🧠 Three patterns that do most of the work
  • Two organisms live inside red cells and both make “rings.” Babesia and Plasmodium. Separate them by geography (New England tick vs tropical mosquito) and fever pattern (Babesia irregular; malaria on a clock).
  • Two organisms are spread by fleas, and the fleas belong to different animals. Cat flea → Bartonella. Rat flea → plague.
  • Two viruses are essentially the same disease. Ebola and Marburg — same bat, same route, same syndrome. Marburg just does it harder: more bleeding, higher mortality, nothing approved to give.
🩺 One rule that explains half the vector biology here

Stated twice, once for the flea and once for the mosquito: “you can't be a vector unless the organism grows in you.” An arthropod that merely carries a pathogen on its mouthparts delivers far too small a dose — a true vector amplifies the organism inside its own body first. This is also why none of them is born infected: each must acquire the organism by feeding on an infected reservoir animal before it can pass anything on.

Filoviruses — Ebola: the filament with no vector

🔑 Family facts, and the one that is high yield
  • Genome: single-stranded RNA — like every hemorrhagic fever virus in Parts 1 and 2.
  • Route in: mucosal surfaces via small abrasions. Intact skin is a real barrier, but the virus “can find a way in.”
  • There is NO insect vector for any filovirus. This is a direct-contact disease from start to finish — the single most testable family fact.
🧠 The genuinely unusual thing: Ebola will grow in almost anything

Most viruses are picky. Filoviruses have an extraordinarily wide host cell range, and that single fact produces the entire syndrome:

  • Monocytes and macrophages → the engine of the cytokine storm, and the vehicle carrying virus to distant organs
  • Dendritic cells → antigen presentation crippled early (panel A immunosuppression)
  • Endothelial cells → capillary leak and hemorrhage
  • Hepatocytes → transaminase rise and loss of clotting factor synthesis
  • Adrenal cells → hypotension, sodium loss, hypovolemia
  • Fibroblasts and epithelial cells → connective tissue, mucosal and glandular involvement

The result is a tissue-factor and pro-inflammatory cytokine cascade that “starts to look like sepsis” — the same four-panel mechanism, aimed at more cell types than usual.

Ebola strainNote
Zaire ebolavirusThe most virulent. Named for what was then Zaire, now the DRC. Every licensed monoclonal and the licensed vaccine target this strain
Sudan ebolavirusAlso found in Sudan
Taï Forest ebolavirusNamed for the forest in Côte d'Ivoire
Bundibugyo ebolavirusThe strain prevalent in the current outbreak — which is exactly why the Zaire-directed treatments are failing
🔑 The healthy-looking reservoir — a pattern across this whole block

The virus grows in the bat and the bat can transmit it, but the bat is not sick. (“Which I think is unfair. They should at least be sick if they're gonna transmit it to people.”) The same was true of livestock in Crimean–Congo hemorrhagic fever. A healthy-appearing reservoir animal is the rule, not the exception.

Animal → human: close contact with blood, secretions, organs or bodily fluids — fruit bats first, but also chimpanzees, gorillas, monkeys, forest antelope, porcupines and pigs. Human → human: body fluids of a sick person, contaminated fomites, and semen.

⚠️ The corpse point is the one people forget ★ HY

“Ebola can last for some period of time in a corpse, so handling this material after the person dies doesn't mean the virus has disappeared.” This is why traditional funerary practices — washing and touching the body — have repeatedly driven outbreaks, and why funeral workers are named as an at-risk group alongside health care workers. If a stem mentions a funeral, that is a deliberate clue.

🩺 A clinical-skills point embedded in the rash slide

The rash is not diagnostic on its own — you need the rest of the findings. And it is more difficult to visualize as skin gets darker. The lecturer includes that comparison slide deliberately: a rash you cannot see is still a rash, and assuming its absence in a patient with darker skin is a real diagnostic error, not a theoretical one.

Diagnosis

practical reality

Antigen or antibody capture tests front-line, confirm with RT-PCR. But “it's not easy to do PCR in some of these remote areas,” so many diagnoses rest on capture kits alone.

Supportive care

the backbone

Early symptomatic treatment and rehydration. “Symptomatic treatment will always improve survival.”

Inmazeb · Ebanga

monoclonals

Both target the surface glycoproteins — the spike-protein logic from COVID-19. Both developed against ZAIRE only.

Ervebo

the vaccine, CDC-cleared 2020

Live attenuated recombinant VSV vector — the VSV glycoprotein genes are replaced with Ebola glycoprotein genes. Zaire strain again.

Remdesivir

experimental

Familiar from COVID-19 — inhibits the virus-specific RNA polymerase. Used experimentally alongside pan-Ebola monoclonals.

In trials

aimed at Bundibugyo

An AstraZeneca viral-vector vaccine and a Moderna mRNA vaccine, both carrying Bundibugyo glycoprotein.

⚠️ Why the current outbreak is so hard to treat — the strain-specificity problem ★ HY

Every licensed product — Inmazeb, Ebanga and Ervebo — was built against the Zaire glycoproteins, because Zaire was what was rampant at the time. In the current Bundibugyo outbreak there is very little cross-protection, whether the person received monoclonals or the vaccine. If a question asks why a vaccinated patient still got Ebola, strain mismatch is the answer.

Naming correction: the recording calls VSV “a pox virus.” Vesicular stomatitis virus is a rhabdovirus — same family as rabies. Same slip appeared for the Lassa candidates, which use the same platform.

Marburg — the same disease, turned up

💡 The name is the mnemonic — the one filovirus not named after Africa

Every other name in this lecture is a place in Africa. Marburg is a university town in Germany, where the first known outbreak occurred in laboratory workers handling African green monkey blood imported from Uganda. African in origin, European in discovery — exactly the kind of detail that tests whether you know the story or just pattern-matched on “African virus.” Compare Lassa, whose first notable US outbreak was in a Yale research group: laboratory-acquired infection is a recurring theme with these agents.

 EbolaMarburg
Family / morphologyIdentical. Filoviridae, ssRNA, 80 nm × up to 800 nm filaments
ReservoirIdentical — the Egyptian rousette fruit bat
Human acquisitionContact with infected animals: bats, chimps, gorillas, monkeys, antelope, porcupines, pigsExposure to infected bats — especially in CAVES
Human → humanIdentical — contaminated body fluids, including semen
Outbreak frequencyRecurrent, sometimes large (~6,300 cases currently)Uncommon and sporadic — ~25 total cases this year
HemorrhagePresentMORE common than in Ebola
Fatality rate25–90% depending on strain50%; 88–90% in severe outbreaks
Immune evasionSubstantialMORE aggressive — blocks the interferon response, far more likely to induce a massive cytokine storm, and destroys blood vessels
DiagnosisAntigen/antibody capture, confirm with PCRRT-PCR
MonoclonalsInmazeb, Ebanga (Zaire only)NONE approved
VaccineErvebo (Zaire only)NONE approved — candidates in development
TreatmentSupportive + monoclonals ± remdesivirSUPPORTIVE ONLY — the goal is to avoid shock
🧠 Why Marburg is deadlier — the mechanism, not just the number
  1. It blocks the interferon response. Type I interferon is the innate antiviral brake, and removing it early is the founding event of the whole pathogenesis — Marburg does it harder.
  2. It is far more likely to induce a massive cytokine storm. Higher viral burden → larger mediator surge → more endothelial activation, more DIC, more shock.
  3. It destroys blood vessels — the direct explanation for why hemorrhage is more common than in Ebola.

“The second deadliest virus.” The deadliest is rabies — “once you start with symptoms, it's over.” Marburg is “pretty close, but you might have a chance.” Recent outbreaks: Rwanda (2024 into 2025), and this year Ethiopia and Uganda.

🩺 Why there is no Marburg drug — an economic fact, not a scientific one

“There's a certain break point for pharmaceutical houses… If you're talking about something that's 25 cases for a half year, that's not going to stimulate their business acumen.” The same platform that produced Ervebo would very likely work. This is why “neglected tropical disease” is a category at all.

Bartonella — one bug, one cat, two completely different diseases ★ HY

One organism, acquired from one animal, producing two diseases told apart by a single variable: the state of the patient's immune system. Immunocompetent gets cat scratch disease. Immunocompromised gets bacillary angiomatosis. Hold that fork and the rest fills in.

⚠️ Two traps set on purpose

Bartonella, not Bordetella. Different genera, entirely different diseases — Bordetella pertussis is whooping cough. He puts five look-alike choices on the board specifically to see whether you read carefully.

And it is cat scratch DISEASE, not cat scratch fever. “Cat Scratch Fever” is a Ted Nugent song.

🔑 The coccobacillus list — flagged explicitly as “this is for boards”

A coccobacillus is neither quite a coccus nor quite a bacillus — “sort of fat rods that look almost round.” An examiner “likes to drop coccobacillus on you,” and if you don't know the short list, “you're doomed.”

  • Bartonella — cat scratch disease, bacillary angiomatosis, trench fever, culture-negative endocarditis
  • Haemophilus — H. influenzae: epiglottitis, otitis, meningitis
  • Bordetella — B. pertussis: whooping cough. The one you must not confuse with Bartonella

Bartonella is additionally pleomorphic, very fastidious (hard to grow), and Gram-negative. The fastidiousness has a direct diagnostic consequence — see below.

SpeciesDiseaseWhere / note
B. bacilliformisOroya feverSouth America. Not examined further
B. quintanaTrench fever · culture-negative endocarditis · sometimes bacillary angiomatosisAn agent of trench fever in World War One. Exam tip: if a bacillary angiomatosis answer key lacks henselae but offers quintana, take it
B. henselae ⭐Cat scratch disease AND bacillary angiomatosisThe most common human pathogen of the genus, and the most common agent of both diseases in this country
🧠 The detail that makes the mechanism click ★ HY

It is tempting to assume the bacterium lives on the cat's claws. It doesn't. The organism is in the FLEA FECES, which contaminates the fur and claws during grooming and scratching. The claw is the delivery needle, not the source. That is why flea control on the cat is genuine prevention, and why the CDC figure spends most of its space on the flea.

Cat → cat is by the cat flea. Cat → human is the scratch (or a bite, via saliva). In the cat, infection may show as cough, anorexia, lethargy or breathing difficulty — or nothing at all.

🔑 Cat scratch disease — the three stages with their timings
  1. Cutaneous papule at the scratch site, which may pustulate. 3–14 days.
  2. Regional lymphadenopathy — head, neck or upper extremities, i.e. draining the scratch. Nodes enlarge, become quite tender, may drain or pustulate. 1–3 weeks.
  3. Systemic infection — another 2–4 weeks, and in immunocompetent people not seen terribly often.

Who: most often children under 10 (rough play, more scratches), and kittens are the most likely source. Incubation 3–10 days — short enough that the patient still remembers the scratch. 25,000–30,000 US cases/year reported, probably twice that unreported. Low-grade fever in about half, plus headache, anorexia, sore throat, rash, arthralgias. Self-limiting, but slowly — 5–6 weeks.

🔑 Argyrophilic organisms — the silver-stain list ★ HY

Argyrophilic means “silver-loving.” Only a handful of organisms do this, which makes it a clean board question:

  • Bartonella — a node, after a cat exposure
  • Spirochetes (e.g. Treponema)
  • Legionella — lung, in a pneumonia
  • Helicobacter pylori — gastric mucosa

Silver stain with black organisms → this list, and the clinical context picks the winner.

Do NOT rely on culture. The organism is fastidious and takes weeks. “Anything that takes 2 or 3 weeks to grow — forget it.” Order EIA/ELISA for IgG and IgM (or indirect immunofluorescence); PCR of node material is definitive. Treat with azithromycin, adding rifampin if severe — realistically this only shortens a 5–6 week illness. Prognosis very good.

⚠️ The look-alike you must not miss — Kaposi sarcoma ★ HY

These lesions “look a little bit like Kaposi's.” Both occur in AIDS patients and they look alike, but one is a treatable bacterial infection and the other a vascular malignancy driven by HHV-8. You cannot tell them apart by looking — which is precisely why the diagnosis rests on lesion biopsy with histopathologic examination.

🔑 Why serology fails in bacillary angiomatosis — understand it, don't memorize it

Serology detects the host's antibody response. These patients are immunocompromised, so they may not be producing much antibody. A test that looks for the host's response will underperform in exactly the population that gets this disease. Contrast cat scratch disease in an immunocompetent child, where serology works fine: same organism, different test strategy, because the host is different.

Diagnose by lesion biopsy + histopathology; PCR is the central test. Treat with erythromycin and/or doxycycline (note: not azithromycin, which is the CSD drug), and start or optimize ART if HIV-positive — “you've got to get that immune system back up before it's going to take care of these organisms.” Antibiotics alone will not hold the line in a host who cannot help.

 Cat scratch disease (CSD)Bacillary angiomatosis (BA)
OrganismBartonella henselae (BA occasionally B. quintana)
HostIMMUNOCOMPETENT — typically a child <10IMMUNOCOMPROMISED — AIDS, chemotherapy, transplant
PathologyLymphocutaneous — papule then regional nodeVascular proliferation of small vessels, skin and viscera
LesionPapule → pustule, then tender regional lymphadenopathy (head, neck, upper extremity)Cherry-red vascular papules and nodules — mimics Kaposi sarcoma
CourseSelf-limiting over 5–6 weeksProgressive; fatal if untreated, especially with organ involvement
DiagnosisHistory + node; EIA/ELISA IgG & IgM; PCR of node definitive; Warthin–Starry silver stain. Do not cultureLesion biopsy + histopathology; PCR. Serology unreliable — the host isn't making antibody
TreatmentAzithromycin (+ rifampin if severe)Erythromycin and/or doxycycline + ART if HIV-positive

Plague — the disease all other epidemics are measured against

A zoonosis with a memorable animal, vector, lesion and stain — almost purpose-built for exam questions. And still endemic in the western United States, so not a medieval curiosity.

💡 Why the mask has a beak — and why it is actually a memory hook

The beak was filled with herbs because the patients did not smell good. That is not a joke about hygiene: people were literally rotting away from acral gangrene. The costume encodes the pathology — plague causes tissue necrosis extensive enough to be smelled across a room.

🔑 Where plague is now — this is the examinable part ★ HY
  • Endemic in at least 17 states, mostly Pacific Coast and Western states.
  • Named repeatedly: New Mexico, Colorado, California, Texas, Arizona, Oregon, Nevada.
  • Only about 150 US cases since the year 2000. Rare, but real.
  • Maine has never had a case. (“We have Powassan virus, but we don't have plague.”)

The geographic rule for this whole lecture: a febrile patient with rodent exposure in the western United States is the plague stem. A tick-bitten patient in New England is Babesia.

🧠 “Peri-domestic” — and why the two rats behave differently

Peri-domestic means rats that live close to humans but not with them. The distinction between the two rats is entirely behavioural, and it is the same logic as Aedes aegypti versus albopictus: the organism grows in both, but only one of them wants to be near you. R. rattus is the ship rat that runs up mooring ropes and lives in human buildings — so it is the one that drove the pandemics.

US epizootics have occurred in squirrels, prairie dogs and chipmunks. Prairie dogs became exotic pets, and there were human plague cases in Indiana and Missouri — states nowhere near the endemic west. The exotic pet trade moves a reservoir animal outside its endemic range, which breaks your geographic reasoning.

🧠 Why a starving flea is the most dangerous flea — the blocked proventriculus ★ HY
  1. The flea ingests Y. pestis in a blood meal. The organisms grow in the proventriculus — the valve between the flea's esophagus and midgut.
  2. The bacterial mass blocks it completely, progressing from a soft mass to an extremely hard one.
  3. Now the flea bites but gets nothing. No blood can pass the blockage. The flea is starving while full.
  4. So it bites frantically — and expands its host range. “They started biting these hairless things that were running around.” Each failed feeding attempt regurgitates bacteria into the wound.

The flea gets no nutrition and dies, but it inoculates far more hosts than a well-fed flea ever would. Blockage converts an efficient parasite into a desperate, indiscriminate transmission machine — and that is why humans, who are otherwise irrelevant to this organism, get bitten at all.

🔑 Humans are a DEAD-END host — “that's not meant to be a joke”

Human infection is accidental and does nothing for the organism. Plague is a classic zoonosis: a disease primarily of animals, for which humans get in the way. Hold this next to dengue and malaria, where humans ARE the reservoir. Incidental host versus reservoir host is a clean discriminator across the whole two-part block.

Other routes: the human flea Pulex irritans · inhalation of contaminated aerosols from rodent waste · handling infected animals or people.

🧠 How a gut bug became the Black Death — two acquired capabilities

Y. pestis evolved from Yersinia pseudotuberculosis, an enterocolitis organism, through step mutations somewhere between 1,500 and 20,000 years ago. Two adaptations were required:

  • The ability to grow in, and be transmitted by, the flea. Without this there is no vector, and without a vector this stays a gut infection.
  • The ability to initiate systemic infection from a peripheral site. A gut bug had to learn to be implanted in skin and still cause systemic disease.

A nice illustration that virulence is not a fixed property of a species — it is a set of acquired capabilities.

  1. Rapid multiplication at the bite site.
  2. Spread to the regional lymph node → the BUBO. Intense hemorrhage and swelling produce the exquisitely tender node that names bubonic plague.
  3. Into the blood → essentially every organ — lungs, pericardium, meninges, kidneys.
  4. Extensive hemorrhage and DIC — the same endgame, arrived at by a bacterial route.
  5. Gangrene at the cool acral sites → “Black Death.” Fingers, toes, ears and nose — the coldest, most distal tissue, where microvascular thrombosis bites hardest. That is literally where the name comes from.

The clinical forms — the table to memorize

FormHow it startsIncubationKey featuresMortality treatedUntreated
BubonicFollows the flea biteDaysAbrupt high fever, chills, weakness; BUBO at the node draining the bite; then dissemination1–15%50%
Primary plague pneumoniaDIRECT INHALATION of the bacillus1–3 days — very shortSudden high fever, chills, headache, tachypnea, dyspnea, hypoxia, hemoptysis. Bilateral multilobar hemorrhagic consolidation; bloody frothy sputum. Highly contagious~50%100%
Secondary plague pneumoniaHematogenous spread after bubonic plague — blood filtered through the lungsA couple of days longerUsual bubonic signs, then productive cough; untreated → hemorrhage, consolidation and death in 3–4 days. Also spreads by aerosol~50%100%
Septicemic plagueCan follow either bubonic or pneumonicRapidSudden very high fever 103–104 °F; frequently WITHOUT a bubo; extremely rapid progression to sepsis, multi-organ failure and shock50%100%
⚠️ Why the 14th century was so catastrophic — the chain that makes the curve go vertical

Most people picture the Black Death as buboes. The pneumonic forms probably did most of the killing. The chain: bubonic plague → secondary plague pneumonia in that patient → they aerosolize the organism → the next person inhales it and gets primary plague pneumonia → 100% fatal untreated within days, and itself highly transmissible.

A flea-borne disease becomes an airborne one — and that is the infection-control point too: you do not need to be exposed to a “pneumonic plague” case to catch pneumonic plague. A bubonic case that progressed is enough.

Get the right specimen

diagnosis, step 1

Aspirate of a lymph node if there are buboes; sputum in a pneumonic presentation.

Demonstrate the organism

the classic

Bipolar-staining Gram-negative rod on Gram or Giemsa stain.

Rapid antigen test

“the go-to”

100% sensitive and 100% specific for Y. pestis antigen.

Culture on blood agar

for sensitivities

Identification and antibiotic sensitivity. Metabolic panels take too long to be useful acutely. Confirm with PCR where available.

Treatment

two drugs

Gentamicin or a quinolone. Naturally occurring plague shows very little drug resistance.

Vaccine

exists, but

Not available in this country.

⚠️ Highly resistant plague is a bioterrorism signal, not a treatment-failure puzzle ★ HY

“If you see a plague where you have very high resistance, you have to suspect something that's been altered by humans to be more resistant.” Plague has historically been developed as a biological weapon — rapid onset, high mortality, and aerosol transmissibility in the pneumonic form. Notify public health immediately.

Babesia microti — the one you can actually catch here

💡 “You must be all from the northeast, right?”

Babesiosis is a New England disease. Elsewhere in the country nobody has heard of it. And when the lecturer asks which of these six agents you could actually go out and acquire today: “you can run out there now and get Babesia.”

What it is

category

A protozoan parasite. Babesia microti is the species.

Where

geography

Primarily the Northeast; sometimes the very upper Midwest.

2,000–3,000

cases/year reported

At best 40% of actual cases — most people get a week or two of fever that resolves.

1–2 µm

trophozoite size

“These are the size of bacteria, not very big.”

🔑 Learn this one mouse and you get five diseases ★ HY

The white-footed mouse (Peromyscus leucopus) is the reservoir for a whole cluster of northeastern diseases:

  • Babesiosis (this section)
  • Lyme disease (Borrelia burgdorferi)
  • Anaplasmosis (Anaplasma phagocytophilum)
  • Powassan virus
  • Hantavirus

One mouse, one tick, five diseases — which is also why co-infection is common. Birds, chipmunks and raccoons can also carry Babesia, but the mouse is primary.

🧠 Why the tiny NYMPH — not the adult — is the one that infects you

Two facts combine, and they are exactly the same two facts as in Lyme disease:

  • Ticks are NOT born infected. There is no transovarial transmission — an infected female does not pass the organism to her eggs. Every tick must acquire the parasite by feeding, and the nymph, the first stage to feed after moulting, gets it from infected white-footed mice.
  • You cannot see a nymph. An adult tick walking on you is noticeable. A nymph is about the size of the dot over the “i” in newsprint. “They look like freckles — unless they're moving. Freckles don't move.”

So the nymph is the primary vector not because it is more infectious, but because it feeds long enough to transmit without being noticed and removed. This is why most patients have no history of a tick bite — and why the absence of that history must never argue against the diagnosis.

  1. The feeding nymph deposits ~100,000 sporozoites under the dermis — the organism has been multiplying inside the tick.
  2. Sporozoites enter the bloodstream and attach specifically to red blood cells. This is an intra-erythrocytic parasite — the same lifestyle as Plasmodium.
  3. Inside the red cell they differentiate into TROPHOZOITES, the adult stage.
  4. They replicate by BINARY FISSION to produce MEROZOITES.
  5. Maturation to merozoites LYSES the red cell — and not just one, a whole population.
  6. Released merozoites infect new red cells, and the cycle continues.
🔑 Where the symptoms come from — two sources, and both matter

(1) Hemolysis of red blood cells causes the fever and the hemolytic anemia. (2) Pro-inflammatory cytokines, which contribute heavily to the symptoms. It is the same two-source model as every hemorrhagic fever — direct cell destruction plus a disproportionate host inflammatory response. Plasmodium works the same way.

SeverityWhoFeatures
Asymptomatic40% or moreNothing at all — which is why the reported count is at best 40% of reality
Mild to moderateMost symptomatic patientsFlu-like — fever, chills, fatigue, myalgia, occasional GI symptoms. “I got a bug, I got the flu, and that's all there is to it”
SevereElderly and immunocompromisedSevere GI symptoms · respiratory involvement / ARDS · DIC · severe hemolytic anemia · shock · congestive heart failure
⚠️ Co-infection — the point that makes this clinically important ★ HY

Co-infection with Anaplasma phagocytophilum or Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme) is common — and the reason is structural, not coincidental: all three use the same reservoir (white-footed mouse) and the same vector (Ixodes scapularis nymph). One bite can deliver more than one pathogen.

Practically: a New England patient not improving on doxycycline for Lyme disease may have babesiosis as well — and doxycycline does not treat Babesia. Incubation is 1–4 weeks, depending on inoculum and immune status.

🩺 Diagnosis and treatment — with the mechanism worth one line

Supporting labs: hemolytic anemia · thrombocytopenia · elevated AST/ALT with liver involvement · elevated BUN and creatinine with renal involvement. Giemsa smear for ring forms; PCR where available. Do not require a tick-bite history.

Treat with azithromycin PLUS atovaquone. Atovaquone targets the parasite's electron transport system — that is the mechanism to be able to state. Intravenous, at least for the azithromycin, in severe cases. Note what is absent: doxycycline, which treats the Lyme and anaplasmosis co-infections but has no useful activity against Babesia.

Plasmodium — malaria, and the clock in the fever

SpeciesStatusFever interval
P. falciparumMost common AND most virulent — the one that killsIRREGULAR
P. vivaxThe other common human agent48 hours
P. ovaleLess common48 hours
P. malariaeLess common72 hours
P. knowlesiLess common24 hours
🔑 The fever-interval table is not four arbitrary numbers ★ HY

The interval is set by the synchronized moment when infected red cells lyse and a new wave of merozoites bursts into the circulation. The parasite's erythrocytic cycle length IS the fever period.

So the pattern makes sense: knowlesi 24 h · vivax and ovale 48 h · malariae 72 h. And falciparum is IRREGULAR precisely because its cycles are not synchronized — which is one reason it is the most dangerous: no reliable rhythm and no fever-free window in which the patient recovers.

~300 million

cases per year

Currently.

~600,000

deaths per year

Reported, annually.

~5 billion

deaths across all history

Statisticians' estimate for malaria's cumulative mortality. Tuberculosis is estimated at ~1 billion; everything else is below that.

Every US state but Alaska

until the 1880s

Malaria was endemic in every state except Alaska. First American epidemic: Jamestown, 1607. Washington, Lincoln and Grant all had malaria, acquired domestically; sessions of the Continental Congress were stopped by outbreaks.

🩺 Transmission — and one contrast worth holding

Essentially human-to-human via the bite of the female Anopheles mosquito. Humans are the reservoir — as with dengue, and in direct contrast with plague, where humans are a dead-end host.

There are more than 40 species of Anopheles and most can transmit, so — unlike dengue, where Aedes aegypti is singled out — genus is enough. And mosquitoes are not born infected: same vector rule as the flea and the tick.

  1. The female Anopheles bites and deposits SPOROZOITES into the dermis. “Very much like the Babesia” — the same deposit-at-the-bite-site mechanism.
  2. Sporozoites reach the LIVER via blood and lymphatics — the exo-erythrocytic (pre-erythrocytic) stage.
  3. They invade hepatocytes and form SCHIZONTS, each containing thousands upon thousands of MEROZOITES.
  4. The hepatocyte lyses, releasing merozoites that infect more hepatocytes and eventually pour into the blood.
  5. Merozoites attach to RED BLOOD CELLS and become RING FORMS — the erythrocytic stage, the stage that makes you sick.
  6. Ring → trophozoite → schizont → new merozoites → lyse the red cell → infect new red cells. The synchrony of this lysis sets the fever interval.
  7. Some parasites become gametocytes, which a feeding mosquito ingests — closing the loop.
🔑 The one structural difference from Babesia, and it matters

Both are deposited at a bite site and both end up multiplying inside red cells producing ring forms. The difference is the liver.

Plasmodium has an obligatory pre-erythrocytic LIVER stage, where a single sporozoite amplifies into thousands of merozoites before the blood stage begins. Babesia goes straight from the dermis to the red blood cell — no liver stage at all.

That liver stage is where the vaccine attacks, and it is why malaria has a 1–4 week incubation — the liver phase is silent.

🩺 Clinical — and the sentence that ties Parts 1 and 2 together

Chills, rigors and fever at regular intervals per the species table, with sweating between. Abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and jaundice, occurring at intervals, driven by the waves of red cell lysis. In severe disease, infected red cells cause infarcts and capillary leakage → liver, kidney, respiratory and neurologic (cerebral malaria) dysfunction → severe anemia, DIC, shock. Some patients go into shock and die within 24 hours.

The lecturer, wearily: “severe anemia, DIC — the story is over and over. It's the same thing for all of these guys.” That is the point of Parts 1 and 2 taken together: the final common pathway is always the same. The front end — the animal, the vector, the geography — is what differs.

🌕

THICK smear — is it there?

The red cells are PRE-LYSED, so the parasites are released and concentrated onto the slide.

  • Purpose: a SCREEN — “a presence/absence test.”
  • More sensitive — far more blood per field.
  • You cannot speciate — the cell context is gone.
🌑

THIN smear — which one?

The parasites are visualized WITHIN intact red cells.

  • Purpose: IDENTIFY the species and estimate parasite density.
  • Preserved cell morphology lets you speciate.
  • Less sensitive — fewer parasites per field.
🪝 Memory hook — thick = there or not; thin = which one

Both use a Giemsa stain, and both take time and a proficient microscopist. In practice, rapid diagnostic tests detect parasite antigens in about 10 minutes — which matters, because “a lot of places you're going to see malaria are going to be in resource-limited areas where you don't have maybe even microscopes,” let alone PCR.

🧠 The chloroquine mechanism — the drug never attacks the parasite at all ★ HY
  1. The parasite eats hemoglobin. It breaks hemoglobin down and uses the globin as an amino acid source.
  2. That leaves free HEME — which is highly TOXIC to the parasite. It has created its own poison as a by-product of feeding.
  3. So it detoxifies it: HEME POLYMERASE converts toxic heme into non-toxic HEMOZOIN. “All right, that's clever.”
  4. Chloroquine, quinine and mefloquine all block that step. Heme accumulates to toxic concentrations and the parasite dies.

Notice the elegance: the drug disables the parasite's own waste-disposal system and lets the parasite poison itself.

Chloroquine-sensitive → chloroquine phosphate, the preferred treatment “as long as it's sensitive to the drug.” Chloroquine-resistant → artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT), e.g. artemether–lumefantrine.

🔑 RTS,S/AS01 (Mosquirix) — take the name apart and the vaccine explains itself
  • Recombinant. P. falciparum surface proteins produced in yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae).
  • Combined with hepatitis B surface protein, which acts purely as a CARRIER. “Nothing special about the hepatitis B itself… it's just a side issue.” Scaffolding, not a target.
  • Plus the AS01 adjuvant.
  • It targets the SPOROZOITE stage — neutralizing the parasite in the blood before it reaches the liver, cutting the life cycle at step 2, before any amplification occurs. Once the erythrocytic stage begins, the burden is orders of magnitude larger.
🩺 The adjuvant — and why Shingrix hurts

AS01 combines an extract derived from the outer lipopolysaccharide (endotoxin) of Salmonella with a saponin from the Chilean soapbark tree. “Mix that together and that's a great adjuvant. It hurts like hell though.” This is the same adjuvant family used in Shingrix — the reactogenicity is the adjuvant, not the antigen.

⚠️ A figure worth checking before you quote it

In class, RTS,S/AS01 protection was given as “about 80 to 90%” — so that is what to reproduce if the exam asks what he said. Be aware that the published phase 3 efficacy is substantially lower, on the order of ~30–50% against clinical malaria in the first year, declining thereafter, which is why it is deployed alongside bed nets and chemoprevention rather than as a stand-alone solution. If a board question asks about RTS,S efficacy, the lower figure is the defensible one.

💡 What he actually wants you to know about malaria

Asked whether all the species need differentiating: “there's only two of them” that are common — falciparum (most common and most virulent) and vivax. Testing the rare ones would be “a really nasty” question. His stated goal: “I would like you to know about HOW MALARIA WORKS.”

Study priorities in order: life cycle > thick vs thin smear > chloroquine mechanism > fever intervals > species minutiae. And if a stem asks which species without other clues — falciparum, because it is the most common.

The one grid, filled in six times

Reservoir and vector. Every other row can be reconstructed; those two cannot, and they are what the question stem hands you.

🔑 Rapid-fire discriminators — see this → think this
  • Filament / “6” shape on EM → filovirus · Cave exposure → Marburg · Handled a corpse → Ebola
  • Coccobacillus → Bartonella, Haemophilus, Bordetella · Kitten scratch + swollen node → cat scratch disease
  • Warthin–Starry silver stain → Bartonella (or spirochete, Legionella, H. pylori) · Cherry-red papules in AIDS → bacillary angiomatosis vs Kaposi
  • Bipolar “safety pin” rod → Y. pestis · Bubo → bubonic plague · Black fingers and toes → acral gangrene · Prairie dog → plague · Blocked proventriculus → the plague flea · Resistant plague → suspect bioengineering
  • White-footed mouse → Babesia, Lyme, anaplasma, Powassan, hanta · Ixodes nymph → Babesia + Lyme co-infection · Rings in RBCs + New England → Babesia
  • Rings in RBCs + tropical travel → malaria · Fever every 48 h → vivax or ovale · every 72 h → malariae · irregular + severe → falciparum · Heme polymerase blocked → chloroquine

Q: A 30-year-old in rural New Mexico develops abrupt fever to 103 °F, chills and profound weakness, with an exquisitely tender 5 cm mass in the right groin. He has been camping and handling dead ground squirrels. Aspirate shows Gram-negative rods that stain darkly at both ends. Diagnosis, form and treatment?

Answer

Bubonic plague, Yersinia pestis. The stem gives you everything: the western United States (endemic in ~17 mostly Pacific Coast and Western states), rodent exposure (squirrels are a named US epizootic host alongside prairie dogs and chipmunks), abrupt high fever with chills and weakness, and a BUBO in the node draining a lower-limb flea bite. The stain confirms it: bipolar “safety pin” Gram-negative rods.

Treat with gentamicin or a quinolone. Send a rapid antigen test (100% sensitive, 100% specific) and culture for sensitivities; PCR if available. Untreated bubonic plague ~50% mortality; treated 1–15%. Watch for progression to secondary plague pneumonia — at which point he becomes infectious by aerosol.

Q: Why does a flea whose gut is completely blocked by bacteria transmit plague far more efficiently than a healthy flea?

Answer

Y. pestis multiplies in the flea's proventriculus until it forms a hard mass that occludes it. The flea can still bite, but no blood can pass the blockage — it is starving despite constant biting. Its response is to bite frantically and repeatedly, and to expand its host range onto animals it would usually ignore, including humans. Each failed attempt regurgitates bacteria into the wound.

So the blockage converts a well-adapted rat parasite into an indiscriminate, high-frequency inoculator. This is also the answer to why humans — a dead-end host that offers the organism nothing — get bitten at all.

Q: Distinguish primary from secondary plague pneumonia, and explain why the distinction drives infection control.

Answer

Primary follows direct inhalation of the bacillus. Incubation 1–3 days, with sudden high fever, chills, headache, tachypnea, dyspnea, hypoxia and hemoptysis, progressing to bilateral multilobar hemorrhagic consolidation with bloody frothy sputum.

Secondary follows hematogenous spread from bubonic plague — organisms reach the lymph, then the blood, then are filtered through the lungs. It takes a couple of days longer and is preceded by the bubonic picture.

Both are ~50% fatal treated, 100% untreated, and both transmit by aerosol. That is the infection-control point: a patient with secondary plague pneumonia — who arrived with an ordinary bubonic presentation — can seed primary plague pneumonia in everyone around them. You do not need exposure to a “pneumonic plague” case to catch it.

Q: An 8-year-old has a tender 3 cm right cervical node and low-grade fever. Two weeks ago a new kitten scratched her right cheek; a small crusted papule is still visible. Diagnosis, what is the actual infectious material, and what do you give?

Answer

Cat scratch disease, Bartonella henselae. Everything fits: a child under 10, a kitten, an inoculation papule at the scratch site, and regional lymphadenopathy draining that site at the right interval — incubation 3–10 days, papule stage 3–14 days, nodal stage 1–3 weeks.

The infectious material is contaminated FLEA FECES, inoculated by the scratch — the claw is the needle, the flea dirt is the inoculum. Treat with azithromycin (rifampin only if severe). Expect a self-limiting 5–6 week course with a very good prognosis. Do not send a culture — Bartonella is fastidious and takes weeks; use EIA serology, or PCR of node material if you need definitive proof.

Q: A man with AIDS and a CD4 count of 40 has multiple friable cherry-red cutaneous papules and a nodular forearm lesion. Bartonella serology is negative. Does that exclude bacillary angiomatosis?

Answer

No — the negative result is close to meaningless here. Serology detects the host's antibody response, and this patient's immune system is severely impaired, so he may not be producing much antibody. Serology in bacillary angiomatosis is supportive but neither sensitive nor definitive, for exactly that reason.

Proceed to lesion biopsy with histopathologic examination and PCR. The critical differential is Kaposi sarcoma, which looks very similar in the same population and cannot be distinguished clinically — one is a curable bacterial infection, the other a vascular malignancy.

Treat with erythromycin and/or doxycycline, and start or optimize antiretroviral therapy — you must restore immune function for the antibiotics to hold. Untreated, especially with organ involvement, the disease can be fatal.

Q: A 72-year-old on Nantucket in July has a week of fever, chills, fatigue and myalgia. Hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, platelets 88,000/µL, AST and ALT mildly elevated, haptoglobin undetectable. He recalls no tick bite. Diagnosis, and how would you prove it?

Answer

Babesiosis (Babesia microti). The stem is a checklist: coastal New England in summer, a flu-like illness, and the lab triad of hemolytic anemia (low hemoglobin, undetectable haptoglobin), thrombocytopenia and transaminase elevation. His age puts him in the severe-disease group alongside immunocompromised patients.

The absence of a tick-bite history is expected and does not argue against the diagnosis — the vector is the Ixodes scapularis NYMPH, the size of a printed full stop and easily mistaken for a freckle.

Prove it with a Giemsa-stained blood smear for trophozoites and merozoites inside red cells; PCR if available. Treat with azithromycin plus atovaquone, intravenously if severe. Also test for Borrelia burgdorferi and Anaplasma phagocytophilum — shared reservoir, shared vector, common co-infection.

Q: Explain why the nymph, not the adult tick, is the principal vector of both babesiosis and Lyme disease.

Answer

Two reasons, and they compound.

First, ticks are not born infected — there is no transovarial transmission from an infected female to her eggs. Each tick must acquire the organism by feeding, and the nymph is the first stage to feed after moulting, taking its meal from the infected white-footed mouse. So it is the first stage that is both infected and hungry.

Second, and decisively, you cannot see a nymph. It is about the size of the dot over an “i” and is easily mistaken for a freckle, so it stays attached long enough to transmit. An adult tick is conspicuous and gets removed. Transmission is a function of going unnoticed, not of biological potency — which is exactly why most patients report no tick bite at all.

Q: Explain precisely how chloroquine kills Plasmodium.

Answer

The parasite digests hemoglobin inside the red cell and uses the globin portion as an amino acid source. This liberates free heme, which is highly toxic to the parasite itself. To survive its own metabolism, the parasite uses heme polymerase to convert toxic heme into inert hemozoin.

Chloroquine — along with quinine and mefloquine — inhibits that conversion. Heme accumulates to toxic concentrations and kills the parasite. The drug never attacks the organism directly; it disables the detoxification step and lets the parasite poison itself. Where chloroquine resistance is present, use artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) such as artemether–lumefantrine.

Q: A traveller returns from Nigeria with fever, rigors and sweats occurring without any discernible pattern, plus jaundice and confusion. A thick smear is positive. Which species, why is the fever irregular, and what does the confusion signify?

Answer

Plasmodium falciparum — the most common and most virulent species, and the expected answer for sub-Saharan Africa.

The fever is irregular because falciparum's erythrocytic cycles are not synchronized. Fever spikes are produced by waves of red cell lysis releasing merozoites; when those waves are synchronous you get the clean 24-, 48- or 72-hour periodicity of knowlesi, vivax/ovale and malariae. Falciparum lacks that synchrony — no rhythm and no fever-free recovery window.

The confusion signifies cerebral malaria — severe disease with neurologic involvement. Infected red cells cause infarcts and capillary leakage producing liver, renal, respiratory and neurologic dysfunction, with severe anemia, DIC and shock; patients can die within 24 hours. This is an emergency. The thick smear told you parasites are present; now get a THIN smear to confirm the species and quantify parasite density.

Q: The malaria vaccine RTS,S/AS01 raises antibodies against the sporozoite. Why is that the stage chosen, and what is the hepatitis B surface protein doing in it?

Answer

The sporozoite is the bottleneck. A mosquito deposits sporozoites into the dermis, and they must reach hepatocytes before the infection amplifies — a single sporozoite becomes a schizont containing thousands of merozoites. Neutralizing antibody at the sporozoite stage stops the parasite in the blood before it reaches the liver, cutting the cycle before any amplification occurs. Once the erythrocytic stage begins, the burden is orders of magnitude larger.

The hepatitis B surface protein is purely a CARRIER. The P. falciparum surface antigens are produced recombinantly in yeast and fused to it so they assemble and present well. It is not itself a target — “nothing special about the hepatitis B itself… it's just a side issue.” The AS01 adjuvant (Salmonella LPS-derived component + Chilean soapbark saponin) supplies the immune stimulation — and the sore arm.

Q: A health care worker in eastern DRC develops fever, vomiting, diarrhea and, on day 7, a maculopapular rash beginning on the face. She received Ervebo two years ago. How is this possible?

Answer

Strain mismatch. Ervebo is a live attenuated recombinant VSV-vectored vaccine built against the Zaire glycoproteins, and the current outbreak strain is Bundibugyo, against which there is very little cross-protection. The same limitation applies to the two monoclonals, Inmazeb and Ebanga, which also target Zaire surface glycoproteins.

Manage with early supportive care and rehydration; experimental options are remdesivir (inhibits the viral RNA polymerase) plus pan-Ebola monoclonals. Confirm with antigen/antibody capture followed by RT-PCR. Bundibugyo-specific candidates are in trials from AstraZeneca (viral vector) and Moderna (mRNA).

Q: A geologist returns from surveying a cave system in Uganda with fever, myalgia, a day-6 maculopapular rash, then prominent bleeding from the gums and venipuncture sites. Agent, and how does treatment differ from Ebola?

Answer

Marburg virus. The tell is cave exposure — Marburg acquisition is specifically exposure to infected bats, especially in caves — combined with prominent hemorrhage, which is more common in Marburg than Ebola. The reservoir is the same Egyptian rousette fruit bat.

Treatment differs by being absent. For Ebola you have two monoclonals (Inmazeb, Ebanga) and a licensed vaccine (Ervebo). For Marburg there are no approved monoclonals, no approved antivirals and no approved vaccine. Management is supportive care aimed at avoiding shock. Confirm with RT-PCR. Expect ~50% fatality, or 88–90% in severe outbreaks.

Q: A lymph node biopsy stained with silver shows clumps of black bacilli. Name the stain and the four organisms this should put on your differential.

Answer

The Warthin–Starry silver stain. The organisms are argyrophilic — literally “silver-loving.” The short list: Bartonella · spirochetes · Legionella · Helicobacter pylori.

The clinical context picks the winner: a lymph node with a cat exposure is Bartonella; gastric mucosa is H. pylori; lung in a pneumonia is Legionella.

LO 13Source: Blood & Lymphoreticular Infections, Part 1 — Viral Hemorrhagic Fevers

Section 22 · Infection

The Viral Hemorrhagic Fevers — One Mechanism, Four Agents, Four Discriminators

Every agent here damages small vessels and cripples clotting by the same four-step pathway, so the mechanism is learned once. What separates them on an exam is never the syndrome — it is which animal, which vector, which geography, and which organ fails out of proportion.

Abbreviations used in this section VHF viral hemorrhagic fever — a febrile illness in which a virus damages small blood vessels and reduces the ability to clot · APC antigen-presenting cell — dendritic cell or macrophage · IFN interferon · NK cell natural killer cell · DIC disseminated intravascular coagulation · MODS multi-organ dysfunction syndrome · AST / ALT aspartate / alanine aminotransferase — liver enzymes · ssRNA single-stranded ribonucleic acid · RdRp RNA-dependent RNA polymerase — the viral replication enzyme · DENV dengue virus (serotypes 1–4) · HFRS hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome · HCPS hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome · AKI acute kidney injury · CCHF Crimean–Congo hemorrhagic fever · LCMV lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus · VSV vesicular stomatitis virus — a rhabdovirus used as a vaccine vector · RT-PCR reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction · ELISA enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay · NSAID non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug · VEGF vascular endothelial growth factor · Gn / Gc the two hantavirus envelope glycoproteins
🔑 The four questions that actually distinguish these viruses ★ HY

The lecturer promises the pathogenesis and the symptom list are essentially identical for every agent, explains them once, and never repeats them. So for each virus, answer only these:

  1. What is the reservoir? A mosquito, a tick, a field mouse, or a multimammate rat — usually the single most identifying detail in a stem.
  2. Is there a vector, and does the virus replicate in it? Dengue and Crimean–Congo have true vectors. Hantavirus and Lassa have none — you inhale or touch rodent excreta instead.
  3. Where in the world? Central/South America and the Caribbean · the Far East · Africa and southeastern Europe · West Africa.
  4. Does one organ fail out of proportion? Only hantavirus HFRS — it destroys kidneys. Everything else fails as a set.

The pathogenesis — four panels that are a causal chain, not a list

Panel A — immunosuppression

the founding event

Virus crosses a mucosal barrier into dendritic cells and macrophages, which then show an immature phenotype: very low co-stimulatory molecules (the second signal a T cell needs) and very low type I interferon. Result: poor NK cell and T cell activity → loss of replication control → viral burden climbs.

Panel B — cytokine storm

scaled to that burden

Infected monocytes and macrophages release massive pro-inflammatory mediators, causing endothelial activation, platelet activation, coagulation cascade activation, and bystander T cell activation with apoptosis — which deepens the immunosuppression of panel A.

Panel C — dissemination

phagocytes as couriers

APCs take up the virus but do not kill it, then migrate normally — to lymph nodes and on to brain, adrenal gland, liver and spleen — carrying still-infectious virus.

Panel D — vascular collapse

the endpoint

Sustained inflammation plus direct endothelial infection: ↑ permeability and leak, vasodilatation and hypotension, DIC, hemorrhage, multi-organ failure, death.

🧠 Why panel A has to come first

Every downstream disaster is proportional to viral burden. The virus does not cause hemorrhage by being cleverly cytopathic — it causes hemorrhage by reaching a burden the innate system was never allowed to cap, then provoking a response scaled to that burden. Blunting the interferon response is the founding event.

And panel B worsens panel A rather than rescuing it: bystander activation kills T cells that were never virus-specific. The patient ends up simultaneously over-inflamed and under-defended.

What panel C does to each organ — and how it shows up in the labs

Organ infectedWhat the infection does thereLaboratory / clinical consequence
LiverHepatocyte injury and loss of synthetic functionVery high AST and ALT; decreased synthesis of clotting factors → prolonged coagulation times
Adrenal glandDecreased steroid-synthesizing enzymesHypotension, sodium loss, hypovolemia
SpleenInfection of a major lymphoreticular organFurther amplification of viral load and immune dysregulation
BrainCentral nervous system involvementConfusion, delirium, seizures, coma in severe disease
🩺 Three independent reasons the patient bleeds — a question can test any one

(1) Consumption — panel B burns through platelets and clotting factors in widespread microthrombosis. (2) Failure of production — panel C's liver injury stops new clotting factors being made. (3) A leaky, damaged vessel — panel D.

🪝 Memory hook — “this is sepsis by a viral route”

Panels B and D are sepsis: dysregulated host response, endothelial activation, capillary leak, DIC, distributive shock, multi-organ failure. You do not need a new mental model — only a new trigger.

One symptom list, taught once, staged in three

🌡️

Stage 1 — febrile prodrome + non-specific systemic features

  • Fever ≥ 100.4 °F (38 °C), typically climbing to 101–103 °F
  • Weakness, headache, bone pain, joint pain, myalgia, dizziness
  • Vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, chest pain, rash
  • Photophobia, hyperesthesia, periorbital edema, retro-orbital pain, facial flushing, conjunctival redness
🩸

Stage 2 — coagulation disorder

  • Petechiae and bleeding under the skin
  • Bleeding from gums, mouth, eyes and ears
  • Bleeding into internal organs
  • Driven largely by the immune reaction, not by the virus lysing vessels directly
💀

Stage 3 — shock and organ failure

  • Hypotension → shock
  • Delirium, seizures, coma
  • Kidney failure, liver failure, proteinuria
  • Endpoint: multi-organ failure
⚠️ The one prescribing rule that spans the entire lecture ★ HY

Acetaminophen for fever and pain. Never NSAIDs — not ibuprofen, not naproxen, not aspirin. NSAIDs inhibit platelet function and increase bleeding risk, and this patient already has bleeding into skin, mucosa and internal organs. The lecturer states the rule for dengue and repeats it verbatim for CCHF: treat it as a class rule for every viral hemorrhagic fever.

There is no antiviral for any agent in this lecture except Lassa (ribavirin, and it is weak). Everything else is fluids, blood pressure support, oxygenation, and correcting what the coagulopathy has consumed.

Five families, four shared properties

🔑 True of every family on this list
  • All are enveloped — which is why they are fragile outside a host. Lipid does not survive drying, detergent or heat.
  • All are RNA viruses, specifically ssRNA. Segmentation varies: Bunyavirales three segments, Arenaviridae two, Flaviviridae non-segmented.
  • All have an animal or insect reservoir. None is a purely human pathogen.
  • Humans acquire them two ways — direct contact with an infected animal or its excreta, or transmission from a vector. Human-to-human then requires blood or body fluid contact.
FamilyAgent(s)Reservoir / vectorCovered where
FlaviviridaeDengue virus (DENV-1 to DENV-4)Human reservoir; vector Aedes aegypti and Ae. albopictusHere, in depth
FlaviviridaeYellow fever virusAedes mosquitoes; non-human primatesGI block — liver-dominant disease
TogaviridaeChikungunya virusAedes mosquitoesMSK block — polyarthralgia-dominant
Bunyaviridae (Bunyavirales)Hantavirus — Hantaan, Seoul, Dobrava, PuumalaRodents (field mice, rats, voles). No vectorHere, in depth
Bunyaviridae (genus Nairovirus)Crimean–Congo hemorrhagic fever virusLivestock and birds (asymptomatic); vector Hyalomma tickHere, in depth
ArenaviridaeLassa fever virus; Junin (Argentine); Machupo (Bolivian); LCMVRodents — Lassa: Mastomys natalensis. No vectorHere, in depth
FiloviridaeEbola virus; Marburg virusBats and non-human primates→ next section (Part 2)
🦟

Vector-borne — an arthropod bite

The virus replicates inside the arthropod, which is what makes it a true vector rather than a passive needle.

  • Dengue — Aedes mosquito. Reservoir is humans themselves.
  • Crimean–Congo — Hyalomma tick. Reservoir is livestock and birds, which stay well.
🐁

Rodent-borne — no vector at all

You acquire it by inhaling or touching rodent urine, feces or saliva. There is no insect in the story.

  • Hantavirus (HFRS) — field mice, rats, voles. Aerosol is the classic route.
  • Lassa — Mastomys natalensis. Contact, aerosol, or eating the rodent.
⚠️ Deliberately taught elsewhere — do not go looking for them here

Yellow fever → GI block (hepatic-dominant). Chikungunya → MSK block (polyarthralgia-dominant). Ebola and Marburg → Part 2, the next section. Hantavirus HCPS, the New World cardiopulmonary disease → respiratory block. Only the Old World renal disease is in scope here.

Flaviviridae — a large, fragile, arthropod-borne family

🧠 Extreme environmental lability — and the two things it rules out clinically

Flavus is Latin for yellow, after yellow fever virus, the first member found. The family holds > 70 types, most of which cause something other than hemorrhagic fever. Flaviviruses are labile to heat, UV light, disinfectants, acid pH and alkaline pH, and are stable only inside their host or inside their vector. Two testable consequences:

  • Not fomite-transmitted. You do not pick dengue up from a doorknob or shared equipment.
  • They do not persist in aerosols. Airborne transmission over meaningful distance or time does not occur.

Most flaviviruses are not hemorrhagic: West Nile, St. Louis encephalitis and Powassan cause encephalitis; Zika causes a mild febrile illness and congenital Zika syndrome.

Dengue — “breakbone fever”

The largest agent in this lecture by case volume, the one with a genuine United States footprint, and the only one with a licensed vaccine. First described in this country in a 1780 Philadelphia outbreak — a bilious (queasy), remittent fever with extreme joint stiffness — with outbreaks continuing here through the 1940s.

~400 million

cases per year, worldwide

With about 40,000 deaths annually.

~13 million

cases per year, the Americas

2024 figure — Central and South America and the Caribbean.

2,725

US cases, Jan–Aug 2025

Most of them in Puerto Rico, not the continental United States.

~24%

clinically apparent

Meaning ~76% are inapparent — yet still transmissible to a mosquito.

🔑 The reservoir is people — and that changes the whole prevention strategy

No animal reservoir has been identified in the Western Hemisphere. The cycle is human → mosquito → human, with no animal amplifier — unlike CCHF (livestock) or hantavirus and Lassa (rodents). Two consequences: you are unlikely to acquire dengue from handling animals, and because ~76% of infections are asymptomatic but still transmissible, the human reservoir is largely invisible. That is why vector control, not case isolation, is the prevention strategy.

⚠️ The climate prediction the lecturer wants noticed

Warming models predict an expanding Aedes aegypti range, its band creeping into New England. That matters more than albopictus already being there, because aegypti is the mosquito that actually prefers to bite humans — and it also transmits yellow fever, chikungunya and Zika, so its expansion brings the whole set.

Other routes worth knowing: vertical transmission (mother → fetus), documented and testable; and contaminated blood products — possible but explicitly low risk, “nothing like what one sees in Ebola.”

Dengue — four serotypes, three severity tiers

TierDefinitionFeatures
Common / acute dengueThe base syndromeFever and chills, headache, rash, musculoskeletal and lumbar (low back) pain, retro-orbital eye pain. The musculoskeletal pain is the “breakbone” component that named it
Moderate infectionTier 1 plus any TWOAbdominal tenderness · persistent anorexia, nausea or vomiting · mucosal bleeding (± hemoptysis, liver symptoms)
Severe dengueDengue plus any ONEHypovolemic shock · severe bleeding · organ failure. The panel D endpoint. Requires hospitalization
🔑 Note the structure — it is how the criteria are written and tested

Tier 2 = tier 1 + any TWO warning features. Tier 3 = dengue + any ONE severe feature. A patient with fever, headache, rash and bone pain who develops abdominal tenderness and persistent vomiting has moderate dengue. The same patient who instead becomes hypotensive has severe dengue — on that one finding alone.

Diagnosis

exposure first

Multiplex RT-PCR — commercial kits test dengue plus the other top hemorrhagic fever viruses in one run. Expensive, but resolves the whole differential. Alternative: ELISA for dengue antigen. Antibody testing is not useful acutely — weeks to turn positive.

Treatment

no antiviral exists

Fluids to prevent dehydration — the single most important intervention. Acetaminophen, never NSAIDs. Hospitalize severe cases.

Prevention

vector control

Control of the Aedes mosquito in endemic areas is the mainstay.

Dengvaxia

FDA-approved 2019

Live attenuated, tetravalent, recombinant. Backbone = the attenuated yellow fever vaccine virus, with inserted genes encoding the surface proteins of all four DENV serotypes.

⚠️ The single most examinable fact about Dengvaxia ★ HY

Do not give it to someone who has never had dengue. It is indicated only for people with documented prior dengue infection; in the dengue-naive the course can be rougher. A vaccine with a prior infection prerequisite is unusual enough to be worth a question on its own.

Hantavirus HFRS — the one where the kidney fails

Every other agent here kills through generalized multi-organ failure. Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome is the exception: the kidney is damaged by a specific immunopathologic mechanism, and acute kidney injury is the usual cause of death. Renal failure out of proportion to everything else = this answer.

SegmentEncodesWhat that protein does
S — smallNucleocapsid (N) proteinSurrounds and coats the viral RNA. Internal — not accessible to antibody
M — mediumEnvelope glycoproteins Gn and GcThe outer surface spike complex — attachment and entry, and the antibody target
L — largeRdRp — RNA-dependent RNA polymeraseThe replication enzyme. Largest segment because it encodes the largest protein
🪝 Memory hook — S, M, L is not arbitrary

S = Surrounds the RNA (nucleocapsid). M = Membrane spikes (Gn/Gc). L = Largest protein, the polymerase. Each segment is named for its size, and the sizes track the size of the protein encoded. A vaccine targeting neutralizing antibody must aim at M — the only segment whose product is exposed on an intact virion.

🩸

HFRS — Old World → kidneys

Far East (especially China and Korea), extending into Western Europe. This is the hemorrhagic disease in scope here.

  • Hantaan virus — Korea (and China); named for the Hantan River
  • Seoul virus — also Korea
  • Dobrava virus — central and western Europe
  • Puumala virus — Scandinavia, carried by voles
🫁

HCPS — New World → heart and lungs

The hantaviruses of the Americas — e.g. Andes virus. Taught in the respiratory block, not here.

  • Same rodent reservoir, same aerosol route, same absence of a vector, same supportive treatment
  • Presents as rapidly progressive respiratory failure and pulmonary edema with normal renal function
⚠️ Old World versus New World is the whole distinction

Old World hantaviruses → kidneys (HFRS). New World hantaviruses → heart and lungs (HCPS). Get the hemisphere right and the syndrome follows. This also means HFRS is genuinely rare in the United States — a US case is someone who has been to the Far East or parts of Western Europe.

🔑 The incubation period is unusually long — and diagnostically useful ★ HY

3 to 9 weeks from inhalation to symptom onset (compare dengue's 4–7 days). A patient who cleaned out a rodent-infested cabin a month or two ago and is now febrile is still within the window — do not dismiss the exposure because it was not recent.

Transmission: virus shed in rodent urine, feces and saliva, acquired by aerosol — classically someone generating aerosols while working in a contaminated building. No vector. Person-to-person is possible but very rare. Burden 60,000–120,000 cases/year worldwide.

🩺 The historical case that named the disease in the West

During the Korean War, roughly 2,000–2,500 United Nations troops acquired what we now recognize as hantavirus HFRS over about two years, with a ~5% fatality rate. That outbreak is why the prototype agent is called Hantaan virus, after the Hantan River.

  1. Infected dendritic cells and macrophages start the cascade. They release IL-12, TNF-α, IL-1 and chemokines (RANTES, IP-10, IL-6, MCP-1, IL-8) plus VEGF — the cytokine storm of panel B.
  2. Cytotoxic T cells are recruited and turn on the endothelium. IL-12 drives cytotoxic T cell activity; these cells produce IL-6 and IL-10 and induce apoptosis in infected endothelial cells.
  3. Infected endothelial cells make themselves targets. They upregulate HLA class I and HLA-DR and the adhesion molecules ICAM-1, VCAM-1, E-selectin, PECAM-1, recruiting antibody-dependent cytotoxicity and complement onto the vessel wall — and secrete VEGF, which directly increases permeability.
  4. The kallikrein–kinin system is switched on, raising bradykinin — a potent vasodilator and permeability agent, adding to the leak and the hypotension.
  5. The renal vascular bed fails in two phases. Early: congestion and permeability disturbance. Oliguric: leakage, extensive interstitial hemorrhage, severe endothelial degenerative change, occasional anemic necrosis in the deep medulla.
🧠 Why “immunopathologic” is the operative word

Almost nothing in that cascade is the virus destroying kidney tissue directly. It is cytokines, cytotoxic T cells, antibody-dependent cytotoxicity, complement and bradykinin attacking an endothelium that has been marked as infected. The lesion is an acute tubulointerstitial nephritis. The kidney is collateral damage from the host's own response — which is exactly why there is no antiviral to give and the treatment is supportive.

Diagnosis: suspect it with fever of unknown origin + thrombocytopenia + renal failure and an endemic exposure. ELISA for anti-hantavirus IgM/IgG is the mainstay (limited by a two-week lag); RT-PCR when the infection may be fulminant and you cannot wait. Treatment: no antiviral, no vaccine available in the United States, supportive care with careful volume and electrolyte management and renal replacement therapy where indicated.

Crimean–Congo hemorrhagic fever — the tick-borne one

💡 Why a rare disease gets its own section

The lecturer's stated reason: “it appears frequently on the USMLE, especially Step 1.” Roughly 1,000 cases per year worldwide — a small disease with a disproportionate examination footprint. Learn it as a pattern: tick bite + livestock contact + southeastern Europe or the Middle East + ~30% mortality.

Number discrepancy worth knowing: the written outline gives ~1,000 cases/year; the recorded lecture said ~10,000/year. Where they disagree, carry the written outline's number.

The name comes from two unrelated discoveries of one agent: first described in Russian soldiers in the Crimea in 1944, then isolated about ten years later from a child in the Congo. It is a Nairovirus, and its morphology resembles hantavirus because both are Bunyaviridae.

⚠️ Hyalomma is not Ixodes — keep the naming straight

The recording describes Hyalomma as “related to the deer tick, but it's not the deer tick.” Right idea — both are hard ticks (Ixodidae) and slow feeders — but the CCHF vector is the genus Hyalomma. If a stem names Ixodes scapularis, it is pointing at Lyme disease, babesiosis or anaplasmosis, not CCHF.

The tick acquires the virus from livestock and birds, which carry it and stay completely well. Second route: direct contact with infected animal or human blood — a slaughterhouse or veterinary exposure — but most of the time it is the tick.

OutcomeProportion / detail
Subclinical~88% — the large majority never come to attention
Symptomatic infectionSudden fever, headache, myalgia, conjunctivitis, photophobia, abdominal pain, nausea and GI upset
Hemorrhagic manifestationsPulmonary hemorrhage, gum bleeding, petechiae, extensive bleeding into skin → cytokine storm → shock → multi-organ failure
Mortality~30% among those who become symptomatic — far higher than dengue or Lassa, and the number most worth remembering
DiagnosisRT-PCR primary; IgM/IgG antibody kits secondary (must wait for antibodies)
TreatmentNo antiviral. Supportive: fluids, electrolytes, ventilation, hemodialysis, vasopressors. Acetaminophen, not NSAIDs. Prevention = tick-bite avoidance

Lassa fever — West Africa, a multimammate rat, and deafness in survivors

🧠 Arena is Latin for sand — arenavirus = “sandy virus”

The granular, speckled interior on electron micrograph is host-cell ribosomes captured during virus assembly. A virion makes no proteins of its own, so a captured ribosome does nothing there — but the appearance named the family. Other members: Machupo (Bolivian hemorrhagic fever), Junin (Argentine hemorrhagic fever), and LCMV, which causes aseptic meningitis and is taught in the neurology block.

Named 1969

Lassa, Nigeria

The village where it was first identified. The first notable US experience was the same year, at Yale University, in a research group working with the virus and infected monkeys.

300–350 thousand

cases per year

With ~5,000 deaths — an overall mortality of about 1%, far below CCHF's 30%.

West Africa

the geography

Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Liberia and Guinea.

Three routes in

all involve the rodent

Direct contact with urine, feces or bodily fluids · inhalation of aerosolized excreta · eating the rodent as a food source. No insect vector. Human-to-human by blood, tissue, secretions or excretions.

🔑 The two no-vector rodent diseases, side by side

Hantavirus HFRS and Lassa are the only agents here with no arthropod vector at all. They differ on three points a question can hinge on: geography (Far East / Western Europe versus West Africa), rodent (field mice, rats and voles versus Mastomys natalensis specifically), and the extra route — Lassa adds eating the rodent, which hantavirus does not have.

StageFeatures
Stage I — ~80% stop hereFever, fatigue, headache, myalgias. Mild; it resolves
Stage IISore throat, cough, retrosternal chest pain, vomiting, abdominal pain, back pain, diarrhea
Stage IIIHead and neck edema, conjunctival injection, shortness of breath, proteinuria, hypotension, anemia
Stage IVAltered mental status, convulsions, mucosal and internal bleeding, coma
Sequelae or deathSensorineural hearing loss (usually bilateral), hair loss, balance difficulty, difficulty speaking, tremor — or death from multi-organ failure, usually a couple of weeks after symptom onset
⚠️ The sequela that identifies Lassa ★ HY

New bilateral sensorineural hearing loss after a febrile illness acquired in West Africa is Lassa until proven otherwise. No other agent in this lecture has that sequela. Survivors also report tremors, balance difficulty, hair loss and difficulty speaking; post-Lassa encephalitis has been described.

🔑 Lassa is the only agent in Part 1 with a drug — and it is a weak one

Ribavirin, a guanosine analog that inhibits viral RNA synthesis. Studies show mixed results; the lecturer's honest summary is that it is “not a great drug, but it is used and it can slow things down.” Contrast dengue, hantavirus HFRS and CCHF, for which no antiviral exists at all. Supportive care remains first: oxygen, blood pressure, fluids.

Diagnosis: endemic travel + rodent or patient exposure, then ELISA for anti-Lassa IgM/IgG, ELISA for Lassa antigen when you need a faster answer, and RT-PCR preferentially if available.

🧠 No licensed vaccine — but the candidates teach a platform worth knowing

The leading candidates are viral vector vaccines: an attenuated measles virus (the kind used in MMR) or an attenuated vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV), into which genes for Lassa surface protein have been inserted. The recipient receives the harmless attenuated vector, which then expresses Lassa surface protein and raises an immune response against it — not measles, and not Lassa.

Correction worth carrying: the recording calls VSV a “vesicular dermatitis virus … a pox virus.” It is vesicular stomatitis virus, a rhabdovirus — same family as rabies — and it is the vector in the licensed Ebola vaccine. The concept described is otherwise exactly right.

🪝 See this in a stem → think this
  • Fever + retro-orbital pain + severe bone pain → dengue
  • Fever + thrombocytopenia + acute renal failure → hantavirus HFRS
  • Fever + petechiae + tick bite in Turkey or the Balkans → Crimean–Congo
  • Fever + West Africa + new sensorineural hearing loss → Lassa
  • Cytokine storm + DIC + capillary leak → the shared panel B/D endpoint, common to all of them

Q: A 30-year-old returns from two weeks in Puerto Rico and, five days later, develops fever to 102 °F, severe headache, retro-orbital pain, and pain in the lower back and long bones. On day 3 a faint macular rash appears and the platelet count is 88,000. Diagnosis, test, and which analgesic must be avoided?

Answer

Dengue fever. Endemic-area travel (Puerto Rico accounts for most US dengue), an incubation of 4–7 days matching the intrinsic incubation period, and the classic tier-1 features — fever, headache, retro-orbital eye pain, musculoskeletal and lumbar “breakbone” pain, rash — with thrombocytopenia. Order multiplex RT-PCR (covers dengue plus the other main VHF agents in one run); ELISA for dengue antigen is the alternative. Avoid NSAIDs — they add platelet inhibition to an existing coagulopathy. Use acetaminophen and give fluids.

Q: A 40-year-old who spent last month renovating an old barn in rural South Korea presents with fever, headache, vomiting, petechiae, conjunctival hemorrhage, hypotension, platelets 40,000 and creatinine 4.2 mg/dL. Agent, route, and what specifically will kill them?

Answer

Hantavirus HFRS — an Old World hantavirus, most likely Hantaan or Seoul given Korea. Acquired by inhaling aerosolized rodent urine, feces or saliva while working in a contaminated building; there is no vector. The exposure a month ago fits the 3–9 week incubation period — do not dismiss it as too remote. The likely cause of death is acute kidney injury from an immunopathologic acute tubulointerstitial nephritis, the most common cause of mortality in this infection. Management is supportive: no antiviral, and no vaccine available in the United States.

Q: A hantavirus is isolated from a patient in New Mexico with rapidly progressive respiratory failure and pulmonary edema and normal renal function. Is this HFRS?

Answer

No — this is hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), caused by a New World hantavirus of the Americas (Andes virus is the lecture's named example). Old World → renal (HFRS); New World → cardiopulmonary (HCPS). HCPS is taught in the respiratory block. Everything else is shared: rodent reservoir, aerosol transmission, no vector, supportive treatment only.

Q: A 45-year-old sheep farmer in eastern Turkey has abrupt fever, severe headache, myalgia, conjunctivitis and abdominal pain, and on day 4 develops bleeding gums, widespread petechiae and hemoptysis. Diagnosis, vector, and approximate mortality?

Answer

Crimean–Congo hemorrhagic fever, a Nairovirus within the Bunyaviridae. The vector is the Hyalomma tick, which acquires the virus from livestock that carry it without becoming ill; this farmer also has the second route available — direct contact with infected animal blood. Mortality is ~30% among the symptomatic, and note that ~88% of infections are subclinical, so he is in the minority. No antiviral: supportive care, and acetaminophen rather than NSAIDs.

Q: A 29-year-old aid worker returns from rural Nigeria with three weeks of fever, sore throat, retrosternal chest pain, vomiting and diarrhea, then facial and neck swelling, conjunctival injection and proteinuria. On recovery she cannot hear properly in either ear. Infection, reservoir, and the one drug with any evidence?

Answer

Lassa fever, an Arenaviridae infection. Reservoir is the multimammate rat, Mastomys natalensis, acquired by contact with or inhalation of its excreta, or by eating the rodent — no insect vector. The course maps onto the staged natural history: stage II (sore throat, retrosternal chest pain, vomiting, diarrhea) progressing to stage III (head and neck edema, conjunctival injection, proteinuria). The bilateral sensorineural hearing loss clinches it. The drug is ribavirin, a guanosine analog inhibiting viral RNA synthesis — mixed results, used alongside supportive care.

Q: Which hantavirus genome segment would you target with a vaccine intended to generate neutralizing antibody, and why?

Answer

The M (medium) segment, because it encodes the envelope glycoproteins Gn and Gc — the outer surface spike complex, and therefore the only viral proteins accessible to antibody on an intact virion. The S segment encodes the internal nucleocapsid protein coating the RNA, and the L segment encodes the internal RdRp; neither is exposed on the particle surface.

Q: Why does the immunosuppression of panel A make the later cytokine storm worse rather than milder?

Answer

Because the mediator surge in panel B is a response to viral burden, and panel A is precisely what let the viral burden climb unchecked. Low type I interferon and low co-stimulatory molecule expression mean poor NK and T cell activity, so there is no early cytotoxic control of replication. Macrophages then meet an enormous antigen load and respond with an enormous mediator release. The weak specific response and the excessive non-specific response are two faces of one failure.

Q: A hospital asks whether a dengue patient needs airborne precautions and terminal fomite disinfection. What do you tell them, on what virologic basis?

Answer

No airborne precautions are needed on the basis of the virus. Flaviviruses are enveloped and extremely labile — sensitive to heat, UV light, disinfectants, acid and alkaline pH — and are stable only inside their host or their vector. They therefore do not survive on fomites and do not persist in aerosols. The residual risk is blood and body-fluid exposure (dengue is transmissible through contaminated blood products, at low risk), so standard blood-borne precautions are the right answer.
