Section 23 · Laboratory foundations

Inside the Analyzer — What Is Measured and What Is Calculated

Three numbers on the complete blood count are measured. The rest are arithmetic. Knowing which is which explains almost every artefact you will ever be handed.

Abbreviations used in this section CBC complete blood count — the standard automated panel · RBC red blood cell, also called an erythrocyte · WBC white blood cell, also called a leukocyte · Hgb hemoglobin, in grams per decilitre · Hct hematocrit, the proportion of blood volume occupied by red cells · MCV mean corpuscular volume — average red cell size · MCH mean corpuscular hemoglobin — average hemoglobin mass per cell · MCHC mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration — hemoglobin density inside the cell · RDW red cell distribution width — how variable the cell sizes are · MPV mean platelet volume · SD standard deviation · SLS sodium lauryl sulfate — the cyanide-free hemoglobin reagent · PLT-F the fluorescent platelet channel · EDTA ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid — the lavender-top anticoagulant · fL femtolitre (10−15 L) · pg picogram · nm nanometre · TAT turnaround time · CD41 / CD61 platelet glycoproteins IIb and IIIa, the flow cytometry reference markers
🔑 The three measured values — everything else is derived

The analyzer physically measures the red cell count, the MCV (both by impedance) and the hemoglobin (photometrically). The hematocrit, MCH, MCHC and RDW are all calculated from those three.

That single fact is the reason artefacts cascade. Corrupt one measured value and every number derived from it goes wrong at the same time — which is exactly what makes an impossible MCHC such a reliable alarm bell in Section 25.

The specimen — what the laboratory will accept

  1. Fresh whole blood in EDTA. The lavender-top tube. Ideal within 3 hours of collection, acceptable within 8 hours; refrigerated samples beyond that may degrade.
  2. Invert the tube several times. EDTA is sprayed on the inside surfaces of the tube, including near the top. Blood that simply runs to the bottom never meets the full dose of anticoagulant, and partial clotting follows.
  3. No clots and no clumps. A clot sequesters platelets and some white and red cells with them, so those cells never reach the aperture and the counts come back falsely low — an artefact that reads as a disease.
  4. Citrate is the fallback for platelets. A blue-top tube may be used when EDTA-dependent platelet clumping is suspected. This is the workaround that reappears in Section 25.
🧠 Two tubes, one principle, opposite requirements

The CBC uses EDTA, which binds calcium irreversibly — fine, because the analyzer only needs to count intact cells. Coagulation testing uses sodium citrate, which binds calcium reversibly so the laboratory can add calcium back and restart clotting on demand (Section 29). Same principle, opposite requirement, different tube. Getting them the wrong way round makes both tests uninterpretable.

One practical footnote on tube brands: in the laboratory's own correlation study, MCV, RDW and hematocrit ran 1–2% higher in one manufacturer's tube than another's. Not clinically significant in isolation — but when you are trending a value over time, such as an MCV rising on iron therapy, use the same tube type and remove the variable.

Four measurement principles cover the whole panel ★ HY

Impedance — the Coulter principle

counting and sizing

Cells in a conductive fluid are drawn through a narrow aperture; each cell crossing changes the electrical impedance. Each pulse is one cell (the count) and pulse height is that cell's volume (the size). Gives RBC + MCV, platelets + MPV, and the total white count.

Flow cytometry

the differential

Separates cells by forward scatter (size) against side scatter (complexity and granularity). Those two axes are what let the machine tell a lymphocyte from a neutrophil — the white cell differential comes from here, not from impedance.

SLS photometry at 555 nm

hemoglobin

Sodium lauryl sulfate lyses red and white cells, the heme is oxidised, SLS binds it into a stable coloured complex, and absorbance is read at 555 nm — a wavelength chosen to minimise interference from turbidity. Cyanide-free, unlike the older cyanmethemoglobin reference method.

Fluorescence — the PLT-F channel

difficult platelet counts

Stains platelet rough endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria with oxazine and counts by fluorescent intensity — identifying platelets by what they contain rather than how big they are. Correlates with CD41/CD61 flow cytometry; especially useful below 50 × 10³/µL.

🪝 Memory hook — the machine decides what a cell is almost entirely from its size

There is more than one aperture, each sized for its population: a small pore for platelets, a mid-size one for red cells, a larger one for white cells. So anything that is the wrong size for its identity is counted as the wrong thing, and that one idea generates most of Section 25:

Too small → counted as a platelet. Schistocytes, microcytes and white cell fragments falsely raise the platelet count. Too big to be a platelet → missed. Platelet clumps and giant platelets falsely lower it.

The formulas, and the ranges to carry ★ HY

IndexMeasured or calculatedFormulaNormal adult rangeWhat it means
RBC — red cell countMeasured (impedance)—3.5–5.5 × 10⁶/µLHow many cells there are
Hgb — hemoglobinMeasured (SLS, 555 nm)—14–18 g/dL male; 12–16 g/dL femaleOxygen-carrying capacity — the number that defines anemia
MCV — mean corpuscular volumeMeasured (pulse height)—80–100 fL; lower in childrenAverage red cell size — the first branch of the anemia algorithm
Hct — hematocritCalculated(RBC × MCV) / 1040–50% male; 36–48% femaleProportion of blood volume that is red cells
MCH — mean corpuscular hemoglobinCalculated(Hgb / RBC) × 1026–34 pg/cellAverage amount of hemoglobin per cell
MCHC — mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentrationCalculated(Hgb / Hct) × 10031–37 g/dLHemoglobin density — a concentration, and therefore bounded by physics
RDW — red cell distribution widthCalculatedSD of volume / MCV11.4–14.5Variation in cell size — the width of the impedance curve
ReticulocytesMeasured (RNA stain)—0.8–4%Is the marrow responding? The branch point in the normocytic column
🧠 MCH versus MCHC — the pair students reliably confuse

MCH is an amount; MCHC is a concentration. A cell can contain little hemoglobin because it is small (low MCH, normal MCHC), or because it is underfilled for its size (low MCHC — true hypochromia).

Because MCHC is a density it has a physical ceiling, and that is what makes it the best artefact detector on the panel. A reported MCHC above about 37 g/dL is usually impossible and points at a laboratory interference rather than a disease. The one genuine exception is hereditary spherocytosis (Section 9), where the cells really are hyperdense — there, a high MCHC is a clue, not an error.

🪝 The rule of three — and why breaking it is itself a finding

Hematocrit ≈ 3 × hemoglobin. Hemoglobin 10 g/dL should give a hematocrit near 30%. The qualifier that makes it usable: this holds only when the MCV is normal, because the two are linked through cell size.

So a hemoglobin and hematocrit that do not fit the rule of three is not merely an oddity — it points either at abnormal red cell size or at one of the interferences in Section 25. The same check appears in Section 2; here you can see exactly why it works.

Reticulocytes and nucleated red cells — what a nucleus is for

🧠 Why a red cell has a nucleus at all, and why losing it matters

A red cell is born with a nucleus because it needs one to manufacture its hemoglobin. Once fully loaded, the nucleus has no further use and gets in the way, so the cell ejects it. A reticulocyte is the stage just after that — no nucleus, but still carrying leftover RNA, which is what the reticulocyte stain detects. A mature red cell has neither.

Three consequences worth carrying:

  1. A nucleated red cell in the blood is a cell released before it was finished. Either the marrow is under stress and rushing output, or something is taking over the marrow and forcing cells out — fibrosis, metastasis. Either way it needs explaining (Section 27).
  2. The analyzer counts nucleated red cells as white cells unless it corrects for them, because it is looking for nuclei. That is one of the interferences in Section 25.
  3. G6PD deficiency behaves the way it does because of this. With no nucleus, the G6PD a red cell carries at birth is all it will ever have — it cannot make more, so a deficient cell runs out of oxidant protection partway through its life (Section 9).
🔑 The immature platelet fraction is the reticulocyte count for platelets

Same logic, different lineage. Its clinical use is monitoring engraftment after a stem cell or marrow transplant: the platelet count is still low, but if immature platelets start appearing, the new marrow has begun producing — and the actual count will start to rise in two or three days. Days of warning you would not otherwise have.

Reticulocyte is to red cell as immature platelet fraction is to platelet. Both answer “is the marrow producing?” before the mature count moves.

The anemia algorithm, as the laboratory draws it ★ HY

Start with a low hemoglobin, split on the MCV, and then — in the normocytic column only — split again on the reticulocyte count. This is the same tree as Section 3, laid out the way the analyzer hands it to you.

MCV < 80 fL · microcyticMCV 80–100 · normocytic, low reticsMCV 80–100 · normocytic, high reticsMCV > 100 fL · macrocytic
Iron deficiency
Thalassemia — may show an increased RBC count
Hemoglobin E variant
Metal toxicity
(chronic disease)

🪝 Two details on this algorithm that are exam gold

Thalassemia may show an increased red cell count. This is the cleanest way to separate it from iron deficiency at the CBC alone. Both are microcytic with a low hemoglobin, but in thalassemia the marrow makes many small cells, whereas in iron deficiency it makes few small cells. And the consequence is not academic: giving iron to a patient with thalassemia trait achieves nothing and risks overload.

Chronic disease and sideroblastic anemia appear in two columns. They are bracketed in the microcytic column and listed plainly in the normocytic one, because they usually start normocytic and only become microcytic later. If they do not fit the first column you try, try the other.

⚠️ The averaging trap — why a normal MCV can lie

The MCV is an average, and averages hide bimodal data. Two named scenarios produce a normal MCV over two abnormal populations:

  • Microcytic anemia with a brisk reticulocytosis — small cells averaged with large young ones.
  • After transfusing normal blood into a microcytic patient — the patient's small cells averaged with the donor's normal ones.

The tell is a raised RDW with a normal MCV, and the confirmation is looking at the smear. This is the strongest single argument for why the smear still exists.

Accuracy, precision, and reading a scattergram

🎯

Systematic bias → decreased accuracy

  • Every result is off in the same direction by a consistent amount.
  • May represent an instrument problem, and is fixable by calibration.
  • Rule of thumb: consistently wrong → suspect the machine.
🎲

Random bias → decreased precision

  • Results scatter around the truth rather than sitting off to one side.
  • May be an intrinsic feature of the assay and not fixable at all.
  • Rule of thumb: inconsistently wrong → suspect the method.
🩺 Precision is partly a property of the analyte, not just the machine

Platelets fluctuate by roughly 15–20% between repeat runs, intrinsically, because they activate. A repeat count differing by 15% is not an instrument fault. The MCV, by contrast, is very tightly precise — so a genuinely shifting MCV means something real.

That distinction is the whole point: some imprecision cannot be engineered away, whereas worsening precision in a test that is normally tight does suggest an instrument problem. Note too that turnaround time is measured across the whole workflow — sample arrival to result reaching the clinician — not just the instrument's run time.

🧠 Where each cell sits on the scattergram

With side scatter on the X-axis and forward scatter on the Y-axis:

  • Lymphocyte — a simple cell: spherical nucleus, thin rim of cytoplasm. Low side scatter, low fluorescence → bottom-left.
  • Eosinophil — very bright granules and a lobed nucleus. Very high side scatter → pushed far right.
  • Monocyte — the largest of the normal white cells. High forward scatter → sits high up.
  • Ghost cells — cells that lysed during collection or processing. Having lost contents and surface markers they show low forward and low side scatter and are gated out as debris. A lot of them means a degraded sample.

This is also how the “abnormal scattergram” and “blasts?” flags are produced: blasts and immature cells are larger and cluster somewhere the normal populations do not. A dense cloud in unexpected territory pulls the slide out of autoverification and onto a microscope — the discrimination Section 27 then has to make.

🔑 Why the automated count beats the manual one — and what it frees people up to do

The analyzer counts about 36,000 cells per sample. A technologist performing a manual differential counts 100–200. That is the entire precision argument in one comparison.

When there are no flags and results are close to normal, the instrument autoverifies and the result reaches the provider without human review. The point of that is not speed for its own sake: it lets technologists spend their time on smear review for atypical cells such as leukemia blasts and on the special hematology testing that remains manual.

Q: Which CBC parameters are directly measured and which are calculated — and why does the distinction change how you read an abnormal panel?

Answer

Measured: the red cell count and MCV (both from impedance — one pulse per cell, pulse height for size), and the hemoglobin (photometrically at 555 nm as the SLS–hemoglobin complex).

Calculated: Hct = (RBC × MCV)/10 · MCH = (Hgb/RBC) × 10 · MCHC = (Hgb/Hct) × 100 · RDW = SD of volume / MCV.

It matters because an error in a measured value propagates into every value derived from it. Cold agglutinins clump red cells, which drops the count and inflates the MCV — and the calculated hematocrit and MCHC both go wrong as a direct consequence. That is why an impossibly high MCHC is such a reliable flag: it is downstream of two other errors.

Q: Two patients both have a hemoglobin of 10.5 g/dL and an MCV of 68 fL. Patient A has a red cell count of 3.1 × 10⁶/µL; patient B has 6.2 × 10⁶/µL. What is the likely diagnosis in each, and why does the distinction matter urgently?

Answer

Patient A: iron deficiency anemia. Few cells, and they are small — the marrow cannot build hemoglobin, so it builds fewer, smaller cells.

Patient B: thalassemia. The algorithm notes explicitly that thalassemia may show an increased RBC count — the marrow produces plenty of cells, each small and underfilled.

It matters because the treatments are opposite. Patient A needs iron. Patient B has normal or high iron stores, gains nothing from supplementation, and is put at risk of iron overload by it. Confirm with iron studies (ferritin, total iron binding capacity) and hemoglobin electrophoresis.

Q: A patient has a normocytic anemia. What single inexpensive test most efficiently divides the differential, and what does each result mean?

Answer

The reticulocyte count — the branch point in the normocytic column. Normal range roughly 0.8–4%.

High reticulocytes → the marrow is working, so the cells are being lost: hemolysis, recovery from an insult, hemoglobinopathies, enzymopathies, membranopathies.

Low reticulocytes → the marrow itself is the problem: renal failure (no erythropoietin), chronic disease, sideroblastic anemia, hypoendocrine states, aplastic anemia, or a mixed deficiency.

The question it answers, in one line: is this low production or increased destruction?

Q: A hematology analyzer produces platelet counts that are consistently 15% lower than the reference method on every quality control sample. Is this an accuracy or a precision problem, and what does it suggest?

Answer

An accuracy problem, from systematic bias. The results are off by a consistent amount in a consistent direction — that is the definition of systematic bias, and it manifests as decreased accuracy. Systematic bias may represent an instrument problem, so the next step is calibration and instrument troubleshooting.

Had the results instead scattered widely around the correct value, that would be random bias reducing precision, which may be an intrinsic feature of the assay rather than a fault — and platelets in particular vary 15–20% between runs for real biological reasons.

LO 5LO 27Source: Complete Blood Count & Blood Smears

Section 24 · Laboratory foundations

The Peripheral Smear — Four Cases and the Morphology Atlas

The analyzer gives you numbers. The smear gives you the diagnosis when the numbers cannot — and it is the only way to catch the two populations hiding under a normal average.

Abbreviations used in this section Monolayer the region of a smear where cells sit evenly spaced without overlapping — the only place morphology should be read · Feather edge the thin trailing end of a smear · Wright–Giemsa the standard smear stain, eosin plus methylene blue · Polychromasia blue-grey young red cells — the smear equivalent of a raised reticulocyte count · Poikilocytosis variation in cell shape (contrast anisocytosis, which is size) · Codocyte target cell · Dacryocyte tear-drop cell · Acanthocyte spur cell · Echinocyte burr cell · Schistocyte a red cell fragment · TIBC total iron binding capacity · MAHA microangiopathic hemolytic anemia · TTP thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura · HUS hemolytic uremic syndrome · DIC disseminated intravascular coagulation · Parasitaemia the percentage of red cells infected · cc/kg millilitres per kilogram of body weight

Where to look, and why it matters ★ HY

1

The feather edge

The thin trailing end. Cells are spread too far apart and distorted, and large cells preferentially collect here. Red cells lose their central pallor as an artefact — which is exactly the feature that defines a spherocyte.

2

The thicker edge

Cells overlap and pile up. Morphology is uninterpretable here for the opposite reason.

3

The monolayer

Between the two, where cells are evenly distributed without touching or overlapping. This is the only region morphology should be assessed in.

4

A consistent smear

An automated spreader produces the uniform slide that image-capture systems need — the software cannot compensate for a badly made slide, and neither can a human.

🧠 What a normal red cell actually is, and where the central pallor comes from

Think of a donut whose hole is filled in. The centre is thinner, not absent — and that dip is where the nucleus used to be before the cell ejected it. Because cells settle flat and you view them top-down, the thin centre reads as the central pallor.

Normal central pallor occupies about one third of the cell. Notably wider than that is hypochromia — the concrete threshold behind the vague phrase “faint staining”.

And the reason the biconcave shape exists at all: it bends and twists, because capillaries are sometimes narrower than the red cell's own diameter. That is precisely what fails in sickle cell disease, where the cells are stiff and deformed, and why spherocytes, having lost that flexibility, are pulled out by the spleen (Section 9).

🪝 Memory hook — opposites attract, and that is where the cell names come from

Individual cells are translucent; without a stain there is essentially nothing to see. Hematoxylin is a basic dye that stains acidic material — nuclear DNA — blue-purple. Eosin is an acidic dye that stains basic material — cytoplasmic protein — pink-orange. The peripheral smear stain is Wright–Giemsa, eosin plus methylene blue, devised in 1902.

The granulocytes are named for which dye they prefer: an eosinophil takes up eosin and goes bright orange-red; a basophil takes up the basic dye and goes dark blue-purple; a neutrophil is indifferent to both and stains a neutral pale lilac.

One clarification worth making explicit: the red you see on a smear is the eosin, not the hemoglobin. A single red cell is essentially colourless — it is only when you pile enough of them together, as in a tube of blood, that you see red.

Four cases where the diagnosis is on the slide ★ HY

Each is read in the same order: microscopic features → pathophysiology → clinical implications → what to send next.

Case 1 — 18-month-old with fatigue

microcytic, hypochromic

Hemoglobin 3.6 g/dL, MCV 58 fL. TIBC 421 mcg/dL (high — more transferrin hunting for iron), ferritin 1 ng/mL (stores essentially absent), electrophoresis normal. Severe iron deficiency. Transfused 15 cc/kg red cells, started on oral ferrous sulfate, and milk restricted.

Case 2 — 5-year-old with pain crises

sickle cells, target cells, polychromasia

Hemoglobin SS disease with prior acute chest syndrome, on hydroxyurea. Admitted with fever 39.3 °C, white count 36,000/µL, streptococcal pharyngitis — treated with ceftriaxone, hydration and bronchodilators. Confirmed on sickle solubility test.

Case 3 — 17-year-old, bruising and confusion

schistocytes, low platelets

Fever, acute mental status change, thrombocytopenia and schistocytes — thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. Worked mechanistically in Section 32 as ADAMTS13 failure.

Case 4 — 5-year-old back from Afghanistan

intraerythrocytic parasites

Mosquito bites, periodic fevers. Hgb 10.7, MCV 70, platelets 47 × 10³/µL. Parasite load 1.8%; morphology and rapid antigen testing indicate Plasmodium vivax, with the falciparum band negative.

🪝 Why milk restriction is the treatment, not an aside

Excessive cow's milk in a toddler causes iron deficiency three separate ways: it is low in iron, its calcium and casein inhibit absorption of what iron there is, and it can cause occult gastrointestinal blood loss. Giving iron without addressing the milk treats the number rather than the cause.

Two numbers worth carrying from the same case. Roughly 10–15 cc/kg of red cells raises hemoglobin by about 2–3 g/dL. And the target was closer to 7, not normal — in a chronic, slowly developing anemia the child has physiologically compensated, so transfusion is deliberately partial and cautious, and the marrow does the rest once given iron.

⚠️ Why fever in sickle cell disease is an emergency, not an observation

These patients are functionally asplenic from repeated infarction, so they cannot clear encapsulated organisms — Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Neisseria meningitidis. That is why case 2 starts with ceftriaxone rather than watchful waiting: fever is treated as presumed sepsis until proven otherwise. Section 11 works through the post-splenectomy version of the same problem.

Hydration is on the treatment list for a mechanistic reason, not a supportive one: dehydration raises intracellular hemoglobin concentration and directly worsens sickling, as does hypoxia.

🔑 The single most actionable next step in this lecture: target cells → send a hemoglobin electrophoresis

Asked directly whether thalassemia can be identified from the smear, the answer was a clear no — you cannot differentiate these conditions from morphology alone. Target cells are a feature of hemoglobin disorders generally, thalassemias and hemoglobinopathies alike, and combinations exist: hemoglobin S with beta thalassemia, hemoglobin S with hemoglobin C. Only electrophoresis separates them (Section 10).

🧬 Malaria on the smear — and the loop that closes back to Section 10

Five species of Plasmodium infect humans. In the P. vivax case the forms seen were mature schizonts — the parasite progressively taking over the cell and consuming its hemoglobin. P. vivax is milder and more common in Afghanistan.

P. falciparum is the one to remember — most aggressive and most widespread, with many more ring forms and occasional gametocytes on the smear. It can present with parasitaemia above 10% (severe cases 15–20%) against the 1.8% here, because it infects red cells of all ages whereas P. vivax prefers young cells, which caps its parasite load. P. vivax and P. ovale additionally form dormant liver hypnozoites, so they need treatment aimed at preventing relapse as well as clearing the blood stage.

And the evolutionary loop: sickle cell, G6PD deficiency and thalassemia persist at high frequency because the heterozygous state protects against malaria — the red cells are less hospitable to the parasite. The Duffy antigen is the receptor P. vivax uses to enter red cells, so Duffy-null individuals are resistant to P. vivax — and the same Duffy-null phenotype gives the constitutionally lower neutrophil count in Section 26. One selection pressure, shaping both the red cell and the white cell findings.

🪝 The pattern that should make you request a malaria smear

Fever + travel + thrombocytopenia. Thrombocytopenia is present in the large majority of malaria cases and is one of the most consistent laboratory clues — in case 4 the platelet count of 47,000 is the abnormality that stands out. Add a periodic fever pattern and mosquito exposure and the smear is mandatory.

Report the parasitaemia as a percentage. It is not optional: it quantifies severity, drives treatment intensity, and is followed to judge response.

The abnormal red cell morphology atlas ★ HY

MorphologyWhat it looks likeClassically associated with
SpherocytesSmall, round, densely stained, no central pallorHereditary spherocytosis; autoimmune hemolytic anemia — membrane removed by splenic macrophages
Ovalocytes / elliptocytesOval to cigar-shapedHereditary elliptocytosis; also iron deficiency and myelodysplasia
StomatocytesCentral pallor is a slit or “mouth” rather than roundHereditary stomatocytosis; alcohol and liver disease
Tear-drop cells (dacryocytes)One pointed endMyelofibrosis; marrow infiltration; also thalassemia. Squeezed as they exit a scarred marrow
Target cells (codocytes)A bullseye — central dot of hemoglobin inside the pallorThalassemia, hemoglobin C, liver disease, post-splenectomy — excess membrane relative to contents
Hemoglobin C crystalsDense, angular, rod- or bar-shaped intracellular crystalsHemoglobin C disease — mild hemolysis with target cells; can be co-inherited with hemoglobin S as HbSC
Acanthocytes (spur cells)Few, irregular, unevenly spaced blunt projectionsSevere liver disease, abetalipoproteinemia, post-splenectomy
Echinocytes (burr cells)Many, regular, evenly spaced short spiculesUremia / renal failure; also a common artefact of slow drying or storage
SchistocytesFragments, no central pallor, two pointed endsMicroangiopathy — TTP, HUS, aHUS, DIC, malignant hypertension, mechanical valves, march hemoglobinuria
Sickle cellsRigid crescent with pointed endsSickle cell disease — β6 Glu→Val polymerisation of deoxygenated hemoglobin S
PolychromasiaLarger, blue-grey cellsReticulocytes — the smear equivalent of a raised reticulocyte count. The marrow is responding
🪝 The two pairs worth being able to separate on sight

Spiky cells. The shortest version of the rule: burr cells point to kidney disorders, spur cells point to liver disorders. Acanthocyte has asymmetric spicules — few, irregular → liver. Echinocyte has even ones — many, regular → kidney, or an artefact. That last possibility is the practical reason to tell them apart: one is a finding, the other is often just a badly handled slide.

Target cells — one mechanism, opposite starting points. A target cell has too much membrane for the hemoglobin inside, so the excess surface folds into a central bump. That happens either because the contents are reduced (thalassemia, iron deficiency) or because the membrane is increased (liver disease, where lipid loading expands it; post-splenectomy, where the spleen is no longer trimming cells). Same final shape, opposite causes.

🔑 Schistocytes narrow the field but do not close it — the coagulation panel does

Schistocytes appear in every entry on the microangiopathy list. The discriminator that separates a thrombotic microangiopathy from disseminated intravascular coagulation is not the smear but the clotting screen:

TTP, HUS, aHUS: PT and aPTT normal, fibrinogen normal — the clotting factors are not being consumed; the problem is platelets and endothelium. DIC: PT and aPTT both prolonged, fibrinogen low or falling, D-dimer markedly raised. Sections 28 and 29 work both sides.

Q: A trainee assesses red cell morphology at the feather edge of a smear and reports numerous spherocytes. Why is that report unreliable?

Answer

Because morphology must be read in the monolayer — the region where cells are evenly distributed without touching or overlapping. The feather edge is the thin trailing end, where cells are dragged out and distorted by the spreading process and where large cells preferentially collect.

Red cells there characteristically lose their central pallor as an artefact of being flattened and over-spread — which is precisely the feature that defines a spherocyte. Reading at the feather edge manufactures spherocytes that are not present.

The other extreme, the thicker edge, is equally useless because cells pile up and overlap. This is also why a consistently made smear matters: automated image-capture systems cannot compensate for a bad slide.

Q: A smear shows numerous cells with many short, evenly spaced projections. The clinician insists the patient has liver disease. What do you tell them?

Answer

Many, regular, evenly spaced spicules describe an echinocyte (burr cell), not an acanthocyte. Echinocytes point toward uremia / renal failure — or, very commonly, toward a preparation artefact from slow drying, prolonged storage before smearing, or a stain pH problem.

The liver disease cell is the acanthocyte (spur cell), which has few, irregular, unevenly spaced blunt projections.

Practically: check renal function, and check when and how the slide was made. If the sample sat before smearing, request a fresh specimen.

Q: A patient's smear shows schistocytes and the platelet count is low. What two laboratory results would you look at immediately to separate a thrombotic microangiopathy from disseminated intravascular coagulation?

Answer

The PT/aPTT and the fibrinogen.

TTP, HUS and aHUS: PT and aPTT normal, fibrinogen normal. The clotting factors are not being consumed — the lesion is in platelets and endothelium.

DIC: PT and aPTT both prolonged, fibrinogen low or falling, with a markedly raised D-dimer.

The smear cannot make this distinction — schistocytes appear in every entry on the list, including obstetric complications, malignant hypertension, march hemoglobinuria and mechanical valves. The coagulation panel can, in one look.

Q: Why does a malaria report state the parasite load as a percentage, and why does species identification change management?

Answer

Parasitaemia quantifies severity and is followed to judge response to therapy. Case 4 was 1.8%; P. falciparum can present above 10%, with severe cases running 15–20%.

Species matters because P. falciparum is the most virulent — it causes cerebral malaria and death, reaches far higher parasite loads because it infects red cells of all ages, and is treated more aggressively. A rapid antigen test distinguishes it: in case 4 the band was for the vivax/malariae/ovale common antigen and the falciparum band was negative.

P. vivax and P. ovale also form dormant liver hypnozoites, so treatment must additionally target relapse, not just the blood stage.

LO 27Source: Complete Blood Count & Blood Smears

Section 25 · Laboratory foundations

Interferences, Artefacts, and When to Redraw

The half of the objective that is usually skipped. Every interference below follows from something already established: the analyzer identifies cells by size, reads hemoglobin by absorbance, and calculates several of the numbers it reports.

Abbreviations used in this section MCHC mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration — the best single artefact detector · Pseudothrombocytopenia a falsely low platelet count from EDTA-dependent clumping · PLT-F the fluorescent platelet channel · nRBC nucleated red blood cell · Lipemia turbid, fat-laden plasma · Cold agglutinin an antibody that clumps red cells at low temperature · Hyperbilirubinemia raised plasma bilirubin, which adds pigment and absorbance · EDTA the lavender-top anticoagulant · Autoverification automatic release of unflagged, near-normal results without human review
🔑 The three failure modes, and what each one produces
  1. Something is the wrong size for its identity. It goes through the wrong aperture and is counted as the wrong thing. This is the entire platelet-counting problem.
  2. Something adds absorbance at 555 nm. Turbidity or pigment inflates the measured hemoglobin — and therefore MCH and MCHC, which are derived from it.
  3. Cells never reach the aperture. A clot traps them; the counts come back falsely low with no flag to explain why.

The interference table ★ HY

InterferenceWhat it does to the CBCMechanismHow to resolve it
Platelet clumping (EDTA-dependent)Falsely low platelet count; may falsely raise the white countClumps are too large to be sized as platelets, so they are missed — or counted as leukocytes. Flagged as “Platelet clumps?”Redraw in citrate (blue top); confirm by looking at the smear
Giant / large plateletsFalsely low platelet countToo large for the platelet size windowFluorescent (PLT-F) channel, which identifies by staining rather than size; smear review. Consider Bernard–Soulier syndrome (Section 30)
Schistocytes, microcytes, white cell fragmentsFalsely high platelet countSmall enough to fall into the platelet size windowFluorescent platelet count; smear review
Cold agglutinins (red cell agglutination)Falsely low RBC, falsely high MCV, impossibly high MCHCClumped red cells are counted as one large cell. Hct is calculated from RBC × MCV so it falls; MCHC = Hgb/Hct then rises absurdly. Flagged as “RBC agglutination”Warm the sample to 37 °C and re-run. Clinically, follow up with a cold agglutinin titre and a direct antiglobulin test
Lipemia, marked leukocytosis, hyperbilirubinemiaFalsely high hemoglobin → falsely high MCH and MCHCTurbidity and pigment add absorbance at the reading wavelength. The 555 nm choice minimises this but cannot eliminate itPlasma replacement or blank correction; recognise that a very high MCHC is usually artefactual
Nucleated red blood cellsFalsely high white cell countThey have nuclei, so they land in the leukocyte gateModern analyzers count and subtract them automatically; otherwise correct the white count manually
Clotted specimenFalsely low platelet and cell countsCells are trapped in the clot and never reach the apertureReject and redraw — “no clots or clumps” is an explicit acceptance criterion
Delayed or refrigerated specimenUnreliable indices, especially the MCVCells swell over time. Ideal ≤ 3 hours, acceptable ≤ 8 hoursRedraw
🪝 The single best artefact detector: an MCHC above ~37 g/dL

MCHC is a concentration, and a red cell can only hold so much hemoglobin per unit volume — the normal range tops out around 37 g/dL. A reported value well above that is almost never a real biological finding. It means either:

the hemoglobin was read too high (lipemia, very high white count, hyperbilirubinemia), or the hematocrit was calculated too low (cold agglutinins clumping red cells). Both point straight at a specimen problem.

The one genuine exception is hereditary spherocytosis, where the cells really are hyperdense. There a high MCHC is a diagnostic clue, not an error — which is exactly how Section 9 uses it.

⚠️ Pseudothrombocytopenia — the clue is the absence of bleeding

A platelet count of 22,000/µL in an entirely asymptomatic outpatient should not be believed before it is checked. Genuine severe thrombocytopenia usually shows petechiae or mucosal bleeding; a very low count with no bleeding at all is the signature of EDTA-dependent platelet clumping.

The mechanism is the impedance size window again: clumps are too large to be counted as platelets and are missed, or misread as white cells. Look at the smear to confirm clumping directly, then redraw in citrate — the responsible antibody is EDTA-dependent. A fluorescent platelet count also helps, since it identifies platelets by staining rather than by size.

Acting on the false number is the real harm: it triggers a hematology referral, a marrow biopsy, or a platelet transfusion the patient never needed.

🩺 The closing instruction — the pathologist is part of the workup

The lecture ends on a point worth taking literally. Sophisticated analyzers provide a great deal of information and can flag abnormal samples, but the pathologist can help interpret interferences and determine whether results are consistent with the rest of the patient's findings — and in some cases you may need to redraw the specimen.

The practical habit that follows: before acting on a startling CBC, ask whether the numbers are internally consistent. Does the hematocrit fit the rule of three? Is the MCHC physically possible? Was the tube full, fresh, and properly inverted? A great many “abnormal” CBCs fail one of those three questions.

Q: A CBC on an elderly patient reports RBC 1.9 × 10⁶/µL, MCV 128 fL, Hgb 11.8 g/dL, Hct 24.3%, MCHC 48.6 g/dL. What is going on, and what should the laboratory do?

Answer

Cold agglutinins causing red cell agglutination. The giveaway is the MCHC of 48.6 g/dL — far above the ceiling of about 37, and physically impossible.

The mechanism runs straight through the calculations: clumped red cells cross the aperture together and are counted as one very large cell, so the RBC count falls and the MCV rises. Because Hct = (RBC × MCV)/10 and the count fell further than the volume rose, the hematocrit is falsely low — and since MCHC = (Hgb/Hct) × 100, the MCHC is driven absurdly high. The hemoglobin itself is measured on lysed cells and stays accurate.

The fix is to warm the sample to 37 °C and re-run it, which disperses the agglutinates. The analyzer should also have raised an “RBC agglutination” flag. Clinically, follow up with a cold agglutinin titre and a direct antiglobulin test.

Q: A patient with severe iron deficiency and marked microcytosis has an automated platelet count of 610,000/µL, but the smear shows only a moderate number of platelets. Explain the discrepancy and how the laboratory would resolve it.

Answer

Microcytes are being counted as platelets. Impedance counting assigns identity by size, and microcytes sit alongside schistocytes and white cell fragments on the list of things mistaken for platelets. In severe iron deficiency the red cells become small enough to fall into the platelet size window, falsely elevating the count.

Resolution is to count by a method that does not depend on size: the fluorescent (PLT-F) channel, which stains platelet rough endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria with oxazine and identifies platelets by their contents. It correlates well with CD41/CD61 flow cytometry and is specifically useful at the extremes of the count.

The clinical stake is real: a falsely high platelet count in an iron-deficient patient can prompt an unnecessary workup for thrombocytosis, while a falsely low one can trigger an unnecessary transfusion.

Q: A blood sample is drawn into a lavender-top tube, set down without inversion, and sent to the laboratory. All three cell lines come back low. What has happened, and why is this dangerous rather than merely inconvenient?

Answer

Partial clotting from inadequate mixing. EDTA is sprayed on the inside surfaces of the tube; blood that runs straight to the bottom never contacts the full dose of anticoagulant. The phlebotomist's several gentle inversions are what prevent this.

The clot then sequesters platelets, and some white and red cells with them. Those cells are no longer in the liquid being analysed, so every count comes back falsely low.

The danger is that the result is plausible: a pancytopenia in a real patient invites a marrow biopsy, a hematology referral, or a transfusion — for an artefact. “No clots or clumps” is an explicit specimen acceptance criterion, and the correct response is to reject and redraw.

LO 76Source: Benign White Blood Cell Disorders

Section 26 · Benign white cell disorders

Normal Leukocytes, the Absolute Neutrophil Count, and Neutropenia

Five cells, three thresholds, and one calculation that a percentage will always mislead you about.

Abbreviations used in this section WBC white blood cell, also called a leukocyte · ANC absolute neutrophil count — neutrophils per microlitre, an absolute number rather than a percentage · Ig immunoglobulin (antibody); the classes are IgG, IgM, IgA, IgD, IgE · ROS reactive oxygen species · CD4 the helper T cell surface marker · Granzyme B / perforin the cytotoxic mediators released by killer lymphocytes · Duffy null a common phenotype giving a constitutionally lower neutrophil count without increased infection risk · CSF colony stimulating factor — a growth factor given to raise the neutrophil count · G-CSF granulocyte colony stimulating factor · Febrile neutropenia fever in a neutropenic patient, treated as an emergency · µL microlitre
🔑 The organising split for this whole group of sections

Benign white cell abnormalities are either quantitative — too many cells or too few — or qualitative, where the count is normal and the cells do not work. Sections 23 and 24 are the quantitative half; Section 28 is the qualitative half.

The components of normal immune function map directly onto the diseases: cell production (marrow), cell maturation (thymus, lymph nodes, spleen), surveillance (lymphoid aggregates near mucous membranes), and enzymes and mediators (immunoglobulins, lysosomes, perforin and granzyme B, reactive oxygen species, complement, cytokines, migration into tissue). Lose the immunoglobulins and you get Bruton agammaglobulinemia; lose the reactive oxygen species and you get chronic granulomatous disease; lose the thymus and you get DiGeorge.

The five circulating white cells ★ HY

Total white cell count is normally 4.3–10.8 × 10⁹/L.

CellPercentage of white cellsPrimary targetRecognising it on a smear
Neutrophils45–74% — bands 0–4% of total granulocytesCombat bacteriaA nucleus of 3 or 4 lobes — which is where “polymorphonuclear” comes from. Granules stain a neutral pale lilac
Lymphocytes16–45%Combat viruses, bacteria, fungiSpherical nucleus, thin rim of cytoplasm. About the same size as a red cell
Monocytes / macrophages4–10%Target bacteria and debrisThe largest of the five, full of vacuoles. Becomes a macrophage once it leaves the circulation — the garbage collector
Eosinophils0–7%Target helminths and parasitesNamed for taking up eosin; bright orange-pink granules. Contain histamine — hence antihistamines for allergy
Basophils0–2%Target parasites; allergyNamed for taking up the basic dye; dark granules that overlie the nucleus
🧠 What to memorise here, and what not to

The instruction from the lecture is unusually direct: there is no reason to memorise these percentages. What matters is the shape — neutrophils and lymphocytes are by far the most common, monocytes are third, and eosinophils and basophils together are only about 1–3%. It is entirely normal to scan a smear and see no basophil at all.

Two caveats that carry more weight than the numbers. First, the classic “one cell, one job” assignment above is a simplification — there is substantial overlap and cooperation. Helper T cells (CD4) are the conductor of the orchestra: they activate macrophages and drive antibody class switching in B cells. Lose them and every other cell is present but the response is inefficient — which is exactly what happens in HIV (Sections 18–19), and why advanced HIV eventually produces the same opportunistic infections as a congenital T-cell defect.

Second, infection does not always raise the count. In newborns, and in certain viral infections, the white cell count can be suppressed instead.

The three ANC thresholds ★ HY

⚠️ Memorise these three numbers
Absolute neutrophil countConsequence
< 1,000/µLSharply increased risk of infection
< 500/µLControl of endogenous (skin, gut) flora is impaired — the patient's own commensals become the threat. This is also the definition of absolute neutropenia
< 200/µLNo inflammatory process in response to immune challenge — there are not enough cells left to mount a response at all

ANC = white cell count × % neutrophils. It is an absolute number, not a percentage — a normal-looking neutrophil percentage in a patient with a very low total white count can still be a dangerous ANC.

🪝 Why fever in a neutropenic patient is treated before a source is found

The second threshold is the one clinicians quote; the third is the one that changes bedside behaviour. The classic signs of infection are the inflammatory response, and that response is made of neutrophils.

Pus is dead neutrophils. Consolidation on a chest film is largely neutrophilic exudate. Erythema, swelling and induration around a wound or line depend on neutrophil recruitment. With too few cells to produce any of it, a serious infection can be present with almost no localising signs — fever may be the only sign.

Hence febrile neutropenia is an emergency, treated with empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics before any source declares itself. The progression the lecture draws is fever and chills → sepsis → multisystem organ failure (Section 18).

Neutropenia — three mechanisms, and one benign variant

🏭

Ineffective production

  • Drugs — the usual cause in adults.
  • Infections — the usual cause in children.
  • Aplastic anemia.
  • Marrow replacement or transplantation.

That adults → drugs, children → infections split is stated explicitly and changes what you ask about first in the history.

💥

Accelerated destruction — and pooling

  • Immune mediated destruction.
  • Splenic sequestration — the hypersplenism mechanism from Section 11, seen here in the white cell line.
  • Excessive peripheral pooling — the cells exist but are marginated along vessel walls rather than circulating, so the measured count understates them.
🧬 Duffy null — a normal count that was called a disease for decades

Duffy is a blood group antigen, and it is the receptor Plasmodium vivax uses to enter red cells. Duffy-null individuals are therefore resistant to P. vivax malaria, which is why the phenotype became common in populations of African ancestry — the same selection story as sickle trait, G6PD deficiency and thalassemia in Section 24.

Separately, and for reasons still being worked out, Duffy-null individuals run a constitutionally lower neutrophil count — with a perfectly functional immune system and no increased infection risk. For a long time these people were labelled abnormal. Applying standard reference ranges to them has historically caused unnecessary workups, and exclusion from clinical trials and from full chemotherapy dosing.

The wider lesson the lecture draws: every time the immune system is better understood, so is the question of what the appropriate reference range is for a given patient.

🩺 Two treatment points that are easy to get backwards

Granulocyte colony stimulating factor (G-CSF) is the “colony stimulating factor” in the therapy list — it instructs the marrow to make more neutrophils, and is used both to help a patient engraft after transplant and to lift a severely neutropenic count. Note the parallel with erythropoiesis-stimulating agents in Section 17: same idea, different lineage.

Bacteriostatic antibiotics need a working immune system. A bactericidal drug kills the organism outright; a bacteriostatic one only stops it multiplying and relies on the patient to clear what is already there. In a neutropenic or immunodeficient patient that second half never happens — which is why an apparently appropriate antibiotic can seem not to work.

Q: A patient has a white cell count of 1.8 × 10⁹/L with 20% neutrophils. Calculate the absolute neutrophil count and state the clinical implication.

Answer

ANC = 1,800 × 0.20 = 360/µL.

That is below 500/µL, so control of endogenous skin and gut flora is impaired — the patient's own commensal organisms become pathogens. It is above 200, so some inflammatory response remains possible.

The teaching point is that percentage alone is misleading. Twenty percent sounds unremarkable; against a white count of 1.8 it is profound neutropenia. Always compute the absolute number.

Q: Why does an ANC below 200/µL make infection harder to detect as well as more likely?

Answer

Because below 200/µL there is no inflammatory process in response to immune challenge — and the classic signs of infection are the inflammatory response.

Pus is dead neutrophils. Consolidation on a chest radiograph is largely neutrophilic exudate. Erythema, swelling and induration around a wound or line site depend on neutrophil recruitment. With too few neutrophils to produce any of it, a serious infection can be present with almost no localising signs.

This is why fever alone is treated as an emergency in the neutropenic patient, with antimicrobial therapy and colony stimulating factors, rather than waiting for a source to declare itself: fever and chills → sepsis → multisystem organ failure.

Q: A healthy 24-year-old of West African ancestry is repeatedly found to have an ANC of 1,300/µL. He has never had an unusual infection. Two previous workups were negative. What is the likely explanation, and what has been the historical harm?

Answer

The Duffy-null phenotype, which is common in people of African ancestry and produces a constitutionally lower neutrophil count with no increased infection risk. The negative infection history across years is the strongest evidence — this is his normal, not a disease.

The historical harm has been threefold: unnecessary investigation (repeat counts, marrow biopsies), exclusion from clinical trials whose entry criteria used a single population reference range, and under-dosing of chemotherapy in patients judged neutropenic when they were not.

The same antigen is the receptor Plasmodium vivax uses to enter red cells, so the Duffy-null phenotype also confers resistance to P. vivax malaria — the reason it became common in the first place.

LO 66Source: Benign White Blood Cell Disorders

Section 27 · Benign white cell disorders

Leukocytosis, Left Shift, and Reactive versus Malignant

The discrimination that decides whether a patient gets antibiotics or a bone marrow biopsy. Six criteria on the smear, six clinical considerations, and one shape you can read in seconds.

Abbreviations used in this section CML chronic myelogenous leukemia · Left shift immature granulocyte precursors circulating in the blood · Auer rod a needle-shaped cytoplasmic inclusion in a myeloblast — a marker of malignancy · Döhle body a pale blue cytoplasmic inclusion in a reactive neutrophil · Toxic granulation coarse dark granules in a reactive neutrophil · nRBC nucleated red blood cell · Dacryocyte tear-drop red cell · Leukoerythroblastic immature white cells plus nucleated red cells plus tear-drop cells together · N:C ratio nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio — how much of the cell is nucleus · Clonality whether the cells all descend from a single clone · B symptoms fever, night sweats and weight loss · Scattergram the analyzer's plot of forward scatter (size) against side scatter (complexity)

Which line is up, and what that suggests

FindingCauses
Neutrophilia(Pyogenic) infections, acute inflammation, various “stresses” — for example tissue necrosis
Lymphocytosis(Viral) infections, pertussis, chronic inflammation
MonocytosisChronic infection and inflammation, recovery from neutropenia
EosinophiliaHypersensitivity, parasites, fungus, malignancy, drug reactions
Basophilia(Viral) infections, drugs, hypersensitivity, (chronic) inflammation, chronic myelogenous leukemia
🪝 Five entries worth flagging individually
  • Neutrophilia does not require an organism. New-onset diabetes presenting in ketoacidosis produces a high white count with a neutrophilia purely as a stress response. Inflammation, not infection.
  • Pertussis is listed under lymphocytosis — a bacterial infection producing a lymphocytic response, the opposite of the usual pattern, and often a striking one.
  • Monocytes arrive late. Neutrophils and lymphocytes mobilise first; monocytes follow and often peak after an infection has been cleared, removing debris. That is why monocytosis reads as chronic or recovering.
  • Eosinophils gather at the edge of a malignancy — for example within an involved node in Hodgkin lymphoma. The immune system recognising that something is wrong.
  • Basophilia is otherwise uncommon, so persistent unexplained basophilia is one of the few CBC findings that should make you think of a myeloproliferative neoplasm directly. CML looks very reactive, but it is driven by the BCR-ABL fusion oncogene — and for reasons that are not obvious it produces a lot of basophils.

The granulocyte maturation series, in order ★ HY

  1. Myeloblast. The most immature form. May contain an Auer rod — a needle-like cytoplasmic inclusion, which is a marker of malignancy, not of reactive change.
  2. Promyelocyte. Carries coarse primary granules.
  3. Myelocyte. Myelo- is simply Greek for marrow, so a myelocyte is literally “the marrow cell”.
  4. Metamyelocyte. Recognised by the characteristic notch in its nucleus.
  5. Band. The last immature form; normally 0–4% of total granulocytes. Bands are “the reticulocytes of the white cell line” — a normal immature form that legitimately circulates, especially during infection.
  6. Segmented neutrophil. The mature circulating cell.

Left shift means the blood contains more of the earlier forms than it should — a marrow releasing cells before they are finished because demand is high. Metamyelocytes and anything earlier belong in the marrow only; seeing them in blood is the definition.

⚠️ A nucleolus is not by itself abnormal

A rule students reliably over-apply. The nucleolus is the site of active transcription and translation, so any reactive cell working hard will have one. What is abnormal is many nucleoli, or very large ones — that indicates uncontrolled proliferation.

Auer rods carry no such ambiguity. Granules arranged into rods mean a malignant cell, and specifically a myeloid leukemia.

The leukemoid reaction

🔑 Definition, and the whole clinical problem in one line

Severe leukocytosis with immature cells in the peripheral blood, which may mimic a neoplastic proliferation. That mimicry is the clinical problem.

On the smear you see: Döhle bodies, toxic granules and vacuolisation — the three reactive changes, all signs of a neutrophil working hard rather than a malignant one; immature white cells, myelocytes and metamyelocytes; and nucleated red cells and tear-drop erythrocytes.

The differential named is myelofibrosis and a space-occupying lesion such as a tumour — both push immature cells out of a marrow under mechanical stress.

🪝 “Leukoerythroblastic” — the word that ties this together

Immature white cells plus nucleated red cells plus tear-drop cells in the same smear is a leukoerythroblastic picture, and it means the marrow architecture is disturbed — either scarred (myelofibrosis) or displaced by something growing in it (a space-occupying lesion).

Notice that this is the same tear-drop cell that appears in the Section 24 morphology atlas pointing at myelofibrosis, and the same nucleated red cell that falsely raises the automated white count in Section 25. One finding, three places it matters.

Reactive versus malignant — the six morphological criteria ★ HY

CriterionFavours reactiveFavours malignant
Nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratioDecreased — more cytoplasmIncreased — the nucleus dominates
Cytoplasm“Skirt” around surrounding red cells — abundant, moulding around neighboursScant
Population uniformityVariety of appearances — a polyclonal response looks heterogeneousMonoclonal appearance — every cell looks like the same cell
ChromatinCoarse, clumped, denseOpen, powdery, with nuclear clefts and folds
NucleoliOccasional, usually smallProminent, can be large
Other cell lines (red cells, platelets)Close to normalDecreased — suggesting marrow impact
🪝 Memory hook — a reactive cell is busy, a malignant cell is young

A reactive lymphocyte is a mature cell responding to something: it has grown abundant cytoplasm (hence the low N:C ratio and the “skirt” moulding around neighbouring red cells), its chromatin is condensed because it is differentiated, and its neighbours all look different because many different clones responded.

A malignant cell is arrested at an immature stage: scant cytoplasm, open powdery chromatin (actively transcribing), prominent nucleoli (ribosome production for rapid division), and every cell looks identical because they descend from one clone.

The sixth criterion is the one that needs no microscope: cytopenias in other cell lines. A reactive marrow keeps making red cells and platelets. A marrow being crowded out by a clone cannot.

The six clinical considerations

  1. Cell morphology — the six criteria above.
  2. Uniformity of the cell population (clonality).
  3. Excess blasts, out of proportion to the left shift.
  4. Cytopenias in other cell lines are concerning for a neoplastic process.
  5. Duration of the leukocytosis — acute versus chronic.
  6. Clinical background — sick contacts, microbiology studies, and B symptoms: fever, night sweats, weight loss.
🔑 The blast pyramid — the most useful single discriminator ★ HY

A reactive left shift keeps the normal proportions. Going from immature to mature you should see a few blasts, more promyelocytes, more myelocytes, and progressively more as you approach the mature end — a pyramid standing on its point.

If the pyramid is the other way up — relatively few mature cells and a lot of immature forms and blasts — that is the concerning pattern. In the lecture's own phrasing: if you're seeing more blasts than anything else, it's probably something like leukemia.

Two supporting points. A few blasts are tolerable in a very young patient, whose marrow is simply not tight about what it releases. And duration settles most cases: reactive morphology resolves as the infection clears, whereas a leukemia persists after the patient gets better.

🩺 When in doubt, send flow cytometry

Explicit advice, and it resolves the “I'm not sure” case: have a low threshold to send flow cytometry. It identifies a clonal population directly, which is the one thing morphology can only hint at. The reasoning given — better to get a flow cytometry that tells you it's reactive than to maybe miss something. The cost of an unnecessary flow is money; the cost of a missed leukemia is not comparable.

The underlying principle behind the whole table: any time in hematology you are seeing a clonal phenomenon, that is not good. Clonal means one cell proliferated and everything descends from it — which is why “all the cells look similar and abnormal” is the finding that matters, not abnormality on its own.

The analyzer contributes here too: because flow cytometry plots cells by forward scatter against side scatter, a population that does not belong shows up as a cluster in the wrong place — which is what generates the “abnormal scattergram” and “blasts?” flags described in Section 23.

Q: A patient has a white cell count of 62,000/µL with myelocytes and metamyelocytes in the blood, Döhle bodies, toxic granulation and vacuolisation. Nucleated red cells and tear-drop erythrocytes are present. Is this reactive or malignant, and what is the differential?

Answer

This is a leukemoid reaction — severe leukocytosis with immature cells in the peripheral blood that may mimic a neoplastic proliferation.

The features favouring reactive are the Döhle bodies, toxic granules and vacuolisation: these are the changes of a neutrophil responding hard to a stimulus, and they do not belong to a malignant clone. The immature cells present are myelocytes and metamyelocytes rather than an excess of blasts — the pyramid is the right way up.

The differential is myelofibrosis and a space-occupying lesion such as a tumour — both consistent with the nucleated red cells and tear-drop erythrocytes, which together make a leukoerythroblastic picture and indicate disturbed marrow architecture.

If persistent basophilia were also present, or the blast proportion were out of keeping with the left shift, the answer would shift toward chronic myelogenous leukemia — confirmed by BCR-ABL testing rather than by morphology.

Q: A smear shows a lymphocytosis. The cells have abundant cytoplasm that moulds around adjacent red cells, coarse clumped chromatin, occasional small nucleoli, and a variety of appearances. Hemoglobin and platelets are normal. Reactive or malignant?

Answer

Reactive. Five of the six criteria point that way:

  • Abundant cytoplasm moulding around red cells — the classic “skirt”, and a decreased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio.
  • Coarse, clumped, dense chromatin — a differentiated cell.
  • Occasional, small nucleoli.
  • A variety of appearances — a polyclonal response, not a monoclonal one.
  • Other cell lines close to normal — no marrow crowding.

The picture fits a viral infection. Confirm clinically with the duration (acute rather than chronic), sick contacts and microbiology, and the absence of B symptoms. If any doubt remains, flow cytometry settles clonality directly.

Q: Why is “the cells look abnormal” a weaker finding than “the cells all look the same”?

Answer

Because reactive cells are supposed to look abnormal. A lymphocyte responding to a virus enlarges, grows cytoplasm and may develop a nucleolus — all of which is a healthy cell doing its job. Abnormality on its own is compatible with a vigorous immune response.

Uniformity is the finding that matters. A polyclonal reaction recruits many different clones, so the cells look heterogeneous. A monoclonal population means one cell proliferated and everything present descends from it — and clonality in hematology is the thing that is never benign.

That is why flow cytometry is the resolving test: it demonstrates clonality directly, rather than inferring it from appearance.

LO 4Source: Benign White Blood Cell Disorders

Section 28 · Benign white cell disorders

Primary Immunodeficiencies — Where the Block Sits

The qualitative half. Normal counts, cells that do not work — and a maturation tree where the height of the block predicts the severity, the organisms, and the treatment.

Abbreviations used in this section PID primary immunodeficiency · CGD chronic granulomatous disease · NADPH nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate — the electron donor for the respiratory burst · ROS reactive oxygen species · NBT nitroblue tetrazolium — the classic CGD screening test · IFN-γ interferon gamma · SCID severe combined immunodeficiency · ADA adenosine deaminase · BTK Bruton tyrosine kinase · TREC T-cell receptor excision circles — what the newborn SCID screen measures · ALC absolute lymphocyte count · CVID common variable immunodeficiency · CD19 / CD20 B lymphocyte surface markers · CMV / RSV cytomegalovirus / respiratory syncytial virus · IL-2 interleukin-2 · GVHD graft-versus-host disease · Catalase-positive an organism that destroys its own hydrogen peroxide
🔑 When to suspect a primary immunodeficiency

Recurrent, frequent infections · unusual pathogens · long resolution time, plus failure to thrive and a positive family history.

With numbers attached, because “recurrent” is meaningless in a toddler otherwise:

  • 8 or more ear infections in a year; serious sinus infections; frequent pneumonias.
  • Recurrent abscesses; persistent thrush — yeast is everywhere and is normally controlled without causing disease.
  • Deep-seated infections needing unusually strong antibiotics.
  • Failure to thrive — a body permanently fighting infection struggles to grow.
  • Family history, since most of these are inherited.

Any one of these is grounds to refer to an immunologist.

Which arm fails, and how often ★ HY

CategoryShare of primary immunodeficienciesExamples named in this lecture
Antibody deficiencies65%Bruton agammaglobulinemia; common variable immunodeficiency, hyper-IgM syndrome, selective IgA deficiency
Combined cellular and antibody15%Severe combined immunodeficiency
Phagocyte disorders10%Chronic granulomatous disease; Kostmann syndrome (hereditary neutropenia); myeloperoxidase deficiency
Cellular deficiencies5%DiGeorge syndrome
Complement deficiencies5%The smallest group

Antibody deficiencies are nearly two thirds of the total — worth knowing on its own, and it explains why immunoglobulin replacement is such a common therapy.

🪝 Read the maturation tree from the top down — the higher the block, the worse the disease
  1. Block at the lymphoid stem cell, before the B and T branches separate → SCID (adenosine deaminase deficiency). Both arms lost.
  2. Block on the T branch, just after pro-T → SCID (defective interleukin-2 receptor / common gamma chain) — the most common form.
  3. Block on the B branch, at pre-B → Bruton agammaglobulinemia.
  4. Block at the immature T cell → DiGeorge syndrome — the thymus is missing, so T cells cannot mature.
  5. Blocks further down the B branch → the partial antibody defects: common variable immunodeficiency, hyper-IgM syndrome, selective IgA deficiency.

A block above the branch point takes out everything; a block at the very bottom takes out a single immunoglobulin class.

Chronic granulomatous disease — the phagocyte that cannot make bleach

🧠 The respiratory burst, and where CGD blocks it
  1. O₂ → superoxide (O₂⁻), catalysed by NADPH oxidase. This is the step that fails in CGD.
  2. Superoxide → hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), via superoxide dismutase.
  3. H₂O₂ → hypochlorous acid (HOCl), via myeloperoxidase — and hypochlorous acid is the active ingredient in bleach. The neutrophil is manufacturing bleach inside a vacuole.

Because the block in CGD is at the first step, nothing downstream can be made — which is exactly why myeloperoxidase deficiency, blocking only the last step, is a far milder disease.

The genetics: mutations in the NADPH oxidase gene, cytochrome b558. 70% X-linked recessive, 30% autosomal recessive; 86% of patients are male. Incidence 1 in 200,000.

🪝 The catalase logic — why only some organisms cause trouble ★ HY

The central sentence: cells can ingest organisms, but catalase-producing organisms are not killed, because reactive oxygen species cannot be generated.

The reason is elegant. A phagocyte with no NADPH oxidase makes no hydrogen peroxide of its own — but many bacteria make hydrogen peroxide as a metabolic by-product, and the phagocyte can simply borrow theirs. Catalase-positive organisms destroy their own hydrogen peroxide, leaving the defective phagocyte nothing to work with, so they survive inside it.

Worked through with E. coli: the neutrophil ingests it perfectly well (phagocytosis is intact), can make little or no hydrogen peroxide itself, and the organism's catalase converts what trace exists back to water and oxygen. The bacterium sits there alive inside the phagocyte. The corollary makes the rule predictive: catalase-negative organisms are still killed, because they supply the peroxide themselves and cannot quench it.

As the lecture puts it: it's kind of like a standoff, and that's what's going to lead to a granuloma. The offenders to name are S. aureus, Aspergillus, Serratia, Nocardia, Burkholderia.

🩺 What a granuloma is actually made of — and why you give steroids to an immunodeficient patient

Layered and organised: a necrotic centre containing dead cells and still-living pathogen; a surrounding barrier of monocytes and macrophages, including multinucleated giant cells; and T and B cells outside that, the T cells signalling to hold the line.

The framing is a siege: as long as the immune system holds, the granuloma persists and the organisms stay contained — but they are still alive, and if they overwhelm the barrier they break out. That is exactly what reactivation of tuberculosis is.

Which explains the counterintuitive treatment. Granulomas that keep growing can compress organs — the example given is intestinal obstruction — so steroids are given to shrink them, accepting some immunosuppression because here the inflammation itself is doing the mechanical damage.

Diagnosis is by the nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) test — normal neutrophils reduce a yellow dye to a blue-black precipitate; CGD neutrophils cannot and stay yellow — or the neutrophil oxidative index, the modern quantitative flow cytometry version. Clinical features: lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, anemia of chronic disease (Section 6), and granulomas in lung, skin, gastrointestinal tract and lymph nodes. Management: prophylactic antibiotics and exposure prevention, recombinant interferon gamma — which reduces the infection rate by up to 70% — and steroids for obstruction.

The four named diseases side by side ★ HY

Chronic granulomatous diseaseBruton agammaglobulinemiaDiGeorge syndromeSCID
Arm affectedPhagocyte (10% of PIDs)B cell / antibody (65%)T cell / cellular (5%)Combined (15%)
DefectNADPH oxidase, cytochrome b558 → no reactive oxygen speciesBTK gene → block at the pre-B cell22q11 deletion → 3rd/4th branchial pouch, thymic aplasiaCommon gamma chain (X-linked) or ADA (autosomal recessive)
Inheritance70% X-linked, 30% autosomal recessive; 86% maleX-linked — presents in boys90% de novo; 10% autosomal dominantX-linked (most common) or autosomal recessive
Incidence1 in 200,000——1 in 100,000
OnsetChildhoodAfter a few months — maternal antibody protects firstBirth — cardiac defect and hypocalcemia often firstFirst months of life
Characteristic infectionsCatalase-positive organisms; granulomasPyogenic bacteria — Haemophilus, Streptococcus, Staphylococcus; also gastroenteritis and chronic intestinal inflammationViral and fungal — the T-cell patternViral, bacterial and fungal — Pneumocystis, candida, CMV, RSV, rubella
Key testNitroblue tetrazolium / neutrophil oxidative indexNo CD19/CD20 B cells; all immunoglobulins low; absent tonsils22q11 deletion; low T cells; low calciumNewborn TREC screen; absolute lymphocyte count < 2,000/µL
TreatmentProphylactic antibiotics; interferon gamma (↓ infection up to 70%); steroids for obstructionMonthly IgG infusions; stem cell transplant may cureThymus or stem cell transplant; calcium and vitamin D; irradiated blood productsAllogeneic stem cell transplant — earlier is better; antimicrobials, immunoglobulins
🔑 CATCH-22 — the mnemonic that is also the chromosome
LetterFeatureDetail
CCardiac abnormalityConotruncal defects
AAbnormal faciesLong, narrow face; prominent nasal bridge with a bulbous tip; small mouth; thin eye openings; low-set or malformed ears; micrognathia
TThymic aplasiaThe immunodeficiency — no thymus, so T cells cannot mature
CCleft palateWith velopharyngeal incompetence
HHypocalcemiaFrom absent parathyroid glands
22Chromosome 22q11 deletion90% de novo

One embryological event explains all five features: a migration defect of neural crest-derived tissues affecting the third and fourth branchial pouches. Those pouches form the thymus (hence T-cell deficiency) and the parathyroids (hence hypocalcemia), and neural crest cells also populate the conotruncal heart and the facial structures. Not five unrelated problems — one developmental failure with five consequences.

⚠️ Irradiated blood products — the transfusion rule to memorise

Donor blood contains viable donor T lymphocytes. In a normal recipient these are recognised and destroyed. A patient with thymic aplasia cannot do that, so the donor T cells engraft and attack the recipient — transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease, which is almost uniformly fatal. Irradiation inactivates the donor lymphocytes so they cannot proliferate.

The same rule applies to SCID and other severe T-cell deficiencies, and it is exactly why congenital T-cell immunodeficiency appears as an absolute indication for irradiated components in Section 12 and why TA-GVHD is worked through in Section 14.

The companion rule: live vaccines are contraindicated in severe T-cell deficiency. “Vaccination” in these patients means inactivated vaccines — plus vaccinating household contacts.

🧠 Why an immunodeficiency causes lymphoma and autoimmunity

The DiGeorge complications list — rheumatoid arthritis, thyroiditis, B-cell neoplasms — looks unrelated to the diagnosis until you hear the mechanism.

When one arm of the immune system fails, the others try to compensate, and that compensation can run out of control. In DiGeorge the T cells are missing, so the body drives B-cell production harder. But T cells are also what regulate and restrain exuberant B-cell proliferation — so the brake has been removed at the same moment the accelerator was pressed.

The result is uncontrolled B-cell proliferation (hence B-cell neoplasms) and loss of regulatory control generally (hence thyroiditis and rheumatoid arthritis). Immunodeficient patients developing lymphoma and autoimmunity is not a paradox; it is the same lesion seen from two sides.

🔑 Two mechanisms worth knowing in detail

Bruton agammaglobulinemia — the maternal antibody window. Patients are generally asymptomatic for the first few months because maternal IgG crosses the placenta and protects them until it wanes around 6 months (the protected window is about the first 2–3 months). That timing is the signature of an antibody defect. Diagnosis: immunoglobulins all low, flow cytometry shows no CD19/CD20 B cells and no plasma cells, marrow shows absent precursor B cells, and BTK sequencing confirms. Absent tonsils and atrophic lymph nodes are a bedside sign, because lymphoid tissue is mostly B cells. Treatment is monthly IgG infusions; marrow transplant is currently the only cure, with gene therapy plausible — the mutation's location is known, and the approach is already in use for thalassemia and sickle cell disease (Section 17).

SCID — and why ADA deficiency is different. The X-linked form mutates the common gamma chain, a protein shared by receptors for many interleukins, so T and B cell development and differentiation fail. The autosomal recessive form is adenosine deaminase deficiency: accumulated purines inhibit ribonucleotide reductase, deoxyribonucleotide synthesis fails, and toxic phosphorylated products drive precursor apoptosis. Lymphocytes are hit first because they are among the most rapidly dividing cells in the body.

The consequence matters clinically: a stem cell transplant replaces blood-forming cells and nothing else. In ADA deficiency the enzyme defect is corrected in the blood but not in other organs — and because neurons are also affected by the toxic metabolites, neurological and developmental problems can persist despite a technically successful transplant. X-linked SCID is a purely haematopoietic defect, so transplant is genuinely curative; ADA deficiency is a systemic metabolic disease that happens to present as an immunodeficiency, which is the argument for enzyme replacement or gene therapy.

🩺 How the newborn screen works — and that it is only a screen

A maturing T cell rearranges its VDJ gene segments, and in cutting out the intervening DNA it produces small circular by-products — T-cell receptor excision circles (TRECs). Their presence is direct evidence that new T cells are being made; a very low level means they are not.

A positive screen requires confirmation: a CBC showing a very low lymphocyte count — an absolute lymphocyte count below 2,000/µL warrants evaluation — then flow cytometry to establish which populations are missing.

The stakes justify the programme. Untreated, patients usually die within 1 year; outcome is determined by allogeneic stem cell transplantation, and survival is better the earlier it is performed. The screen exists to get the transplant done before the first serious infection. Meanwhile these children need a near-sterile environment — the “bubble boy” — because they acquire organisms otherwise seen only in advanced HIV, such as Pneumocystis jirovecii, which classically appears only when CD4 is undetectable (Section 20).

The diagnostic toolkit, by arm

Arm suspectedFirst-line testsConfirmatory
Neutrophil numberCBC with differential; calculate the ANCBone marrow examination
Neutrophil functionNitroblue tetrazolium test, neutrophil oxidative indexGenetic testing of NADPH oxidase components
AntibodySerum immunoglobulin assay — IgG, IgA, IgM (and IgD, IgE)B-cell immunophenotyping: CD19, CD20; marrow precursor B cells; molecular testing (e.g. BTK)
Cellular / combinedAbsolute lymphocyte count — < 2,000/µL warrants evaluation; newborn TREC screenT-cell subsets (CD4, CD8); genetic testing (common gamma chain, ADA); 22q11 deletion testing
ComplementCH50 (classical pathway) and AH50 (alternative pathway) — total haemolytic complement screensIndividual component assays
🪝 Why HIV belongs at the end of this section

HIV is the acquired counterpart to everything above: a CD4 T-cell deficiency that develops over years rather than being present from birth. The chronic phase is explicitly compared to a granuloma — contained, not eradicated — until CD4 falls below a critical level, viraemia rebounds, and that is AIDS.

Read against the maturation tree: HIV depletes CD4 helper T cells, and helper T cells activate macrophages and drive antibody class switching. So losing them degrades the cellular arm directly and the antibody arm indirectly — which is why advanced HIV eventually produces the same opportunistic infections as SCID: Pneumocystis jirovecii, candida, cytomegalovirus.

Same final phenotype, opposite origin: one is a congenital block on the maturation tree, the other is acquired destruction of a mature population. Sections 18 and 19 work the acquired side in full.

Q: A 3-year-old boy has recurrent abscesses with Staphylococcus aureus and Aspergillus, hepatosplenomegaly, and granulomas in the gut. His neutrophil count is normal. What is the defect, what test confirms it, and why are only certain organisms a problem?

Answer

Chronic granulomatous disease — mutations in the NADPH oxidase gene, cytochrome b558, causing failure of phagocytic cells to generate reactive oxygen species. Note the normal neutrophil count: this is a qualitative defect, not a quantitative one. 70% are X-linked recessive and 86% of patients are male, which fits.

Confirmed with the nitroblue tetrazolium test or the neutrophil oxidative index.

Only certain organisms cause trouble because the cells can ingest organisms but catalase-producing organisms are not killed. Catalase-negative bacteria supply their own hydrogen peroxide, which the defective phagocyte borrows; catalase-positive organisms — S. aureus, Aspergillus, Serratia, Nocardia, Burkholderia — destroy it and survive intracellularly. The walled-off survivors become the granulomas.

Management: prophylactic antibiotics and exposure prevention, recombinant interferon gamma (reduces infection rate by up to 70%), and steroids if granulomas cause obstruction.

Q: Two infants present with recurrent infections. Infant A was well for the first 6 months and then developed recurrent otitis media and a perineal abscess. Infant B has had chronic diarrhoea, thrush and Pneumocystis pneumonia since 2 months of age. What does the difference in timing tell you?

Answer
