Infant A has an antibody deficiency — Bruton agammaglobulinemia. Patients are asymptomatic for the first few months because of maternal antibodies: maternal IgG crosses the placenta and protects the infant until it wanes around 6 months. The pyogenic bacterial infections fit an antibody defect. Expect no CD19/CD20 B cells, low levels of all immunoglobulins, and absent tonsils.

Infant B has SCID. Infections start in the first months of life because maternal antibody never covered the T-cell arm, and the organisms named — Pneumocystis jirovecii, candida, chronic diarrhoea — are the T-cell-deficiency pattern. Check the absolute lymphocyte count (below 2,000/µL warrants evaluation); the newborn TREC screen should have flagged it.

Timing is the discriminator: maternal IgG protects the antibody arm, not the cellular arm.

Q: A neonate with a conotruncal cardiac defect, hypocalcemic seizures and an unusual facies is going to theatre and will need transfusion. What is the diagnosis, what single embryological event explains it, and what must be specified about the blood products?

Answer

DiGeorge syndrome — 22q11 deletion, CATCH-22: Cardiac abnormality, Abnormal facies, Thymic aplasia, Cleft palate, Hypocalcemia, chromosome 22.

The single event is a migration defect of neural crest-derived tissues affecting the third and fourth branchial pouches. Those pouches form the thymus and the parathyroid glands, and neural crest cells also populate the conotruncal heart and the facial structures — so one developmental failure produces all of the features.

The blood products must be irradiated, to prevent transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease. With thymic aplasia the recipient cannot reject viable donor T lymphocytes, which would otherwise engraft and attack the host; irradiation inactivates them. Also avoid live vaccines.

Q: A 4-month-old with failure to thrive, chronic diarrhoea and oral thrush has an absolute lymphocyte count of 900/µL. What is the concern, what should have caught this earlier, and what determines the outcome?

Answer

Severe combined immunodeficiency. An absolute lymphocyte count below 2,000/µL should lead to further evaluation, and 900 is well under that. The presentation matches: failure to thrive, chronic diarrhoea and profuse candidiasis, all beginning in the first months of life.

The newborn screen should have caught it — it measures T-cell receptor excision circles, a by-product of normal T-cell receptor rearrangement in the thymus, so an absent TREC count identifies an infant making no new T cells before any symptoms appear.

Outcome is determined by immune reconstitution with allogeneic stem cell transplantation, and survival is better the earlier it is performed — which is the entire point of screening. Untreated, patients usually die within 1 year. Meanwhile: high-dose antibiotics and antivirals, immunoglobulins, parenteral nutrition if needed, no live vaccines, and irradiated blood products if transfused.

LO 50LO 32Source: Coagulation I — Cascade & Bleeding Disorders

Section 29 · Coagulation I · bleeding

The Cascade, PT and aPTT, and the Mixing Study

Two clotting times and one follow-up test carry most of the diagnostic weight. Which test is prolonged tells you which arm is broken; the mixing study then tells you whether something is missing or something is blocking.

Abbreviations used in this section PT prothrombin time — the clotting test for the extrinsic pathway · INR international normalised ratio — a standardised PT so results compare across laboratories · aPTT activated partial thromboplastin time — the clotting test for the intrinsic pathway · TT thrombin time · VWF von Willebrand factor · TF tissue factor, also called factor 3 · tPA tissue plasminogen activator · FDP fibrin degradation products · DIC disseminated intravascular coagulation · GPIb glycoprotein Ib — the platelet receptor for von Willebrand factor · ADAMTS13 the enzyme that trims von Willebrand factor multimers · TEG / ROTEM thromboelastography / thromboelastometry — viscoelastic whole-blood tests · EDTA ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid, the lavender-top anticoagulant
🔑 The four specifications of a working coagulation system

Worth learning as a list, because every disease in Sections 26–31 is a failure of exactly one of them:

  1. Balance protection from bleeding against protection from clotting. Neither extreme is survivable.
  2. Maintain hemostasis and the patency of the circulatory system. Seal holes without blocking the pipe.
  3. Respond at the site of injury quickly and in a localised fashion. Systemic activation is disseminated intravascular coagulation (Section 31).
  4. Return to the usual state once healing is complete. This is fibrinolysis — the clot has to be dismantled again.

And the three ingredients, which is why the count is three rather than one: platelets (right number and right function), a fibrin clot (correctly produced and correctly broken down), and blood vessels with healthy endothelium. A patient can bleed with a perfect coagulation panel.

Primary and secondary hemostasis — the seam that everything sorts along ★ HY

🩹

Primary hemostasis — the platelet plug

  • Vessel injury exposes subendothelial collagen.
  • Von Willebrand factor binds that collagen and unfurls.
  • The platelet receptor glycoprotein Ib/IX/V binds the tethered von Willebrand factor — the adhesion step.
  • Platelets then activate, release their granules, and aggregate to one another.

Hold on to the chain collagen → VWF → GPIb → platelet: two separate diseases break it at two different links (Section 30).

🕸️

Secondary hemostasis — the fibrin mesh

  • The serial protease cascade converts fibrinogen to fibrin, reinforcing the fragile plug.
  • Factor 13 then cross-links the fibrin to stabilise it.
  • Failure here bleeds into spaces — joints and muscles.

The two stages happen essentially at once, but bleeding disorders sort cleanly along the seam — which is what makes the bedside pattern in Section 30 diagnostic.

The procoagulants, the brakes, and the demolition crew

ComponentAlso calledRole in the cascade
Numbered factors 2, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13FII, FV, FVII, FVIII, FIX, FX, FXI, FXII, FXIIIThe serial protease chain. Each activates the next
FibrinogenFactor 1The substrate. Thrombin cleaves it into fibrin, the structural polymer of the clot
Von Willebrand factorVWFPlatelet adhesion, plus it is the carrier protein for factor 8
Tissue factorFactor 3Exposed by injury; the trigger for the extrinsic pathway
Calcium“Factor 4”Required cofactor throughout — which is exactly why the collection tube works the way it does
PhospholipidPlatelet surfaceThe membrane surface the reactions have to assemble on
🧠 Why factors 3, 4 and 6 are missing from the list

The gaps are historical, not an oversight. Factor 3 is tissue factor and nobody calls it factor 3 any more. Factor 4 is calcium — identified early as a required “factor”, then recognised as simply an ion. Factor 6 was retired: what had been numbered separately turned out to be an already-numbered factor in its activated form, so the number was dropped rather than reused.

The practical consequence of calcium being “factor 4”: a hypocalcemic patient has a problem with clotting. Carry that into massive transfusion, where citrated blood chelates the patient's calcium (Section 14), and into DiGeorge syndrome, where hypocalcemia is part of the phenotype (Section 28).

🪝 Memory hook — read the cascade as two arms joining one trunk ★ HY

The left arm starts at a negatively charged surface and runs 12 → 11 → 9 → 8 — the intrinsic pathway, measured by the aPTT. The right arm starts at tissue factor exposure and is just 7 — the extrinsic pathway, measured by the PT. They meet at factor 10 and run down the shared trunk 10 → 5 → 2 (prothrombin → thrombin) → fibrinogen → fibrin — the common pathway, which moves both tests.

The dotted feed-forward arrows are the part people skip: thrombin activates factors 5, 8, 11 and 13. It accelerates its own production, which is what makes the response fast enough to be useful.

On numerals: read Roman and Arabic interchangeably (II = 2, V = 5, VII = 7, VIII = 8, IX = 9, X = 10, XI = 11, XII = 12, XIII = 13). The pairs that actually get mixed up are VII (7) versus VIII (8) — extrinsic versus intrinsic, PT versus aPTT — and XI (11) versus XII (12), where one causes bleeding and one does not.

🔑 Where the coagulation proteins are made — and the one exception that does the most work

The liver makes all of the coagulation factors except von Willebrand factor and factor 8. Von Willebrand factor comes from endothelial cells (stored in Weibel–Palade bodies) and megakaryocytes; factor 8 is largely endothelial in origin and is carried in plasma bound to von Willebrand factor.

Two payoffs. In liver disease everything falls except these two, so factor 8 is characteristically normal or even high — which is one way to separate liver disease from DIC, where factor 8 is consumed along with everything else (Section 31). And it is why the endothelium, not the hepatocyte, is the organ of interest in von Willebrand disease.

The natural anticoagulants — what keeps the clot local

  • Protein C and protein S — together they inactivate factors 5a and 8a. Two of the most important thrombophilias in Section 33 are deficiencies of these.
  • Antithrombin III — neutralises thrombin and factor 10a. This is the protein heparin works through, which is why antithrombin deficiency makes heparin less effective.
  • Plasmin — the enzyme that digests fibrin. Tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) converts plasminogen to plasmin.
  • Intact endothelial surface — expresses heparans, so a healthy vessel lining is actively anticoagulant rather than merely neutral. Heparin therapy is essentially borrowing a mechanism the endothelium already uses.
⚠️ A naming trap that costs marks

Protein C and protein S are anticoagulants. Factor 5 and factor 8 are procoagulants. Because protein C inactivates factor 5, a mutation that makes factor 5 resistant to protein C — factor V Leiden — produces the same net effect as losing protein C: more clotting. That equivalence is stated explicitly in Section 33 and is a favourite question stem.

The mirror image completes the logic: too much antiplasmin, or overexpression of the fibrinolysis inhibitors, causes a clotting problem, because clots are not taken down when they should be.

🧠 Where the name “D-dimer” comes from — and why it means what it means

Fibrin monomers contain regions labelled D and E. When factor 13 cross-links fibrin it locks two adjacent D regions together. Plasmin then cuts the mesh up, but it cannot break that cross-link — so the fragment released carries two D regions: a D-dimer.

Therefore a D-dimer can only exist if fibrin was formed, cross-linked by factor 13, and then broken down. It is a marker of clot turnover, not merely of clotting. It reappears as one of the four laboratory legs of DIC (Section 31) and in the workup of thrombosis (Section 34).

🪝 Why factor 13 is drawn off to the side of the cascade

Because it acts on the fibrin clot after the clot has already formed, changing its configuration so the finished mesh is stronger.

That placement is the clinical picture. Patients with factor 13 deficiency do make a clot — so the PT, aPTT and platelet count are all normal, because every one of those stops timing at the point the first fibrin appears. The clot is simply not as strong as it should be and falls off sooner than it should. Hence delayed bleeding, and delayed wound healing. It needs a specific factor 13 assay — classically a clot solubility test.

The collection tube — before any of this ★ HY

⚠️ A short-draw blue top is one of the commonest reasons a “coagulopathy” turns out not to exist

Coagulation samples go into sodium citrate tubes — the light blue top. Citrate reversibly chelates calcium, so the laboratory can add calcium back and start the reaction on demand. (Contrast the lavender-top EDTA tube used for the CBC in Section 23, where the calcium binding is not reversed.)

The critical detail: the ratio of whole blood to anticoagulant must be 9:1. An underfilled tube carries proportionally too much citrate, so when calcium is added back there is not enough of it — producing an artificially prolonged clotting time. Such samples are rejected.

Which test covers which pathway ★ HY

TestPathway measuredMost sensitive toProlonged by
PT (prothrombin time)Extrinsic + commonFactor 7Warfarin, vitamin K deficiency, liver disease, factor 7 deficiency
INRStandardised PTSame as PTReported so PT results compare between laboratories; the number warfarin is dosed against
aPTTIntrinsic + commonFactors 8, 9, 11, 12Hemophilia A and B, heparin, lupus anticoagulant, factor 12 deficiency
Both PT and aPTTCommonFactors 2, 5, 10 and fibrinogenLiver disease, DIC, common-pathway factor deficiency
D-dimer, FDPFibrinolysis—Any active clot formation and breakdown — thrombosis, DIC
Platelet count / functionPrimary hemostasis—Thrombocytopenia, platelet function defects — not reflected in PT or aPTT
Thromboelastography (TEG/ROTEM)All phases—Monitors clot initiation, strength and lysis together, in whole blood
🧠 What the analyzer physically does — and why this test cannot see platelets
  1. Spin the citrate tube and take the plasma only. The cells, including every platelet, are discarded with the pellet.
  2. Load the plasma; the instrument adds calcium back, reversing the citrate and restoring clotting capability.
  3. Add the activator — thromboplastin for the PT, partial thromboplastin for the aPTT.
  4. Time until a clot forms, in seconds. A longer time means a factor is missing.

Step 1 is the whole explanation of the blind spot. These are plasma assays. The platelets were removed before the test began, so the PT and aPTT are structurally incapable of detecting a platelet problem — and von Willebrand factor's platelet-tethering role is invisible to them for the same reason. This is not a sensitivity limitation a better reagent could fix.

⚠️ A normal PT and aPTT does not exclude a bleeding disorder

Von Willebrand disease and platelet function disorders do not significantly affect the PT or aPTT. Both are diseases of primary hemostasis, and neither clotting time looks at platelets at all.

A patient with a lifetime of nosebleeds, heavy periods and easy bruising can have a perfectly normal coagulation screen. Ordering a PT and aPTT and stopping there is how von Willebrand disease gets missed for decades. The first-pass bleeding workup is therefore PT, aPTT, fibrinogen, platelet count — plus von Willebrand testing, which has to be requested separately.

The 50% rule, and why a slightly long clotting time may mean nothing ★ HY

Factor levels of roughly 50% are enough for hemostasis. That single number explains three separate things: a clotting time only prolongs once a factor drops well below normal; thresholds vary with the laboratory's reagent; and it is why the mixing study works, since adding an equal volume of normal plasma lifts a deficient patient to about 50%.

Factor levelWhat the clotting time doesWhat it means for the patient
~50%aPTT just begins to prolong (PT at around 55%)Flags as abnormal on the report
30–40%Mildly prolongedProbably fine — no spontaneous bleeding
< 20%aPTT above ~45 secondsHemophilia territory
< 1% (severe)aPTT over 100 secondsSpontaneous bleeding
🩺 Why a marginally abnormal result may be nothing at all

A reference range is built by running healthy volunteers and taking the 95% confidence interval. By construction, about 5% of perfectly healthy people fall outside it. A value a little past the line may simply be a normal person, not a diagnosis — and a negative bleeding history through prior surgery is the strongest single piece of contrary evidence you can get.

The mixing study — missing, or blocked? ★ HY

  1. Mix patient plasma with normal pooled plasma, usually 1:1. This supplies every factor at roughly half the normal concentration.
  2. Repeat the clotting time and read the result against the 50% rule.
  3. It corrects → factor deficiency. The donated factors were enough to restore clotting, so the patient was simply short of something.
  4. It does not correct → inhibitor. Something in the patient's plasma is neutralising the added factors too — an acquired factor 8 antibody, or a lupus anticoagulant.
🪝 “Corrects = missing, stays long = blocked” — and the incubated study that catches a slow inhibitor

Deficiency is a subtraction problem, so adding plasma fixes it. An inhibitor is an opposition problem, so adding plasma just gives the inhibitor more to attack.

The refinement that matters clinically: some inhibitors — classically the acquired factor 8 antibody — are slow-acting. On an immediate 1:1 mix they appear to correct, because the antibody has not had time to neutralise the added factor. The fix is to incubate the mix at 37 °C for 30–60 minutes and re-time it. If the clotting time drifts back out, the antibody has been slowly destroying the donated factor 8.

An immediate mix that corrects does not by itself exclude an inhibitor. If the clinical picture is a new bleeding diathesis, ask for the incubated study.

The same test is the front end of the lupus anticoagulant workup in Section 33 — there, the extra twist is that the clotting time also corrects with added phospholipid, which is what proves the inhibitor is aimed at phospholipid rather than at a factor.

Q: A patient has an isolated prolonged aPTT with a completely normal PT. Which factors could be responsible, and which single one of them will not cause bleeding?

Answer

An isolated prolonged aPTT points at the intrinsic pathway: factors 8, 9, 11 and 12. If a common-pathway factor (2, 5, 10) or fibrinogen were low, the PT would be prolonged too.

The exception is factor 12 deficiency, which prolongs the aPTT but does not cause bleeding. In vivo you do not need factor 12 at all — there is a backup contact system using other contact factors. The in vitro test, however, genuinely depends on factor 12 being present. It is a case where the assay is not the same as the body.

It is the classic distractor when a question gives you a long aPTT in an asymptomatic patient found on pre-operative screening — and it still matters to make the diagnosis, because otherwise every aPTT this patient ever has will be re-investigated.

Ranked by what they mean: factor 8 = hemophilia A (1 in 5,000 males); factor 9 = hemophilia B (1 in 30,000 males); factor 11 = hemophilia C, autosomal, milder; factor 12 = no bleeding.

Q: A blue-top tube arrives half-filled. The aPTT comes back markedly prolonged in a patient with no bleeding history. What is the most likely explanation, and what should happen next?

Answer

A pre-analytic artefact from an underfilled citrate tube. The 9:1 whole-blood to citrate ratio is broken, so there is excess citrate relative to blood. When the laboratory recalcifies the sample, that excess citrate soaks up the added calcium and the clotting time comes out artificially prolonged.

The sample should be rejected and redrawn, properly filled. This is a laboratory-error question, not a hematology question — and it is exactly the kind of thing a coagulation laboratory director puts on a test.

Q: A 68-year-old with new spontaneous bruising has an aPTT of 62 seconds. A 1:1 mix with normal plasma corrects to 34 seconds. The team concludes there is no inhibitor. What have they missed?

Answer

They have missed a slow-acting inhibitor, and they need an incubated mixing study.

Acquired factor 8 antibodies are time- and temperature-dependent. On an immediate mix the antibody has not yet had time to neutralise the donated factor 8, so the clotting time corrects and looks like a simple deficiency. Incubating at 37 °C for 30–60 minutes and re-timing lets the antibody act, and the aPTT drifts back out.

The clinical setting should have prompted this from the start: a new bleeding diathesis in an older patient with no lifetime history is acquired hemophilia A until proven otherwise (Section 31). Confirm with a factor 8 level and a Bethesda titre; treat with a bypassing agent plus immunosuppression to eradicate the antibody.

Q: Both PT and aPTT are prolonged. A 1:1 mix with normal plasma corrects neither. Give two categories of cause.

Answer

Failure to correct means an inhibitor, and involvement of both tests points at the common pathway or at something non-specific:

  1. A specific factor inhibitor against a common-pathway factor — for example an acquired antibody to factor 5.
  2. A non-specific inhibitor, classically a lupus anticoagulant, or an interfering substance such as heparin contamination from a line draw, or a paraprotein.

Remember the paradox carried into Section 33: a lupus anticoagulant prolongs clotting in vitro but increases thrombosis risk in vivo.

LO 32LO 36LO 48LO 68LO 79Source: Coagulation I — Cascade & Bleeding Disorders

Section 30 · Coagulation I · bleeding

Reading a Bleeding Pattern — Hemophilia, von Willebrand, and the Platelet

The single highest-yield idea in the lecture is that where a patient bleeds tells you which half of hemostasis has failed — before a single assay is sent.

Abbreviations used in this section F8 / FVIII factor 8 — deficient in hemophilia A · F9 / FIX factor 9 — deficient in hemophilia B, also called Christmas disease · VWD von Willebrand disease · VWF:Ag von Willebrand factor antigen — how much protein is present · VWF:RCo ristocetin cofactor activity — how well that protein works · HMWM high molecular weight multimers · DDAVP desmopressin — a vasopressin analogue that releases stored von Willebrand factor · GPIb/IX/V the platelet receptor for von Willebrand factor, absent in Bernard–Soulier syndrome · GPIIb/IIIa (CD41/CD61) the fibrinogen receptor, absent in Glanzmann thrombasthenia · Inhibitor an alloantibody against infused factor · Hemarthrosis bleeding into a joint · Menorrhagia heavy menstrual bleeding · Petechiae pinpoint non-blanching skin haemorrhages · Lumi-aggregometry a platelet study reading aggregation by light transmission and secretion by ATP luminescence
🔑 The match game — three bleeding patterns, three disease families ★ HY
Bleeding patternDisease familyWhich half of hemostasis
Mucocutaneous — nosebleeds, gum bleeding, heavy periods, bruisingvon Willebrand disease (and platelet disorders)Primary — the platelet plug
Joint and muscle — hemarthrosis, deep hematomaHemophilia A or B (factor 8 or factor 9)Secondary — the fibrin mesh
Delayed — stops, then restarts hours laterFactor 13 or antiplasmin deficiencyClot stabilisation / fibrinolysis
🪝 Memory hook — surfaces, spaces, and the second act

Platelets patch surfaces, so when platelets fail you bleed from surfaces — skin and mucosa. Fibrin fills spaces, so when fibrin fails you bleed into spaces — joints and muscles. Factor 13 cross-links the finished clot, so when it fails the plug forms normally and then falls apart — bleeding that is delayed, not immediate.

Delayed bleeding after circumcision or a dental extraction with a normal PT, aPTT and platelet count is the classic factor 13 stem, because factor 13 deficiency does not prolong either clotting time.

Bleeding symptomPlatelet defects (primary hemostasis)Coagulation disorders (secondary hemostasis)
General patternMucocutaneous — oral, nasal, gastrointestinal, genitourinaryDeep tissue — joints and muscles
Excessive bleeding after minor cutsYesNot usually
PetechiaeCommonUncommon
Ecchymoses (bruises)Small and superficial (larger with severe thrombocytopenia)Large subcutaneous and soft-tissue hematomas
Hemarthroses, muscle hematomasUncommonCommon in severe deficiency, or with injury in mild/moderate deficiency
Bleeding with surgery or proceduresImmediate; severity tracks the defectMay be immediate or delayed
⚠️ One honest caveat, stated in the lecture itself

“It is never as clear-cut as you only get one type.” These are the predominant patterns, not exclusive ones — and if any of these patients goes to surgery, all of them bleed. The pattern is a pointer for the undifferentiated patient, not a rule.

The lecturer's own expansion is worth keeping: hemophilia → joint bleeding, deep muscle bleeding, and retroperitoneal bleeding — with joint arthropathy as a major cause of morbidity, because repeated bleeds scar a joint and it progressively stops working. That is what prophylaxis exists to prevent. von Willebrand disease → heavy periods, gum bleeding, purpura. Factor 13 → delayed bleeding and delayed wound healing.

The full differential of bleeding — including what is not the coagulation system

Factor problems

secondary hemostasis

Deficiency of, or inhibitors to, factors 8 and 9 (hemophilia A and B) or factors 2, 5, 7, 10, 11.

Fibrinogen problems

the substrate

Afibrinogenemia (none), hypofibrinogenemia (too little), dysfibrinogenemia (present but non-functional — and this one can cause clotting as well as bleeding).

Clot stabilisation

the second act

Factor 13 or antiplasmin deficiency — delayed bleeding with entirely normal screening tests.

Platelet problems

primary hemostasis

Thrombocytopenia (too few) or platelet function defects (enough, but they do not work).

von Willebrand disease

the common one

The most common inherited bleeding disorder, and the one the routine screen misses.

Not the coagulation system at all

normal panel, real bleeding

Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia; Kasabach–Merritt phenomenon, where a vascular tumour consumes platelets inside itself; connective tissue disorders such as Ehlers–Danlos; small vessel vasculitis; paraproteins; skin disease, infection, psychogenic causes; and trauma and surgery — the commonest cause of bleeding overall, and the one a hematology lecture forgets.

Hemophilia A and B — two diseases, one phenotype ★ HY

Hemophilia AHemophilia BHemophilia C
Missing factorFactor 8Factor 9 (Christmas disease)Factor 11
InheritanceX-linked — presents in males, carried by femalesAutosomal — affects both sexes; enriched in Ashkenazi Jewish populations
Incidence1 in 5,000 males1 in 30,000 males — six times rarer—
Coagulation screenProlonged aPTT, normal PT, normal platelet count; mixing study correctsProlonged aPTT
Bleeding patternJoint (hemarthrosis) and muscle bleeding — deep tissue, not mucocutaneousTypically milder, correlates poorly with the factor level; often only after surgery or trauma

Hemophilia C is the reason to say “factors 8, 9, 11 and 12” when listing what prolongs an isolated aPTT — and then to remember that 11 bleeds and 12 does not.

🔑 Severity is defined by the factor level, not by the symptoms
Factor level (% of normal)SeverityWhat it means clinically
< 1%SevereSpontaneous bleeding, including into joints, with no identifiable trauma
1–5%ModerateBleeding with minor trauma
> 5–30%MildBleeding usually only with surgery or significant trauma

Line this up against the 50% rule from Section 29: a level of 30% is below what full hemostasis needs but well above the severe range — which is why mild hemophilia can go undiagnosed until a first operation.

The treatment target is not a normal factor level. Keeping a patient above roughly 20–30% is good, and above 5% already sharply reduces the spontaneous bleeding that drives joint damage. Higher targets, sustained longer, are used around major surgery.

🩺 Why these patients no longer receive plasma — a rule with a history behind it

In the 1980s, patients with hemophilia began developing AIDS with no sexual risk factors, and that observation is one of the ways HIV transmission through blood was established — because they were receiving chronic plasma transfusions as their source of factor 8 and factor 9.

Modern pharmaceutical factor concentrates undergo viral inactivation, giving essentially zero viral transmission risk. So the rule that follows is now firm: patients with hemophilia should not receive plasma or cryoprecipitate, except as an absolute last resort when no concentrate is available. The same reasoning drives the “avoid cryoprecipitate” instruction in von Willebrand disease below, and connects to the infectious-risk discussion in Section 14.

🪝 Emicizumab is a molecular clamp, not a replacement

Inhibitors — alloantibodies against the infused factor — are the single biggest management problem in hemophilia. Once a patient develops one, ordinary replacement is neutralised and stops working. The clue is loss of response to a dose that previously worked; the mixing study fails to correct, and the antibody is quantified with a Bethesda titre.

Factor 8a does not cut anything — it is a cofactor that holds factor 9a and factor 10 next to each other so the reaction can happen. Emicizumab (Hemlibra) is a bispecific antibody with two arms: one grabs factor 9a, the other grabs factor 10. It reproduces the geometry without reproducing the protein, which is exactly what makes it invisible to an anti-factor-8 antibody.

A practical trap: a patient on emicizumab will have an aPTT that looks falsely normal or short, because the drug drives the intrinsic pathway in the tube.

von Willebrand disease — the common one ★ HY

How common

the most common inherited bleeding disorder

~1% of people have asymptomatic von Willebrand factor abnormalities; ~1 in 8,000 have symptomatic disease.

Inheritance

contrast with hemophilia

Most often autosomal dominant — so it affects both sexes, unlike X-linked hemophilia.

Presentation

primary hemostasis

Bruising and mucosal bleeding — epistaxis, menorrhagia, gingival bleeding; also soft-tissue hematomas and surgical bleeding.

The protein's two jobs

why one gene, two failures

(1) Bind platelet GPIb and mediate adhesion to exposed collagen. (2) Act as the carrier for factor 8, prolonging its half-life.

🧠 Why the protein's size is the whole story

Von Willebrand factor is a large multimeric glycoprotein made by endothelial cells (stored in Weibel–Palade bodies) and megakaryocytes. It is made as a propolypeptide; the propeptide is cleaved off and the rest polymerises into high molecular weight multimers.

Hemostatic activity tracks molecular weight. Put physically: von Willebrand factor has to stretch from the collagen at the injury site out into the flowing blood to catch a passing platelet. A short multimer cannot span that distance. So a patient who makes only the small forms has plenty of antigen and still bleeds — which is exactly the type 2 pattern.

The enzyme ADAMTS13 trims the multimers down to size. In Section 32 the failure of that trimming causes thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. Same molecule, opposite disease.

🔑 The two assays that make the diagnosis

Ristocetin cofactor assay (VWF:RCo) — measuring function. Normal fixed platelets are supplied by the laboratory, so the platelets are never the variable; patient plasma supplies the von Willebrand factor; ristocetin artificially induces it to bind GPIb, forcing the adhesion reaction to happen in a tube; agglutination is read as increased light transmission.

Why ristocetin? It was developed as an antibiotic. Patients taking it turned up with bruising and falling platelet counts, and the cause was traced to the fact that ristocetin activates von Willebrand factor, driving it onto platelets and clearing them. Nobody takes it as an antibiotic any more — but the laboratory kept it, precisely because that side effect is a controllable, quantifiable trigger of the GPIb interaction. The drug's failure is the assay's mechanism.

Multimer analysis — measuring size distribution. A Western blot: separate the multimers by electrophoresis, transfer, and detect with an anti-VWF antibody. Loaded at the top, the ultra-large and high molecular weight multimers are too bulky to navigate the gel and stay near the origin; smaller forms migrate further down. Three results: normal ladder, abnormal pattern (usually loss of the high molecular weight forms), or essentially absent. Not a front-line test — it is sent after the activity-to-antigen comparison has already shown something is wrong. The antigen itself is measured by a standard ELISA.

🪝 The diagnostic algorithm in one sentence

Are activity and antigen similar? If yes, the protein present works normally — there is just not enough of it: a quantitative problem, types 1 and 3. If no — antigen much higher than activity — the protein is present but broken: a qualitative problem, type 2.

TypeProblemVWF levelActivity : antigen ratioMultimersFirst-line treatment
Type 1Quantitative — partial deficiency. The most common formDecreased, < 30%Similar — roughly normal ratioNormal pattern, reduced amountDesmopressin (DDAVP) — releases stored VWF from endothelial Weibel–Palade bodies; the stored protein is normal, there is simply more available on demand
Type 2 (2A, 2B, 2M, 2N)Qualitative — the protein is abnormalMay be near-normalReduced, < ~0.5–0.7Abnormal — usually loss of high molecular weight forms2A/2M: DDAVP may work if there is residual activity, otherwise plasma-derived factor 8 concentrates (Humate P, Alphanate). 2B: concentrate, not DDAVP
Type 3Quantitative — essentially complete absence. The severe formEssentially absent, < 3%Both near zeroEssentially absentConcentrate — there is nothing stored to release

Also available: plasma-derived von Willebrand factor (Wilate) or recombinant von Willebrand factor (Vonvendi). Avoid exposing these patients to cryoprecipitate when virally-inactivated concentrates exist.

⚠️ Two grey zones the lecture flags explicitly

“Low von Willebrand factor” of 30–50% sits between normal and type 1. It may be von Willebrand disease if there is a bleeding history — the clinical history, not the number alone, decides.

Blood group O individuals have lower von Willebrand factor levels at baseline. A group O patient can test in the low range and be entirely normal. Interpret the level against the patient's blood type, or you will over-diagnose.

And a practical note on desmopressin: it is available as a nasal spray as well as parenterally, so a patient can take it themselves before a planned challenge. It releases both von Willebrand factor and factor 8 from endothelial stores, targeting a level above roughly 30–40%. Response is tested before it is relied upon — the DDAVP trial draws a baseline level, gives the drug, then draws serial levels and plots the response curve. A non-responder is identified before the operation, not during it.

When the platelet itself is abnormal

🔑 Two diseases, one broken handshake ★ HY

Recall the chain: collagen → von Willebrand factor → GPIb → platelet. Adhesion fails if you remove either partner in the handshake.

DiseaseWhat is missingSide of the handshake
von Willebrand diseaseVon Willebrand factor — the ligandThe plasma side
Bernard–Soulier syndromeGPIb/IX/V — the receptorThe platelet side

Both produce decreased adhesion and both bleed mucocutaneously. This is why the ristocetin cofactor assay uses normal fixed platelets — it deliberately removes the platelet side of the equation so the test reads the plasma side only.

🧠 Two thirds of a clot's strength comes from the platelets

A number that converts Glanzmann thrombasthenia from a curiosity into something intuitive: roughly two thirds of the mechanical strength of a clot comes from the platelets enmeshed in it, not from the fibrin alone.

So in Glanzmann thrombasthenia, where GPIIb/IIIa cannot bind fibrinogen and platelets therefore cannot be knitted into the mesh, the patient does form a fibrin clot — it is just mechanically weak, and it fails. Adhesion is intact (ristocetin normal); incorporation is not.

What the aggregometer is detecting when it measures secretion: activated platelets change shape and release calcium, serotonin and ATP from their granules. The ATP is what the luciferase channel sees — the firefly reaction — while aggregation is read as light transmission. Hence lumi-aggregometry. The serotonin is what the serotonin release assay measures in the HIT workup in Section 34.

🪝 How to read the platelet disorder table — look at the ristocetin column first

Ristocetin tests the GPIb–von Willebrand factor axis specifically. The other agonists — arachidonic acid, collagen, ADP — test activation and aggregation through other receptors. So:

Ristocetin low, everything else normal → the GPIb receptor is the problem → Bernard–Soulier (or von Willebrand disease, which the fixed-platelet design excludes). Ristocetin normal, the others low → the receptor is fine but aggregation is broken → classically Glanzmann thrombasthenia.

B for Bernard, b for bind — cannot bind the vessel wall, GPIb is missing, so ristocetin fails, and the smear gives you a free extra clue: big platelets, low count. G for Glanzmann, g for glue together — the fibrinogen bridge is missing, so everything except ristocetin fails.

Platelet disorderATP release (thrombin)Arachidonic acidCollagenADPRistocetinThe defining note
Bernard–Soulier syndromeNormalNormalNormalNormalDecreasedGPIb/IX/V abnormality (interacts with VWF). Smear shows thrombocytopenia with large platelets
Glanzmann thrombastheniaNormalDecreasedDecreasedDecreasedNormalGPIIb/IIIa abnormality (interacts with fibrinogen) — adhesion intact, aggregation fails
Delta (δ) granule storage poolDecreasedVariably decreasedVariably decreasedVariably decreasedNormalElectron microscopy needed. Includes Hermansky–Pudlak and Chediak–Higashi
Alpha (α) granule storage poolNormalVariably decreasedVariably decreasedVariably decreasedNormalSmear shows gray platelets without typical granules
Arachidonic acid / thromboxane A2 pathwayNormalDecreasedVariably decreasedVariably decreasedNormalAspirin produces identical findings — always ask about aspirin before diagnosing this
Primary secretion defectsVariably decreasedVariably decreasedVariably decreasedVariably decreasedNormalSignal transduction problem — decreased granule release with a normal number of granules
🩺 Where platelet studies sit in the workup

Explicit sequencing advice: rule out hemophilia and von Willebrand disease first. Platelet function disorders are rare, and platelet aggregometry belongs in a second- or third-tier workup, not the initial panel. Platelet electron microscopy is added only when a granule storage pool defect is suspected.

🔑 Historical features that suggest a bleeding disorder is hereditary ★ HY
  • Lifelong, not new. Bleeding dating from childhood — circumcision, tooth eruption, first dental extraction — points at a congenital defect. A diathesis that appears suddenly in a patient's 50s or 70s with no prior history is acquired until proven otherwise (Section 31).
  • Family history, read for the right pattern. Affected males across generations through unaffected mothers → X-linked (hemophilia A or B). Affected men and women in every generation → autosomal dominant (most von Willebrand disease). Both sexes with consanguinity or an isolated case → autosomal recessive (Bernard–Soulier, Glanzmann, hemophilia C).
  • Bleeding at first haemostatic challenge. Mild hemophilia and type 1 von Willebrand disease often surface at a first operation, a first delivery, or the start of menstruation — not before.
  • Menorrhagia is the most commonly missed presentation. Von Willebrand described the disease in families from the Åland islands of the Baltic where teenage girls died of blood loss from heavy menstrual bleeding. Heavy periods still get normalised for years before anyone sends a von Willebrand panel — and the routine coagulation screen will be entirely normal.
  • A mixing study that corrects supports a deficiency (usually inherited); one that fails to correct supports an inhibitor (usually acquired).

The thrombotic counterpart of this list — young age, unusual site, recurrence, family history — is in Section 34.

Q: A 6-year-old boy is brought in with a swollen, painful, warm knee after a minor fall. There is no history of nosebleeds. Which half of hemostasis is failing, and what should the coagulation screen show?

Answer

Secondary hemostasis. Hemarthrosis — bleeding into a joint — is the signature of a coagulation factor deficiency, not a platelet problem, and the absence of mucocutaneous bleeding supports that. In a boy this age the answer is hemophilia A or B until proven otherwise.

Expect a prolonged aPTT with a normal PT (factors 8 and 9 are both intrinsic), a normal platelet count, and a mixing study that corrects — because this is a deficiency, not an inhibitor. Factor 8 and factor 9 activity assays then separate hemophilia A from B; they are clinically indistinguishable at the bedside.

Q: A woman with lifelong heavy periods and easy bruising has a normal PT, aPTT and platelet count. Von Willebrand antigen is 60%, ristocetin cofactor activity is 22%. Which type of von Willebrand disease is this, and should she be given desmopressin?

Answer

Type 2 — a qualitative defect. The activity-to-antigen ratio is 22/60 = 0.37, well under the 0.5–0.7 threshold, meaning plenty of protein is present but it does not work. A type 1 patient would have activity and antigen falling together. Multimer analysis is the next test, and would be expected to show loss of high molecular weight multimers.

Not desmopressin as a reflex. In types 2A and 2M it may help if there is residual activity; in type 2B it can make things worse by driving abnormal von Willebrand factor onto platelets and deepening the thrombocytopenia. The subtype must be established first — and if it cannot be, use a plasma-derived factor 8 / von Willebrand factor concentrate.

Q: Why does von Willebrand disease cause mucocutaneous bleeding when hemophilia — also a “clotting protein” problem — causes joint bleeding? And why can severe von Willebrand disease prolong the aPTT?

Answer

Because von Willebrand factor's dominant role is in primary hemostasis. It is the tether between subendothelial collagen and the platelet receptor GPIb, so losing it is functionally a platelet adhesion defect — and platelet problems bleed from surfaces: nose, gums, uterus, gut. Hemophilia is a defect of secondary hemostasis, and fibrin failure bleeds into spaces: joints and muscles.

The aPTT can prolong because of the protein's second job: it is the carrier for factor 8. Losing it means factor 8 is cleared faster and its level falls — a secondary factor 8 deficiency, and factor 8 is an intrinsic-pathway factor.

This is why severe (type 3) von Willebrand disease can look like mild hemophilia A on a screen, and why the two must be separated with von Willebrand antigen and activity assays rather than the aPTT.

Q: Aggregometry shows decreased response to arachidonic acid, collagen and ADP, with normal ristocetin and normal ATP release. Give two possible explanations and say how to separate them.

Answer

Glanzmann thrombasthenia (GPIIb/IIIa deficiency) or an aspirin effect — the table notes explicitly that aspirin shows similar findings. Normal ristocetin rules out Bernard–Soulier and von Willebrand disease, because the GPIb axis is intact.

Separate them with the history first: recent aspirin or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory exposure. Then by pattern — a pure arachidonic acid / thromboxane defect tends to hit arachidonic acid hardest with only variable effects elsewhere, whereas Glanzmann abolishes aggregation to all of arachidonic acid, collagen and ADP.

Definitive testing is flow cytometry for GPIIb/IIIa (CD41/CD61) expression. If aspirin is suspected, stop it and repeat after 7–10 days — aspirin is an irreversible inhibitor, so recovery requires an entirely new platelet population (Section 16).

LO 32LO 36Source: Coagulation I — Cascade & Bleeding Disorders

Section 31 · Coagulation I · bleeding

Acquired Bleeding — Liver Disease, DIC, Vitamin K and Inhibitors

The inherited disorders are the ones with names. The acquired ones are the ones you will actually meet on the wards — and they move both clotting times, because they knock out several factors at once.

Abbreviations used in this section DIC disseminated intravascular coagulation · FDP fibrin degradation products · PCC prothrombin complex concentrate — a concentrated preparation of the vitamin K-dependent factors · FFP fresh frozen plasma · INR international normalised ratio · ADAMTS13 the protease that trims von Willebrand factor multimers · HMWM high molecular weight multimers · Bethesda titre the quantitative measure of a factor inhibitor

Liver disease — a coagulopathy in both directions

🧠 Why liver disease is not simply “a bleeding state”

The liver makes almost all the coagulation proteins — the procoagulant factors and the natural anticoagulants protein C, protein S and antithrombin. Losing both sides at once produces a rebalanced but fragile hemostasis, which is why patients with end-stage liver disease can bleed and clot.

The practical consequence: a prolonged PT/INR in liver disease does not predict bleeding the way it does in warfarin therapy, and is not by itself a reason to transfuse plasma.

But the rebalancing does not protect them through surgery. These patients bleed a great deal intra-operatively — it is routine for the blood bank to set aside 20–30 units for a liver transplant.

Disseminated intravascular coagulation ★ HY

🔑 DIC is specification 3 failing — clotting that is not localised

Go back to the four specifications in Section 29: the system must respond to injury quickly and in a localised fashion. In DIC, coagulation is triggered systemically. Widespread microvascular thrombosis consumes platelets and factors, and simultaneously drives fibrinolysis. The patient therefore clots and bleeds at the same time — the defining paradox.

TestDirection in DICWhy
Platelet countFallsConsumed in microthrombi
PT and aPTTBoth prolongedFactors consumed — and a common-pathway and fibrinogen deficit hits both tests
FibrinogenFallsConsumed converting to fibrin. A falling trend is more useful than a single value, since fibrinogen is an acute-phase reactant and starts high in sepsis
D-dimer / FDPRise, often markedlyActive fibrin formation and breakdown
SmearSchistocytesRed cells sheared on intravascular fibrin strands — a microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (Section 24)
⚠️ The management principle for DIC

Treat the underlying cause. DIC is always secondary — to sepsis, malignancy, obstetric catastrophe, major trauma. Product support (platelets, plasma, cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate) is given for bleeding or before a procedure, not to correct a number on a panel.

Two cross-references worth holding: DIC is one of the causes of schistocytes in Section 24, and it is the entity the thrombotic microangiopathies must be distinguished from in Section 32 — a distinction the coagulation panel makes in one look.

Vitamin K deficiency ★ HY

🔑 Vitamin K — factors 2, 7, 9, 10, plus proteins C and S

Vitamin K is required to make factors 2, 7, 9 and 10 functional, plus the anticoagulants protein C and protein S. Deficiency follows malnutrition, malabsorption, or prolonged antibiotics.

Because factor 7 has the shortest half-life of the four, the PT prolongs first — an isolated long PT with a normal aPTT is the classic early picture. This is the same mechanism warfarin exploits (Sections 14 and 31).

Vitamin K injection is part of standard neonatal care. Newborns are relatively deficient — little placental transfer, low stores, sterile gut — and without it they are at risk of hemorrhagic disease of the newborn, including intracranial hemorrhage. Practical history point: babies born outside a hospital may miss the routine injection, so ask about the birth setting.

🪝 Factor 5 — how to tell vitamin K deficiency from liver disease

Both prolong the PT. Both eventually prolong the aPTT. The clean discriminator is a factor most people forget to order:

Factors 2, 7, 9, 10Factor 5Why
Vitamin K deficiency (or warfarin)LowNormalFactor 5 is not vitamin K dependent, so it is untouched
Liver diseaseLowAlso lowThe liver makes factor 5 too, so synthetic failure takes it down as well

Low 2, 7, 9, 10 with a normal factor 5 = vitamin K. Everything low including factor 5 = liver.

A supporting check runs the other way, from Section 29: factor 8 is normal or high in liver disease (hepatocytes do not make it) but low in DIC, where it is consumed with everything else. When liver disease and DIC are hard to separate, that is the discriminating assay.

Acquired inhibitors and acquired von Willebrand disease

🩺 The patient who looks like hemophilia but has no history

Acquired factor inhibitors are associated with autoimmune disorders, malignancy, and cardiac valvular disease. The typical patient is older, presenting with a new bleeding diathesis and no lifelong bleeding history — often in their 50s, with a diathesis that appears suddenly. That contrast with a congenital disorder is the diagnostic clue.

The mixing study is the discriminator: an acquired inhibitor fails to correct — and remember from Section 29 that a slow-acting factor 8 antibody may need the incubated study to declare itself.

Management has two halves, and the second is what distinguishes acquired from congenital disease: treat the bleeding as you would in hemophilia (bypassing agents, since infused factor is neutralised), and suppress the antibody with immunosuppressants — because here the antibody can actually be eradicated.

🧠 Acquired von Willebrand disease with aortic stenosis — Heyde syndrome

A mechanism worth knowing because it explains a clinical pairing that otherwise looks like coincidence. Shear stress across a stenotic valve unfolds von Willebrand factor and exposes it to ADAMTS13, which strips out the high molecular weight multimers.

The result is a type-2-like picture — antigen present, activity reduced, abnormal multimers — in a patient with a murmur and gastrointestinal bleeding. Same enzyme as Section 32's TTP, same molecule as Section 30's inherited disease, arriving by a mechanical route.

🔑 The lecture's closing summary, worth reproducing whole
  • There is a wide range of bleeding disorders.
  • Evaluate with PT, aPTT, fibrinogen, platelet count, and von Willebrand testing — von Willebrand testing is listed separately because the first four will not find it.
  • Factor deficiency; von Willebrand disease, challenging because of the variety of subtypes; dysfibrinogenemia, which can also cause clotting; platelet disorders, which are rare.
  • Proper coagulation also depends on blood vessels and endothelium — the panel can be normal and the patient can still bleed.

Q: A septic patient in intensive care has a falling platelet count, prolonged PT and aPTT, fibrinogen dropping from 480 to 140 mg/dL over two days, a markedly raised D-dimer, and schistocytes on the smear. What is the diagnosis, and what is the most important treatment?

Answer

Disseminated intravascular coagulation, secondary to sepsis. Every leg is present: consumption (falling platelets and fibrinogen, prolonged clotting times), fibrinolysis (high D-dimer) and microangiopathy (schistocytes).

Note that the fibrinogen at 140 is still within many reference ranges — the downward trend from 480 is the finding, because fibrinogen is an acute-phase reactant and should be high in sepsis.

The most important treatment is aggressive treatment of the sepsis (Section 18). Blood products are given for bleeding or before procedures, not to normalise numbers.

Q: Two patients each have a prolonged PT. Patient A has factors 2, 7, 9 and 10 all low with a normal factor 5. Patient B has factors 2, 7, 9, 10 and 5 all low. What distinguishes them?

Answer

Patient A has vitamin K deficiency (or is on warfarin). Patient B has liver disease.

Factor 5 is not vitamin K dependent. Vitamin K is required only for factors 2, 7, 9, 10 and proteins C and S — so a pure vitamin K problem leaves factor 5 untouched. The liver, by contrast, synthesises factor 5 as well, so hepatic synthetic failure drags it down with everything else.

A supporting check runs the other way: factor 8 is normal or high in liver disease (it is not made by hepatocytes) but low in DIC.

For patient A, ask about nutrition, malabsorption, prolonged antibiotics — and in a neonate, whether the birth happened outside a hospital, where the routine vitamin K injection may have been missed.

Q: A 74-year-old with no prior bleeding history develops large spontaneous hematomas. aPTT is prolonged, PT normal, platelet count normal. A 1:1 mix does not correct. What is going on?

Answer

An acquired factor inhibitor — most commonly an acquired factor 8 inhibitor (acquired hemophilia A). Three features point there: an isolated prolonged aPTT (intrinsic pathway), a mixing study that fails to correct (inhibitor rather than deficiency), and above all a new bleeding diathesis in an older patient — a congenital factor deficiency would have declared itself decades earlier.

Look for an underlying autoimmune disorder or malignancy. Confirm with a factor 8 activity level and a Bethesda titre.

Treat the bleeding with a bypassing agent, since infused factor is neutralised, and suppress the antibody with immunosuppression — unlike congenital hemophilia, here the antibody can be eradicated.

Q: A patient with cirrhosis has an INR of 2.1. The surgical team asks for plasma before a paracentesis. What do you say?

Answer

A prolonged INR in liver disease does not reliably predict bleeding, and by itself is not a reason to transfuse plasma.

The reason is that the liver makes both sides of the system — the procoagulant factors and the natural anticoagulants protein C, protein S and antithrombin. Losing both produces a rebalanced but fragile hemostasis. The INR measures only the procoagulant half, so it reports a coagulopathy that the patient may not clinically have. That is the opposite of warfarin, where the anticoagulants are also suppressed but the INR is a validated, dose-calibrated measure.

Manage individually: transfuse for bleeding or for a genuinely high-risk procedure, not to normalise a number. And note the honest caveat — rebalancing does not protect these patients through major surgery, where they bleed a great deal, which is why a liver transplant has 20–30 units set aside.

LO 33LO 44Source: Coagulation II — Thrombophilia & Anticoagulation

Section 32 · Coagulation II · clotting

The Thrombotic Microangiopathies — TTP, HUS and aHUS

Small-vessel thrombosis that shreds red cells as they pass. The clinical presentations overlap heavily; the classification is by mechanism, and the mechanism decides the treatment.

Abbreviations used in this section TMA thrombotic microangiopathy — the umbrella term for small-vessel thrombosis with red cell destruction · TTP thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura · HUS hemolytic uremic syndrome · aHUS atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome · MAHA microangiopathic hemolytic anemia — red cells shredded in small vessels · ADAMTS13 the protease that cleaves von Willebrand factor multimers · VWF von Willebrand factor · CFH complement factor H · MCP / CD46 membrane cofactor protein, a membrane-bound complement regulator · MAC membrane attack complex · HELLP Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets · DIC disseminated intravascular coagulation · SLE systemic lupus erythematosus
🔑 The mechanistic classification — the master table ★ HY
PathologyMechanismClinical disease
Systemic platelet thrombiInability to degrade large von Willebrand factor multimers (ADAMTS13)TTP
Predominantly renal, platelet–fibrin-rich thrombiShiga toxin causing endothelial cell damage (E. coli)HUS
Renal, platelet–fibrin-rich thrombiFactor H deficiency and complement activationFamilial, or aHUS
Systemic and renal thrombiDrugs and stem cell transplant, endothelial damageFeatures of both TTP and HUS
🪝 Memory hook — systemic vs renal, platelets vs fibrin

TTP is systemic and platelet-rich — ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers grab platelets everywhere, so the brain is involved and the presentation is neurological. HUS is renal and fibrin-rich — Shiga toxin damages glomerular endothelium, so the presentation is renal failure.

The overlap is real, but “brain = TTP, kidney = HUS” is the correct first instinct.

TTP — the ADAMTS13 story ★ HY

  1. Endothelial cells secrete von Willebrand factor from Weibel–Palade bodies. It emerges as ultra-large multimers, anchored to the cell surface.
  2. Normally, ADAMTS13 cleaves them. The enzyme trims the ultra-large multimers into normal-sized ones — hemostatically useful, but not dangerous.
  3. In TTP, ADAMTS13 is absent or blocked. Either a congenital deficiency (Upshaw–Schulman) or an acquired IgG inhibitor — an autoantibody against the enzyme. The acquired form is far more common.
  4. Uncleaved ultra-large multimers seize platelets. They act as enormous adhesive ropes, driving adhesion and aggregation in the microvasculature — consuming platelets and producing thrombocytopenia.
  5. Red cells are shredded on the resulting strands. This is microangiopathic hemolytic anemia — the source of the schistocytes.

Incidence is 0.37 per 100,000 per year in the United States — rare, and lethal if missed.

⚠️ Why TTP is a medical emergency — and the one thing not to do

Untreated TTP has a mortality above 90%. The treatment is plasma exchange, and it is started on clinical suspicion, before the ADAMTS13 level returns.

The trap: do not transfuse platelets in suspected TTP unless there is life-threatening bleeding. The thrombocytopenia is consumptive — adding platelets adds fuel to ongoing microvascular thrombosis.

🧠 Why plasma exchange, and not plasma infusion

Because it does two things at once. The plasma you give back replaces ADAMTS13, supplying the missing enzyme. The plasma you remove takes the antibody with it, stripping out the autoantibody that was neutralising the patient's own enzyme. Infusion alone would only do the first. Immunosuppression is added when the patient is likely to relapse.

Two details that change how you read the case. The acquired form has a characteristic age: an autoimmune antibody against ADAMTS13 typically brings a patient in during their 20s or 30s, whereas the congenital deficiency presents much earlier. And you do not want zero large multimers either — ADAMTS13 is a balancing enzyme, and the large multimers are the active ones that recruit platelets to a genuine injury. The disease is having only those, so platelets are recruited everywhere.

Vocabulary worth having: schistocytes are described as “triangular helmet cells”, and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia decodes literally — micro-angio (small vessels) -pathic (something wrong) hemolytic anemia.

HUS — Shiga toxin and the kidney

🔑 Etiologic classification — what is actually understood
Etiology understoodSubtypes
1. Infection-inducedShiga toxin / Shiga-like toxin (E. coli); neuraminidase and T antigen (Streptococcus pneumoniae)
2. Disorders of complement regulationGenetic; or acquired — anti-factor-H antibodies
3. von Willebrand proteinase (ADAMTS13) deficiencyGenetic; or acquired — autoimmune, drug-induced
4. Defective cobalamin metabolismGenetic
5. QuinineDrug-induced

Etiology not understood: HIV; malignancy, radiation, chemotherapy; calcineurin inhibitors and transplantation; pregnancy, HELLP syndrome, oral contraceptives; systemic lupus erythematosus and antiphospholipid antibodies; glomerulonephropathy; familial not otherwise specified; unclassified.

🧠 How an intestinal infection ends up causing clotting

The organism is enterohemorrhagic E. coli, classically O157:H7 (also Shigella dysenteriae), and the classic exposure is undercooked or contaminated meat, producing bloody diarrhoea and then kidney failure.

The step that is easy to miss is why an infection triggers coagulation at all. The toxin kills endothelial cells directly — and dying cells activate the immune system, releasing interleukins and chemokines. Coagulation and immunity are wired together: an inflammatory signal is also a “there may be bleeding here” signal. So fibrinogen and von Willebrand factor, both acute-phase reactants, are released — and the surge of high molecular weight von Willebrand factor reproduces the same end result as TTP by a completely different route.

That acute-phase behaviour recurs twice more in this file: it is why fibrinogen starts high in sepsis (so a falling trend matters more than one value in DIC, Section 31), and why factor 8 is elevated in the acute period, making thrombophilia testing unreliable then (Section 34).

aHUS — complement out of control

🧠 What complement does, and how that becomes a clotting disease

Complement has two jobs. Opsonisation — proteins coat a target and mark it for destruction, making it far easier for neutrophils and macrophages to phagocytose. And the membrane attack complex (MAC) — a pore that lyses the target cell outright.

Now run that without a brake. The alternative complement pathway is constitutively ticking over — it is held in check by regulatory proteins rather than being switched on by a trigger. In atypical HUS the suppression is defective, so the pathway is continually on, and unregulated complement binds the patient's own cells. The membrane attack complex destroys their endothelium; destroyed endothelium exposes collagen and tissue factor — the exact trigger from Section 29 — and coagulation is switched on.

The defects are in complement factor H (CFH), complement factor I, membrane cofactor protein (MCP/CD46), and thrombomodulin. The pattern that follows: a patient carries a regulatory mutation and is fine for years, until something triggers the system — and because the feedback that would switch it off is broken, it keeps amplifying itself. Named triggers include HIV, cancer, transplantation, tacrolimus, and pregnancy — including HELLP syndrome, associated with pre-eclampsia and eclampsia.

⚠️ Why the genetics must be sorted out before a transplant

The recurrence rate after renal transplantation is so high that children must be genetically tested before receiving a kidney. The reason is mechanistic:

If the defective regulator is made in the liver (factor H, factor I), a new kidney enters the same hostile circulation and is attacked in turn. If the defect is in a membrane-bound regulator made by the kidney itself (MCP/CD46), a transplanted kidney brings its own working copy and does far better.

Prognosis follows the same logic: a factor H mutation carries a high rate of recurrence and of death or end-stage renal disease, whereas other mutations recur far less. That is what makes the genotype worth knowing — for treatment, and for family counselling and screening.

Targeted treatment is complement blockade with eculizumab, an anti-C5 antibody — which is why establishing complement as the mechanism changes management, not just the label.

🪝 The single most useful discriminator: the clotting times

In every thrombotic microangiopathy the PT and aPTT are normal, because the clotting factors are not being consumed — the problem is platelets and endothelium. In DIC they are both prolonged and fibrinogen falls.

If you are handed schistocytes plus thrombocytopenia, the coagulation panel is what separates the microangiopathies from DIC, and it takes one look. The smear cannot do it (Section 24).

🩺 The TTP pentad — and why you should not wait for it

Fever · thrombocytopenia · microangiopathic hemolytic anemia · neurological changes · renal impairment.

The practical instruction is not to wait for all five. Recognition has improved to the point that anyone with some of these features, or with schistocytes, should be treated as TTP while confirmatory results are pending — because untreated TTP kills, and plasma exchange works. The Section 24 smear case supplies four of the five and is the same patient seen from the microscope.

Q: A 17-year-old woman presents with bruising, fever, confusion, a platelet count of 14,000/µL and schistocytes on the smear. PT and aPTT are normal, fibrinogen is normal. What is the diagnosis, what is the enzyme defect, and what is the treatment?

Answer

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. The combination of neurological change, thrombocytopenia and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with normal clotting times is the classic picture — and normal PT, aPTT and fibrinogen is what excludes DIC.

The defect is ADAMTS13 — deficient or, more often, blocked by an acquired IgG inhibitor. Without it, ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers are not cleaved and recruit platelets into systemic microthrombi. Her age fits the acquired autoimmune form, which typically presents in the 20s or 30s.

Treatment is urgent plasma exchange, started on suspicion rather than waiting for the ADAMTS13 result — it both replaces the enzyme and removes the antibody. Do not give platelets unless there is life-threatening bleeding.

Q: A 4-year-old develops acute kidney injury, thrombocytopenia and a hemolytic anemia with no preceding diarrhoea. Stool studies are negative for Shiga toxin. Why does establishing the mechanism change management, and why must this be sorted out before any transplant?

Answer

This is the third branch of the recognition algorithm — no diarrhoeal prodrome and no pneumococcal infection — so a full investigation for alternative causes is required, and the leading candidate is atypical HUS from a complement regulation defect (factor H, factor I, membrane cofactor protein, thrombomodulin).

It changes management because aHUS has a targeted therapy — complement blockade with eculizumab — whereas typical Shiga toxin HUS is managed supportively.

It matters before transplant because the recurrence rate is very high. If the faulty regulator is a circulating protein made in the liver, the new kidney meets the same unregulated complement and is attacked; if the defect is in a membrane-bound renal protein, the graft supplies its own working copy and does far better. A factor H mutation in particular carries a high rate of recurrence and of death or end-stage renal disease — which also makes it worth knowing for family screening.

Q: Von Willebrand factor causes a bleeding disease in one lecture and a clotting disease in the next. Explain how one molecule does both.

Answer

Because hemostatic activity tracks multimer size, and the disease depends on which direction the size distribution goes wrong.

Too little, or too small → bleeding. In von Willebrand disease (Section 30) there is either not enough protein (types 1 and 3) or the high molecular weight multimers are missing (type 2). A short multimer cannot span from collagen out into flowing blood to catch a platelet, so adhesion fails and the patient bleeds mucocutaneously.

Too large, uncleaved → clotting. In TTP, ADAMTS13 — the enzyme that normally trims ultra-large multimers to size — is deficient or inhibited. The uncleaved ropes seize platelets across the entire microvasculature, consuming them and shredding red cells on the resulting strands.

Same molecule, same enzyme, opposite disease — and a third variant sits in between: in Heyde syndrome (Section 31), shear across a stenotic aortic valve exposes von Willebrand factor to ADAMTS13 and strips out the large multimers mechanically, producing a type-2-like bleeding picture.

LO 45LO 46LO 48Source: Coagulation II — Thrombophilia & Anticoagulation

Section 33 · Coagulation II · clotting

Inherited Thrombophilias and Antiphospholipid Syndrome

Two mechanisms, and only two: either you have too little of an anticoagulant, or too much (or too resistant) a procoagulant. Every inherited thrombophilia sorts into one of those buckets — and the bucket predicts how dangerous it is.

Abbreviations used in this section VTE venous thromboembolism · DVT deep vein thrombosis · PE pulmonary embolism · FVL factor V Leiden · R506Q the common factor V Leiden mutation, named for the amino acid change · G20210A the common prothrombin mutation, named for the DNA position · 3′ UTR three-prime untranslated region — the non-coding tail of a messenger RNA · AT III antithrombin III · APS / APLA antiphospholipid (antibody) syndrome · LA lupus anticoagulant · dRVVT dilute Russell viper venom test — a phospholipid-dependent clotting assay · anti-β2-GP1 anti-beta-2-glycoprotein-1 antibody · VDRL / RPR the non-treponemal syphilis tests, which use a cardiolipin antigen · OCP oral contraceptive pill · Lp(a) lipoprotein(a) · ET / PV essential thrombocythemia / polycythemia vera
🔑 Virchow's triad — the frame for everything in this section ★ HY

Three categories of risk factor for thrombosis, and every disease and drug below maps onto one of them:

1

Endothelial cell damage

Surgery, trauma, central lines, inflammation.

2

Blood stasis

Immobilisation, prolonged travel, paralysis, pregnancy.

3

Hypercoagulable state

The thrombophilias — inherited and acquired. This is where this section lives.

🧠 How common is this? — and why that argues against testing everyone

Some form of thrombophilia is present in roughly 25% of the general population, and about 60% of patients presenting with a deep vein thrombosis will have one. Overall incidence of thrombosis is 1–2 per 1,000 per year, rising steeply with age — about 1 in 100,000 per year in children and up to 1 in 100 per year in the elderly.

A finding present in a quarter of everyone does not, by itself, explain a clot. That single statistic is the strongest argument in Section 34 for testing selectively rather than reflexively.

The full list, split by mechanism ★ HY

🚫

Deficit in antithrombotic proteins — lose a brake

  • Protein C deficiency
  • Protein S deficiency
  • Antithrombin III deficiency

Rarer, but much higher risk per patient — relative risk 15–19×.

⚡

Excessive activation of prothrombotic factors — push the accelerator

  • Factor V Leiden mutation
  • Prothrombin G20210A mutation
  • Dysfibrinogenemia

Far more common, lower risk each — relative risk 3–5×.

ThrombophiliaPrevalenceMechanismHow it is detectedThe detail that gets tested
Factor V Leiden~5% of Caucasians; accounts for 20–30% of VTE events — the most common thrombophiliaR506Q prevents deactivation of factor 5 by protein C — “activated protein C resistance”Molecular testingNet effect is similar to protein C deficiency. Homozygotes carry substantially higher risk; can coexist with protein C deficiency, which is additive
