🪝 Memory hook — three lesions, one shared failure

The reaction is activated protein C cleaves factor 5a. You can break it three ways, and all three converge on the same end result — factor 5a survives and thrombin generation runs on:

Remove the scissors → protein C or protein S deficiency. Armour-plate the paper → factor V Leiden. Poison the scissors → hyperhomocysteinemia, which inhibits protein C.

That is why the lecture says the effect of factor V Leiden is “similar overall” to protein C deficiency — and why having both is additive.

⚠️ Purpura fulminans — why the skin bleeds in a clotting disease

Homozygous protein C or S deficiency causes potentially fatal purpura fulminans shortly after birth — widespread dermal microvascular thrombosis with skin necrosis. It is a neonatal emergency.

The name looks contradictory until you follow the mechanism: disseminated clotting in the capillaries; the occluded capillaries then rupture, and blood leaks into the surrounding tissue. The purpura is the consequence of the thrombosis, not of a bleeding tendency.

The same protein C mechanism, arriving pharmacologically rather than genetically, produces warfarin-induced skin necrosis in Section 34.

🩺 Antithrombin deficiency is the one that changes what drug you reach for

Antithrombin III is a small protein and is easily lost, so a low level does not automatically mean an inherited disorder. Acquired causes: nephrotic syndrome (the kidneys leak protein), chest tube drainage, protein-losing enteropathies, severe heart failure.

It matters because heparin works by increasing antithrombin's enzymatic activity — heparin has essentially no anticoagulant action of its own. With little antithrombin present, more heparin achieves little: the classic picture of heparin resistance.

The answer is not more heparin. It is either antithrombin III supplementation, so that the heparin can work to its full effect, or an agent that does not depend on antithrombin at all — a direct thrombin inhibitor (Section 15).

🧠 The acquired thrombophilias, for contrast
  • Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome — lupus anticoagulant, anti-cardiolipin, anti-β2-glycoprotein-I. Worked below.
  • Elevated platelet count or fibrinogen. Essential thrombocythemia is a myeloproliferative disorder producing a persistently high platelet count — at a million or more, in the lecture's phrase, “a lot of fuel there to generate a clot.” Distinguish it from a reactive thrombocytosis, which is temporary.
  • Elevated levels of factors 8, 9, 11.
  • Malignancy.
  • Hormones — oral contraceptives, estrogen, pregnancy. Oral contraceptives plus smoking carries a very high clotting risk, and importantly a reversible one: stopping both may remove the need for anticoagulation altogether, which is why identifying the combination matters more than treating around it.
  • Lipoprotein(a) — associated mainly with atherosclerotic disease, with a possible additional thrombotic contribution.

Antiphospholipid syndrome — the double misnomer ★ HY

⚠️ “Lupus anticoagulant” is wrong on both counts

Not lupus. Patients with a lupus anticoagulant do not necessarily have lupus — about 8% may develop it later. The relationship is a Venn diagram with partial overlap: you can have lupus without a lupus anticoagulant, and a lupus anticoagulant without meeting criteria for lupus. It is not part of the diagnostic criteria for lupus at all. The two were linked by the order of discovery, not by definition.

Not an anticoagulant. It increases clotting time in vitro — which is where the name came from — but increases the risk of thrombosis in vivo. The test tube and the patient point in opposite directions.

🧠 Why the paradox exists — and why it hands you the confirmatory test

The clotting assays are run on a phospholipid surface. The antibody binds phospholipid, so in the tube it competes with the clotting complexes for a limited amount of surface and the reaction is slowed — a prolonged clotting time. In the patient, phospholipid is not limiting; instead the antibodies activate endothelium and platelets and interfere with natural anticoagulant pathways, which promotes thrombosis.

And because the inhibition is phospholipid-dependent, adding extra phospholipid corrects the clotting time. Adding normal plasma does not. That asymmetry is the diagnostic algorithm.

  1. Mixing study. Patient plasma plus normal plasma. A lupus anticoagulant does not correct — it is an inhibitor, not a deficiency (Section 29).
  2. aPTT and/or dilute Russell viper venom test (dRVVT). Both are phospholipid-dependent clotting assays; the dRVVT is more specific for a lupus anticoagulant.
  3. Confirm with excess phospholipid. Adding extra phospholipid corrects the prolongation — proving the inhibitor is directed at phospholipid rather than at a specific factor.
  4. Immunoassays for the individual antibodies. Anti-cardiolipin IgG and IgM; anti-β2-glycoprotein-1 IgG and IgM; anti-phosphatidylserine; anti-prothrombin — note the exception, that at a high level this may cause a hemorrhagic disorder rather than thrombosis, by clearing prothrombin from the circulation.
🔑 Diagnostic criteria — one clinical plus one laboratory
Clinical criteria (at least one)Laboratory criteria
a. Vascular thrombosis — arterial, venous, or small vessel. Not superficial venous thrombosis.

b. Pregnancy morbidity, any one of:
i. Three or more unexplained consecutive miscarriages before the 10th week.
ii. One or more unexplained deaths of a morphologically normal fetus at or beyond the 10th week.
iii. One or more premature births of a morphologically normal neonate before the 34th week due to eclampsia, severe pre-eclampsia, or placental insufficiency.		 Prolonged clotting times that do not correct on mixing with plasma, but do correct with extra phospholipid.

Persistent — positive on two occasions at least 12 weeks apart. Timing relative to the event: 12 weeks to 5 years.
🪝 The “12 weeks apart” rule is the whole point

After a recent clot, during an infection, or in any severely ill patient, you can transiently form antibodies that look like they bind phospholipid — and these disappear once the patient recovers. A genuine antiphospholipid antibody gives a strong reaction and persists. Requiring persistence over at least 12 weeks is what separates a real, thrombosis-associated syndrome from a passing epiphenomenon.

Notice also that the number of events scales with gestational age — three early losses, but only one after 10 weeks — because a late loss is a far rarer and more specific event.

⚠️ Having the antibody is not having the syndrome

More people have antiphospholipid antibodies than have antiphospholipid syndrome. The syndrome requires both a clinical and a laboratory criterion.

The management consequence is the part most often got wrong: a patient with antiphospholipid antibodies but no thrombosis and no pregnancy morbidity is generally not anticoagulated. Treatment follows the syndrome, not the serology.

Q: A patient with nephrotic syndrome fails to achieve a therapeutic aPTT despite escalating heparin doses. What is the likely explanation?

Answer

Acquired antithrombin III deficiency from urinary protein loss. Antithrombin III is a small protein that is easily lost, and proteinuria is named explicitly as a cause — as are chest tube drainage, protein-losing enteropathy and severe heart failure.

It matters because heparin works by activating antithrombin III; heparin has essentially no anticoagulant action of its own. With little antithrombin present, more heparin achieves little — the classic picture of heparin resistance.

Management is to check an antithrombin level and either replace antithrombin so the heparin can work, or use an agent that does not depend on it — a direct thrombin inhibitor.

Q: Explain why the prothrombin G20210A mutation causes thrombophilia even though it does not alter a single amino acid of the prothrombin protein.

Answer

Because it is a regulatory mutation, not a coding one. G20210A sits in the 3′ untranslated region of the gene and increases pre-messenger-RNA stability. A more stable transcript is translated more, so the patient makes more prothrombin.

The protein itself is entirely normal — there is simply more substrate available for the cascade to convert into thrombin, which shifts the hemostatic balance toward clotting.

This is why the diagnosis is made by molecular testing rather than a functional assay: a protein activity test would look normal. It is also why the test can be run at any time and only ever needs running once (Section 34).

Q: A woman with three first-trimester miscarriages has a prolonged aPTT. She has never bled abnormally. The mixing study does not correct. Should she be given fresh frozen plasma before her next procedure?

Answer

No. This is a lupus anticoagulant, and the prolonged aPTT is an in-vitro artefact: the antibody competes for the phospholipid surface the assay depends on. Clinically she is at risk of thrombosis, not bleeding — the second half of the “double misnomer”.

Confirm by showing the prolongation corrects with added phospholipid (and with a dilute Russell viper venom test), then check anti-cardiolipin and anti-β2-glycoprotein-1 antibodies. Diagnosis requires persistence on repeat testing at least 12 weeks apart.

With three unexplained consecutive losses before 10 weeks she meets the clinical criterion, so a persistent laboratory finding would establish antiphospholipid syndrome.

Q: A patient has a positive non-treponemal syphilis test but treponemal-specific testing is negative. What hematological condition should you consider, and why does the false positive happen?

Answer

Antiphospholipid syndrome, specifically anti-cardiolipin antibodies.

The non-treponemal syphilis tests (VDRL, RPR) use a cardiolipin-based antigen. A patient whose own antibodies are directed against cardiolipin will bind that antigen and produce a biological false-positive. The treponemal-specific test, which uses actual Treponema pallidum antigens, stays negative.

Follow up with lupus anticoagulant testing and anti-β2-glycoprotein-1 antibodies, repeated at 12 weeks to establish persistence — and remember that the antibody alone, without a clinical criterion, is not the syndrome and is generally not anticoagulated.

LO 43LO 52LO 46Source: Coagulation II — Thrombophilia & Anticoagulation

Section 34 · Coagulation II · clotting

Prothrombotic Complications, HIT, and How Long to Treat

The objective that asks you to design an approach rather than recall a fact. Two questions drive it: should this patient be tested for thrombophilia at all, and how long should they be anticoagulated? The second turns out to depend far more on the circumstances of the clot than on any genetic result.

🩺 Where this section sits relative to Sections 14 and 15

The drug pharmacology — mechanisms, dosing, pregnancy use, contraindications and the full reversal bench — is worked in Section 15 and Section 16 from the Key Drug List. This section adds what the Coagulation II lecture contributes on top: why the monitoring test differs between heparins, the HIT decision rules, and how the circumstances of a clot set the duration of therapy.

Where clots actually form, and the two things every admission gets assessed for

🧠 Stasis is where clots start — the mechanism is mundane

Veins are pumped by the surrounding muscles and kept unidirectional by one-way valves, so blood only moves up the leg when you do. When it stops moving, platelets come into contact with each other and red cells settle — add dehydration on a long flight and that is a deep vein thrombosis.

Clots therefore form in dependent areas, usually the legs. Which is exactly why an unusual site is a red flag: mesenteric vessels, upper extremity, or cerebral venous sinus.

Two practical consequences follow. Every adult admission includes a thromboprophylaxis decision — compression stockings, prophylactic heparin, or both. And central lines must be locked with heparin, because the body treats indwelling plastic as foreign: platelets adhere to it and fibrin forms on it. (They are also a major infection route — the other reason not to leave one in past its usefulness.)

And the reason any of it matters: the deep vein thrombosis itself is painful, but what you dread is that clot dislodging into the lungs. A pulmonary embolism can kill the patient.

TransientPersistentInherited

Pregnancy deserves its own note: the hypercoagulability is deliberate physiology, protecting against haemorrhage at delivery — and it peaks postpartum, when the placental bed must clot down.

Complications of a prothrombotic state ★ HY

Venous thromboembolism

the common endpoint

Deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. The DVT is painful; the PE can kill. Post-thrombotic syndrome follows recurrent or extensive leg thrombosis.

Thrombosis at unusual sites

the red flag

Mesenteric, upper extremity, cerebral venous sinus. Unusual location is itself an indication to investigate for thrombophilia.

Pregnancy morbidity

antiphospholipid syndrome

Recurrent early loss, fetal death at or beyond 10 weeks, or premature birth before 34 weeks from eclampsia, severe pre-eclampsia or placental insufficiency (Section 33).

Purpura fulminans

homozygous protein C / S

Neonatal dermal microvascular thrombosis with skin necrosis — occluded capillaries rupture and blood leaks out. The purpura is a consequence of clotting.

Warfarin-induced skin necrosis

the iatrogenic version

Protein C falls before the procoagulant factors do, so the first days of warfarin are transiently more prothrombotic. Classically in patients with underlying protein C deficiency.

Venous limb gangrene

warfarin alone in HIT

The same protein C mechanism in a patient who is already thrombosing. This is why warfarin alone is prohibited in heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.

Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia ★ HY

⚠️ The counterintuitive core of HIT

HIT is a prothrombotic state. The platelet count falls, but the danger is thrombosis, not bleeding — new venous and arterial clots at a ratio of roughly 4:1 venous to arterial. Every management error below follows from forgetting this.

🧠 Why it takes 5–14 days, and why past HIT closes off the whole class

The delay is an immune delay. Heparin binds platelets and forms a complex with platelet factor 4; the patient's immune system then has to recognise that complex and manufacture antibodies against it, which takes 5–14 days. The antibody then binds platelets and activates them — which is why the count falls (they are being consumed into clots) and why the patient clots rather than bleeds.

That also explains the variants: with pre-existing antibody from exposure in the past 100 days there is no immunisation delay, so onset is within hours. A few patients present days after heparin has been stopped — easy to miss, because the drug is already gone.

And the consequence for the future: once a patient has had HIT, low-molecular-weight heparin and fondaparinux are closed off too. They are structurally related and the existing antibody can cross-react. A lower risk of causing HIT is not the same as being safe once the antibody exists.

🔑 The 4T score — a decision rule, not a description
Criterion2 points1 point0 points
Thrombocytopenia> 50% fall, or nadir 20–100 × 10⁹/L30–50% fall, or nadir 10–20 × 10⁹/LFall < 30%, or nadir < 10 × 10⁹/L
Timing of the fallClear onset days 5–10; or < 1 day if heparin exposure within the past 100 daysConsistent with immunisation but not clear, or onset after day 10Fall too early, without recent heparin exposure
Thrombosis or other sequelaeNew thrombosis; skin necrosis; post-heparin-bolus acute systemic reactionProgressive or recurrent thrombosis; erythematous skin lesions; suspected but unproven thrombosisNone
oTher cause for thrombocytopeniaNo other cause evidentPossible other cause evidentDefinite other cause present

6–8 = high · 4–5 = intermediate · 0–3 = low pre-test probability. The score exists to tell you whether to test at all:

High (6–8) → treat as HIT. Stop the heparin, start an alternative. Do not wait for a result. Low (0–3) → do not send the test. It is not HIT, and a false positive will cause harm — plenty of people carry the anti-PF4 antibody without having HIT, and an indiscriminate assay generates positives that force you to stop heparin in patients who never had the disease. Intermediate (4–5) → this is where testing actually helps decide.

🪝 How to read the result once you have it

Negative is genuinely useful. The anti-heparin/PF4 immunoassay is very sensitive, so a negative result essentially rules HIT out.

Positive leaves you stuck. It is not specific, so you must treat as HIT while sending the serotonin release assay — a functional test that takes the patient's platelets, adds heparin, and measures whether serotonin is released. It is complex and run only in reference laboratories, so the answer is not quick. Which is precisely why clinical impression is the most important element, listed ahead of any assay.

Read honestly: laboratory testing does not exclude a diagnosis of HIT, but the negative predictive value approaches 100% when both the serotonin release assay and the PF4 assay are negative. And positive results alone do not mean the thrombocytopenia can be attributed solely to heparin — anti-PF4 antibodies are common in hospitalised patients. Co-existing causes must be considered.

⚠️ Treatment — and the three errors the lecture names explicitly

HIT is a hypercoagulable state, but you cannot use any heparin compound and you cannot use warfarin. Institute an alternative antithrombotic: argatroban or lepirudin (direct thrombin inhibitors).

  1. Do not use warfarin alone — associated with gangrene. Warfarin drops protein C before it drops the procoagulant factors, transiently deepening the prothrombotic state in a patient who is already thrombosing. Venous limb gangrene is the result.
  2. Do not switch to low-molecular-weight heparin — the antibody cross-reacts.
  3. Do not stop anticoagulation altogether. The instinct to stop everything because the platelets are low is exactly wrong.
🧠 The tail — why aPTT monitors unfractionated heparin but not the low-molecular-weight ones

Heparin is a chain of sugars, and it comes in different lengths — much like von Willebrand factor multimers.

To inactivate thrombin, antithrombin and thrombin must be bridged together, and it is the heparin molecule's long tail that provides that bridge. Only a long chain can do it. To inactivate factor 10a, no bridge is needed — antithrombin does it well on its own once heparin has activated it. A short chain is enough.

AgentAnti-thrombin effectAnti-factor-10a effectSo monitor with
Unfractionated heparin (long tail)StrongStrongaPTT works — it senses the thrombin effect. Anti-Xa also valid
LMWH, fondaparinux (short)WeakStrongAnti-factor 10a only — the aPTT has little to detect

Targets: unfractionated heparin aPTT 1.5–2.5× normal or anti-Xa 0.3–0.7 U/mL; low-molecular-weight heparin generally needs no monitoring, but if measured, anti-Xa 0.5–1.0 U/mL twice-daily dosing, 1.0–2.0 U/mL once daily. A practice note: anti-factor 10a has largely replaced the aPTT even for unfractionated heparin in many laboratories, so a modern chart saying “therapeutic heparin level” usually means the anti-Xa result.

Risk stratification — the numbers that decide duration ★ HY

🔑 Recurrence risk in the first year, by the circumstances of the clot
Situation at the time of thrombosisExampleRecurrence risk in the first year
Major transient risk factorProlonged bedrest in hospital, surgery3%
Minor reversible risk factorOral contraceptive, long airplane trip5%
Unprovoked VTE, or a persistent risk factorNo identifiable trigger; ongoing malignancy10%

This is the core of the objective: determine which risk factors were present at the time of the thrombosis, because that — more than any genetic test — predicts recurrence and therefore therapy length.

Thrombophilic defectAnnual risk of first DVTRelative risk vs controlsRisk of recurrence
Antithrombin · protein C · protein S deficiency1.52–1.90%15–19×At 5 years 40%; at 10 years 55%
Factor V Leiden · prothrombin G20210A · high factor 80.34–0.49%3–5×At 5 years 11%; at 10 years 25%
High factor 9 · high factor 11 · high TAFI · hyperhomocysteinemiaNot independent risk factors for venous thrombosis — the risk is associated with high factor 8
🪝 The clinically important asymmetry: common ≠ dangerous

Compare the two rows. Losing a brake (antithrombin, protein C, protein S) gives a relative risk of 15–19×. Pushing the accelerator (factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A) gives only 3–5×.

Factor V Leiden is by far the most common thrombophilia and by no means the most dangerous one — which is exactly why finding it in a patient with a provoked clot rarely changes management.

When to test, and when not to ★ HY

🔑 The rule that governs all of this

Put more forcefully in the recording than on the slide: “If you're sending the test and the result doesn't impact anything you're doing, you probably didn't need to send that test.” These assays cost money and, worse, generate findings that invite unnecessary lifelong therapy.

So before sending, be able to finish this sentence: if it is positive I will <do X>; if it is negative I will <do Y>. If X and Y are the same, don't send it. The two answers that legitimately justify testing are “it will change whether or how long I anticoagulate” and “it will trigger family counselling and screening”.

When to evaluate for thrombophilia — and note how closely this list mirrors the hereditary-bleeding features in Section 30:

  • Family history of clotting.
  • Young age — under 45 years.
  • Absence of risk factors — no recent surgery, long flight, or malignancy.
  • Recurrent thromboses.
  • Unusual location — upper extremity, mesenteric vessels, cerebral venous sinus.
  • Specific paediatric scenarios — single ventricle physiology, ventricular assist device evaluation.
⚠️ Why thrombophilia testing in the acute period is unreliable
SituationEffect on testing
PregnancyAlters multiple factor and protein levels
Acute period and inflammationElevated factor 8 and fibrinogen
HeparinDecreases antithrombin III levels
WarfarinDecreases protein C and protein S levels
The thrombosis itselfAntithrombin III and proteins C and S may be consumed by the clot
Lupus anticoagulantMay be transient — hence the 12-week repeat requirement

Genetic testing is the one exception. Factor V Leiden and prothrombin G20210A may be run at any time — DNA does not change with acute illness or drugs — and only ever need running once. It is expensive, and the answer will never change.

The recommendation for everything else: wait several months after the thrombotic episode, and if possible, off anticoagulation.

🩺 Diagnosing the clot itself — what this lecture gives you, and what it does not

This lecture supplies the pre-test probability half of the deep vein thrombosis workup: Virchow's triad, the transient/persistent/inherited risk-factor table, the dependent-site rule, and the D-dimer as a marker of clot turnover (Section 29) that rises whenever fibrin is being formed and broken down.

What it does not supply is the formal diagnostic algorithm — a validated clinical decision rule, the D-dimer's role as a rule-out in low-probability patients, compression ultrasonography, or CT pulmonary angiography for suspected embolism. That part of objective 15 is still pending a dedicated lecture, and is flagged as partial in the coverage map for that reason.

🔑 The lecture's closing summary
  • Several abnormalities increase thrombosis risk: decreased anticoagulant proteins (antithrombin, proteins C and S) and increased procoagulant proteins (mutated factor 5, prothrombin overexpression, increased factor 8).
  • Diagnosis in the acute period may be difficult.
  • Before testing for thrombophilia, consider whether the patient has other clotting risk factors — cancer, obesity, immobility.
  • A variety of blood clotting medications are available. Therapy length should be based on risk factors and risk of recurrence, not on the presence of a thrombophilia alone.

Q: A post-operative patient on unfractionated heparin has a platelet count fall from 240,000 to 85,000/µL on day 7, and develops a new deep vein thrombosis. What is the 4T score, and what are the two most important immediate actions?

Answer

4T score = 8, high probability. Thrombocytopenia: a > 50% fall with a nadir between 20 and 100 × 10⁹/L — 2 points. Timing: clear onset on day 7, within the 5–10 day window — 2 points. Thrombosis: new thrombosis — 2 points. Other cause: none evident — 2 points.

Two immediate actions: (1) stop all heparin, including flushes and heparin-bonded lines, and (2) start an alternative anticoagulant — argatroban. Send heparin–PF4 antibodies, but do not wait for the result to act.

Do not switch to low-molecular-weight heparin (cross-reactivity), do not start warfarin alone (gangrene risk from the early protein C drop), and do not simply stop anticoagulation because the platelets are low.

Q: A 28-year-old woman has a deep vein thrombosis two weeks after starting a combined oral contraceptive. Testing while she is on heparin shows a low antithrombin III level and heterozygous factor V Leiden. How should you interpret these results, and how long should she be treated?

Answer

The antithrombin result is uninterpretable. Heparin decreases antithrombin III levels, and antithrombin can also be consumed by the acute thrombosis itself. It must be repeated several months later, off anticoagulation.

The factor V Leiden result is valid, because genetic testing may be run at any time. But heterozygous factor V Leiden carries a relative risk of only 3–5× — far less than an anticoagulant-protein deficiency at 15–19× — and roughly 5% of Caucasians carry it.

Duration is set by the circumstances of the clot, not the genotype. The oral contraceptive is a minor reversible risk factor, giving about a 5% recurrence risk in the first year. Standard-duration treatment with removal of the trigger (stopping the contraceptive) is appropriate; the factor V Leiden result does not by itself justify indefinite anticoagulation.

Q: Given that roughly 25% of the general population has some thrombophilia, why is finding one in a patient with a provoked clot rarely useful?

Answer

Because a finding that common has poor specificity — with a quarter of everyone carrying something, a positive result is close to expected and does not establish causation for this clot.

More decisively, the result does not change management. Duration of anticoagulation is driven by the recurrence risk, which is set by the circumstances: 3% after a major transient risk factor, 5% after a minor reversible one, 10% for unprovoked or persistent risk. A provoked clot sits in the low-risk group whether or not factor V Leiden is present.

This is exactly why the lecture insists on asking first how a positive result will be used. If the answer is “it will not change therapy”, the remaining justification is family counselling — and that is a separate discussion, best had months later and off anticoagulation.

Q: A patient is started on low-molecular-weight heparin. The house officer orders a daily aPTT and is puzzled that it is normal. What has gone wrong, and what should be measured instead?

Answer

The aPTT is the wrong test for a low-molecular-weight heparin, and a normal result does not mean the patient is under-anticoagulated.

The mechanism is chain length. To inactivate thrombin, antithrombin and thrombin must be bridged together, and only a long heparin tail can provide that bridge. To inactivate factor 10a, no bridge is needed — a short chain is enough. So low-molecular-weight heparins have a strong anti-factor-10a effect and a weak anti-thrombin effect, and the aPTT, which senses the thrombin effect, has little to detect.

Most patients on low-molecular-weight heparin need no monitoring at all — that predictability is the point of the drug. When monitoring is genuinely indicated (pregnancy, obesity, renal impairment), measure anti-factor 10a activity: 0.5–1.0 U/mL for twice-daily dosing, 1.0–2.0 U/mL for once-daily.

LO 63LO 66Source: Lymph Node — Normal Architecture & Reactive Lymphadenopathy (Sirotnikov)

Section 35 · Lymph node pathology

The Normal Lymph Node, and the Benign Mimics of Lymphoma

Before you can call a node abnormal you have to know exactly what a normal one looks like — which zone holds which cell, and why a reactive node can look alarming and still be benign. Nearly every high-yield fact here exists because it separates a benign process from a lymphoma.

Abbreviations used in this section LN lymph node · LAD lymphadenopathy · GC germinal center — the reactive centre of a secondary follicle · FDC follicular dendritic cell · TBM tingible body macrophage — a macrophage full of apoptotic debris · IM infectious mononucleosis · EBV Epstein–Barr virus · HHV-8 human herpesvirus 8 · KFD Kikuchi–Fujimoto disease · HLH hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis · RDD Rosai–Dorfman disease · IHC immunohistochemistry · H&E hematoxylin and eosin · MPO myeloperoxidase · AFB acid-fast bacilli stain (mycobacteria) · GMS Grocott methenamine silver (fungi) · FISH fluorescence in situ hybridization · VDJ variable–diversity–joining gene segments · CHL classic Hodgkin lymphoma · FL follicular lymphoma · DLBCL diffuse large B-cell lymphoma · Emperipolesis intact cells passing through a histiocyte without being digested · Atretic shrunken / regressed
🧠 The organizing habit: blue versus pink at low power ★ HY

Before you go to high power, ask one question: where is it blue and where is it pink? Blue means lymphocytes — a dense population of small dark nuclei. Pink means something that is not lymphocytes: necrosis, fibrosis, histiocytes with abundant cytoplasm, or a carcinoma.

The distribution of blue and pink IS the pattern, and the pattern is what generates your differential. A pathologist who starts at 40× has already lost the architecture — the most informative thing on the slide.

Normal architecture — a filter with a fixed floor plan

Lymph enters through afferent lymphatics into the subcapsular sinus, percolates through the cortex and paracortex, and leaves through the efferent lymphatic at the hilum. Every zone houses a specific cell population — and every reactive or neoplastic pattern is simply one of those zones expanding.

🔵

Cortex — the B-cell zone

The outer rim, packed with follicles.

  • Primary follicles have no germinal center — a uniform ball of small naive B cells that has not yet met antigen.
  • Secondary follicles contain a reactive germinal center — the B cell has met antigen and the follicle has switched on.
  • Finding both in one node is normal, not a red flag — different lobules drain different tissue fields.
🔴

Paracortex — the T-cell zone

Also called the interfollicular or deep cortical area.

  • Predominantly small T lymphocytes.
  • Also histiocytes, dendritic cells, plasma cells and scattered activated immunoblasts.
  • Dendritic cells have pale chromatin, irregular contours, abundant cytoplasm — when they accumulate, the paracortex looks pale at low power.
  • Contains the high endothelial venules through which circulating lymphocytes enter.
🟩

Medulla — cords and vessels

The inner zone, toward the hilum.

  • Medullary cords (plasma cells and lymphocytes) alternating with medullary sinuses.
  • Where the draining vascular structures sit.
  • Neoplasms arise from any of these normal structures — which is why the map of the node doubles as a map of the lymphomas.
🔑 Two structural habits worth having

Always look for the capsule. A capsule with a subcapsular sinus underneath confirms you are looking at a lymph node rather than tonsil, MALT, spleen or thymus. It sounds trivial; it changes the entire differential.

The subcapsular sinus is where you hunt for metastasis. Lymph empties there first, so that is the first place tumor cells land. A small cohesive cluster sitting in a sinus is the earliest metastatic finding.

🩺 What the heterogeneity is telling you

In the low-power image the germinal centers vary in size and shape, some large and irregularly outlined. That heterogeneity is characteristic of reactive follicular hyperplasia. Follicular lymphoma tends toward the opposite: monotonous follicles of similar size, crowded back-to-back.

The germinal center — the most examinable structure in the node

A reactive germinal center at high power is “a scary image” — large cells, prominent nucleoli, brisk mitoses, apoptotic debris. It looks like a high-grade lymphoma and it is entirely normal. Knowing the features that certify it as reactive is what keeps you from over-calling.

Dark zone

centroblast-rich

Centroblasts: large activated cells — round nuclei, open vesicular chromatin, prominent nucleoli, brisk mitotic activity. Where somatic hypermutation happens, so also where cells fail and die.

Light zone

centrocyte-rich

Centrocytes: smaller cleaved cells being selected on affinity. Paler because the cells are smaller; holds the follicular dendritic cell meshwork.

Tingible body macrophages

the pale holes

Macrophages engulfing the apoptotic bodies of B cells that failed selection — the “starry sky”. Strong evidence of a reactive process.

Mantle zone

the rim

A cuff of small naive B cells. Well-defined in reactive follicles; attenuated or absent in follicular lymphoma.

Marginal zone

beyond the mantle

A paler outer rim of memory B cells with more abundant cytoplasm. The normal counterpart of marginal zone lymphoma.

Polarization

the architectural clue

A reactive germinal center is polarized — dark zone at one pole, light zone at the other. Follicular lymphoma loses polarization and looks uniform end to end.

FeatureReactive germinal centerFollicular lymphoma
Polarization (dark/light zone)PresentLost — uniform cell population
Tingible body macrophagesNumerousAbsent
Mantle zoneWell definedAttenuated or absent
Spacing of folliclesVaried size, separated by paracortexMonotonous, back-to-back, effacing the paracortex
BCL2 immunostain ⭐NEGATIVE in the germinal centerPOSITIVE in the neoplastic follicles
Ki-67 proliferation indexHigh and polarized — higher in the dark zoneOften lower and non-polarized
🧠 Why BCL2 is negative in a normal germinal center — the logic, not the fact ★ HY

BCL2 is an anti-apoptotic protein. The whole purpose of the germinal center is somatic hypermutation followed by ruthless selection: B cells randomly mutate their immunoglobulin variable regions, and the ones whose receptors got worse must die. To make that possible, normal germinal center B cells switch BCL2 OFF — they are deliberately kept easy to kill. That is why the tingible body macrophages have so much to eat.

Follicular lymphoma arises when t(14;18) puts BCL2 (chromosome 18) under the immunoglobulin heavy chain promoter (chromosome 14), forcing BCL2 back on. The cells become unkillable and accumulate. So a BCL2-positive germinal center is the single most useful stain here — and the reason is mechanistic, not arbitrary.

🩺 Ki-67 across the lymphoid differential

Ki-67 labels every cell not in G0. Its value here is comparative:

  • Reactive germinal center: brisk, and polarized — visibly higher in the centroblast-rich dark zone. That gradient is itself reassuring.
  • Mantle cell lymphoma and most indolent B-cell lymphomas (including marginal zone): low Ki-67.
  • Burkitt lymphoma: over 95% — essentially every cell cycling.

Lymphoid development — why the normal map predicts the lymphomas

Every lymphoid neoplasm recapitulates the phenotype of the normal cell it came from. Know where a normal cell lives and which markers it carries, and you can predict where its tumor will present and what the flow cytometry will show.

🧬

Antigen-INdependent development

Largely fetal, neonatal and childhood. Does not require ever having seen a foreign antigen.

  • B cells: in the bone marrow. Stem cell → pro-B → pre-B → immature B → mature naive B.
  • T cells: in the thymus. Marrow stem cell migrates → T-cell receptor rearrangement → selection → mature naive T cell.
  • This is where the precursor (lymphoblastic) neoplasms arise — which is why B-lymphoblastic leukemia fills the marrow and T-lymphoblastic lymphoma presents as a mediastinal mass.
🎯

Antigen-DEPENDENT development

In secondary lymphoid tissue — the lymph node — after the naive cell meets its antigen.

  • Naive B cells undergo the germinal center reaction.
  • Naive T cells blast-transform into CD4 helper or CD8 cytotoxic effectors, plus memory cells.
  • This is where the peripheral (mature) lymphomas arise — follicular, Burkitt, DLBCL, marginal zone, peripheral T-cell.
🔑 Why so many B-cell translocations involve chromosome 14 ★ HY

The germinal center B cell deliberately breaks and re-joins DNA at the immunoglobulin loci during class switch recombination and somatic hypermutation (and earlier, during VDJ recombination in the marrow). These are controlled double-strand breaks — but an error can join an oncogene to the transcriptionally hyperactive immunoglobulin heavy chain promoter, which then drives it permanently.

That single mechanism explains t(14;18) BCL2 in follicular lymphoma, t(8;14) MYC in Burkitt, and t(11;14) cyclin D1 in mantle cell lymphoma.

⚠️ The double-positive stage — a normal-development fact with a diagnostic payoff

Developing thymocytes normally express BOTH CD4 and CD8 before committing to one lineage. No mature peripheral T cell does this. So when flow cytometry on a mediastinal mass shows a population co-expressing CD4 and CD8, you are looking at cells frozen at a thymic stage — a strong pointer to T-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma.

Normal counterpartWhere it livesNeoplasm(s)Practical consequence
B-cell precursorBone marrowB-lymphoblastic leukemia / lymphomaMarrow replacement, ± circulating blasts
T-cell precursorThymusT-lymphoblastic leukemia / lymphomaMediastinal mass; may co-express CD4 and CD8
Mature naive B cell (pre-germinal center)Mantle zone and circulationCLL/SLL, mantle cell lymphomaBoth are CD5 positive, CD10 negative
Germinal center B cellThe follicleFollicular, Burkitt, many DLBCLAll are CD10 positive, BCL6 positive — the germinal centre signature
Marginal zone / memory B cellMarginal zone; extranodal mucosaMarginal zone lymphoma (nodal, splenic, MALT)CD5 negative AND CD10 negative — partly a diagnosis of exclusion
Plasma cellBone marrow, beside the vesselsMyeloma, Waldenström / lymphoplasmacytic lymphomaDisease is caused by the secreted immunoglobulin, not the mass
Mature peripheral T cellParacortex; skinPeripheral T-cell lymphomas, mycosis fungoidesNode shows paracortical expansion rather than follicles

Handling the specimen, and what the site already tells you

⚠️ Formalin is a one-way door ★ HY

Once tissue goes into formalin, flow cytometry and conventional cytogenetics are no longer possible. Flow needs a viable single-cell suspension; karyotype needs living cells that can be driven into metaphase. IHC, FISH and most molecular studies (PCR, NGS) still work on fixed paraffin tissue — but flow and karyotype are lost forever. That is exactly why the protocol triages fresh tissue first.

Touch preparations exploit the fact that lymphocytes are discohesive — tap the cut surface against a slide and they transfer readily. A rapid read of that imprint drives every subsequent decision while the tissue is still fresh.

What you see on the touch imprintWhat you start worrying about
Sheets of immature cells (blasts)Lymphoblastic leukemia / lymphoma
Scattered large atypical cells in a MIXED backgroundHodgkin lymphoma
Sheets of large atypical cellsDiffuse large B-cell lymphoma
Very large, bizarre, cohesive-looking cellsAnaplastic large cell lymphoma — and in adults, metastatic carcinoma or melanoma

Cervical, generally

think infection first

The commonest cause of cervical lymphadenopathy overall is reactive / infectious.

Anterior cervical

mononucleosis

Infectious mononucleosis and other viral pharyngitides.

Posterior cervical

toxoplasmosis

Classically toxoplasmosis; also mononucleosis and Kikuchi–Fujimoto disease.

Supraclavicular — hard and fixed

the worrying one

Hodgkin lymphoma especially, but also metastatic carcinoma from an intrathoracic or intra-abdominal primary. Malignant until proven otherwise — fixation implies extracapsular extension.

Axillary and mesenteric

non-Hodgkin

Non-Hodgkin lymphoma characteristically involves these; Hodgkin rarely involves mesenteric nodes.

Mediastinal

Hodgkin

Particularly nodular sclerosis. Also primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma and T-lymphoblastic lymphoma in the young.

🩺 MIAMI — a workable way to think broadly without a list
  • M — Malignancies: lymphomas, leukemias, metastases, Kaposi sarcoma, skin neoplasms.
  • I — Infections: bacterial (cat-scratch, tularemia, syphilis), granulomatous (TB, histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis), viral (EBV, CMV, HIV, adenovirus, rubella), other (fungal, Lyme, toxoplasmosis).
  • A — Autoimmune: rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, Sjögren, dermatomyositis, Still disease.
  • M — Miscellaneous: Castleman, Kikuchi, Kimura, sarcoidosis, histiocytoses, Kawasaki.
  • I — Iatrogenic: medications, serum sickness.

Then narrow by site, exposures and history. Tenderness generally favors inflammation (rapid capsular stretch); painless, hard, matted nodes favor neoplasm.

The pattern-based approach — the core method

🔑 The pattern is the question; the stains are the answer

Rather than trying to recall every entity that can involve a node, read the low-power architecture, decide which pattern you are in, and inherit a differential of two or three — which stains then settle.

For each pattern, hold one idea: every benign pattern has a malignant counterpart that produces the same low-power look. The pattern tells you which pair you are choosing between. It is not a classification scheme — it is a way of framing the actual decision.

✅

Pattern 1, follicular — favors reactive hyperplasia

  • Germinal centers of varying size and shape
  • Follicles not back-to-back — paracortex still visible between them
  • Tingible body macrophages present; polarization preserved
  • BCL2 negative within germinal centers
⚠️

Pattern 1, follicular — favors follicular lymphoma

  • Monotonous follicles, back-to-back, effacing the paracortex
  • No tingible body macrophages; polarization lost
  • Attenuated or absent mantle zones
  • BCL2 positive within the follicles; t(14;18) on molecular testing
🩺 Stain anyway — and correlate with the history

However benign it looks, you still stain and still correlate. A reactive-appearing follicular pattern in a 68-year-old with widespread painless lymphadenopathy is a different proposition from the same picture in a 6-year-old with a sore throat.

🧠 Patterns 2 and 3 — what expands the paracortex, and the trap
  • Paracortical T-cell hyperplasia with increased dendritic cells → dermatopathic lymphadenopathy, the reactive node draining chronically inflamed skin. This matters enormously in mycosis fungoides, where a dermatopathic node must be distinguished from true nodal involvement — because that distinction changes the stage.
  • Numerous eosinophils in this pattern → Kimura disease (recognize by name only).
  • Diffuse pattern with numerous immunoblasts → benign consideration is infectious mononucleosis; sheets of large cells throughout → DLBCL.
  • The trap: mixed cellularity classic Hodgkin lymphoma characteristically expands the interfollicular zone while leaving reactive follicles standing — which is why it is the hardest subtype to separate from a reactive paracortical process. Other malignant counterparts: peripheral T-cell lymphoma, angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma.

Sinus histiocytosis

normal reactive

Mild expansion of subcapsular and medullary sinuses by bland histiocytes. A normal phenomenon, not a disease.

Rosai–Dorfman disease

the neoplastic version

Same compartment, massively expanded sinuses and enlarged nodes. S100 positive, buzzword emperipolesis.

Hemophagocytosis

debris inside histiocytes

Histiocytes containing engulfed red cells, apoptotic bodies and degenerated cells. Distinct from emperipolesis.

Metastatic carcinoma

the one you must exclude

Tumor arrives via afferent lymphatics into the subcapsular sinus. Cohesive clusters in a sinus are the earliest deposit.

Anaplastic large cell lymphoma

the mimic

Can grow in a sinusoidal distribution, looking cohesive and epithelioid — a classic mimic of metastatic carcinoma or melanoma in adults. Needs CD30.

Castleman-type change

pattern 6

Kept separate because these follicles look nothing like hyperplastic ones: small atretic follicles of dendritic cells, onion-skinning, and a penetrating vessel.

Pattern 5 findingThinkWhat to do next
Non-necrotizing granulomas, asteroid bodiesSarcoidosisStill exclude infection — sarcoid is a diagnosis of exclusion
Necrotizing granulomasMycobacterial or fungalAFB (mycobacteria stain red) and GMS (fungi stain black)
Suppurative, STELLATE granulomas with numerous neutrophilsCat-scratch disease (Bartonella henselae)Serology; Warthin–Starry silver stain — see the Bartonella section
Necrosis with abundant nuclear debris and NO neutrophilsKikuchi–Fujimoto diseaseCD68 and MPO on the histiocytes; exclude lupus
Necrosis with any large atypical cells nearbyHodgkin lymphoma can necrose tooAlways look for Reed–Sternberg cells before settling on an infectious cause
⚠️ The departmental reflex when a node shows necrosis

When you see necrosis in a lymph node, do an AFB and a GMS. Mycobacteria stain red on acid-fast staining; Grocott methenamine silver stains fungi black. And separately: necrosis does not exclude Hodgkin lymphoma — hunt for Reed–Sternberg cells at the edge of the necrotic zone.

Infectious mononucleosis — the most dangerous benign mimic of Hodgkin lymphoma ★ HY

EBV infection of B cells with a massive reactive T-cell response. Benign and self-limited — and it contains large atypical cells that can be CD30 positive with weak PAX5, exactly the Hodgkin profile.

🔑 The clinical triad — present in more than 50%

Fever · pharyngitis · cervical or generalized lymphadenopathy. Add splenomegaly and profound fatigue and the picture is essentially made. Blood count classically shows lymphocytosis with > 10% atypical lymphocytes.

Duncan syndrome (X-linked lymphoproliferative disease), from a mutation in the SAP gene: affected boys cannot control EBV, and a trivial first exposure can cause fulminant mononucleosis, HLH, or lymphoma.

🩺 The pathology, and the one architectural point that matters most
  • Gross: moderately enlarged node.
  • Architecture distorted but INTACT or only PARTIALLY effaced — this is the key architectural point separating it from lymphoma.
  • Three changes together: paracortical hyperplasia (most prominent), follicular hyperplasia, and sinus histiocytosis.
  • The paracortex holds a polymorphous mixture: small and larger lymphocytes, immunoblasts, histiocytes, plasma cells.
  • Patchy pale areas give the classic “mottled” low-power appearance. Focal necrosis can be present.
  • Occasional very large mono- or polynucleated cells with prominent nucleoli — the Reed–Sternberg-like cells.
FeatureInfectious mononucleosisClassic Hodgkin lymphoma
ArchitectureIntact or partially effaced, with follicular hyperplasia and paracortical expansionEffaced or partially effaced; the mixed cellularity subtype can be interfollicular — which is what makes it tricky
Atypical cellsPolymorphous: small lymphocytes, plasma cells, immunoblasts and RS-like cells — a spectrum of sizesBona fide Reed–Sternberg cells and variants standing out from a polymorphous background
NucleoliMore basophilic (blue-grey)Well-rounded, cherry-red macronucleoli with a perinuclear halo
CD20 ⭐POSITIVE in the large cellsNEGATIVE
OCT2 ⭐POSITIVENEGATIVE or inconsistently expressed
PAX5Retained at normal intensityWEAK compared with background B cells
CD30Can be positive — an activation marker, not a lymphoma markerStrong and uniform, membranous with Golgi accentuation
CD15NegativePositive in ~75%; co-expression with CD30 is helpful
EBVPositive — expected, this is the causeAlso can be positive — so EBV alone does not settle it
🪝 The single sentence that resolves it

The RS-like cells of infectious mononucleosis RETAIN their B-cell program; the Reed–Sternberg cells of classic Hodgkin lymphoma have LOST theirs.

Everything else — CD30, EBV positivity, large cells in a mixed background — is shared between the two and therefore cannot decide the case. CD20 and OCT2 are the discriminating stains. Using CD30 to call Hodgkin lymphoma in a mononucleosis node is one of the classic ways to make a catastrophic error.

Kikuchi–Fujimoto disease — necrosis without neutrophils

A benign, self-limited necrotizing lymphadenitis that at high power can look like a high-grade lymphoma or even histiocytic sarcoma. The two facts that save you are the absence of neutrophils and the MPO-positive, crescent-shaped histiocytes.

🔑 The clinical profile that appears in question stems
  • Young adults; women more than men; more common in Asian populations — the stem is usually a young Asian woman.
  • Cervical nodes, typically unilateral, mildly enlarged and often tender.
  • Fever, weight loss, night sweats, skin rash, sore throat, arthromyalgias — a B-symptom-like picture, which is exactly what makes lymphoma the clinical worry.
  • Does not respond to antibiotics — a common feature of the presenting history.
  • Self-limited with spontaneous remission — which is why the diagnosis matters so much: the alternative diagnoses lead to chemotherapy.
🧠 The pathology, and the three phases
  • Paracortical process with partially preserved architecture.
  • Necrosis and single-cell apoptosis are prominent, with abundant nuclear debris. The necrosis is eosinophilic — hence the low-power pink zones against blue preserved node.
  • Crescent-shaped (C-shaped) histiocyte nuclei — the morphologic signature. Note they are non-phagocytic.
  • ABSENCE OF NEUTROPHILS (and of eosinophils) — the finding that separates it from suppurative infectious causes such as cat-scratch disease, which is full of neutrophils.
  • Immunophenotype: histiocytes are CD68 positive AND myeloperoxidase positive; CD8 T cells predominate; very few B cells. Clonality studies show no monoclonality.

Three phases: proliferative (~5%, plasmacytoid dendritic cells and histiocytes, minimal necrosis) → necrotizing — the one to recognize → xanthomatous (~one third, lipid-laden macrophages appearing first at the margins).

⚠️ The differential that actually matters
  • Lupus lymphadenitis — the closest mimic: also necrotizing, also neutrophil-poor. Favor Kikuchi when the histiocytes are MPO positive; lupus classically shows hematoxylin bodies and abundant plasma cells. Always check the serology.
  • Suppurative / cat-scratch lymphadenitis — neutrophils present; cat-scratch shows stellate suppurative granulomas.
  • High-grade lymphoma — Kikuchi has no monoclonal population, and the atypical cells are histiocytes (CD68+/MPO+), not lymphoid.
  • Histiocytic sarcoma — Kikuchi histiocytes are cytologically bland and the process is partially architecture-preserving.
  • Mycobacterial / fungal — AFB and GMS; Kikuchi lacks granulomas.

Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis — where the pathologist supplies one criterion of eight

A sudden-onset systemic inflammatory response secondary to macrophage activation. Macrophages become uncontrolled, consume blood cells, and flood the body with cytokines. Diagnosis requires 5 of 8 criteria.

👶

Primary (familial) HLH

Occurs in infants, from inherited mutations in the granule-mediated cytotoxicity pathway.

🦠

Secondary (acquired) HLH

Triggered by infection — particularly EBV and CMV. Also with aggressive lymphomas and autoimmune disease, where it is called macrophage activation syndrome.

DomainFindings that count toward the diagnosis
ClinicalFever, splenomegaly, cytopenias
LaboratoryHigh ferritin (the one to remember), high triglycerides, LOW fibrinogen
PathologicHemophagocytic histiocytes in bone marrow, spleen or lymph node
⚠️ Hemophagocytosis is not specific — and that is the point

Hemophagocytic histiocytes are seen in many settings. Their value is that, in the right clinical and laboratory context, they satisfy ONE of the eight criteria. A pathologist reporting hemophagocytosis is contributing one line of evidence, not making a diagnosis. Do not let a stem convince you the marrow finding alone establishes HLH.

 HemophagocytosisEmperipolesis
What is inside the histiocyteDebris, apoptotic bodies and degenerated cells — the material is being destroyedIntact, VIABLE lymphocytes and plasma cells passing through — they are not being digested
Where you see itHLH (and reactive states)Rosai–Dorfman disease
Helper stainCD68 highlights the histiocyteS100 positive in the histiocyte, negative in the engulfed cells — a built-in negative control

Castleman disease — two buzzwords and one classification split

Uncommon (~6,500–7,700 new US cases/year). It is a disease of dendritic cells, which explains why its follicles look small, pale and atretic rather than hyperplastic.

🔢

Axis 1 — how many nodes?

  • Unicentric: a single node or closely related group. Usually curable by excision.
  • Multicentric (20–25%): multiple groups, systemic disease. Subdivided into HHV-8-associated (particularly in HIV), idiopathic multicentric, and syndrome-associated (POEMS, TAFRO).
🔬

Axis 2 — what does it look like?

  • Hyaline vascular variant — a benign neoplasm derived from lymph node stromal cells. The one with the classic morphology.
  • Plasma cell variant — sheets of plasma cells between follicles; more often with the systemic/multicentric presentations.
🔑 The morphologic buzzwords — hyaline vascular variant ★ HY
  • Hyalinization — very dense pink material around the vessels; the feature the variant is named for.
  • Atretic follicles — small, composed mainly of pale dendritic cells, a normal germinal centre constituent that here becomes the dominant population.
  • “Lollipop sign” — a penetrating blood vessel running into the atretic follicle.
  • Onion-skinning — mantle-zone lymphocytes in concentric rings.
  • “Twinning” — two germinal centers within one follicle.

Gross: a large, firm node, median 7 cm. Complication to know: the hyaline vascular variant is prone to developing FOLLICULAR DENDRITIC CELL SARCOMA — which follows logically once you accept this is a disease of dendritic cells.

Rosai–Dorfman disease — sinus histiocytosis with massive lymphadenopathy

The same compartment as ordinary reactive sinus histiocytosis, expanded to the point of producing bulky nodes. Now recognized as a histiocytic neoplasm, with MAP kinase pathway mutations in about a third of cases.

🔑 Distribution and associations
  • Lymph node involvement in 50–60%.
  • Extranodal sites in 30–40% — including skin and central nervous system.
  • 10% have an associated immunologic disorder. Can be associated with IgG4-related disease, can be familial, and can arise with or after other histiocytic diseases, lymphoma or leukemia.
  • Gross: large, matted nodes with capsular and pericapsular fibrosis.
🧠 S100 as its own negative control — the elegant bit

S100 stains the nucleus and cytoplasm of the neoplastic histiocytes but is negative in the lymphocytes and plasma cells they have engulfed. The engulfed cells therefore appear as clear, unstained holes inside a brown histiocyte — the stain highlights emperipolesis while simultaneously providing a built-in internal negative control.

Phenotype: S100 + · CD68 + · CD163 + · cyclin D1 + · OCT2 + · CD1a − · CD207 (langerin) −

⚠️ CD1a and CD207 negativity is what excludes Langerhans cell histiocytosis

Langerhans cell histiocytosis is also S100 positive, so S100 alone cannot separate them. Langerhans cells are CD1a positive and CD207 (langerin) positive; Rosai–Dorfman histiocytes are negative for both. Langerhans cell histiocytosis also shows grooved “coffee-bean” nuclei and eosinophils rather than emperipolesis.

Melanoma is the other S100-positive sinus mimic — but it is SOX10 positive, CD68 negative, and has no emperipolesis.

Genetics and treatment: MAP kinase / ERK alterations (MAP2K1, NRAS, KRAS) in about one third — shared with the other histiocytic neoplasms, and what makes the disease targetable with MEK inhibitors. Spontaneous regression occurs and observation is often appropriate; relapsed disease gets steroids, chemotherapy, radiation or MEK inhibition.

Two worked cases — the method in action

🩺 Case 1 — a 28-year-old woman with a painful neck lump

Three weeks of fever to 102.5°F, extreme fatigue, and a progressively painful left neck lump. No response to 10 days of doxycycline. Evening fever spikes with chills and drenching night sweats. 5 lb weight loss. Exam: tender, mobile, firm left POSTERIOR cervical node, 3 × 2 cm. Labs: WBC 2.8 × 109/L with neutropenia and lymphopenia, hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL, normal platelets, elevated ESR and CRP, LDH 310 U/L; infectious and autoimmune workup negative.

Reading the stem before the slide: a posterior cervical node narrows to toxoplasmosis, mononucleosis or Kikuchi. Fever, night sweats and weight loss read like B symptoms and put lymphoma on the list. Failure of antibiotics argues against bacterial lymphadenitis. Cytopenias with a negative workup in a young woman → Kikuchi — but lymphoma has to be excluded on tissue.

🩺 Case 3 — a 15-year-old boy with sore throat and fatigue

Ten days of headache and myalgia progressing to high fever, severe sore throat and profound fatigue, with painful neck and axillary glands. Exam: 38.6°C, pharynx red with whitish-yellow tonsillar exudate, enlarged tender posterior cervical nodes, petechiae on the soft palate, spleen palpable 2 cm below the costal margin. Rapid strep negative; CBC shows leukocytosis with > 50% lymphocytes and > 10% atypical lymphocytes.

Q: A lymph node shows numerous follicles. The germinal centers contain many macrophages full of apoptotic debris, show a clear dark and light zone, and are surrounded by crisp mantle cuffs. BCL2 stains the mantle and paracortical lymphocytes but leaves the germinal centers blank. Diagnosis?

Answer

Reactive follicular hyperplasia. Four independent features all point the same way: tingible body macrophages present, polarization preserved, mantle zones intact, and BCL2 negative within the germinal centers.

The BCL2 pattern is the clincher — a positive germinal center would be the abnormal result, because normal germinal center B cells suppress BCL2 so that failed clones can undergo apoptosis. A BCL2-positive follicle means t(14;18) has forced it back on: follicular lymphoma.

Q: A 16-year-old has a cervical node with an expanded, mottled paracortex containing scattered very large binucleate cells with prominent nucleoli. They are CD30 positive, PAX5 positive at normal intensity, CD20 strongly positive, OCT2 positive, and EBV positive. Diagnosis?

Answer

Infectious mononucleosis — not Hodgkin lymphoma. CD30 positivity and EBV positivity are compatible with either and are therefore uninformative here.

What settles it is the retained B-cell program: strong CD20, positive OCT2, and normal-intensity PAX5. In classic Hodgkin lymphoma the Reed–Sternberg cells would be CD20 negative, OCT2 negative, and PAX5 weak relative to background B cells. The intact-to-partially-effaced architecture with follicular hyperplasia supports the reactive interpretation.

Q: If you could order only ONE immunostain to separate the large cells of infectious mononucleosis from Reed–Sternberg cells, which would it be — and why is CD30 the wrong choice?

Answer

CD20 (or equivalently OCT2). CD30 is an ACTIVATION marker, not a lineage or malignancy marker — it is expressed by normal activated lymphocytes, so the immunoblasts of infectious mononucleosis are frequently CD30 positive. Using CD30 to call Hodgkin lymphoma in a mononucleosis node is one of the classic ways to make a catastrophic error.

CD20 asks the question that actually differs between the two: is the B-cell program intact?

Q: A 26-year-old woman of Korean descent has a tender left cervical node, fever and night sweats that did not respond to antibiotics. The node shows patchy eosinophilic necrosis with abundant nuclear debris, crescent-shaped histiocytes, and no neutrophils. Diagnosis, the one serology you must send, and the treatment?

Answer

Kikuchi–Fujimoto disease (histiocytic necrotizing lymphadenitis). The absence of neutrophils despite necrosis is the discriminating morphologic finding.

Send serology for systemic lupus erythematosus — lupus lymphadenitis is the closest histologic mimic, and some patients later develop lupus. Treatment is supportive only: the disease is self-limited with spontaneous remission. Confirm with CD68 and myeloperoxidase positive histiocytes, predominant CD8 T cells, very few B cells.

Q: A lymph node shows markedly expanded sinuses filled with large histiocytes containing intact lymphocytes within their cytoplasm. They are S100 positive, CD68 positive, CD1a negative and CD207 negative. Name the finding, the diagnosis, and the two entities the phenotype excludes.

Answer

The finding is emperipolesis; the diagnosis is Rosai–Dorfman disease (sinus histiocytosis with massive lymphadenopathy).

The phenotype excludes Langerhans cell histiocytosis (which would be CD1a and CD207/langerin positive) and, with CD68 positivity and the morphology, metastatic melanoma (also S100 positive but SOX10 positive, CD68 negative, and without emperipolesis). Remember that S100 is negative in the engulfed cells, which is what makes the emperipolesis so conspicuous.

Q: A lymph node arrives fresh in the laboratory at 4 p.m. and the resident drops the entire specimen into formalin. Which studies has this made impossible, and why?

Answer

Flow cytometry and conventional cytogenetics (karyotype). Flow requires a viable single-cell suspension; conventional cytogenetics requires living cells that can be cultured and driven into metaphase. Formalin cross-links proteins and kills the cells, so both are lost.

Immunohistochemistry, FISH and most molecular studies (PCR, next-generation sequencing) still work on fixed paraffin-embedded tissue — but flow and karyotype are one-way doors. This is exactly why the protocol triages fresh tissue before fixation.

Q: A 14-year-old has a large anterior mediastinal mass and respiratory compromise. Flow cytometry shows an immature population co-expressing CD4 and CD8. Diagnosis, and what normal developmental fact explains it?

Answer

T-lymphoblastic lymphoma. The mass is in the mediastinum because that is where the thymus sits, and the thymus is where T cells undergo antigen-independent maturation.

The phenotype is explained by the fact that normal developing thymocytes pass through a DOUBLE-POSITIVE stage expressing both CD4 and CD8 before committing to a single lineage — the neoplasm is frozen at that stage, and no mature peripheral T cell does this. Note the naming logic too: “-oma” means mass, so the lymphoma form presents as the thymic mass while the leukemic form fills the marrow.

Q: A lymph node contains numerous small follicles with regressed germinal centers made largely of pale dendritic cells, surrounded by concentric rings of mantle lymphocytes, with hyalinized vessels running into them. Diagnosis, and what malignancy is this variant at risk of?

Answer

Hyaline vascular Castleman disease. Three buzzwords are present: atretic follicles composed of dendritic cells, onion-skinning of the mantle, and the lollipop sign (penetrating hyalinized vessel).

Because the underlying lesion is a benign neoplasm of lymph node stromal / dendritic cells, the variant is prone to developing follicular dendritic cell sarcoma. Also know the other axis: unicentric versus multicentric, and that multicentric disease may be HHV-8-associated (especially in HIV), idiopathic, or syndrome-associated (POEMS, TAFRO).

Q: A 4-month-old has fever, hepatosplenomegaly and pancytopenia. Ferritin 12,000 ng/mL, triglycerides elevated, fibrinogen low. Diagnosis, marrow finding, and what should be sought as a trigger?

Answer

Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. The marrow will show hemophagocytic histiocytes containing engulfed red cells, nucleated red cells and cellular debris.

In an infant, suspect the primary/familial form from an inherited mutation in the granule-mediated cytotoxicity pathway — but you must still hunt for a trigger, classically EBV or CMV. The three laboratory findings given (high ferritin, high triglycerides, low fibrinogen) plus fever, splenomegaly and cytopenias is already most of the way to 5 of 8 criteria.

Q: Why is the diffuse/paracortical pattern the one that most often causes serious diagnostic trouble?

Answer

Because its benign entity and its malignant entity look genuinely alike. Infectious mononucleosis produces paracortical hyperplasia with numerous immunoblasts, some so large and nucleolated they are called Reed–Sternberg-LIKE cells. Classic Hodgkin lymphoma — particularly mixed cellularity — also expands the interfollicular zone and contains scattered large cells in a mixed background.

The resolution is immunophenotypic: the large cells of mononucleosis retain their B-cell program (CD20 and OCT2 positive), while Reed–Sternberg cells have lost it (CD20 and OCT2 negative).

LO 6LO 58Source: Introduction to Hematologic Malignancy

Section 36 · Hematologic malignancy · the frame

The Core Construct, and the Acute Leukemia Emergencies

One idea organizes every blood cancer: a cell somewhere along the path from pluripotent stem cell to fully differentiated cell acquires a mutation — and where on that path it happens determines which disease you get, and how fast it will kill.

Abbreviations used in this section AML acute myeloid leukemia · ALL acute lymphoblastic leukemia · APL acute promyelocytic leukemia · MDS myelodysplastic syndrome · MPN myeloproliferative neoplasm · DIC disseminated intravascular coagulation · TLS tumour lysis syndrome · Blast an immature, undifferentiated precursor cell · Indolent slow-growing · Pluripotent stem cell the earliest marrow cell, able to become any blood cell · Progeny the descendant cells of a dividing cell · ANC absolute neutrophil count
🔑 The principal construct ★ HY

A hematopoietic cell in the bone marrow or lymph system acquires a mutation, or a series of mutations, that disrupts the differentiation and maturation of its progeny. The resulting disease depends on the maturation stage of the cell that undergoes transformation:

  • Less differentiated → AGGRESSIVE
  • More differentiated → INDOLENT

Note the phrase of its progeny. The mutated cell itself is not usually the problem — the problem is that everything descended from it is frozen at a stage where it should not be, and keeps dividing.

The map — two lineages across, differentiation stage along each ★ HY

LineageAggressive (less differentiated)IntermediateIndolent / normally differentiated
MYELOIDAcute myeloid leukemia — over 20% blastsMyelodysplastic syndrome — abnormal differentiation, a disruption in maturationPolycythemia vera · essential thrombocythemia · myelofibrosis · chronic myeloid leukemia
LYMPHOIDAcute lymphoblastic leukemia · Burkitt lymphoma · diffuse large B-cell lymphoma—Follicular lymphoma · chronic lymphocytic leukemia / small lymphocytic lymphoma · marginal zone lymphoma · lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma
PLASMA CELL——Multiple myeloma — a fully mature plasma cell

Read left to right and the tempo changes from weeks (acute leukemia) to years or decades (myeloma, follicular lymphoma).

🧠 Why myeloma sits at the far right

The plasma cell is the fully differentiated end-point of the B-cell lineage — an antibody factory and nothing else. A cancer of that cell keeps doing what plasma cells do: it makes a single antibody in enormous quantity (the monoclonal protein). It does not blast the marrow the way an acute leukemia does.

That is why multiple myeloma is a chronic disease measured in years, and why its complications — kidney failure from light chains, bone lesions, hypercalcemia — come from the product of the cell rather than from its proliferation.

The darkest corollary runs the other way: in the very least differentiated cancers you can get an acute leukemia with both myeloid and lymphoid features — transformation before the myeloid/lymphoid branch point — and the prognosis is correspondingly dismal.

🪝 Memory hook — differentiation is a one-way street

A highly specialized cell can never go back and become something else. A cancer arising early on that street therefore inherits the proliferative capacity of an undifferentiated cell. That single fact is why acute leukemias are aggressive and plasma cell disorders are chronic — and it makes the whole taxonomy predictable rather than a list to memorize.

Acute leukemia — the defining features ★ HY

  • Unregulated growth of undifferentiated cells in the marrow called blasts.
  • Cells rapidly overwhelm the marrow and spill out into the peripheral blood.
  • Diagnosis requires more than 20% blasts in the bone marrow OR the peripheral blood. Either compartment suffices. Memorize this number — it is also the line that separates myelodysplastic syndrome and chronic myeloid leukemia blast phase from acute leukemia.
  • May have a high, normal, or LOW white blood cell count at presentation. A normal white count does not exclude acute leukemia.
  • Universally present with bone marrow failure — anemia, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia.
  • Rapidly fatal: untreated, death within 12 weeks in most cases.
🩺 The presenting vignette, and why every element points one way

A 57-year-old previously healthy woman with 3 weeks of progressive malaise and spontaneous bruising. Pulse 110, pallor, scattered ecchymoses. White cells 87,000 · hemoglobin 6.2 · platelets 45,000 · neutrophils 0.6 with 90% blasts.

The white count is enormous but she is functionally neutropenic — the cells are all blasts, which do nothing. She is anemic, thrombocytopenic and neutropenic simultaneously: trilineage marrow failure with a packed marrow, which is the signature of acute leukemia.

“Extinguish the fire” — the initial management

  1. Treat the marrow failure — transfusion support. Transfuse for hemoglobin below 7, platelets below 10,000 — or below 50,000 if actively bleeding. Identify and treat infection, which in a neutropenic patient is the thing most likely to kill them this week.
  2. Buy time — control the unchecked white cell growth. Hydroxyurea. This is cytoreduction, not cure — it holds the count down while the diagnostic workup proceeds and definitive therapy is arranged.

The two metabolic emergencies ★ HY

🩸

Disseminated intravascular coagulation

Uncontrolled intravascular consumption of clotting factors.

  • Low fibrinogen
  • High partial thromboplastin time and prothrombin time
  • Low platelets
  • Accompanied by thrombotic microangiopathy — hemolysis with schistocytes on the smear

Most strongly associated with acute promyelocytic leukemia, where it is the cause of early death.

💥

Tumour lysis syndrome

Rapid cell turnover and death releasing intracellular contents. Four derangements, each with its own treatment:

  • Hyperuricemia → renal failure. Prevention: allopurinol. Severe: rasburicase
  • Hyperphosphatemia
  • Hypocalcemia — may need calcium replacement
  • Hyperkalemia → arrhythmia. Treatment: sodium polystyrene

Watch for it in acute leukemias and aggressive lymphomas — particularly Burkitt — either spontaneously or on starting treatment.

🔑 The tumour lysis pattern in one line

Everything goes UP except calcium. Potassium up, phosphate up, uric acid up, calcium down — because the released phosphate binds and precipitates the calcium. If a question lists three highs and one low in a patient starting chemotherapy, this is the diagnosis.

Note the discrimination against DIC: DIC is a coagulopathy (low fibrinogen, prolonged times, schistocytes); tumour lysis is metabolic. They are both emergencies of the first week, and they are not the same problem.

🧠 Grade and stage — how they change prognosis and treatment

In hematolymphoid neoplasms, “grade” is essentially the aggressive/indolent axis of the core construct, and it inverts the usual intuition about what a bad diagnosis means:

  • High-grade / aggressive disease kills in 3–6 months untreated — but is treated with curative intent, because rapidly dividing cells are exactly what chemotherapy kills.
  • Low-grade / indolent disease is compatible with decades of life — but is not curable by standard therapy, because most cells are never cycling when the drug is present. A third of follicular lymphoma patients are never treated at all.

Stage (Ann Arbor) behaves differently in each: advanced stage drives urgency in aggressive lymphoma, while indolent lymphoma is usually stage III/IV at diagnosis and that fact alone changes nothing. Molecular findings can outweigh clinical stage entirely — a double hit lymphoma does worse than the highest clinical risk score.

Q: A patient presents with a white cell count of 87,000, of which 90% are blasts, plus anemia and thrombocytopenia. Absolute neutrophil count is 0.6. Why is this patient at high risk of infection despite a white count of 87,000?

Answer

Because blasts are non-functional. The white count measures cells, not function — the patient is functionally neutropenic with an absolute neutrophil count of 0.6 despite a hugely elevated total. Identifying and treating infection is one of the two immediate priorities, alongside transfusion support.

Q: Two days after starting induction chemotherapy, a patient has potassium 6.4, phosphate 7.1, calcium 6.8 and uric acid 14. Name the syndrome and give the treatment for each abnormality.

Answer

Tumour lysis syndrome. Hyperuricemia → allopurinol for prevention, rasburicase if severe (it degrades existing urate rather than merely blocking production); this is the abnormality that causes renal failure. Hyperkalemia → sodium polystyrene, with urgent attention because of arrhythmia risk. Hyperphosphatemia drives the hypocalcemia, which may need calcium replacement.

Q: Two patients transform at different points in the B-cell lineage. One develops Burkitt lymphoma, the other multiple myeloma. Using only the core construct, predict the difference in tempo and explain why.

Answer

Burkitt lymphoma is highly aggressive; multiple myeloma is chronic. Burkitt arises from a less differentiated B cell, which retains enormous proliferative capacity — it is one of the fastest-growing human tumours. Myeloma arises from the fully differentiated plasma cell, whose job is secretion rather than division, so the disease is measured in years and its damage comes from the monoclonal protein and light chains rather than from raw growth.

LO 39LO 54LO 80LO 82Source: Introduction to Hematologic Malignancy

Section 37 · Hematologic malignancy · myeloid, acute

Acute Myeloid Leukemia — and Its One Curable Variant

The disease you stabilize first and subtype second — except for one variant, where you must start the treatment before the diagnosis is confirmed, because the coagulopathy kills before the cytogenetics come back.

Abbreviations used in this section AML acute myeloid leukemia · APL acute promyelocytic leukemia · ATRA all-trans retinoic acid, a vitamin A derivative that forces differentiation · PML-RARA the fusion gene of t(15;17), joining the promyelocytic leukemia gene to the retinoic acid receptor alpha gene · Flow cytometry a laser-based technique identifying cell surface antigens, used to assign lineage · 7 + 3 7 days of cytarabine infusion plus 3 days of an anthracycline · Anthracycline daunorubicin or idarubicin · CR complete remission · Allo-SCT allogeneic stem cell transplant, using donor stem cells · Hypomethylating agent decitabine or azacitidine · Cytogenetics analysis of chromosome structure · Performance status a standardized measure of how much a patient can do for themselves
DomainWhat to know
DiagnosisBone marrow biopsy and aspirate showing more than 20% blasts, with myeloid cell surface antigens on flow cytometry. Flow cytometry is what assigns lineage — blast morphology alone will not
Risk factorsPrior cytotoxic chemotherapy · a history of myelodysplastic syndrome or a myeloproliferative disorder · Down syndrome. Note that two of the three are iatrogenic or antecedent hematologic disease — this is often a second cancer
Prognostic featuresAge · performance status · comorbidities · prior cytotoxic chemotherapy or radiation · antecedent myeloid disorders · cytogenetic and molecular findings. The last stratifies patients into high, intermediate and low risk — and that stratification decides who gets a transplant

Treatment — two intents, decided by fitness rather than by age alone

🎯

Curative intent — younger / fit

Induction: “7 + 3” — daunorubicin or idarubicin plus cytarabine. Requires at least a 3–4 week hospitalization. The goal is complete remission.

Consolidation: more intensive chemotherapy. Allogeneic stem cell transplant for intermediate or high risk disease.

🤝

Palliative intent — older / unfit

Hypomethylating agent — decitabine or azacitidine — with or without venetoclax.

Supportive care: transfusions, antibiotics, hospice.

The choice between columns turns on whether the patient can survive a month of marrow aplasia in hospital, not simply on a birthday.

⚠️ Acute promyelocytic leukemia — the one you must not miss ★ HY

A biologically and genetically distinct variant of acute myeloid leukemia, and the single highest-yield disease in this section.

  • Translocation t(15;17) → the PML-RARA fusion gene.
  • Severe disseminated intravascular coagulation causes early death from bleeding in unrecognized cases. The patient does not die of the leukemia — they die of hemorrhage, often within days, often before the diagnosis is confirmed.
  • Treat with all-trans retinoic acid, which does not kill the cells but forces the arrested promyelocytes to differentiate — the purest possible illustration of the core construct.
  • 90% overall survival. This transforms the most rapidly lethal leukemia into the most curable one — but only if it is recognized.

The practical rule: in a new acute leukemia with a coagulopathy, start all-trans retinoic acid on suspicion, before the cytogenetics come back. The cost of being wrong is small; the cost of waiting is a fatal bleed.

🧠 Why differentiation therapy is the perfect proof of the core construct

The lecture's central idea is that disease arises from arrested differentiation. All-trans retinoic acid does not poison the cell — it releases the block, and the promyelocytes mature into cells that then die naturally. A drug that cures a cancer without conventional cytotoxicity is only conceivable if the disease was a maturation problem in the first place.

🩺 Complications of acute leukemia — what actually kills, and when
  • Week one: infection in a functionally neutropenic patient; hemorrhage from thrombocytopenia or DIC (above all in APL); tumour lysis syndrome on starting treatment.
  • During induction: a month of profound marrow aplasia — neutropenic sepsis, transfusion dependence, mucositis.
  • Longer term: relapse; graft-versus-host disease after allogeneic transplant; and, for survivors of prior cytotoxic therapy, therapy-related AML itself as a second malignancy.
