CLL / SLL — CD5 positive, CD10 negative

🔑 The CD5 / CD10 framework — used for the rest of this section ★ HY
  • CD5 POSITIVE (mature B cells aberrantly expressing a T-cell marker): CLL/SLL · mantle cell lymphoma
  • CD10 POSITIVE (germinal center origin, usually BCL6 positive too): follicular · Burkitt · a subset of DLBCL
  • CD5 and CD10 both NEGATIVE (post-germinal-center / marginal zone): marginal zone (incl. MALT) · lymphoplasmacytic · hairy cell
⚠️ CD23 is what separates CLL/SLL from mantle cell lymphoma

Both are CD5 positive, CD10 negative mature B-cell lymphomas. CLL/SLL is CD23 POSITIVE; mantle cell is CD23 NEGATIVE (and carries t(11;14) with cyclin D1 overexpression). If a stem gives you a CD5-positive B-cell lymphoma, CD23 is the next thing to look for.

CLL/SLL phenotype: CD5 + · CD19 + · CD20 + · CD23 + · CD10 − · dim surface Ig light chain.

🧠 Proliferation centers are NOT reactive germinal centers

The pale nodules at low power are proliferation centers (pseudofollicles), containing prolymphocytes (slightly bigger, more open chromatin, distinct nucleoli) and paraimmunoblasts (larger, more activated). But the bulk of the cellularity is still the small CLL cells.

Do not mistake them for reactive germinal centers — the surrounding architecture is effaced, and there are no tingible body macrophages and no mantle zones.

And always judge cell size by an internal comparison: in blood, against a red cell; in a node, against the background small lymphocytes or an endothelial cell. “Small” and “large” are meaningless in isolation — this one habit answers many image-based questions.

🔑 Richter transformation, and the one genetic fact ★ HY

Richter transformation is progression of CLL/SLL to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Patients develop a rapidly enlarging mass within a lymph node or the spleen. Driven by newly acquired mutations in TP53 or MYC.

Commonest genetic abnormalities in CLL: del(13q14.3), del(11q), del(17p) (TP53), and trisomy 12q. TP53 on 17p is ALWAYS associated with a poor prognosis — in CLL, in AML, everywhere. “It's always bad.”

Low stage disease with no adverse indicators is managed with watchful waiting — treatment is not automatic. CLL is the most common leukemia in Europe and North America; median age 65.

Follicular lymphoma — CD10 positive, germinal center origin

10–20%

of all lymphomas

Middle-aged to elderly; median age 65. Widespread disease at diagnosis, but typically asymptomatic.

Splenomegaly typical

distribution

Peripheral nodes (cervical, axillary, inguinal) and central nodes (mesenteric, thoracic).

PARATRABECULAR

marrow, in 40–70%

Lymphoid aggregates hugging the bony trabeculae. The mimic is CLL/SLL's nodular/paratrabecular pattern — phenotype resolves it.

Indolent and incurable

median survival > 17 years

Characteristic waxing and waning of involved sites.

🧠 The translocation you should be able to recite ★ HY

t(14;18): IgH (chromosome 14) :: BCL2 (chromosome 18). The translocation puts BCL2 under the transcriptionally hyperactive immunoglobulin heavy chain promoter, forcing it ON. Anti-apoptosis is restored, and germinal-center-origin cells accumulate because they cannot die.

Normal germinal center B cells are BCL2 NEGATIVE — the germinal center exists to run somatic hypermutation and then eliminate the defective cells, so the cells must be easy to kill. Follicular lymphoma is defined by BCL2 EXPRESSION, and that is how you distinguish it from follicular hyperplasia.

Phenotype: CD10 + · CD20 + · BCL6 + · BCL2 + · CD5 −.

🩺 Grading — the pathologist's job does not stop at the diagnosis

Graded on the proportion of centrocytes to centroblasts. Centrocytes = the small cleaved lymphocytes. Centroblasts = the larger, more activated cells. More than 15 centroblasts in multiple abnormal follicles → higher grade.

Think of it as a continuum: more and more centroblasts, until you reach sheets of those cells — which is diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Transformation to DLBCL occurs at 1–3% per year, median time to progression 2.5–4.1 years. In practice, a new PET-avid site gets excised or biopsied specifically to look for it.

Primary effusion lymphoma

HHV-8 positive

Presents as a malignant effusion WITHOUT a mass. Associated with HHV-8, often in HIV.

Immune-privileged sites

e.g. primary CNS lymphoma

Commonest example is primary central nervous system lymphoma. Also testis and vitreoretinal.

EBV-positive DLBCL

virus-driven

A recognized entity in its own right.

Primary mediastinal LBCL

thymic origin

Arises in the thymus; young adults and adolescents. A mediastinal mass in a young person that is not Hodgkin and not T-lymphoblastic.

Extranodal marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma — CD5 and CD10 both negative

These arise in chronically inflamed tissue, and they sit on a continuum between reactive lymphoid hyperplasia and lymphoma — which is exactly why they are hard to diagnose and why so many ancillary studies get used. 5–8% of B-cell lymphomas; median age 61; indolent (5-year survival 90%, 10-year 80%).

OrganismSiteNote
Helicobacter pyloriStomach — the one to rememberResponds to eradication therapy
Campylobacter jejuniSmall intestine 
Borrelia burgdorferiCutaneous 
Chlamydia psittaciOcular (conjunctiva)Rarely encountered
🧠 Why BCL6 is negative — a logic check, not a fact to memorize

The marginal zone lies OUTSIDE the germinal center. BCL6 and CD10 are germinal center markers, so a marginal-zone-derived neoplasm should not express them. Remember the anatomy of the follicle (germinal center → mantle zone → marginal zone) and the phenotype follows.

Phenotype: CD20 + · CD79a + · PAX5 + · CD5 − · CD10 − · BCL6 − · CD23 −. CD21 and CD23 are follicular dendritic cell markers and are useful differently — they reveal expanded FDC meshworks left behind as the lymphoma colonizes and disrupts pre-existing follicles.

Two buzzwords: MONOCYTOID cells (round nuclei, condensed chromatin, abundant pale cytoplasm producing clearing around each nucleus; admixed plasma cells common) and LYMPHOEPITHELIAL LESION.

Treatment: H. pylori-directed therapy alone can cure gastric MALT lymphoma — remove the antigenic drive and the clone regresses. Alternative: rituximab (anti-CD20).

Burkitt lymphoma — CD10 positive, and the fastest tumor here

SubtypeAssociationClassic presentation
EndemicEBVA child with a large JAW mass — mandible or maxilla. The most common childhood cancer in much of equatorial Africa and Papua New Guinea
Non-endemic (sporadic)—ABDOMEN — often nodules in the omental fat. Can present with volvulus, because the mass creates an anchor point for the bowel to twist around. Also orbit, Waldeyer ring, thyroid, ovary
Immunodeficiency-associatedHIVNodal involvement
🧠 Burkitt versus follicular — both germinal center, opposite BCL2 ★ HY

Both are CD10 positive, BCL6 positive, which places both in the germinal center. But:

  • Follicular lymphoma is BCL2 POSITIVE — t(14;18) forces the anti-apoptotic gene on. The cells accumulate because they cannot die. Indolent.
  • Burkitt lymphoma is BCL2 NEGATIVE — the driver is MYC on chromosome 8, with the defining t(8;14). The cells accumulate because they divide furiously. Aggressive, Ki-67 > 95% — both highly mitotically and highly apoptotically active.

Grow-fast versus die-slow. Two germinal center lymphomas with opposite mechanisms and opposite tempos. Both translocations put an oncogene under the immunoglobulin heavy chain promoter on chromosome 14 — the mechanism from the pathogenesis section.

Hairy cell leukemia — CD5 and CD10 both negative

Middle-aged white males

demographics

Median age 55; M:F 5:1.

BRAF

genetics

> 90% have activating MAP kinase pathway mutations — think BRAF. Targetable with BRAF inhibitors.

The “DRY TAP”

a clinical clue

Marrow aspirate yields hemodilute blood, no spicules — because of prominent marrow fibrosis produced by the infiltrating hairy cells.

MONOCYTOPENIA

the stem's giveaway

A lymphoproliferative disease in blood and marrow accompanied by monocytopenia should raise hairy cell leukemia.

Pancytopenia + splenomegaly

yet indolent

Diffuse marrow involvement → marrow failure → pancytopenia; frequent splenomegaly. Despite all that, the course is INDOLENT. Patients are prone to infection.

The unique markers

essentially specific

CD19 + · CD20 + · CD11c + · CD25 + · CD103 + · annexin A1 + · CD5 − · CD10 −.

Mycosis fungoides and Sézary syndrome — skin, then blood

Mycosis fungoides is the most common cutaneous T-cell lymphoma — over 50% of cases. Sézary syndrome is the leukemic counterpart. Mycosis fungoides is the skin; Sézary syndrome is the blood. Peak in the late 50s, M:F 2:1, indolent over years or decades.

🔑 The four microscopic features — and the “bathing trunk” distribution ★ HY
  1. Small to medium haloed lymphocytes with hyperchromatic, hyperconvoluted (CEREBRIFORM) nuclei — the nuclear outline folded like a brain surface, with a clear rim around each cell.
  2. EPIDERMOTROPISM — the atypical lymphocytes preferentially move up into the epidermis.
  3. PAUTRIER MICROABSCESSES — clusters of lymphocytes forming small collections within the upper epidermis.
  4. Large cell transformation — defined as > 25% large lymphoid cells; may carry a worse prognosis.

Distribution: sun-protected areas — axilla and groin — plus lower trunk and buttocks: the “bathing trunk” distribution. Skin and soft tissue infections and pneumonia are frequent causes of sepsis and hospitalization, because of the disrupted barrier.

Phenotype — a disrupted T-cell program: CD2 + · CD3 + · CD5 + (sometimes lost) · CD4 +, CD8 − · CD7 dim or partially lost. Confirmation usually needs T-cell clonality by PCR. Staged T / N / M / B — skin, node, viscera, blood.

🔑 Diagnostic criteria for Sézary syndrome

In a patient with erythroderma, the diagnosis rests on:

  • An absolute Sézary cell count > 1,000 cells/µL.
  • Flow showing an expanded CD4-positive population with a skewed CD4:CD8 ratio > 10:1.
  • Loss of markers — CD2, CD3, CD7 or CD26.
  • Ideally, T-cell receptor gene rearrangement showing the SAME clone in blood and skin — this is what cements the diagnosis.

Sézary cells alone are not specific, so they must be correlated with the flow phenotype and the clinical picture.

⚠️ Dermatopathic lymphadenopathy — the staging trap ★ HY

Patients with mycosis fungoides frequently develop dramatic dermatopathic lymphadenopathy — a reactive phenomenon in the node draining chronically inflamed skin. It is essential to distinguish this from true nodal involvement, because that distinction changes the stage.

Recognize the reactive node by: architecture preserved but distorted, superficial cortex still showing reactive germinal centers, and paracortical expansion that is pale at low power because it is filled with histiocytes and dendritic cells plus increased pigment-laden macrophages — not atypical lymphocytes. Flow cytometry and immunostains are used to compare the node's phenotype with the skin lesion.

Anaplastic large cell lymphoma — the other CD30-positive lymphoma

⚠️ A tricky diagnosis, because it often does not look lymphoid

These cells can be so large and atypical that lymphoma is not the first thing you think of. In a sinusoidal pattern with cohesive-looking cells it mimics melanoma or poorly differentiated carcinoma, especially in adults. It should be on your differential for any ugly, undifferentiated malignancy in a node — and an ALK stain is done routinely whenever Hodgkin lymphoma is being considered.

10–15% of pediatric and adolescent NHL, but only 3% of adult NHL. Median age 30; male predominance 3:1. Involves nodes and extranodal sites: skin, bone, soft tissue, lung.

Growth patternMimic to consider
SinusoidalMetastatic carcinoma or melanoma — especially in adults
ParacorticalThe normal T-cell zone; other peripheral T-cell lymphomas
IntravascularIntravascular large B-cell lymphoma
Diffuse (occasionally nodular with fibrous bands)Classic Hodgkin lymphoma — but here the atypical cells form uniform sheets, whereas in Hodgkin the RS cell is never the predominant cell
🔑 Phenotype and prognosis — ALK status is what matters

Defined by strong, diffuse CD30 expression. ALCL and classic Hodgkin lymphoma are the two CD30-positive lymphomas — which is why brentuximab works in both.

Can express pan-T-cell markers such as CD2, but is often CD3 negative, which makes proving T-cell lineage harder; some show complete T-marker negativity — the “null cell” phenotype. More likely CD4 positive; EMA positive; CD45 positive (unlike CHL).

  • ALK POSITIVE: long-term survival ~80% — and more likely in adolescents.
  • ALK NEGATIVE: 5-year overall survival ~50%.

Different ALK staining patterns encode different translocation partners — cytoplasmic, or combined nuclear and cytoplasmic.

Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma — geography is the clue

🔑 The question-stem signature ★ HY

A stem that mentions a patient from Japan or the Caribbean is telling you about HTLV-1. The full endemic list: Japan, the Caribbean, intertropical Africa, the Middle East, South America, Papua New Guinea. Median age 68.

Presentation: generalized lymphadenopathy, skin lesions, hepatosplenomegaly — and hypercalcemia. Four clinical subtypes (acute, lymphoma, chronic, smoldering) defined by organ involvement, LDH and calcium levels, and degree of leukemic manifestation. Aggressive.

🪝 Flower cell versus Sézary cell — a deliberate contrast

Both are abnormal circulating T cells with strange nuclei, but the shapes differ:

  • Flower cell (ATLL): MULTILOBATED — distinct petal-like lobes radiating from a center, like a clover or flower.
  • Sézary cell (MF / SS): CONVOLUTED / CEREBRIFORM — one folded mass with a brain-like surface, not separate lobes.

The two translocations to be able to recite cold

🔑 Both put an oncogene under the IgH promoter on chromosome 14
  • Follicular lymphoma: t(14;18) — IgH (14) :: BCL2 (18). Anti-apoptotic → indolent.
  • Burkitt lymphoma: t(8;14) — MYC (8) :: IgH (14). Pro-proliferative → aggressive.

(And the third, from the CD5 group: mantle cell lymphoma, t(11;14) — cyclin D1 :: IgH.)

🩺 Do not forget the secondary neoplasms — look in the sinuses

Malignant lymphadenopathy splits two ways. Primary = the lymphoid malignancies themselves. Secondary = something that arrived from elsewhere: metastatic carcinoma (the commonest), metastatic melanoma, occasionally metastatic sarcoma. The sinuses under the capsule are the first place to look.

Immunohistochemistry

fixed tissue

Monoclonal antibodies against cell-surface antigens — the CD targets. Works on paraffin-embedded tissue.

Flow cytometry

needs FRESH tissue

Defines patterns of expression across a whole population. More colors = more antibodies per tube = better characterization on the same cells.

NGS

next-generation sequencing

Identifies mutations that define particular lymphomas — narrows a broad category further.

PCR

clonality

IgH / light chain rearrangements (B cells) or TCR rearrangements (T cells) — i.e. to prove clonality.

Cytogenetics

karyotype and FISH

Several lymphomas are defined by specific rearrangements, so this is often the confirmatory test.

Q: A lymph node contains scattered large binucleate cells with cherry-red nucleoli in a polymorphous eosinophil-rich background. They are CD30 +, CD15 +, PAX5 weakly +, CD20 −, OCT2 −, CD45 −, ALK −. Diagnosis, and what do the last two negatives rule out?

Answer

Classic Hodgkin lymphoma. The profile is complete: CD30 strong, CD15 co-expressed, PAX5 weak versus dark background B cells, pan-B-cell markers lost, OCT2 negative.

CD45 negativity — CD45 is a pan-hematopoietic marker — helps separate CHL from NLPHL and B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphomas, which retain it. ALK negativity excludes ALK-positive anaplastic large cell lymphoma, the other major CD30-positive lymphoma.

Q: Why is PAX5 more useful than CD20 for confirming classic Hodgkin lymphoma, even though both are B-cell markers?

Answer

Because PAX5 gives you a graded, comparative result rather than a binary one. In CHL, PAX5 is weak but present, and the background small B cells in the same section stain strongly — so a single slide carries its own internal control, and the weakness itself is the positive finding.

CD20 is simply negative, which is less informative because many things are CD20 negative. The PAX5 comparison is “probably your most helpful clue” — the background B cells are always something to look for.

Q: A 24-year-old woman has a mediastinal mass and cervical adenopathy. The node is divided into nodules by thick collagen bands; within them are numerous large cells sitting in clear spaces, in an eosinophil-rich background. Subtype, expected stage, prognosis?

Answer

Nodular sclerosis classic Hodgkin lymphoma. The broad bands of collagen and lacunar cells (large cells in clear spaces from retraction artifact) are diagnostic of the subtype.

It is the subtype most likely to occur in females, typically in young adults, usually presents at early stage (I–II), is the subtype most associated with mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and has an excellent prognosis.

Q: How do you separate mixed cellularity from nodular sclerosis when both show a polymorphous eosinophil-rich background with Reed–Sternberg cells?

Answer

Fibrosis. Nodular sclerosis has broad bands of collagen dividing the node into nodules; mixed cellularity does not.

Supporting differences: nodular sclerosis occurs in young adults, equally in both sexes, at early stage, excellent prognosis, numerous lacunar cells. Mixed cellularity occurs in elderly males (and children), presents at high stage, is aggressive, and shows many typical RS cells with an interfollicular pattern that preserves reactive follicles.

Q: A 38-year-old man has an isolated cervical node and no B symptoms. Vague nodules contain large multilobated cells with pale chromatin, rosetted by small lymphocytes. They are CD20 +, OCT2 +, BOB1 +, CD45 +, CD30 −, CD15 −. Diagnosis, and what are the rosetting cells?

Answer

Nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma (nodular lymphocyte predominant B-cell lymphoma). The large cells are popcorn cells. The fully retained B-cell program (CD20 +, OCT2 +, BOB1 +, CD45 +) with CD30 and CD15 negative is the mirror image of classic Hodgkin lymphoma.

The rosetting cells are T-follicular helper cells: CD4 +, CD57 +, PD-1 +. The absence of B symptoms and the localized cervical presentation in a 30–50-year-old man (M:F 3:1) both fit.

Q: Why is R-CHOP a rational choice for advanced NLPHL, when it is a DLBCL regimen?

Answer

Because the R in R-CHOP is rituximab, an anti-CD20 antibody — and unlike classic Hodgkin lymphoma, the popcorn cells of NLPHL are strongly CD20 positive. The neoplasm has retained its full B-cell program, so a B-cell-directed regimen has a target. This is precisely why the entity has been renamed nodular lymphocyte predominant B-cell lymphoma.

Classic Hodgkin lymphoma, being CD20 negative, would not respond to rituximab — it is targeted instead with anti-CD30 brentuximab.

Q: A 68-year-old has a lymphocyte count of 40,000/µL, with monotonous small lymphocytes, clumped chromatin and numerous smudge cells. Flow: CD5 +, CD19 +, CD20 +, CD23 +, CD10 −, dim surface light chain. Diagnosis, and what one further marker excludes the main alternative?

Answer

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Smudge cells and clumped “soccer ball” chromatin in monotonous small lymphocytes plus a CD5-positive, CD10-negative B-cell phenotype makes it.

The main alternative in the CD5-positive group is mantle cell lymphoma, and the discriminator is CD23: CLL is CD23 POSITIVE, mantle cell is CD23 NEGATIVE. Confirmation for mantle cell would be cyclin D1 / t(11;14). Dim surface light chain also favors CLL.

Q: A patient with stable CLL for six years develops a rapidly enlarging cervical mass, fever and a rising LDH. What has happened, what will the biopsy show, and which two mutations drive it?

Answer

Richter transformation — progression of CLL/SLL to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. The biopsy will show sheets of large cells replacing the previous small lymphocytic population. Driven by newly acquired TP53 or MYC mutations. The clinical signature is a rapidly enlarging mass in a node or spleen in a patient with previously indolent disease.

Q: A 64-year-old with painless generalized lymphadenopathy has a node effaced by crowded, uniform, back-to-back follicles with no tingible body macrophages and attenuated mantle zones. Which single stain confirms it, what result do you expect, and what is the translocation?

Answer

BCL2 — and it will be POSITIVE within the follicles, which is abnormal because normal germinal center B cells are BCL2 negative. Diagnosis: follicular lymphoma.

Translocation: t(14;18), IgH::BCL2 — putting BCL2 (chromosome 18) under the immunoglobulin heavy chain promoter (chromosome 14). Supporting phenotype: CD10 +, BCL6 + (germinal center origin), CD5 −.

Q: A 7-year-old in Kenya has a rapidly growing jaw mass. Biopsy shows a diffuse sheet of monotonous medium-sized cells with numerous pale macrophages containing debris. Subtype, virus, translocation, and what would Ki-67 show?

Answer

Endemic Burkitt lymphoma, associated with EBV, with the defining t(8;14) — IgH::MYC (MYC is on chromosome 8). The morphology described is the starry sky.

Ki-67 would exceed 95% — essentially every cell cycling, which is why the macrophages have so much apoptotic debris to clear and why the tumor doubles so fast. Phenotype: CD10 +, BCL6 +, CD20 +, MYC +, BCL2 NEGATIVE.

Q: A gastric biopsy shows sheets of small lymphoid cells with abundant pale cytoplasm invading and destroying the glands, with admixed plasma cells. Flow: CD20 +, CD5 −, CD10 −, BCL6 −. Diagnosis, the two named morphologic features, and first-line treatment?

Answer

Extranodal marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma of the stomach. The named features are monocytoid cells (abundant pale cytoplasm) and lymphoepithelial lesions (lymphoid invasion of glands).

The CD5-negative, CD10-negative, BCL6-negative phenotype places it outside both the CD5 group (CLL, mantle cell) and the germinal center group (follicular, Burkitt) — consistent with a marginal zone, i.e. extra-germinal-center, origin.

First-line treatment is Helicobacter pylori eradication; rituximab (anti-CD20) is the alternative.

Q: A 56-year-old man has pancytopenia, splenomegaly, and a marrow aspirate yielding only blood with no spicules. Blood shows rare mononuclear cells with irregular cytoplasmic projections, and the monocyte count is very low. Diagnosis, why the aspirate failed, and which mutation is present in over 90%?

Answer

Hairy cell leukemia. The failed aspirate is the “dry tap,” caused by prominent marrow fibrosis induced by the infiltrating hairy cells — so you get a hemodilute sample instead of spicules. Monocytopenia is a characteristic and useful clue.

Over 90% carry an activating MAP kinase pathway mutation — BRAF, which is targetable. Phenotype: CD5 −, CD10 −, with CD11c, CD25, CD103 and annexin A1 positive. Despite pancytopenia and splenomegaly the course is indolent.

Q: A 58-year-old man has a 12-year history of scaly red plaques on his buttocks and groin. Skin biopsy shows small atypical lymphocytes with folded nuclei in clear halos, some clustering within the epidermis. Diagnosis, the two morphologic terms, and the expected phenotype?

Answer

Mycosis fungoides. The terms are epidermotropism (atypical lymphocytes migrating into the epidermis) and Pautrier microabscesses (clusters within the upper epidermis). The nuclei are hyperchromatic and hyperconvoluted — cerebriform.

Phenotype: CD2 +, CD3 +, CD5 +, CD4 +, CD8 negative, with CD7 dim or partially lost. The sun-protected “bathing trunk” distribution and the indolent decade-long course both fit.

Q: The same patient develops total-body erythroderma. Blood shows 1,800 cells/µL with hyperconvoluted nuclei; flow shows an expanded CD4 population, CD4:CD8 ratio 18:1, loss of CD7 and CD26. What has happened, and what one further test do you want?

Answer

Sézary syndrome — the leukemic phase. All three criteria are met: erythroderma, an absolute Sézary cell count above 1,000/µL, and flow showing an expanded CD4 population with a CD4:CD8 ratio > 10:1 plus loss of CD7 and CD26.

The further test is T-cell receptor gene rearrangement, to demonstrate the SAME clone in the blood and in the skin — that is what cements the diagnosis, since Sézary cells alone are not specific.

Q: An axillary node from a patient with mycosis fungoides shows preserved follicles with reactive germinal centers and a pale expanded paracortex full of bland dendritic cells and pigment-laden macrophages. Is this nodal involvement? Why does the answer matter?

Answer

No — this is dermatopathic lymphadenopathy, a reactive response of the node draining chronically inflamed skin. The giveaways are preserved (though distorted) architecture, reactive germinal centers, and a paracortex expanded by histiocytes, dendritic cells and pigment-laden macrophages rather than by atypical lymphocytes.

It matters because mycosis fungoides is staged by T/N/M/B — skin, node, viscera, blood — so calling a reactive node “involved” would upstage the patient incorrectly. Flow cytometry and immunostains compare the node's phenotype with the skin lesion.

Q: A 14-year-old has a cervical node with sheets of very large atypical cells, some with eccentric horseshoe-shaped nuclei. They are strongly and diffusely CD30 +, CD3 −, CD4 +, EMA +, ALK +. Diagnosis, name the diagnostic cell, and what does ALK mean prognostically?

Answer

ALK-positive anaplastic large cell lymphoma. The diagnostic cell is the hallmark cell — eccentric, horseshoe-shaped nucleus with a pale paranuclear area.

ALK positivity carries a long-term survival of about 80%, versus about 50% five-year overall survival for ALK-negative cases; ALK positivity is also more common in adolescents. Note the CD3 negativity, which is typical and makes proving T-cell lineage harder.

Q: A node shows fibrous bands dividing it into nodules, with large atypical CD30-positive cells. Why is this not automatically nodular sclerosis classic Hodgkin lymphoma, and what one stain settles it?

Answer

Because ALCL can also form a nodular pattern with fibrous bands, and both entities are CD30 positive. Two things settle it.

First, at higher power ALCL shows uniform SHEETS of atypical cells, whereas in classic Hodgkin lymphoma the RS cell is never the predominant cell (< 10%, often 1–2%).

Second, the stain: ALK — positive in a substantial fraction of ALCL, always negative in classic Hodgkin lymphoma. Supporting: ALCL is CD45 and EMA positive; classic Hodgkin lymphoma is CD45 negative.

Q: A 66-year-old who emigrated from Japan has generalized lymphadenopathy, skin lesions, hepatosplenomegaly and hypercalcemia. The smear shows lymphocytes with multilobated, petal-like nuclei. Diagnosis, virus, and how do those cells differ from Sézary cells?

Answer

Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma, caused by HTLV-1. The cells are flower cells — multilobated, with distinct petal-like lobes.

Sézary cells are convoluted/cerebriform: one folded nuclear mass with a brain-like surface, not separate lobes. The geography (Japan, Caribbean, intertropical Africa, Middle East, South America, Papua New Guinea) is the intended clue, and calcium and LDH help define the clinical subtype (acute, lymphoma, chronic, smoldering).

Q: A patient with long-standing Helicobacter pylori gastritis develops a low-grade gastric B-cell lymphoma. Why might antibiotics alone cure this lymphoma, when antibiotics obviously do not cure lymphoma in general?

Answer

Because in gastric MALT lymphoma the neoplastic clone remains, at least early on, dependent on chronic antigenic stimulation from the organism. Remove the antigen and the growth stimulus is removed — these tumors respond remarkably well to H. pylori-directed therapy.

It is the clearest clinical demonstration of the “chronic inflammation drives lymphomagenesis” principle. The same logic applies to celiac disease and enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma, and to breast implants and ALCL.

LO 3Source: Introduction to Hematologic Malignancy

Section 42 · Hematologic malignancy · plasma cell

Plasma Cell Disorders — Myeloma, MGUS and Smoldering Myeloma

The far right of the map: a cancer of the fully differentiated plasma cell. Its damage comes from what the cell secretes — and uniquely, it has two well-defined precursor states managed by surveillance rather than treatment.

Abbreviations used in this section MM multiple myeloma · MGUS monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance · SPEP serum protein electrophoresis — separates serum proteins to reveal a monoclonal spike · Serum light chains free immunoglobulin light chains, measured separately because they cause renal failure · Heavy chain / light chain the two protein components of an antibody · CMP comprehensive metabolic panel · Skeletal survey a series of plain radiographs looking for lytic bone lesions · Beta-2 microglobulin a serum marker of tumour burden and prognosis · Paraprotein / monoclonal protein a single antibody species produced in excess by one clone · LPL lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma (Waldenström macroglobulinemia) · Auto-SCT autologous stem cell transplant · PET/CT positron emission tomography with computed tomography

Workup

  • Serum protein electrophoresis — detects and quantifies the monoclonal protein
  • Serum light chains — measured separately, and the reason is below
  • Comprehensive metabolic panel — for calcium and renal function
  • Complete blood count
  • Skeletal survey; equivocal findings confirmed with PET/CT or magnetic resonance imaging
🧠 Why light chains matter so much ★ HY

Antibodies are made of a heavy chain and a light chain. A myeloma clone can produce light chains in very high concentration, and because they are small they are filtered by the glomerulus and precipitate in the tubules — causing kidney failure.

This is why serum light chains are measured separately from the electrophoresis: a patient can have significant light chain disease with an unimpressive monoclonal spike, and the kidney is the organ that pays.

🔑 The complications of plasma cell disorders — the CRAB tetrad and beyond

The end organ damage that converts a watched precursor state into a treated cancer:

  • hyperCalcemia — from bone resorption
  • Renal failure — light chain cast nephropathy, the mechanism above
  • Anemia — marrow occupation by the plasma cell clone
  • Bone lesions — lytic lesions, pathological fracture, cord compression, bone pain

Add to these: recurrent infection (the clone crowds out normal immunoglobulin production, so the patient is functionally hypogammaglobulinemic despite a high total protein), hyperviscosity, and amyloidosis from deposited light chains.

⚠️

High risk features

  • Severe anemia
  • Chronic renal failure
  • Very high monoclonal protein concentration
  • Severe hypercalcemia
  • High beta-2 microglobulin
  • FISH: 17p = bad
📆

Prognosis and treatment

Highly dependent on age, fitness, stage and FISH. Many patients will live 7–10 years or beyond.

Treatment classes: thalidomide derivatives (the “-amides”) · proteasome inhibitors · chemotherapy · monoclonal antibodies · autologous stem cell transplant · palliative radiotherapy · CAR-T · BiTE.

The precursor states — the distinction to memorize ★ HY

MGUSSmoldering myeloma
Plasma cells in marrowUnder 10%10–60%
Monoclonal proteinUnder 3 g/dL3 g/dL or more
Risk of progression1% per year — flat10% per year for the first 5 years, then 3% per year for 5 years, then 1% per year
SurveillanceSPEP, serum light chains, CBC and CMP every 6 months; skeletal survey at least annuallyThe same, except labs every 4 months, and consider an annual PET scan
TreatmentNeither is treated. Both are watched. What converts either into active myeloma is end organ damage
🔑 The two numbers that separate them: 10 and 3

10% plasma cells and 3 g/dL monoclonal protein. Below both → MGUS. Above either (up to 60% plasma cells) → smoldering.

Note the shape of the smoldering risk curve: front-loaded. A patient who gets through the first five years without progressing has a substantially lower annual risk thereafter — which is why surveillance is more intensive early.

🩺 How common is MGUS, and what to tell the patient

Most patients with MGUS will never develop myeloma — at 1% per year, an 80-year-old diagnosed with MGUS is far more likely to die of something else. The counselling point is real reassurance combined with genuine commitment to surveillance, because the 1% per year does not stop.

Myeloma versus Waldenström macroglobulinemia / lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma ★ HY

FeatureMultiple myelomaLymphoplasmacytic lymphoma (Waldenström)
Cell of originFully differentiated plasma cellLymphoplasmacytic cell — a B cell with plasmacytic differentiation; an indolent lymphoma
Paraprotein classUsually IgG or IgA; light-chain-only disease occursIgM — and the pentameric structure drives every complication
GeneticsFISH abnormalities; 17p adverseMYD88 mutation
Bone lesionsLytic lesions characteristic — skeletal survey is part of the workupTypically absent
Renal failureCommon — light chain cast nephropathyUncommon
HypercalcemiaCommonUncommon
Lymphadenopathy / splenomegalyUncommonAdvanced diffuse lymphadenopathy, with or without splenomegaly
HyperviscosityUncommonCharacteristic — and an emergency needing plasmapheresis
Signature complicationsCRAB: hypercalcemia, renal failure, anemia, bone lesionsHyperviscosity · peripheral neuropathy · cold agglutinin hemolysis · cryoglobulinemia · bleeding from impaired fibrin polymerization
🪝 Memory hook — bone versus blood viscosity

Myeloma attacks the skeleton and the kidney. Waldenström thickens the blood and injures nerves. If the stem gives you lytic lesions, hypercalcemia and renal failure, it is myeloma. If it gives you blurred vision, vertigo, ataxia and a neuropathy in someone with lymphadenopathy, it is the IgM disease — and the treatment is plasmapheresis first, chemotherapy second.

Q: A 66-year-old has an IgG monoclonal protein of 1.8 g/dL, 6% plasma cells on marrow biopsy, normal calcium, creatinine and hemoglobin, and no bone lesions. Diagnosis, risk, and plan?

Answer

MGUS — under 10% plasma cells and under 3 g/dL monoclonal protein, with no end organ damage. Risk of progression to multiple myeloma is 1% per year. No treatment. Surveillance with SPEP, serum light chains, CBC and CMP every 6 months, plus a skeletal survey at least annually.

Q: Why can a myeloma patient develop renal failure even when the serum protein electrophoresis spike is modest?

Answer

Because of free light chains. Antibodies comprise heavy and light chains, and a clone may secrete light chains in very high concentration. Being small, they are filtered at the glomerulus and precipitate in the tubules, causing kidney failure — while contributing little to the electrophoresis peak. This is precisely why serum light chains are measured separately in the workup.

Q: How does the progression risk of smoldering myeloma differ from MGUS, and how does that change surveillance?

Answer

MGUS progresses at a flat 1% per year. Smoldering myeloma is front-loaded: 10% per year for the first 5 years, then 3% per year for 5 years, then 1% per year — roughly ten times the early risk. Accordingly surveillance is intensified: labs every 4 months rather than every 6, and consider an annual PET scan.

LO 64Source: Pharmacology of Antineoplastic Agents · Part 1

Section 43 · Antineoplastic pharmacology

Traditional Chemotherapy — Principles, Resistance and Mechanisms

The most toxic group of medications in medicine, for one reason: the thing that makes a cancer cell vulnerable is the same thing that makes your marrow, your gut lining and your hair follicles vulnerable.

Abbreviations used in this section CCS / CCNS cell cycle-specific / cell cycle-nonspecific · DHFR dihydrofolate reductase · TS thymidylate synthase · MDR1 the multi-drug resistance gene · P-glycoprotein the ATP-dependent efflux pump it encodes; the P stands for “permeability” · ATP adenosine triphosphate · 5-FU 5-fluorouracil · 6-MP / 6-TG mercaptopurine / thioguanine · HGPRT hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase · Mesna mercaptoethanesulfonate · Log kill reduction in tumour burden expressed in orders of magnitude · Narrow therapeutic index a small gap between an effective and a toxic dose
💊 Pharm review — what they said to know, and what they said to skip

From the antineoplastics review session. Everything flagged 💊 PHARM REVIEW in Sections 43–46 was named there. Their frame: study chemotherapy as three parts — Part 1 traditional cytotoxics, Part 2 immunotherapy/targeted, Part 3 hormonal — because the class predicts the toxicity.

On the examExplicitly NOT on the exam
Adverse effects and dose-limiting toxicities, by class The general principles themselves (log kill, the definitions) — background only
Drug names for Parts 1 and 3, recognised from their endings Which cell cycle phase a drug hits — not on their exam; boards may still ask
Chemo Man and the supportive-care drugs Differences within the platinums (cisplatin vs carboplatin vs oxaliplatin) — know them as one class
Part 2: the circled drugs, –nib / –mab / –leucel, ADCs, checkpoints, engagers, CAR-T Receptor targets and the big Part 2 tables; monoclonal antibody naming structure (in flux)
The T-cell-engager timing table — “the one you should really know” Diagnosing the cancer — their vignette states it (the oncologist's questions may not)
Part 3: names, mechanism, adverse effects Telling one drug from another inside a class

And the question technique they spent the most time on: never stop at the name of the toxicity. The exam describes how the patient walks in.

🔑 The four classes, one frame

Every antineoplastic drug belongs to exactly one of four columns, and the column tells you most of what you need to predict about it:

  • Traditional cytotoxic chemotherapy — poisons that hit any dividing cell. Toxicity = the toxicity of every fast-dividing normal tissue you own.
  • Targeted therapy — aimed at one molecule the tumour depends on. Toxicity follows the target, not the mitotic rate.
  • Immunotherapy — makes the patient's own immune system do the killing. Toxicity is autoimmunity, cytokine storm and neurotoxicity.
  • Hormonal therapy — starves a hormone-dependent tumour. Toxicity is the toxicity of hormone withdrawal.

If you can predict the adverse effect from the class before you memorize the drug, you have understood the block.

When the drug is given defines the word

Primary chemotherapy

chemotherapy alone

Used for advanced disease, or when no alternative exists. No surgery or radiation is doing part of the work.

Neoadjuvant chemotherapy

given BEFORE surgery

Goal: reduce tumour size prior to resection — turn an unresectable or morbid operation into a smaller one.

Adjuvant chemotherapy

given AFTER surgery or radiation

Goal: decrease recurrence risk by treating occult micrometastases that imaging cannot see.

🪝 Memory hook — “neo-” means before

The prefix is the whole mnemonic. Neoadjuvant comes before the local therapy; plain adjuvant comes after it. Both are add-ons to a local treatment — that is what “adjuvant” means. Primary chemotherapy has no local treatment to be adjuvant to.

Basic chemotherapeutic principles that enhance efficacy ★ HY

🔑 Why almost nobody gets one drug
  • Larger spectrum of activity — a heterogeneous tumour contains subclones with different vulnerabilities; more mechanisms hit more of them.
  • Use drugs with differing mechanisms of action AND differing adverse drug reactions. Different mechanism means additive kill; different toxicity means you can give each at full dose.
  • If two drugs share the same adverse reaction, you may have to dose-reduce — the practical cost of overlapping toxicity, and exactly why the “different organ toxicity” rule exists.
  • Decrease the rate of resistance development — a cell must acquire several independent resistance mechanisms at once rather than one.

The worked example, R-CHOP — each letter is a different mechanism and a different toxicity: Rituximab (anti-CD20 antibody) · Cyclophosphamide (alkylator) · Hydroxydaunorubicin/doxorubicin (anthracycline) · Oncovin/vincristine (vinca alkaloid) · Prednisone (corticosteroid).

🧠 The log-kill hypothesis — why chemotherapy must be repeated

Cytotoxic agents follow first-order kinetics: a constant FRACTION of cells is killed by each dose, not a constant absolute number. A drug that takes the burden from 10⁸ to 10⁵ has produced a “3-log kill”.

The consequence: no single dose can ever sterilize a tumour, because a fixed fraction of any remaining population always survives. Repeated cycles are mathematically necessary, not just conventional.

The 1-gram threshold: 10⁹ cells is the smallest physically detectable burden — about 1 gram, the size of a small grape — and roughly where symptoms first appear. Everything below that line is subclinical disease you are treating blind, which is the entire justification for adjuvant chemotherapy.

Rescue therapy — giving an antidote on purpose 💊 PHARM REVIEW

Rescue agentRescues fromHow it works
Leucovorin (folinic acid)MethotrexateSupplies reduced folate downstream of the blocked dihydrofolate reductase, bypassing the block in normal cells
MesnaCyclophosphamide and ifosfamideBinds the urotoxic metabolite acrolein in the bladder, preventing haemorrhagic cystitis
DexrazoxaneAnthracyclinesChelates intracellular iron so it cannot react with superoxide and hydrogen peroxide to generate free radicals — protecting cardiac muscle
⚠️ Leucovorin cuts both ways

Leucovorin is a rescue agent for methotrexate but an ENHANCER for 5-fluorouracil. Same molecule, opposite intent. Do not assume “leucovorin = antidote”.

Mechanisms of drug resistance ★ HY

Three definitions first: primary (inherent) resistance is present without prior exposure — the tumour never responded. Acquired resistance develops after exposure — the tumour responded, then stopped. Cross-resistance is resistance to one agent conferring resistance to others, including structurally unrelated ones.

MechanismWhat the cell doesDrugs affected
Increased DNA repairRepairs adducts and cross-links faster than they accumulateAlkylating agents and cisplatin
Formation of trapping agentsProduces thiol-rich molecules that bind and sequester the drug before it reaches DNABleomycin, cisplatin, anthracyclines
Changes in target enzymesAlters or amplifies the enzyme so the drug no longer inhibits itMethotrexate (dihydrofolate reductase)
Decreased activation of prodrugsLoses the activating enzyme, so the prodrug is never convertedPurine and pyrimidine antimetabolites (mercaptopurine, thioguanine, cytarabine, fluorouracil)
Drug inactivationMetabolizes the active drug to an inactive formPurine and pyrimidine antimetabolites
Decreased drug accumulationEfflux of the drug out of the cellMany anticancer drugs
Pharmacologic sanctuaryThe tumour sits where the drug cannot reachClassically the central nervous system behind the blood–brain barrier, or the testes
🧠 Multi-drug resistance and the P-glycoprotein pump

Multi-drug resistance arises from increased expression of a normal gene, MDR1, encoding the cell-surface P-glycoprotein — an ATP-dependent pump that exports drugs out of the cell. The P stands for “permeability”.

Because the pump recognizes a broad range of hydrophobic substrates, cross-resistance occurs with structurally unrelated drugs — vincristine, vinblastine, doxorubicin, bleomycin and etoposide all leave through the same door.

The same transporter is why so many anticoagulant interactions are described as “P-glycoprotein inhibitors and inducers” — verapamil, amiodarone, clarithromycin, ketoconazole, rifampicin (Section 15). One transporter, one job, many organs.

💊 Pharm review #1 — the principles are scaffolding; the toxicities are the exam

What they said: “All the general principles, I don't ask questions about it — this is to help set you up. But yes, you should know the adverse effects, and the dose-limiting toxicity.”

  • Know cold: the four high-turnover tissues (oral mucosa, bone marrow, gastrointestinal mucosa, hair follicles) and the dose-limiting toxicity of each class — the toxicity bad enough to force a dose reduction or a stop.
  • Not asked by them: which drug acts in which phase. They teach the cycle to frame the drugs, and said plainly they will not ask it — while adding that they cannot promise the boards won't.
  • The confusion they stopped to clear up: “cell cycle-specific” does not mean one single phase. Irinotecan works in S and G2; that is still cell cycle-specific, because every phase it hits is a proliferative phase. Cell cycle-nonspecific means it also reaches the resting cell — and anthracyclines count as nonspecific because they intercalate DNA and generate free radicals whatever phase the cell is in.

Cell cycle specificity ★ HY

🔑 The G0 problem is the whole reason cure is hard

Cells in G0 — the resting phase — are less susceptible to cancer therapy. Cell cycle-specific (CCS) drugs can only kill a cell that is currently cycling, so a tumour with a large G0 fraction is intrinsically less responsive — and slow-growing solid tumours have exactly that profile.

Cell cycle-nonspecific (CCNS) agents — alkylators, platinums, anthracyclines — do not have this limitation, which is why they remain the backbone of many regimens.

PhaseClassDrugsMechanism
G1EnzymePegaspargase, L-asparaginaseDeaminates asparagine, which leukemic cells cannot make → inhibits protein synthesis
SFolate antagonistsMethotrexate, pemetrexed, pralatrexateInhibit dihydrofolate reductase and thymidylate synthase
SPyrimidine antagonists5-fluorouracil, capecitabine, cytarabine, gemcitabine5-FU → 5-FdUMP → inhibits thymidylate synthase → “thymidine-less death”
SPurine antagonistsMercaptopurine, thioguanine, azathioprine, fludarabineActivated by HGPRT → inhibit purine metabolism enzymes

Late S / early G2Topoisomerase II — podophyllotoxinsEtoposide, teniposidePersistent cleavable complex → double-strand breaks

☐ Fatal route error — vincristine is NEVER given intrathecally 💊 PHARM REVIEW

Intrathecal vincristine is uniformly fatal — it causes an ascending myeloencephalopathy. This is a named, tested, absolute rule, and it is why vincristine is dispensed in a minibag rather than a syringe in most institutions.

🪝 Memory hook — stabilizer versus destabilizer

Both taxanes and vincas act on microtubules in M phase, and their effect on tubulin is opposite. Paclitaxel promotes microtubule formation and prevents disassembly — the cell is frozen in metaphase. Vincristine blocks assembly of tubulin dimers — the spindle dissolves. Both end in mitotic arrest. (Ixabepilone behaves like the taxanes; eribulin like the vincas, with less neuropathy.)

💊 Pharm review #2 — learn Parts 1 and 3 by the ending of the name

What they said: “Out of all the drug classes, you should definitely learn the traditional cytotoxic drugs and the hormonal agents — not just for the exam, but for your boards, because if they test you on chemotherapy it is probably the older agents.” Learn the class first, then read the ending to place a name inside it.

⚠️ The alkylator class signature

Myelosuppression + mucositis · neurotoxicity · SECONDARY MALIGNANCIES. The secondary-malignancy risk is the alkylators' signature — they are mutagens, which is the mechanism behind therapy-related leukemia.

FeatureCisplatinCarboplatinOxaliplatin
EmetogenicityHighly emetogenic↓—
KidneyNephrotoxicity↓—
EarOtotoxicity↓—
NervePeripheral neuropathy↓Pharyngolaryngeal dysesthesia and COLD-INDUCED neuropathy

Shared by all three: delayed hypersensitivity reaction · metallic taste with infusion · taste changes
🔑 The platinum trade-off, in one line

Carboplatin trades cisplatin's organ toxicity for marrow toxicity. Everything cisplatin does to the kidney, the ear, the nerve and the vomiting centre, carboplatin does less of — and it pays for that with more myelosuppression. Oxaliplatin is the odd one out: its signature is cold-induced neuropathy, which patients describe as choking on cold air or cold drinks.

Q: A tumour treated with doxorubicin initially responds, then progresses. On re-challenge it is also resistant to vincristine and etoposide — drugs it has never seen and which are structurally unrelated. What is the mechanism?

Answer

Multi-drug resistance from increased expression of MDR1, producing P-glycoprotein. This is acquired resistance (it developed after exposure) that is also cross-resistance — the ATP-dependent efflux pump exports a broad range of structurally unrelated hydrophobic drugs, so resistance to one selects for resistance to all of its substrates.

Q: Why is a slowly growing solid tumour with a large G0 fraction relatively resistant to methotrexate but not to cyclophosphamide?

Answer

Methotrexate is cell cycle-specific (S phase) — it can only kill a cell actively synthesising DNA, and cells in G0 are less susceptible. Cyclophosphamide is cell cycle-nonspecific — it alkylates the DNA backbone regardless of phase, so a resting cell is still damaged and dies when it next attempts to divide.

Q: A patient on high-dose cyclophosphamide develops haematuria. Mechanism, and what should have been co-administered?

Answer

Haemorrhagic cystitis, caused by the urotoxic metabolite acrolein concentrating in the bladder. It should have been prevented with mesna, which binds acrolein in the urine, plus hydration. The same toxicity and the same prevention apply to ifosfamide.

Q: Two weeks after starting a platinum regimen, a patient reports that drinking cold water makes their throat feel like it is closing. Which platinum, and is this an allergic reaction?

Answer

Oxaliplatin. This is pharyngolaryngeal dysesthesia and cold-induced neuropathy — a neurotoxic, not an allergic, phenomenon, and specific to oxaliplatin among the three platinums. Patients are counselled to avoid cold food, drinks and air. (A separate delayed hypersensitivity reaction is shared by all three platinums, but does not present this way.)

LO 17Source: Pharmacology of Antineoplastic Agents · Part 1

Section 44 · Antineoplastic pharmacology

Toxicities of Traditional Chemotherapy — “Chemo Man” and Supportive Care

The general toxicities belong to nearly every agent and therefore discriminate nothing. The drug-specific ones are what examiners actually test.

Abbreviations used in this section DLT dose-limiting toxicity — toxicity severe enough to require dose or therapy modification · CSF colony-stimulating factor · G-CSF granulocyte colony-stimulating factor · GM-CSF granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor · CXCR4 C-X-C chemokine receptor type 4 · 5-HT3 5-hydroxytryptamine-3 (serotonin) receptor · NK1 neurokinin-1 receptor · Acrolein the urotoxic metabolite of cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide · Hand–foot syndrome painful palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia
🔑 Why the adverse effects are so predictable

Chemotherapy is aimed at killing dividing cells. Effects on normal host cells that are also dividing produce the adverse effects — and the highest-turnover normal tissues are always the same four:

  • Oral mucosa → stomatitis, mucositis
  • Bone marrow → myelosuppression, all three lineages
  • Gastrointestinal mucosa → nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, constipation
  • Hair follicles → alopecia

Chemotherapeutic agents also have a narrow therapeutic index, and many are mutagens — and therefore cause other cancers, most notably the alkylating agents.

💊 Pharm review #3 — “If you don't have any time, know this”

What they said, about the Chemo Man figure below: “If you don't want to study anything — you need to know chemo man, especially for the boards.” The drug sits on the body part it poisons: bleomycin on the chest, cisplatin at the ear and the kidney.

Paired with it, they told the room to know the supportive-care drugs: filgrastim (granulocyte colony-stimulating factor) to lift the neutrophils, because the predictable consequence of a low white count is infection — and the –setron antiemetics you already learned. Both are worked further down this section.

🔑 The single highest-yield sentence in the three decks 💊 PHARM REVIEW

“The most common dose-limiting toxicities of chemotherapy (and the drugs that cause them) include haemorrhagic cystitis (cyclophosphamide/ifosfamide), pulmonary toxicity (bleomycin), ototoxicity with nephrotoxicity and nausea/vomiting (cisplatin), cardiotoxicity (doxorubicin/daunorubicin/trastuzumab), peripheral neuropathies (oxaliplatin/vincristine/taxanes), and potentially fatal diarrhoea (irinotecan).” Six pairings — learn them as a block.

💊 Pharm review #4 — how the question will actually be written

What they said: “The board is not going to say it caused cardiotoxicity. It might not even say pulmonary fibrosis — that's too easy. They'll say the patient is on this drug, and ask how they present.”

So for every toxicity you memorise, take one more step: what does this patient look like walking through the door? Their two worked examples:

Drug → toxicityWhat the vignette actually says
Bleomycin → pulmonary fibrosisCough and shortness of breath; imaging with interstitial changes. Not “gastrointestinal symptoms” — respiratory ones
Cyclophosphamide / ifosfamide → haemorrhagic cystitisHaematuria and dysuria; urinalysis with red blood cells and NO infection — the negative culture is there to rule out a urinary tract infection for you

Run the same translation on the rest of the table below: anthracycline → breathless, swollen ankles, falling ejection fraction. Cisplatin → can't hear the conversation, creatinine climbing. Vincristine → numb fingers, lost ankle jerks. Cytarabine → can't touch finger to nose, red sore eyes.

🪝 Memory hook — the vinca split is a classic distractor

Within one class, vincristine's dose-limiting toxicity is neurotoxicity while vinblastine's and vinorelbine's is myelosuppression. Hook: vinCRIStine → CRIS-py nerves; vinBLAStine → BLASts, i.e. the marrow.

And the myelosuppression ranking: strong — cyclophosphamide, cytarabine, doxorubicin, nitrosoureas, vinblastine. Intermediate — carboplatin, etoposide, 5-FU, methotrexate, procarbazine. Mild — bleomycin, vincristine, and methotrexate given with leucovorin. The two famously non-myelosuppressive drugs are exactly the two whose DLT is something else entirely.

🩺 Map each growth factor onto the cytopenia it fixes

Red cells → epoetin alfa. Neutrophils → filgrastim. Granulocytes + macrophages → sargramostim. Platelets → the “-ostim / -opag” thrombopoietin agents. Stem cell mobilisation → plerixafor + G-CSF.

Note that epoetin alfa reappears in Section 17 as an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent, where its boxed warnings are covered in detail — the same drug, seen from the other lecture's side.

🔑 Antiemetics — the suffixes are the exam gift 💊 PHARM REVIEW
  • -setron → 5-HT3 receptor antagonists: ondansetron, granisetron, dolasetron, palonosetron
  • -pitant → neurokinin-1 receptor antagonists: aprepitant, netupitant, rolapitant
  • Promethazine — phenothiazine / dopamine antagonist, the older option
  • Synthetic cannabinoids — dronabinol, nabilone

When a suffix is flagged in a lecture, it is because a question will give you an unfamiliar generic name and expect you to classify it from the ending alone.

Q: A patient who has completed six cycles of a doxorubicin-containing regimen now needs treatment for a second, unrelated malignancy, and the proposed regimen also contains an anthracycline. What is the specific concern?

Answer

Cumulative lifetime anthracycline dose. Anthracycline cardiomyopathy is dose-cumulative across a patient's entire lifetime, not per regimen — prior exposure counts. Total the lifetime exposure, obtain baseline cardiac function, and consider liposomal doxorubicin or dexrazoxane (which chelates intracellular iron and prevents free-radical injury to cardiac muscle), or select a non-anthracycline regimen.

Q: Which single traditional cytotoxic agent would you expect to spare the bone marrow almost entirely, and what is its dose-limiting toxicity instead?

Answer

Bleomycin. It sits in the mildest myelosuppression tier alongside vincristine and methotrexate-with-leucovorin. Its dose-limiting toxicity is pulmonary — pulmonary fibrosis, “bleomycin lung”. Mechanistically the bleomycin–iron complex generates free oxygen radicals; the lung is uniquely vulnerable because it lacks the inactivating enzyme bleomycin hydrolase.

Q: A patient receiving highly emetogenic chemotherapy is prescribed netupitant. What receptor does it block, and how do you know from the name?

Answer

The -pitant suffix identifies it as a neurokinin-1 (NK1) receptor antagonist — the same class as aprepitant and rolapitant. If the name had ended in -setron it would have been a 5-hydroxytryptamine-3 (5-HT3) receptor antagonist instead.

Q: A patient on procarbazine eats aged cheese and cured meats and develops a hypertensive crisis. Why?

Answer

Procarbazine is a monoamine oxidase inhibitor. Tyramine-rich foods are normally degraded by monoamine oxidase in the gut wall; with that enzyme inhibited, tyramine reaches the circulation and displaces noradrenaline from sympathetic nerve terminals, producing a hypertensive crisis. Procarbazine is a triazene alkylating agent, and the MAO inhibition is its named drug-specific toxicity.

LO 11LO 16Source: Pharmacology of Antineoplastic Agents · Part 2

Section 45 · Antineoplastic pharmacology

Targeted Therapy and Immunotherapy — Mechanisms and Toxicities

Where targeted therapy hands the tumour a poison addressed to it, immunotherapy hands the immune system the tumour's address. In both, the toxicity follows the mechanism — not the mitotic rate.

Abbreviations used in this section mAb monoclonal antibody · TKI tyrosine kinase inhibitor · ADC antibody-drug conjugate · EGFR epidermal growth factor receptor · HER2 human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 · VEGFR vascular endothelial growth factor receptor · ALK anaplastic lymphoma kinase · mTOR mechanistic target of rapamycin · BTK Bruton tyrosine kinase · PARP poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase · PI3K phosphoinositide 3-kinase · CDK4/6 cyclin-dependent kinase 4 and 6 · CDC / ADCC complement-dependent cytotoxicity / antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity · CTLA-4 cytotoxic T-lymphocyte associated antigen 4 · PD-1 / PD-L1 programmed cell death protein 1 / its ligand · LAG-3 lymphocyte activation gene-3 · CAR-T chimeric antigen receptor T-cell · BiTE bispecific T-cell engager · CRS cytokine release syndrome · ICANS immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome · irAE immune-related adverse event · PML progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy
🔑 Size decides where a drug can act — the whole classification in one fact

An antibody is roughly 145,000 daltons; a tyrosine kinase inhibitor is a few hundred. Therefore:

  • Antibodies work only on the OUTSIDE of the cell — the extracellular domain of a transmembrane receptor.
  • Small molecules can cross the membrane and hit intracellular kinases.
  • Consequently every signal-transduction inhibitor is a small molecule — there are no monoclonal antibodies in that group, because an antibody cannot get inside the cell.
💊 Pharm review #5 — Part 2 is where they cut the most

What they said: “Do I expect you to know all these drugs and all these tables? No. Do I ask questions about the receptor target? No.” The receptor handout on Brightspace is for information — it tells you what the drug hits and what cancer it treats, and they will not examine it.

  • Know the drugs they circled in the slides and the video — go back through Part 2 and collect exactly those.
  • Three endings do the classifying: –nib = small-molecule inhibitor · –mab = monoclonal antibody · –leucel = CAR-T cell therapy. Seeing any of them should put you in Part 2 — and a –leucel name can often be eliminated, since they are not asking CAR-T questions.
  • Know the concepts, not the catalogue: the antibody-drug conjugate as a “biological missile” (a cytotoxic drug addressed to the cancer cell), bispecific T-cell engagers, checkpoint inhibitors — the example drugs and how they work — and CAR-T in outline. Rituximab comes back later for rheumatoid arthritis.
  • They will state the diagnosis. “I will tell you this patient has this type of cancer.” That exemption is theirs alone — the oncology faculty's questions may still expect you to diagnose it.
  • Monoclonal antibody naming structure is not required — the –omab/–ximab/–zumab system is being rewritten and biosimilars muddy it further. The table below is worth reading once, not memorising.

⚠️ Trastuzumab is on Chemo Man for a reason

Trastuzumab causes heart failure — the only targeted agent listed on the cardiotoxicity arm alongside doxorubicin and daunorubicin. HER2 is expressed on cardiomyocytes, so blocking it damages the heart. This is the cleanest example of the general principle: targeted-therapy toxicity follows the target's normal tissue distribution.

🧠 Patterns worth noticing in that table
  • QT prolongation appears in five of the ten rows — along with diarrhoea and raised liver function tests, it is a class effect of small-molecule targeted agents.
  • Skin cancers appear with both RAF and MEK inhibitors — paradoxical MAPK activation in RAS-mutant keratinocytes.
  • PI3K inhibitors cause autoimmune dysfunction and opportunistic infections because PI3Kδ is a lymphocyte signalling node. The toxicity follows the target's normal job.
  • mTOR inhibitors cause metabolic dysregulation for the same reason — mTOR is the cell's nutrient sensor.

Antibody nomenclature and antibody-drug conjugates

-omab

murine

Fully mouse-derived.

-ximab

chimeric

Mouse variable region on human constant region — cetuximab, rituximab.

-zumab

humanised

Human except the complementarity-determining regions — trastuzumab, bevacizumab, alemtuzumab.

-umab

fully human

Panitumumab.

IgG subclass matters. Half-lives: IgG1, IgG2 and IgG4 ≈ 21 days; IgG3 ≈ 7 days. Most approved mAbs are IgG1, which has a long half-life and triggers potent effector functions — complement-dependent cytotoxicity and antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity. IgG4 cannot activate the classical complement pathway at all, which is exactly why it is chosen for checkpoint inhibitors: you do not want to lyse the T cell you are trying to activate.

Antibody-drug conjugateTargetPayloadToxicities
Trastuzumab emtansineHER2Anti-microtubuleThrombocytopenia, raised transaminases, neuropathy, anaemia
Trastuzumab deruxtecanHER2Topoisomerase inhibitorNausea, fatigue, alopecia, neutropenia, anaemia, thrombocytopenia, diarrhoea
Sacituzumab govitecanTROP2Topoisomerase inhibitorNausea, diarrhoea, neutropenia, anaemia, alopecia
