🔑 Read the payload out of the generic name

The second word of an ADC's name is the payload. -emtansine and -vedotin are anti-microtubule agents (expect peripheral neuropathy); -deruxtecan and -govitecan are topoisomerase inhibitors (expect myelosuppression and gastrointestinal toxicity). This is why the two HER2-targeted conjugates have different toxicity profiles despite sharing an antibody: the antibody determines where the drug goes; the payload determines what the toxicity looks like.

Immunotherapy — checkpoints, engagers and CAR-T

CheckpointNormal roleBlocked by
CTLA-4Downregulates T-cell function; essential for normal immunologic homeostasisIpilimumab, tremelimumab
PD-1Limits autoimmunity by dampening T cells in peripheral tissues. The major immune resistance mechanism in tumoursPembrolizumab, nivolumab, cemiplimab, dostarlimab, toripalimab
PD-L1The tumour-side ligand for PD-1Atezolizumab, avelumab, durvalumab
LAG-3Inhibitory receptor highly expressed by exhausted T cellsRelatlimab — given with nivolumab in a single infusion

Bispecific T-cell engagers bridge a tumour antigen to CD3 on a passing T cell: blinatumomab (CD19, acute lymphoblastic leukemia), teclistamab (BCMA, myeloma), mosunetuzumab / epcoritamab / glofitamab (CD20, B-cell lymphomas). Tebentafusp is the exception — it uses a T-cell receptor arm to recognize an intracellular peptide presented on HLA-A*02:01, which is why patients must be HLA-typed before treatment.

CAR-T cell therapy collects the patient's T cells, engineers a chimeric antigen receptor into them ex vivo, and re-infuses them. CD19-directed: tisagenlecleucel, axicabtagene ciloleucel, brexucabtagene autoleucel, lisocabtagene maraleucel. BCMA-directed: idecabtagene vicleucel, ciltacabtagene autoleucel. US boxed warning: secondary malignancies — added in 2024, with the FDA stating benefits still outweigh risks.

⚠️ Daratumumab breaks the blood bank

CD38 is expressed on red blood cells, so daratumumab (anti-CD38, for myeloma) coats them and causes interference with cross-matching and red-cell antibody screening — a panreactive indirect antiglobulin test that can mask a genuine alloantibody. The blood bank must be told, and a baseline type-and-screen obtained before the first dose. Cross-reference Section 13.

Toxicities of the newer agents ★ HY

💊

Small molecules

  • Almost all: drug–drug interactions via CYP3A4
  • Drug–food interactions — most should be taken on an empty stomach
  • Many: QT prolongation, diarrhoea, raised liver function tests
  • Multi-kinase inhibitors have more adverse reactions — hitting more kinases means hitting more normal tissue
🧪

Monoclonal antibodies

  • Many: infusion reactions
  • Mostly mechanism-of-action-dependent toxicity — it follows wherever the target is normally expressed
  • Worked example: acne-like rash, which is EGFR-specific
  • A few: progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy — rare, devastating JC virus reactivation
🔑 The format predicts the toxicity family

Small molecule → pharmacokinetic problems (CYP3A4 interactions, food effects) and off-target kinase effects (QT prolongation, transaminitis, diarrhoea). Antibody → immunologic and on-target problems (infusion reactions, mechanism-based toxicity in whatever normal tissue expresses the antigen). You can answer most “which toxicity would you expect?” questions from format alone.

⚠️ Checkpoint inhibitor toxicity — “any organ ending in -itis”

All immune-mediated, across eight organ systems: colitis · rash · pneumonitis · hepatitis · musculoskeletal (arthritis, myositis) · endocrinopathies (thyroiditis, hypophysitis, adrenal insufficiency, new diabetes — often permanent) · ophthalmologic (uveitis) · neurologic.

Checkpoint inhibitors work by removing the brakes that maintain self-tolerance; the predictable cost is autoimmunity anywhere. The corollary that follows from the mechanism: the treatment for a serious immune-related adverse event is corticosteroids — you put a brake back on. Note that checkpoint colitis is autoimmune inflammation needing steroids, not loperamide.

FeatureCheckpoint inhibitors (irAEs)T-cell engagers
Relationship with dose intensityQuite unrelatedHighly related
Variability of profileHighly variableConstant profile
Systems affectedAny organMainly cytokine release syndrome and neurological events
Time courseVery variable, even after the end of therapyMostly during step-up dosing or just beyond
PredictabilityLargely unpredictableQuite predictable
💊 Pharm review #6 — “This table is the one you should really know”

What they said: the reactions to a T-cell engager are individually indistinguishable — fever belongs to all of them — so the discriminator is the timing.

ReactionWhenHow it presentsWhy
Infusion-related reactionMinutes into the infusion, or on the second administrationAnaphylaxis, hypotension, angioedema, bronchospasmIgE hypersensitivity — which is why patients are watched closely through every infusion
Cytokine release syndromeSeveral hours after the infusionFever, hypotension, hypoxiaCytokines, interleukin-6 above all
Tumour flare reaction1–3 daysPain at the tumour itself, transientInflammatory swelling of the treated deposit
ICANS3–9 daysSpeech difficulty, memory trouble, confusion, headache, seizure — looks like a strokeInflammation breaks down the blood–brain barrier
Cytopenias (they call it febrile cytopenia; the haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis end of the spectrum)LaterNeutropenia, anaemia, thrombocytopeniaMarrow suppression and immune consumption

The strategy they attached to it: “You're going to come down to 2 answer choices and think either could be right. They want you to take that little step further.” Decide on timing first, then on the symptom pattern. Immediate or on the second dose → infusion reaction. Hours → cytokine release syndrome. Days, with neurology → ICANS. And in real patients these overlap — cytokine release syndrome often runs on into ICANS — but an exam item that lists them all is asking you to pick on timing.

🩺 Cytokine release syndrome versus ICANS — and the two different steroids 💊 PHARM REVIEW
  • Cytokine release syndrome — the most common reaction to a T-cell engager or CAR-T. Fever, hypotension, hypoxia, typically 4–16 hours after a dose (an infusion reaction occurs within the first 6 hours and is generally afebrile). It is interleukin-6 driven, so the specific treatment is tocilizumab, an anti-IL-6 receptor antibody, plus corticosteroids and vasopressors in severe cases.
  • ICANS — immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome, 3–9 days after infusion: speech difficulty, confusion, behaviour change, headache, seizure. The mechanism is endothelial and blood–brain barrier disturbance, not IL-6 storm — so tocilizumab is NOT the treatment. Use dexamethasone (it penetrates the central nervous system) plus a non-sedating anticonvulsant, since sedation would obscure the neurologic assessment.
⚠️ Two other toxicities to name cold

Aldesleukin (interleukin-2) → capillary leak syndrome. IL-2 makes the endothelium leak; the patient becomes hypotensive and third-spaces fluid.

Thalidomide / lenalidomide / pomalidomide → thromboembolism, and contraindicated in pregnancy. The teratogenicity is the historical reason these drugs are dispensed under strict pregnancy-prevention programmes. Proteasome inhibitors (bortezomib, ixazomib, carfilzomib) → neuropathy (less with subcutaneous than intravenous) and herpes zoster reactivation.

Q: Why is there no monoclonal antibody in the signal-transduction group of targeted therapies?

Answer

Because those targets are intracellular. BCR-ABL, RAF, MEK, mTOR, BTK, PARP, PI3K and CDK4/6 all sit inside the cell. A monoclonal antibody is a ~145,000-dalton protein that cannot cross the cell membrane, so it can only engage the extracellular domain of a transmembrane receptor. Every signal-transduction inhibitor is therefore a small molecule.

Q: A patient on a monoclonal antibody targeting the epidermal growth factor receptor develops a florid acneiform rash over the face and upper trunk. Is this an allergy?

Answer

No — it is an on-target, mechanism-based toxicity. The epidermal growth factor receptor is highly expressed in normal skin, so blocking it produces the characteristic acne-like rash. Both the small molecules (erlotinib, gefitinib, afatinib, osimertinib) and the antibodies (cetuximab, panitumumab, necitumumab) cause it. An infusion reaction would be the separate, antibody-specific toxicity.

Q: Two antibody-drug conjugates both target HER2 in breast cancer, yet one causes prominent peripheral neuropathy and the other prominent myelosuppression and diarrhoea. Explain.

Answer

The payloads differ. Trastuzumab emtansine carries emtansine, an anti-microtubule agent — hence neuropathy (plus thrombocytopenia and transaminitis). Trastuzumab deruxtecan carries deruxtecan, a topoisomerase inhibitor — hence neutropenia, anaemia, thrombocytopenia, nausea and diarrhoea. The antibody determines where the drug goes; the payload determines what the toxicity looks like.

Q: Six hours after a step-up dose of a bispecific T-cell engager, a patient develops a temperature of 39.4 °C, blood pressure 82/50, and oxygen saturation 89% on room air. Diagnosis and specific treatment?

Answer

Cytokine release syndrome. The discriminators are timing beyond 6 hours (4–16 hours is typical) and the triad of fever, hypotension and hypoxia — an infusion-related reaction occurs within the first 6 hours and is generally afebrile. Treatment: tocilizumab (anti-IL-6 receptor), plus corticosteroids and vasopressors in severe cases. CRS is largely confined to the first administrations during step-up dosing, which is exactly when this patient presented.

Q: Day 6 after a T-cell engager infusion a patient becomes confused, cannot name objects, and has a witnessed seizure. Fever has resolved. What is this, and which steroid do you choose?

Answer

ICANS — immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome, occurring 3–9 days after infusion. The pathophysiology is endothelial and blood–brain barrier disturbance, not an IL-6 storm — so tocilizumab is not the answer here. Choose dexamethasone, which penetrates the central nervous system, plus a non-sedating anticonvulsant (sedation would obscure the neurologic assessment).

LO 15Source: Pharmacology of Antineoplastic Agents · Part 3

Section 46 · Antineoplastic pharmacology

Hormonal Therapy — Mechanisms and Toxicities

Three families: anti-estrogens, anti-androgens, and gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonists. The mechanistic question in every case is the same: are you blocking the receptor, or removing the hormone? And the toxicity is the toxicity of inducing menopause or andropause on purpose.

Abbreviations used in this section SERM selective estrogen receptor modulator · GnRH gonadotropin-releasing hormone · LHRH luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone — the same thing · LH / FSH luteinizing hormone / follicle-stimulating hormone · Aromatase the enzyme converting androgenic precursors to estrogens · CYP17 17α-hydroxylase / C17,20-lyase, required for androgen biosynthesis · DHEA dehydroepiandrosterone · BMD bone mineral density · ACTH adrenocorticotropic hormone
💊 Pharm review #7 — Part 3: names, mechanism, adverse effects

What they said: “If you're going to learn any drug names, know Part 1 and Part 3 — and their mechanism. Do they inhibit estrogen? Do they inhibit testosterone?”

  • Predict the adverse effects instead of memorising them: you are depriving the body of a sex hormone, so think of menopause — fatigue, hot flashes, bone loss. That single frame covers most of the list.
  • The SERM question they asked the room: raloxifene treats osteoporosis because it is an agonist in bone (building bone mineral density) while being an antagonist in breast — breast and ovarian tumours feed on estrogen, so you starve them there and mimic estrogen where you want it.
  • Prostate cancer feeds on testosterone, so the anti-androgens block it. –lutamide (flutamide, bicalutamide) → gynecomastia, which they flagged twice: “the boards love it if it's unusual,” and it is a real counselling point for the patient.
  • The GnRH agonist paradox — why give an agonist? The surge in luteinizing and follicle-stimulating hormone briefly feeds the tumour (the flare); then, because the dose far exceeds anything the body makes, the axis desensitises and shuts down. Leuprolide is the name to be sure of.

Anti-estrogens — two points on one pathway ★ HY

🔑 The pathway, and where each drug cuts it

Adrenal cortex → androgens → [AROMATASE — blocked by anastrozole, letrozole, exemestane] → estrogens → [RECEPTOR — blocked by tamoxifen, fulvestrant] → breast tumour growth.

Aromatase inhibitors deplete the hormone (upstream). SERMs and fulvestrant block the receptor (downstream).

Selective estrogen receptor modulatorAntiestrogenAromatase inhibitor
DrugsTamoxifen, raloxifene, toremifeneFulvestrantAnastrozole, letrozole, exemestane
MechanismBoth agonist and antagonist effects in different tissues — antagonist in breast, agonist in bone and endometriumPure antiestrogenic; inhibits receptor dimerisation and promotes degradation of the estrogen receptorInhibit aromatase, reducing synthesis of estrogens from androgenic precursors
UsePrevention and treatment of breast cancer; osteoporosis (raloxifene)Breast cancer treatmentBreast cancer treatment — postmenopausal women only
Toxicities↑ Endometrial cancer · protective bone properties · thromboembolic risk · vaginal dryness and discharge—Osteoporosis · hot flashes · arthralgias
🪝 Memory hook — bone is the giveaway 💊 PHARM REVIEW

SERMs protect bone; aromatase inhibitors destroy it. A SERM is an estrogen agonist in bone, so it preserves bone mineral density — and an agonist in endometrium, so it raises endometrial cancer risk. An aromatase inhibitor removes estrogen from every tissue, so bone loses its protection and you get osteoporosis, hot flashes and arthralgias instead. Give the bone finding and you can name the class.

⚠️ Why aromatase inhibitors only work after menopause

In a premenopausal woman the ovary is still making estrogen directly, and there is far more of it than peripheral aromatisation can account for — so blocking aromatase cannot suppress estrogen adequately, and may even trigger a compensatory gonadotropin rise. Appropriate options there are tamoxifen (effective regardless of menopausal status) or ovarian suppression with a GnRH agonist, with an aromatase inhibitor added afterwards.

Anti-androgens

Receptor antagonistsTestosterone depleter
Drugs1st generation: flutamide, bicalutamide, nilutamide
2nd generation: enzalutamide, apalutamide		Abiraterone
MechanismCompete with the natural hormone for the androgen receptor and prevent its action in the prostateInhibits CYP17, required for androgen biosynthesis (the testosterone precursors DHEA and androstenedione) — expressed in testicular, adrenal and prostatic tumour tissue
ToxicitiesGynecomastia and rare hepatotoxicityHepatotoxicity; electrolyte disturbance — hypokalaemia
🧠 Why abiraterone causes hypokalaemia — and why it is given with prednisone

Blocking CYP17 shunts adrenal steroid precursors down the mineralocorticoid pathway, producing a state of mineralocorticoid excess: hypokalaemia, fluid retention and hypertension. This is exactly why abiraterone is given with prednisone — the corticosteroid suppresses the ACTH drive generating the excess precursors.

GnRH (LHRH) agonists

DomainDetail
DrugsLeuprolide, goserelin, triptorelin
MechanismBind LHRH receptors on pituitary gonadotropin-producing cells: (1) initial surge in LH and FSH — the tumour “flare”; (2) therefore use concurrent anti-androgen therapy in prostate cancer; (3) induce menopause in patients with breast cancer
UseProstate cancer and premenopausal breast cancer
ToxicitiesHot flashes, sexual dysfunction, decreased bone mineral density
⚠️ The tumour flare is the counter-intuitive step 💊 PHARM REVIEW

An agonist at the GnRH receptor initially increases LH and FSH — and therefore testosterone — before continuous stimulation downregulates the receptor and shuts the axis down. In a man with bony metastatic prostate cancer, that transient testosterone surge can produce tumour flare: worsening bone pain, urinary obstruction, or spinal cord compression. The mandated fix is concurrent anti-androgen therapy to cover the flare window.

Q: A 48-year-old premenopausal woman with estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer is started on anastrozole alone. What is wrong with this plan?

Answer

Aromatase inhibitors are for postmenopausal women. They reduce synthesis of estrogens from androgenic precursors — the peripheral route that dominates after menopause. In a premenopausal woman the ovary produces estrogen directly, so the drug cannot suppress estrogen adequately. Appropriate options: tamoxifen (effective regardless of menopausal status), or ovarian suppression with a GnRH/LHRH agonist — leuprolide, goserelin or triptorelin — with an aromatase inhibitor added afterwards.

Q: A woman on long-term tamoxifen reports postmenopausal vaginal bleeding. What is the concern, and why does tamoxifen cause it while anastrozole does not?

Answer

Endometrial cancer. Tamoxifen is a selective estrogen receptor modulator — antagonist in breast (the therapeutic effect) but AGONIST in endometrium, which drives proliferation and raises endometrial cancer risk. It is also an agonist in bone, the origin of its protective bone properties. An aromatase inhibitor removes estrogen from every tissue, so it has no endometrial agonist effect — but for the same reason causes osteoporosis, hot flashes and arthralgias instead. Tamoxifen additionally carries thromboembolic risk.

Q: A man with metastatic prostate cancer and vertebral metastases is started on leuprolide. Two weeks later he develops severe back pain and leg weakness. What happened, and what should have been given?

Answer

Tumour flare from the initial surge in LH and FSH that a GnRH agonist produces before it downregulates the pituitary. The resulting testosterone surge stimulates the tumour, and in a patient with vertebral metastases that can mean cord compression. Concurrent anti-androgen therapy — bicalutamide, flutamide or nilutamide — should have been started to cover the flare window.

LO 63Source: Surgery — The Lymphatic System

Section 47 · The lymphatic system

Lymphatic Structure, the Thoracic Duct, and Mucosal Immunity

Why a surgeon lectures on lymphatics: because most of the damage is ours — a groin dissection that produces a heavy leg, and a left internal jugular line that fills a chest with chyle.

Abbreviations used in this section MALT mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue — the umbrella term · GALT gut-associated lymphoid tissue · BALT bronchus-associated lymphoid tissue · M cell microfold cell, the antigen-sampling epithelial cell · IgA / IgG / IgE immunoglobulin A / G / E · IJ internal jugular vein · Chyle lymph rich in fat absorbed from the intestine, giving it a milky appearance · Chylothorax chyle in the pleural space · Interstitium the fluid-filled space between cells, outside blood vessels · Oncotic pressure the osmotic pull exerted by proteins in a fluid compartment · Peyer's patches non-encapsulated lymphoid nodules of the ileum · NEC necrotizing enterocolitis · Positive selection survival of thymocytes that appropriately recognize antigen
🎯 Surgery review — the seven things he said to know

Everything flagged 🎯 SURGERY REVIEW in this document was named in the surgery review session. Each item links to where it is worked in full.

  1. Cancer spreads through the lymph nodes, with abdominal primaries heading for the portal system. If it's in the lungs, it got there through the thoracic duct.
  2. The mechanics of lymphedema — and compression therapy is really the only viable treatment.
  3. The four ligaments of the spleen — splenorenal, splenocolic, splenophrenic, gastrosplenic.
  4. Severe pancreatitis is a problem — thromboses, varices, GI (gastrointestinal) bleeds; splenic vein thrombosis gives splenomegaly AND ischemia.
  5. Why people get big spleens — TTP, ITP, Hodgkin / some non-Hodgkin lymphoma, sickle cell, infectious mononucleosis.
  6. OPSS (overwhelming post-splenectomy sepsis) — unstoppable once it starts, death in 8 hours or less; vaccinate against H. influenzae, N. meningitidis, S. pneumoniae.
  7. Splenic trauma standard of care — stable → no splenectomy; grades IV and up, or unstable at any grade (SBP < 90 and HR > 100) → splenectomy.

Structure and physiology — a low-pressure, protein-scavenging drainage system

🔑 The primary function — and it is not the immune one

The primary function of the lymphatic system is to return proteins and fluids to the blood. Immune function is real but secondary in this framing. When the system goes awry and proteins cannot get from the interstitial space back into the circulation, that is when complications set up.

Low pressure

versus blood vessels

Pressure within lymph vessel walls is LOWER than in blood vessels, and lymph flows more slowly. Lymphatic vessels have valves and behave much like veins; when those valves are damaged or inflamed, flow fails.

High permeability

the key property

Lymphatic vessel walls are MORE permeable than blood capillary walls — which is why they can admit what capillaries cannot.

Protein-rich contents

the consequence

Proteins too large to re-enter the capillaries enter the lymphatic vessels for return to the bloodstream. Lymphatic fluid is therefore very heavy in protein — and that single fact explains lymphedema.

Tiny caliber

why we cannot repair them

The thoracic duct is only 2–3 mm; peripheral lymphatics are the width of pencil lead. You cannot sew pencil lead — which is why there is no good surgical option for lymphatic injury.

🧠 Why lymphatic obstruction swells so much more than venous obstruction

Because lymph is protein-rich. Lymphatic capillaries admit large proteins that cannot re-enter the venous capillaries at all. Block the lymphatic route and those proteins have no alternative drainage path — they accumulate in the interstitium, raising oncotic pressure and drawing water with them. Venous obstruction, by contrast, raises hydrostatic pressure but leaves the protein-clearing route intact.

Node enlargement follows the same logic: bacteria, allergenic particles and cancerous cells collected in the nodes stimulate lymphocyte proliferation, greatly enlarging the node.

The thoracic duct — and the one line you must never place ★ HY

Thoracic duct (LEFT)Right lymphatic duct
Territory drainedEverything except the right upper body — entire lower body, abdomen, left thorax, left arm, left head and neckRight upper body only
Entry pointConfluence of the LEFT subclavian and LEFT internal jugular veins — on the POSTERIOR wallConfluence of the right subclavian and right internal jugular veins
Size2–3 mm — the major ductSmaller, superficial
Consequence of injuryCHYLOTHORAX and chylous ascitesFar less significant — smaller volume
⚠️ Never place a LEFT internal jugular central line

Anatomy: the thoracic duct enters at the posterior wall of the internal jugular vein at the confluence of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins — directly in the path of a left internal jugular needle.

Mechanism of injury: you place the needle, pass the wire, and believe you are in the vein — but you may be in the thoracic duct. You then pass the dilator, which is what does the damage. The line will not thread, so you pull everything and try again, succeed on the second pass, and the chest radiograph shows no pneumothorax, so all seems well. The next morning the film is white.

Why it is so hard to fix: repair requires entering the left chest and working at the apex of the lung, and roughly 90% of the time nothing can be done. The maneuver of last resort is instilling high-fat feeds to increase chyle flow and make the leak visible enough to place a stitch. Usually the duct is simply ligated, relying on the right-sided duct to compensate.

Use instead: the RIGHT internal jugular, a subclavian, or a femoral vein.

Lymph node architecture ★ HY

ZoneCellsWhat happens there
Cortex (outer)B cells, in folliclesThe B-cell zone. Primary follicles become secondary follicles with germinal centres on antigen encounter — the site of the germinal-centre reaction
Paracortex (deep cortex)T cells, plus dendritic cellsThe T-cell zone, where antigen-presenting cells engage T cells. Expands in viral infection
Medulla (inner)Medullary cords (plasma cells, macrophages) and medullary sinusesWhere antibody-secreting plasma cells sit, and lymph collects before leaving via efferent lymphatics
🧠 Antigen-independent versus antigen-dependent maturation

Lymphocyte development happens in two stages, in two different places:

  • Antigen-INdependent maturation occurs in the primary (generative) lymphoid organs — bone marrow for B cells, thymus for T cells. The cell rearranges its receptor genes and is selected for functionality and self-tolerance without ever meeting its antigen. The product is a naive lymphocyte.
  • Antigen-DEPENDENT maturation occurs in the secondary (peripheral) lymphoid organs — lymph nodes, spleen, and mucosal tissue. Here the naive cell meets its antigen and undergoes clonal expansion, class switching, somatic hypermutation and affinity maturation in the germinal centre, producing plasma cells and memory cells.

The overall architecture: marrow → thymus (T cells) → lymph nodes, spleen and mucosa, with continuous recirculation. Generative organs feed the peripheral organs — and it is the peripheral end organs that surgeons have to address.

🔑 T-cell training in the thymus

The thymus is a soft, triangular organ in the mediastinum, anterior and superior to the heart, posterior to the sternum. It receives immature T cells from the marrow and trains them:

  1. T cells first reside in the CORTEX, where they contact antigen-presenting epithelial cells.
  2. Those that respond are selected to survive, mature, and migrate to the MEDULLA.
  3. Non-responders die by APOPTOSIS and are cleared by macrophages.

The slide names this positive selection. The thymus secretes thymulin, thymopoietin and thymosins, and involutes from the onset of puberty, being replaced by adipose tissue — because the immune system produces most of its T cells during childhood and requires very few new ones after puberty.

MALT, GALT and BALT — “mucosal antiseptic paint” ★ HY

🔑 The three-letter families

MALT — mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue, the umbrella term. It includes:

  • GALT — gut-associated lymphoid tissue (Peyer's patches, appendix)
  • BALT — bronchus-associated lymphoid tissue (tonsils)

Major function: generation and dissemination of antigen-sensitized B cells, which require presentation to antibody-producing plasma cells in secretory tissues.

Peyer's patches (GALT)Tonsils (BALT)
LocationThroughout the ILEUM of the small intestineGateway of the respiratory and alimentary tracts
CapsuleNOT encapsulated — unlike lymph nodesNOT encapsulated
How antigen arrivesM (microfold) cells line the luminal side and sample antigen by endocytosisDIRECT and continuous exposure at the crypts — unlike lymph nodes, which receive antigen via the bloodstream
Predominant antibodyIgA — “MUCOSAL ANTISEPTIC PAINT”IgG, and to a lesser degree IgE
FunctionMonitor intestinal bacterial populations and prevent growth of pathogenic bacteriaAntigen presented to T helper and B cells → immunoglobulin-secreting plasma cells
🪝 Memory hook — “mucosal antiseptic paint”

The chain to memorize: Peyer's patches → ileum / ileocecal region → IgA → “mucosal antiseptic paint” → coats the bowel → prevents bacterial invasion of the mucosa.

The surgical consequence: a child who undergoes ileocecal resection — classically for necrotizing enterocolitis — loses the major site of IgA production and is therefore at risk of gastrointestinal sepsis from bacterial translocation across an unprotected mucosa.

🩺 The age shift — the thread that ties this lecture together

In young children, gut and mucosal lymphoid tissue (Peyer's patches, tonsils, appendix) and the thymus carry enormous immunological weight. As we age, that responsibility shifts toward the bone marrow and other parts of the lymphatic system.

This is why the same operation carries different risk at different ages: an ileocecal resection or tonsillectomy in a small child removes a meaningful fraction of their immune capacity, while in an adult it does not. It is also why splenectomy is deferred past early childhood whenever possible, and why tonsillectomy is now rare and generally deferred to about age 12 or older. The appendix, too, is a wealth of immunological importance in very young children.

🧠 Selective IgA deficiency is a different thing — and the transfusion link

Selective IgA deficiency is the most common primary immunodeficiency — an inherited failure to produce IgA. It causes recurrent respiratory and gastrointestinal infections, is often asymptomatic and found incidentally, and is associated with autoimmune disease and allergies. These patients are at risk of anaphylactic transfusion reactions to IgA-containing blood products (Section 14).

Surgical IgA loss after ileocecal resection is by contrast an ACQUIRED, LOCAL deficit of mucosal IgA production. The final common pathway — a less-protected mucosal barrier — is genuinely similar, which is why the two get confused.

Q: A resident places a left internal jugular central line. The immediate post-procedure chest radiograph shows no pneumothorax and correct catheter position. The following morning the left hemithorax is opacified. What has happened, and why did the first film look normal?

Answer

Thoracic duct injury with chylothorax. The duct enters the posterior wall at the confluence of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins, directly in the needle's path; the dilator does the damage.

The first film was normal because chyle accumulates over hours — flow depends on lymphatic return, which is slow, and increases substantially only once the patient is fed. The correct lesson is preventive: do not place a left internal jugular line; use the right internal jugular, subclavian, or femoral vein.

Q: A 6-week-old infant undergoes ileocecal resection for necrotizing enterocolitis. Which immunoglobulin is most reduced, and what is the clinical consequence?

Answer

IgA — the “mucosal antiseptic paint” produced by Peyer's patches, which are concentrated in the ileum and ileocecal region. Losing that tissue removes the major site of IgA production, leaving the intestinal mucosa vulnerable to bacterial invasion and placing the infant at risk of gastrointestinal sepsis through bacterial translocation.

Q: How do tonsils differ structurally from lymph nodes in the way they encounter antigen, and which immunoglobulin predominates in each of tonsils and Peyer's patches?

Answer

Tonsils are directly and continually exposed to antigen at the gateway of the respiratory and alimentary tracts, whereas lymph nodes receive antigen via the bloodstream and afferent lymphatics. Tonsils are also non-encapsulated, unlike lymph nodes. Tonsils: predominantly IgG, less IgE. Peyer's patches: predominantly IgA.

Q: Where do immature T cells first encounter antigen-presenting cells in the thymus, and what happens to those that fail to respond?

Answer

They first reside in the CORTEX, where they contact antigen-presenting epithelial cells. Those that respond are selected to survive, mature, and migrate to the MEDULLA. Non-responders die by apoptosis and are cleared by macrophages. This is positive selection.

Section 48 · The lymphatic system

Lymphedema — Square Toes, and a Diagnosis That Depends on Geography

The one lymphatic diagnosis you will certainly meet. It hinges on a single physical sign, and on a history question about where the patient has lived.

Abbreviations used in this section Stemmer sign inability to tent the skin of the interdigital web space — the “square toes” of lymphedema · Peau d'orange literally “orange peel” — dimpled skin from dermal edema tethered by hair follicles · Hyperkeratosis thickening of the outer skin layer · Lichenification leathery skin thickening from chronic irritation · Praecox / tarda Latin for early / late · Filariasis parasitic infection by filarial nematodes · Elephantiasis gross limb enlargement from chronic lymphatic obstruction · Lymphoscintigraphy nuclear imaging of lymphatic transit after interdigital tracer injection · Lymphangiosarcoma malignancy arising in chronically lymphedematous tissue · DVT deep vein thrombosis
🔑 Pathophysiology in one sentence 🎯 SURGERY REVIEW

Lymphedema ensues if the production of lymph exceeds the maximal transport capacity of the lymphatic conduits. Accumulation of protein and cellular metabolites in the extracellular space generates water accumulation, collagen deposition, and elevated interstitial pressure.

The collagen deposition is why chronic lymphedema becomes firm and fibrotic rather than remaining soft and pitting.

🔥

Acute findings

  • Skin is pink or red with a mildly elevated temperature — easily mistaken for cellulitis or deep vein thrombosis
  • Pain: aching or heaviness of the limb
  • Severe pain is rare — a useful discriminator against infection and acute ischemia
🪨

Chronic findings

  • Thickened skin with hyperkeratosis, lichenification and peau d'orange
  • Progressive fibrosis from collagen deposition
  • Disfiguring and debilitating; requires sequential wrapping and special garments
🔑 The Stemmer sign — square toes ★ HY

Edema extends to the distal aspects of the feet, resulting in “SQUARE TOES”.

The formal definition: loss of cutaneous elasticity with an INABILITY TO TENT the skin of the interdigital web space. At the bedside: with ordinary edema you can usually pinch it; with lymphedema the skin is firm and tough and cannot be pinched, despite obvious swelling.

Classification

TypeSubtypeDefining feature
Primary lymphedema
Females affected 2- to 10-fold more often than males		CongenitalOnset before age 1 year
Lymphedema praecoxOnset age 1 to 35 years
Lymphedema tardaOnset after age 35 years
Secondary lymphedema
The most common form of lymphatic disease — more common than primary		Developed countriesIATROGENIC — lymphatic trauma or dissection · cancer or radiotherapy · also large burns, pregnancy, and bacterial and fungal infection
Developing countriesFILARIASIS — Wuchereria bancrofti, the most frequent cause worldwide (elephantiasis)
🩺 The two vignettes — and why the history question is “where have you lived?”

Case 1 — the United States. A patient with a swollen, painful, heavy UNILATERAL leg. History reveals a hernia repair or kidney transplant 6–8 weeks ago — both approached through the groin, where the lymphatics run. There is pitting edema, erythema, warmth, pain.

First thought must be deep vein thrombosis — because DVTs are deadly — so you obtain an ultrasound. It is negative. Then, on examination, you notice square toes and a positive Stemmer sign → iatrogenic lymphedema from surgical injury to the groin lymphatics.

Note the deliberate rule-out: unilateral is doing real work here. Heart failure gives BILATERAL lower extremity edema, so a unilateral heavy leg is not heart failure.

Case 2 — overseas. A woman from the Philippines with a swollen, painful arm and breast, unilateral. Everyone fears malignancy; the mammogram is clear. The answer is filariasis. And the prognostic difference matters: the parasitic one is easier to treat, because you give medication. The surgical damage is probably not reversible.

Differentiating lymphedema from deep vein thrombosis ★ HY

FeatureLymphedemaDeep vein thrombosis
OnsetGradual, over weeks to months — often 6–8 weeks after a groin operationAcute, over hours to days
PainAching or heaviness. Severe pain is rareOften genuinely painful, with calf tenderness
Stemmer signPOSITIVE — skin of the interdigital web space cannot be tented; square toesNEGATIVE — skin remains pinchable
DistributionExtends to the distal foot and toesTypically calf or whole limb, sparing the toes
Skin over timeHyperkeratosis, lichenification, peau d'orange, fibrosisNormal texture; may be warm and erythematous acutely
PittingPits early; becomes non-pitting and firm as fibrosis developsPits
Definitive testLymphoscintigraphy (after a negative ultrasound)Duplex/Doppler ultrasound
Order of testingUltrasound FIRST, always — because a deep vein thrombosis can kill and lymphedema cannot. Lymphedema is the diagnosis you reach after the ultrasound is negative and you look at the toes
🪝 Memory hook — the discriminating triad

Unilateral (so not heart failure) + negative ultrasound (so not a clot) + square toes with a positive Stemmer sign (so lymphedema). Add a groin operation 6–8 weeks ago in a developed country, or a childhood spent in an endemic region, and you have the cause as well as the diagnosis.

Diagnosis, treatment and complications

Diagnosis

clinical first

Clinical presentation, history and physical findings. Inspect for cutaneous and subcutaneous fibrosis, peau d'orange, and Stemmer sign.

Lymphoscintigraphy

the confirmatory study

Reliable and reproducible. A radiolabeled macromolecular tracer is injected into an interdigital space of the affected limb and its transit imaged.

Nonsurgical management 🎯 SURGERY REVIEW

first line, always

Elevation, therapeutic exercise, manual massage, and compression therapy (wraps, pumps, garments). Compression is the one that actually works.

Surgical therapy

rarely, and late

Only after a trial of conservative therapy. Heroic attempts — such as sewing an opened vein onto a lymph node — do not pan out well.

Preventive measures

the durable win

Skin hygiene, clothing precautions, trauma avoidance, infection control.

Complications

including a malignancy

Infection, malnutrition, immunodeficiency — and LYMPHANGIOSARCOMA.

🎯 Surgery review #2 — the mechanics of lymphedema

What he said: understand the mechanics of lymphedema — compressive therapy is really the only viable treatment.

  • The mechanics: lymph production exceeds what the lymphatic channels can carry → protein is left behind in the interstitium → it pulls water in by oncotic pressure → swelling → the stagnant protein drives inflammation and collagen deposition → soft pitting edema becomes firm, non-pitting fibrosis.
  • Why compression is the answer: the defect is a transport failure, and there is nothing to fix surgically — lymphatics are the width of pencil lead and cannot be sewn. External pressure (wraps, pumps, garments) raises interstitial pressure, pushes fluid back into the remaining lymphatics and veins, and stops re-accumulation. Surgery is rare, late, and works poorly.
🩺 The professional point embedded in the case

There is a phrase in surgery: if you are operating somewhere in the body and something bad happens, it is your fault, and you need to identify the problem. Applied here — a patient with a swollen leg weeks after your groin operation deserves an honest consideration that the lymphatics were injured, rather than a reflexive search for another explanation.

Q: A 54-year-old woman has a heavy, aching, swollen right leg that began 6 weeks after an inguinal hernia repair. Duplex ultrasonography shows no deep vein thrombosis. The skin of the second interdigital web space cannot be tented. Diagnosis and underlying cause?

Answer

Secondary lymphedema from iatrogenic injury to the groin lymphatics. The inability to tent the interdigital web space is a positive Stemmer sign (square toes). Unilateral involvement excludes heart failure, which gives bilateral edema; the negative ultrasound excludes DVT. In developed countries the leading cause of secondary lymphedema is iatrogenic — lymphatic trauma or dissection. Treatment is conservative: elevation, exercise, manual massage, compression — and it is unlikely to reverse.

Q: A 40-year-old woman who emigrated from the Philippines has a unilateral swollen, painful arm and breast. Mammography shows no malignancy. Most likely cause and causative organism?

Answer

Filariasis — the most frequent cause of secondary lymphedema worldwide, producing elephantiasis. The organism is Wuchereria bancrofti. It typically enters through skin invasion or injury and destroys the lymphatic system. Importantly, unlike surgical lymphedema, the parasitic form is treatable with medication and may be reversible.

Q: Distinguish the acute from the chronic skin findings of lymphedema, and name the malignancy that can arise in a chronically lymphedematous limb.

Answer

Acute: pink or red skin with mildly elevated temperature. Chronic: thickened skin with hyperkeratosis, lichenification and peau d'orange, reflecting progressive collagen deposition and fibrosis. In both, pain is typically only aching or heaviness — severe pain is rare. The malignant complication is lymphangiosarcoma; other complications are infection, malnutrition and immunodeficiency.

LO 10LO 43Source: Hypercoagulable States & Thrombophilia

Section 49 · Thrombosis · treating the clot

Deep Vein Thrombosis and Pulmonary Embolism — Starting, Choosing and Stopping Anticoagulation

Two structurally different ways to start, one score to gauge the harm of continuing, and a decision about duration where the arithmetic genuinely does not resolve it.

Abbreviations used in this section VTE venous thromboembolism · DVT / PE deep vein thrombosis / pulmonary embolism · DOAC direct oral anticoagulant — apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran · VKA vitamin K antagonist, i.e. warfarin · UFH / LMWH unfractionated / low molecular weight heparin · INR international normalized ratio · PTT partial thromboplastin time · CrCl creatinine clearance · CHEST the journal of the American College of Chest Physicians · ASH American Society of Hematology · Grade 2B a weak recommendation on moderate-quality evidence · 4F-PCC four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate · CTEPH chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension · BNP brain natriuretic peptide · V/Q scan ventilation-perfusion scan · Phlegmasia cerulea dolens limb-threatening massive iliofemoral thrombosis with a swollen, blue, painful leg
🔑 The diagnostic approach — imaging first, and it differs by site ★ HY
  • Suspected deep vein thrombosis → Doppler (duplex) ultrasound, the standard imaging test. It is the first move in any unilateral swollen limb — because a DVT can kill and the alternatives on the differential cannot (see the lymphedema discrimination in Section 48).
  • Suspected chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension → the ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scan is the screening test of choice, NOT computed tomography angiography. Work it up with brain natriuretic peptide, echocardiography and a V/Q scan.
  • D-dimer is a fibrin degradation product. Beyond its role in initial exclusion, a persistently elevated D-dimer AFTER stopping anticoagulation predicts recurrence — which is why it appears in the duration decision below.

Starting treatment — two-drug versus one-drug ★ HY

2️⃣

Two-drug — a parenteral lead-in is required

Warfarin route (bridging). Start unfractionated heparin (intravenous, monitored by PTT) or low molecular weight heparin (subcutaneous) overlapping with warfarin for at least 5 days AND until the INR is above 2 for 1–2 days. Warfarin starts on day 1; target INR 2–3.

Dabigatran or edoxaban route (switching). The registration trials used 5–10 days of initial low molecular weight heparin and only then switched to the oral drug. These two are not monotherapy agents.

1️⃣

One-drug — oral from the first dose

Apixaban and rivaroxaban only. No heparin lead-in, no monitoring. Both use a loading phase then maintenance:

  • Rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily for 3 weeks, then 20 mg daily
  • Apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 1 week, then 5 mg twice daily

Apixaban is the choice in renal failure — the one DOAC that remains usable when creatinine clearance is low.

🪝 Memory hook — “the two that start with A and R go it alone”

Apixaban and Rivaroxaban are monotherapy with a loading dose. Dabigatran and Edoxaban need Days of heparin first. Note the trap: dabigatran and edoxaban are otherwise unrelated — dabigatran is a direct thrombin inhibitor, edoxaban a factor Xa inhibitor — but they share the lead-in requirement because of how their trials were designed.

🔑 The 2021 CHEST position: a DOAC over warfarin — and why
  • Efficacy is equal. DOACs equal warfarin at preventing recurrent clot. The advantage is not efficacy.
  • The four agents are similar to one another, on indirect comparison — there are no adequate head-to-head trials.
  • Bleeding is lower, especially intracranial bleeding. This is the real advantage.
  • Apixaban may have the lowest bleeding risk of the four.
  • Lack of a specific reversal agent does not make a major bleed more likely to be fatal — the important counterargument to “you cannot reverse them.”
  • Preferred for both initial and long-term treatment in patients without cancer — note the carve-out.

When NOT to use a direct oral anticoagulant ★ HY

SituationWhy the DOAC fails hereUse instead
Pregnancy or breastfeedingNot established as safe; crosses into fetal circulation / breast milkUnfractionated heparin; LMWH while breastfeeding
Severe VTE / large clot burden — massive PE, phlegmasia cerulea dolens, iliofemoral DVTFixed oral dosing cannot be titrated or stopped fast, and thrombolysis may be neededAdmit; unfractionated heparin, consider thrombolysis
Extremes of weight — above 300 lb or below 110 lbFixed dosing was never validated at these extremesLMWH / warfarin
Altered gastrointestinal anatomy — gastric bypassUnreliable absorption of apixaban and rivaroxaban specificallyWarfarin with monitoring
Renal dysfunction — CrCl below 30 mL/minRenal clearance of the drugApixaban or warfarin
Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia with thrombosisRequires a specific alternative strategyNon-heparin parenteral agent
Splanchnic vein thrombosisUnder-studied populationHeparin / warfarin
Antiphospholipid antibody syndromeRandomized evidence of HARMWarfarin, target INR 2–3
Major drug interactions — HIV drugs, phenytoin, carbamazepineEnzyme induction lowers drug levels unpredictablyWarfarin with monitoring

Bleeding risk — the VTE-BLEED score

Risk factorPoints
Active cancer2
Anemia1.5
History of bleeding1.5
Creatinine clearance 30–60 mL/min1.5
Age over 601.5
Uncontrolled hypertension in a male1
2 or more points = HIGH risk13% bleeding risk
0–1.5 points = LOW risk2.9% bleeding risk

Note how low the threshold is: a single active cancer, or any two of the 1.5-point items, tips a patient into the high-risk band — roughly a four-fold separation between bands.

🩺 Reversal — the first question is always “when was the last dose?”

For the factor Xa inhibitors and the direct thrombin inhibitor, half-lives are short enough that time and holding the drug are themselves the reversal strategy in most cases.

  • Rivaroxaban — half-life 5–9 hours; effect wanes quickly with holding.
  • Apixaban — half-life 8 hours; a dose taken more than 18 hours before presentation is likely at minimal concentration.
  • Dabigatran — allow more than 24 hours with good renal function; more than 36 hours if CrCl is below 30.

Andexanet alfa is narrow, expensive and protocol-driven: it requires severe or life-threatening bleeding AND confirmed apixaban or rivaroxaban within the previous 18 hours. It is explicitly NOT indicated for edoxaban, enoxaparin, fondaparinux, dabigatran or warfarin, nor for surgical reversal — and not if the hemorrhage is judged non-survivable. Otherwise: 4F-PCC. See the reversal bench in Section 15.

Duration of anticoagulation — the 2021 CHEST table ★ HY

IndicationDuration
Proximal DVT or PE secondary to a transient risk factor3 months
Idiopathic (unprovoked) proximal DVT or PE“At least 3 months”, then STOP or go LONG-TERM
Second unprovoked DVT or PELong-term
VTE in the setting of active cancerLow molecular weight heparin for at least 3 months
🩺 Choosing Wisely, recommendation 6

“Don't treat with an anticoagulant for more than 3 months in a patient with a first venous thromboembolism occurring in the setting of a major transient risk factor.” The provoked case is genuinely settled: 3 months, then stop.

🔑 Why the unprovoked decision is genuinely close
Recurrent VTE (if you stop)Bleeding (if you continue)
Risk per year5–8%2–6%
Case fatality rate4–12%—
Fatal events per year0.3–1%0.2–0.6%

Look only at the bottom row. The ranges overlap. That is the entire reason both the 2021 CHEST guideline and the 2020 ASH guideline say “suggest” rather than “recommend”, why the CHEST grade is 2B (a weak recommendation on moderate-quality evidence), and why this is a shared decision rather than a rule.

🧠 The four things to weigh before extending beyond 3 months
  1. Recurrence risk — unprovoked status, and D-dimer after stopping.
  2. Bleeding risk — patient characteristics, and the stability of anticoagulation; an erratic INR is itself a risk factor.
  3. Patient preference — the deciding vote. Values, lifestyle, occupation. Does this person race motorcycles? And on the other side, “I never want to have a pulmonary embolism again” is a legitimate and often decisive answer.
  4. Alternatives — it is not all-or-nothing. Low-intensity anticoagulation, a reduced-dose DOAC, or aspirin.
🔑 Low-intensity extended anticoagulation — two landmark trials

AMPLIFY-EXTEND (apixaban 2.5 mg vs 5 mg twice daily vs placebo, after 6–12 months of anticoagulation): recurrence reached ~8–9% on placebo but stayed under ~2% on both apixaban doses — essentially superimposed. Bleeding on the 2.5 mg arm tracked placebo almost exactly. The half dose gave the full benefit at essentially no excess bleeding — which is what created “low-intensity extended anticoagulation” as a real third option.

EINSTEIN-CHOICE (rivaroxaban 20 mg vs 10 mg vs aspirin 100 mg, 3,396 patients): aspirin recurrence ~4.5% versus ≤1.5% on either rivaroxaban dose, with major bleeding low and comparable across all three arms. For extended prevention, aspirin is markedly inferior to a low-dose DOAC and is not meaningfully safer. Aspirin remains an option only where anticoagulation is genuinely unacceptable.

⚠️ Inferior vena cava filters — one solid indication, and a long list of harms

The one indication carrying real confidence: acute venous thromboembolism in a patient with an absolute contraindication to anticoagulation. Beyond that, confidence falls away quickly.

Complications include filter thrombosis, insertion-site thrombosis, filter migration and fracture, caval perforation, and — the important one — an increased rate of recurrent deep vein thrombosis. A filter stops emboli reaching the lung; it does not treat the clotting disorder, and it introduces a thrombogenic foreign body. Retrievable filters should actually be retrieved.

🩺 Long-term complications after venous thromboembolism
  • Post-thrombotic syndrome — chronic limb swelling, pain, skin changes and ulceration from valve damage after a proximal DVT.
  • Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension. Risk is highest after submassive or massive pulmonary embolism and where there was right ventricular strain at presentation. Work up new dyspnea with BNP, echocardiography and a V/Q scan. If confirmed: indefinite anticoagulation, referral for pulmonary thromboendarterectomy, and lung transplantation for refractory disease. Untreated it progresses to cor pulmonale and death.

Q: A patient with a new proximal deep vein thrombosis is to be started on dabigatran. The intern plans to give the first oral dose today with no other agent. What is wrong?

Answer

Dabigatran requires a parenteral lead-in. Its registration trials used 5–10 days of initial low molecular weight heparin before switching to the oral drug — the same is true of edoxaban. Only apixaban and rivaroxaban are true monotherapy agents, each with a loading phase (rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily for 3 weeks then 20 mg daily; apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 1 week then 5 mg twice daily).

Q: A 68-year-old with active colon cancer, hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL and creatinine clearance 45 mL/min is being considered for extended anticoagulation. Estimate the VTE-BLEED score and interpret it.

Answer

Active cancer 2 + anemia 1.5 + CrCl 30–60 1.5 + age over 60 1.5 = 6.5 points. Far above the 2-point cut-off, placing them in the 13% bleeding risk band. This does not automatically forbid anticoagulation — cancer-associated VTE usually requires it — but it means the risk-benefit conversation is genuinely close, and the agent, dose and duration all need care.

Q: A 44-year-old has completed 6 months of anticoagulation after a first unprovoked pulmonary embolism. She wants ongoing protection but is worried about bleeding. What does the evidence support?

Answer

Low-intensity extended anticoagulation. AMPLIFY-EXTEND showed apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily gave the same reduction in recurrence as 5 mg (both under ~2% versus ~8–9% on placebo) while its bleeding curve was indistinguishable from placebo. EINSTEIN-CHOICE similarly showed rivaroxaban 10 mg was at least as good as 20 mg, and both were far superior to aspirin. So the honest answer is not “stop” and not “switch to aspirin” — it is continue at a reduced dose.

Q: A patient with antiphospholipid antibody syndrome and a new deep vein thrombosis asks to be treated with apixaban rather than warfarin. What do you say?

Answer

No — antiphospholipid antibody syndrome is one of the situations with randomized evidence of HARM from direct oral anticoagulants. Use warfarin with a target INR of 2–3. This is the most important of the DOAC exclusions to know, because it runs directly against the general 2021 CHEST recommendation to prefer a DOAC over warfarin — and the carve-outs are exactly what gets tested.

Section 50 · Bleeding · the platelet-destruction disorder

Immune Thrombocytopenia — One Antibody, Two Completely Different Diseases

Immune thrombocytopenic purpura is an antibody problem with a spleen problem attached. An IgG autoantibody coats the platelet, the spleen eats it, and the marrow responds by making more megakaryocytes — which is the finding that separates ITP from every other cause of a low platelet count. The reason this objective is worth its own section is that the childhood disease and the adult disease behave nothing alike, and the exam tests that split.

Abbreviations used in this section ITP immune thrombocytopenia, historically “idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura” — both names are still in use · IgG immunoglobulin G, the antibody class involved · GP2b/3a glycoprotein IIb/IIIa — the platelet surface receptor most often targeted · PT prothrombin time · PTT partial thromboplastin time · IVIG intravenous immunoglobulin · Anti-D anti-RhD immunoglobulin · ICH intracranial hemorrhage · URI upper respiratory infection · SLE systemic lupus erythematosus · RA rheumatoid arthritis · CLL chronic lymphocytic leukemia · Petechiae pinpoint non-blanching skin haemorrhages · Wet purpura blood blisters on the oral mucosa, a marker of higher bleeding risk
🔑 The mechanism, in one line ★ HY

Autoimmune production of IgG directed against platelet surface antigens (GP2b/3a). The antibodies are produced in the spleen AND the antibody-coated platelets are consumed in the spleen — the same organ does both jobs. That single fact explains the entire treatment ladder: steroids blunt antibody production, IVIG saturates splenic Fc receptors so the spleen stops eating platelets, and splenectomy removes the source of antibody and the site of destruction at once.

ITP is the most common cause of thrombocytopenia in both children and adults.

The two diseases that share one name

 Acute ITPChronic ITP
Duration defining itLess than 1 yearMore than 1 year
Who gets itChildren, typically after a viral infection or upper respiratory infectionAdults, predominantly women
TriggerPost-viral; often 1–4 weeks after the illnessPrimary (idiopathic), or secondary to autoimmune disease — SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, thyroid disease, inflammatory bowel disease — or to chronic lymphocytic leukemia
Natural historySelf-limited — 80% recover spontaneously, often with no treatment at allPersistent; relapsing and remitting
Default managementWatchful waiting. Initial treatment is observation, because the risk of life-threatening bleeding is very low (intracranial hemorrhage under 0.1%)Treat; most will need something
Obstetric footnote—Maternal IgG crosses the placenta, so a pregnant woman with chronic ITP may deliver an infant with short-lived neonatal thrombocytopenia
🩺 What the patient looks like — and the one exam sign that raises the stakes
  • Typically a well-appearing child or an otherwise well adult. Unexplained ecchymoses or petechiae are the presenting complaint.
  • Petechiae are NON-BLANCHING — press them and they do not fade. That is what makes them haemorrhage rather than rash.
  • “Wet purpura” — blood blisters in the oral mucosa — is the finding that should worry you. Mucosal bleeding marks a higher risk of serious haemorrhage than skin findings alone.
  • Splenomegaly is RARE. A big spleen argues against ITP and points you toward hypersplenism, a lymphoproliferative disorder, or portal hypertension instead.
🔑 The laboratory signature — isolated, profound, and with a busy marrow ★ HY
TestResult in ITPWhy it matters
Platelet countProfoundly low — under 100,000/mm³, often under 50,000/mm³Diagnostic threshold is <100,000/mm³
Haemoglobin, white cell countNormalIsolated thrombocytopenia. Involvement of other lines sends you to the marrow instead
PT and PTTNormalThis is a platelet problem, not a coagulation-factor problem — excludes disseminated intravascular coagulation and liver disease
Peripheral smearMarkedly reduced platelets, occasional large forms; red cells and white cells normalNo schistocytes — excludes the thrombotic microangiopathies
Bone marrow (when done)INCREASED megakaryocytes — megakaryocytic hyperplasia★ HY The marrow is working harder, not failing. This is the single finding that separates destruction from underproduction

A marrow biopsy is not required in a typical case — a well child with isolated thrombocytopenia and a normal smear does not need one. It is obtained when the picture is atypical, when other cell lines are involved, or before starting steroids in an adult where leukemia is a genuine competitor.

Treatment — and the reason splenectomy sometimes fails

LineOptionHow it works / what to know
First lineObservationThe correct answer in most children, and in adults with a safe count and no bleeding
CorticosteroidsReduce antibody production and splenic clearance. Only about 20% of patients achieve a sustained response — most relapse when steroids are tapered
IVIGRaises the platelet count quickly in symptomatic bleeding by saturating splenic Fc receptors. The effect is short-lived — a bridge, not a cure
Anti-D immunoglobulinSame Fc-blockade principle; only for RhD-positive patients with a spleen
RefractorySplenectomyRemoves both the source of antibody and the site of destruction. Sustained remission in 75–85%
Post-splenectomy failureRituximab (anti-CD20) or romiplostim (thrombopoietin receptor agonist)Rituximab removes the B cells making the antibody; romiplostim pushes production instead of protecting the platelets
EmergencyPlatelet transfusion + IVIG + steroidsFor intracranial haemorrhage or life-threatening bleeding. Transfused platelets are also destroyed, so this buys time only
⚠️ Why ITP comes back after a “successful” splenectomy ★ HY

Accessory spleens are present in about 20% of the population, and more than 80% of them sit right next to the spleen. They are functional. If an accessory spleen is present but not found and removed at operation, ITP will recur — the antibody source and the destruction site are still there. This is the standard explanation for relapse after splenectomy and it is a favourite question.

⚠️ Two things to avoid during the acute phase

Avoid aspirin (it adds a qualitative platelet defect on top of a quantitative one) and avoid high-risk activities while the count is low. In children, the most important intervention is often anticipatory guidance rather than a drug.

Q: A 5-year-old boy is brought in with petechiae over both shins and a blood blister inside his cheek, three weeks after a cold. He is otherwise well. Platelets 18,000/mm³; haemoglobin, white cell count, PT and PTT all normal; smear shows few platelets with occasional large forms and no other abnormality. What is the diagnosis, what would a marrow show, and what is the management?

Answer

Acute immune thrombocytopenia — post-viral, in a child, with isolated profound thrombocytopenia, a normal smear apart from the platelets, and normal coagulation times. The blood blister is wet purpura, which flags a higher bleeding risk and is worth noting out loud.

A marrow, if obtained, would show increased megakaryocytes — the marrow is compensating, which is the hallmark of peripheral destruction rather than marrow failure. It is not required here: a well child with an isolated cytopenia and a clean smear does not need a biopsy.

Management is observation. Eighty percent of children recover spontaneously and the risk of intracranial haemorrhage is under 0.1%. Add IVIG or steroids only if there is significant bleeding. Avoid aspirin and contact sports until the count recovers.

Section 51 · Pediatrics · marrow failure, prognosis, and the crises

Pediatric Hematology — Marrow Failure, Childhood Leukemia Prognosis, and Sickle Cell Crises

Children are not small adults in haematology. A pancytopenic child has a different differential than a pancytopenic adult, childhood leukemia has a different biology and a vastly better prognosis, and the sickle cell complications that kill in childhood are not the ones that kill in adulthood. This section covers the three things the objectives ask for.

Part 2 — Prognostic factors in childhood leukemia (LO 67)

🔑 Favourable versus unfavourable — the list the objective is asking for ★ HY

Acute lymphoblastic leukemia is the most common childhood malignancy, with a bimodal incidence — first peak at 2–5 years, second peak over 50. Roughly 80% of childhood acute leukemia is ALL and 20% is AML, and within ALL about 80% is B-ALL and 20% T-ALL.

VariableFAVOURABLEUNFAVOURABLE
Age2–10 years — that is, being a child. Peak incidence ~4 years does bestUnder 1 year, or adolescent/adult
ImmunophenotypePrecursor B-cellPrecursor T-cell
PloidyHyperdiploid — 51–65 chromosomesHypodiploid — 43 or fewer chromosomes
Translocationt(12;21) → ETV6-RUNX1t(9;22) → BCR-ABL1 (Philadelphia chromosome); t(1;19) → TCF3-PBX1
Presenting white cell countLowHigh
Central nervous systemNot involvedCNS involvement at diagnosis
Early responseRapid clearance of blasts (for example by day 8 of induction)Slow early response

Risk-based treatment follows directly: low risk / favourable → low-intensity standard chemotherapy; high risk / unfavourable → high-intensity therapy and bone marrow transplant.

🪝 Two memory hooks worth stealing
  • B-ALL markers are the big numbers: CD19, CD20, CD22. T-ALL markers are the tiny numbers: CD2, CD3, CD4, CD7, CD8.
  • T-ALL = Thymic mass in a Teenager. Roughly 70% present with a mediastinal mass, and it is more common in adolescent males.
  • Down syndrome: ALL when older than 5 years (“ALLder”), AML when younger than 5 years.
🧠 Why the same disease name carries three different prognoses

Survival in ALL falls from over 90% in children to 50–70% in adolescents and young adults to about 30% in older adults. It is not simply that children tolerate chemotherapy better. Adult ALL is enriched for adverse cytogenetics — including BCR-ABL1 — while childhood disease is enriched for favourable ones. Different biology wearing the same name, with reduced tolerance of intensive protocols widening the gap further.

Two practical points: morphology does not predict immunophenotype, so immunophenotyping is mandatory to separate B-ALL from T-ALL and assign risk; and ALL treatment requires prophylactic chemotherapy into the cerebrospinal fluid (and, historically, the scrotum) because those are pharmacologic sanctuary sites behind the blood-brain barrier.

Total treatment duration is roughly 2.5 years: induction (~4 weeks, 3–4 drugs) → consolidation (~8 weeks, clears sanctuary sites) → interim maintenance (8 weeks) → delayed intensification (8 weeks) → maintenance (~1.5 years). AML is different: 4–5 courses of intensive therapy with no role for maintenance.

Part 3 — The pediatric sickle cell crises (LO 7)

⚠️ Splenic sequestration — the one that kills in hours ★ HY

Sudden trapping of blood within the spleen. Usually occurs in infants under 2 years of age with homozygous sickle cell disease (and at older ages in HbSC or sickle-β-thalassemia, because those spleens survive longer).

  • The spleen is enlarged on examination, and it may not be accompanied by fever, pain or any other symptom — the child can simply become pale and shocked.
  • Haemoglobin more than 2 g/dL below baseline, often with relative thrombocytopenia.
  • A severe sequestration crisis can be fatal within a few hours.
  • Treatment: fluids, transfusion, and splenectomy for recurrent episodes.
🩺 The other crises, and the fever rule
  • Vaso-occlusive (painful) crisis — ischaemia from occluded vessels; chest, abdomen and joints. Mild to moderate pain: NSAIDs and opioids. Severe: hospitalisation.
  • Aplastic crisis — parvovirus B19 infects erythroid precursors and halts erythropoiesis. The reticulocyte count falls, which is what separates it from every other crisis.
  • Functional asplenia develops early from repeated infarction, bringing an increased risk of stroke and acute chest syndrome.
  • ★ HY Fever above 38.5 °C (101.1 °F) in a child with sickle cell disease is an EMERGENCY — obtain basic diagnostic labs and administer broad-spectrum antibiotics immediately. These children need earlier pneumococcal and meningococcal vaccination than the standard schedule.
🔑 Hydroxyurea — the disease-modifying drug, and why it works
  • Increases haemoglobin F, which does not participate in HbS polymerisation — the primary mechanism.
  • Decreases the white cell count, decreases endothelial adhesion, increases nitric oxide, decreases haemolysis.
  • Recommended for all patients, starting as infants. Titrated against clinical and laboratory parameters.

Chronic PRBC transfusion protects against stroke and acute chest syndrome, at the cost of iatrogenic iron overload, alloimmunisation (use sickle-negative, antigen-matched units) and infectious risk. Bone marrow transplant is the first proven curative option, mostly reserved for a perfectly matched sibling, with roughly 5% mortality and potential for significant morbidity.

⚠️ Anticoagulation in children — what is and is not approved

Usable: heparins (unfractionated, enoxaparin, fondaparinux) monitored with PTT and anti-factor Xa; warfarin monitored with INR; DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban) — no monitoring needed.

NOT approved for children: the direct thrombin inhibitors — bivalirudin, argatroban and dabigatran.

And one anatomical cause worth knowing: May-Thurner syndrome — compression of the LEFT iliac vein by the RIGHT iliac artery, presenting with thrombosis of the left lower extremity. In children it is rarely idiopathic, so image and investigate.

Q: Two children present with pancytopenia. Child A is 7, well-appearing, with short stature, café-au-lait macules and an absent right thumb; marrow is acellular. Child B is 4, sick-appearing, with splenomegaly and bone pain; marrow is packed with cells. Name each diagnosis, the confirmatory test for A, and the single finding in B that would most worsen the prognosis.

Answer

Child A: Fanconi anemia. Pancytopenia with an acellular marrow in a well-appearing child, plus the extra-haematologic triad of short stature, café-au-lait macules and a radial ray anomaly (absent thumb). Confirm with a chromosome breakage assay using diepoxybutane or mitomycin C, which shows markedly increased breaks and radial forms. Note the discriminator from TAR syndrome: TAR has absent radii with thumbs present; Fanconi takes the thumbs.

Child B: acute lymphoblastic leukemia. A sick-appearing child with splenomegaly, bone pain and a hypercellular marrow. Age 4 sits in the favourable 2–10 year window.

The single finding that would most worsen the prognosis is t(9;22), the BCR-ABL1 Philadelphia chromosome — historically the worst-prognosis group in ALL, and the one item that would move an otherwise favourable child into a high-intensity, transplant-directed protocol. Hypodiploidy, a T-cell phenotype, a high presenting white count, CNS disease and a slow day-8 response are the other adverse factors.

LO 73Source: Ciraulo, Lymphatics & Spleen (Surgical Approach) · Kendyll's Study Guide

Section 52 · Spleen · the overactive filter

Secondary Hypersplenism — Why an Enlarged Spleen Lowers Every Count

Hypersplenism is functional hyperactivity of the spleen resulting in the loss of one or more haematologic cell populations. The cells themselves are normal; an enlarged, overactive organ simply removes too many of them. On the classification of haemolysis it therefore sits as an extrinsic cause of increased red cell destruction, alongside antibody-mediated destruction and mechanical trauma.

Abbreviations used in this section Hypersplenism functional overactivity of the spleen causing cytopenias · Splenomegaly gross enlargement of the spleen — a size statement, not a function statement · Portal HTN portal hypertension · SMV superior mesenteric vein · ITP immune thrombocytopenia · TTP thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura · OPSS overwhelming post-splenectomy sepsis · MCC most common cause · LUQ left upper quadrant · Marsupialization surgically opening a cyst and suturing its edges open rather than excising it · Splenosis autotransplanted splenic tissue seeded after rupture
🔑 Primary versus secondary — and why the distinction matters ★ HY
  • Primary hypersplenism — functional change in the absence of a haematologic disorder or infection. Rare, and affects women far more than men.
  • Secondary hypersplenism — commonly occurs secondary to another disease process. This is the one the objective is about, and the one you will actually see.

Haematologic disorders of the spleen present with the same short list: anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and splenomegaly with pain secondary to capsular distension.

🧠 The anatomy that explains the commonest cause

The spleen's only venous outflow runs through the portal system. The splenic vein travels along the LOWER (inferior) border of the pancreas and merges with the superior mesenteric vein to form the portal vein; the splenic artery is a branch of the celiac trunk and runs along the SUPERIOR border of the pancreas to terminate at the hilum.

Two consequences follow directly, and both are examinable:

  • Anything that raises portal pressure backs blood up and the spleen enlarges — congestive splenomegaly. That is why portal hypertension is the most common cause of secondary hypersplenism.
  • Because the splenic vein runs behind the pancreas, pancreatitis is the most common cause of splenic vein thrombosis — which produces gastric varices and an upper gastrointestinal bleed, and for which splenectomy is curative.
🎯 Surgery review #4 — severe pancreatitis is a problem

What he said: pancreatitis can cause thromboses, varices and GI (gastrointestinal) bleeds; splenic vein thrombosis results in both splenomegaly and ischemia.

  1. The inflamed pancreas (or a pseudocyst) compresses the low-pressure splenic vein running behind it → splenic vein thrombosis.
  2. The spleen cannot drain → congestive splenomegaly.
  3. Blood backs up into the short gastric veins → isolated gastric varices (left-sided, “sinistral” portal hypertension — the liver is normal) → upper GI bleed.
  4. Venous outflow obstruction plus a swollen organ → splenic ischemia / infarction.
  5. Fix: splenectomy is curative for the bleeding gastric varices, because it removes the inflow.

His CT rule: in a pancreatitis patient, do not look only at the pancreas — look at the spleen too.

🎯 Surgery review #5 — why people get big spleens

What he said: know why people get big spleens — TTP, ITP, Hodgkin / some non-Hodgkin lymphoma, sickle cell, infectious mono.

CauseWhy the spleen is involvedBoard caveat
TTP (thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura)The spleen clears platelets and damaged red cells; splenectomy for relapsing diseaseThe spleen is usually not large; plasma exchange first
ITP (immune thrombocytopenia)The spleen is where antibody-coated platelets are destroyed and where the antibody is made — splenectomy for refractory ITPOn boards, a palpable spleen argues AGAINST ITP — splenomegaly is rare
Hodgkin / some non-Hodgkin lymphomaInfiltration of the spleen's lymphoid tissueSplenic marginal zone lymphoma and hairy cell leukemia give the biggest spleens
Sickle cell diseaseSequestration and congestionChildren only — repeated infarcts leave adults with a small, fibrotic spleen (autosplenectomy)
Infectious mononucleosis (Epstein-Barr virus)Lymphoid hyperplasia → transient splenomegalyRisk of rupture — no contact sports for several weeks

The full etiologic list — what causes it, and whether surgery helps

CategoryCauseWhat it looks likeRole of splenectomy
VascularPortal hypertension★ HY The most common cause of secondary hypersplenism. Splenic congestion with splenomegaly, on a background of cirrhosisGenerally NOT indicated for portal hypertension — treat the portal pressure
