🩺 The surgical spleen — the short list worth carrying
  • Splenic rupture. Broken and unstable → take it out, no question. Broken and haemodynamically stable → look for the “blush sign” (active contrast extravasation, meaning the spleen is bleeding) → interventional radiology. No blush → watch 2–4 days and discharge. ★ HY Rupture during medical management classically happens on day 5–6.
  • Splenic artery aneurysm. Women have a higher risk, and it ruptures during childbirth — the patient crashes and is bleeding from something that is not the uterus.
  • Iatrogenic trauma is commonly caused by retractors; the operating room accounts for 20% of all splenectomies. Blunt trauma is the leading cause overall.
  • Splenosis — spilled splenic tissue seeds the omentum and mesentery. It has no function and is usually left alone; the surgical concern is that spillage can cause the underlying disease to recur, which is why tear-resistant retrieval bags are used laparoscopically.
  • Practical threshold quoted by the lecturer: if they are going to need more than 2 units of blood, take it out.
⚠️ Overwhelming post-splenectomy sepsis — the complication to prevent (LO 51) ★ HY
  • Mechanism: the spleen can no longer opsonise encapsulated bacteria. Incidence is genuinely rare, under 1% — but the mortality is what makes it matter.
  • Organisms: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, Haemophilus influenzae.
  • Timing: most septic episodes occur within 2 years of splenectomy. Risk is greatest if the spleen is removed in the first 2–4 years of life — which is exactly why hereditary spherocytosis splenectomy is deferred past age 4.
  • Presentation: nonspecific, mild, influenza-like symptoms that progress rapidly to high fever, shock and death.
  • Prevention: for an elective splenectomy, vaccinate 2 weeks before operating; for an unplanned splenectomy, vaccinate before discharge. A trivalent preparation covering all three organisms is available.
  • If symptoms begin — initiate penicillin therapy immediately. Do not wait for confirmation.

Other post-splenectomy complications: postoperative haemorrhage (inadequate haemostasis of the splenic pedicle or short gastric vessels); subphrenic abscess, usually accompanied by a left pleural effusion; thrombocytosis — if the platelet count exceeds 1 million, start aspirin; injury to the tail of the pancreas at the hilum causing a pancreatic leak; injury to the short gastric vessels causing gastric wall necrosis; and colonic injury.

Q: A 54-year-old man with alcohol-associated cirrhosis has a haemoglobin of 10.6 g/dL, a white cell count of 2,700/mm³ and platelets of 58,000/mm³. His spleen is palpable 7 cm below the costal margin. The smear shows normal morphology with no dysplasia, blasts or schistocytes, and a marrow biopsy is normocellular with adequate, morphologically normal megakaryocytes. Explain the cytopenias, and say whether splenectomy is indicated.

Answer

Secondary hypersplenism from congestive splenomegaly due to portal hypertension — the most common cause of secondary hypersplenism. The logic is that three cell lines are down while the marrow is normocellular with adequate megakaryocytes and the morphology is normal: the cells are being made properly and removed peripherally. Cirrhosis raises portal pressure, and because the spleen's only venous outflow is through the portal system, the organ engorges and sequesters otherwise normal cells.

The normal morphology also does the differential work for you: no schistocytes excludes a thrombotic microangiopathy and disseminated intravascular coagulation, no dysplasia excludes myelodysplasia, and adequate megakaryocytes with a normocellular marrow excludes both marrow failure and alcohol-induced marrow toxicity.

Splenectomy is generally NOT indicated for portal hypertension. The cytopenias of congestive hypersplenism are typically moderate and do not by themselves require treatment; managing the portal hypertension is what matters. Removing the spleen here also strips a cirrhotic patient of encapsulated-organism defence for a problem that was not threatening his life.

LO 77Source: Stein, Clinical HIV · Kendyll's Study Guide · Heme Summary Sheets · Aronson, Anemia Overview

Section 53 · Across the lifespan · what changes and what to watch

Age-Related Haematologic Change — What Shifts, and What You Monitor Because Of It

This section answers the haematologic half of objective 77 only. The objective’s lecture source is Armstrong’s geriatric functional assessment, worked in Section 58 — read both. Haematologic normals are not fixed numbers. Marrow cellularity falls predictably with age, the newborn passes through a physiologic anemia, disease prevalence is age-banded, and in one specific population — people living with HIV — chronic immune activation ages the cardiovascular, skeletal and cognitive systems ahead of schedule. This section gathers the age-dependent material the objective asks for and pairs each change with what it obliges you to monitor.

Abbreviations used in this section Inflammaging chronic, low-grade, age-associated immune activation and inflammation · ART antiretroviral therapy · CD4 the helper T-cell surface marker used to stage HIV · U = U “undetectable equals untransmittable” · MGUS monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance · MDS myelodysplastic syndrome · ALL acute lymphoblastic leukemia · CLL chronic lymphocytic leukemia · LDL low-density lipoprotein · DXA dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry, the bone density scan · PAP Papanicolaou (cervical or anal cytology) screening
🔑 The one number you can actually calculate ★ HY

Normal marrow cellularity = (100 − the patient's age) percent. An 80-year-old should have roughly 20% cells and 80% fat; a young adult is around 70–80% cellular. This is why “hypocellular for age” is a different judgement in a child than in an octogenarian, and it is the reason a marrow report always states cellularity against age.

Alongside it, the myeloid-to-erythroid ratio is normally about 3:1 — most of what is in a marrow is granulocyte precursors. A fall in that ratio (as in polycythemia vera) means erythroid hyperplasia; a rise means the opposite.

🧠 Where blood is made changes three times before birth — and once after
  • Embryo → yolk sac. The first, primitive wave, in blood islands outside the embryo proper. Hepatic colonisation begins around day 23, spreading to arterial clusters by day 27.
  • Fetus → liver and spleen. The fetal liver is the dominant site through mid-gestation.
  • Late fetus onward → bone marrow. Marrow colonisation is underway by about week 11 and takes over before birth.
  • Adulthood → the marrow retreats inward. Haematopoiesis withdraws from the appendicular skeleton into the axial skeleton. That is why a marrow biopsy is taken from the iliac crest or sternum, not the femoral shaft.

Under extreme demand the body reopens the sites it abandoned — extramedullary haematopoiesis in liver and spleen, and expansion of the skull and facial marrow cavities producing the frontal bossing, chipmunk facies and “crew cut” skull of thalassemia major.

Age-banded disease prevalence — the epidemiology that is really a diagnostic prior

ConditionAge bandWhat it means at the bedside
Acute lymphoblastic leukemiaBimodal: peak 2–5 years, second peak over 50Most common childhood malignancy. Age 2–10 is a favourable prognostic factor; under 1 year or adult is unfavourable
Acute myeloid leukemiaMedian around 65; in Down syndrome, under 5 yearsOlder age is itself a poor prognostic factor, partly through performance status and comorbidity
Chronic lymphocytic leukemiaOver 60The exception to the rule that neoplasms of mature virgin B cells follow the antigen-independent pattern — CLL/SLL occurs only in adults
Chronic myeloid leukemiaPeak 5th–6th decade 
Myelodysplastic syndromeMedian age at diagnosis 77; generally 60–70sAn unexplained macrocytic cytopenia in an older adult is myelodysplasia until proven otherwise
MGUS3% of people over 50; 5% over 70Common enough that finding a small M spike in an older adult is usually MGUS, not myeloma — but it converts at about 1% per year
Hodgkin lymphomaBimodal: 15–35 and over 55Nodular sclerosis clusters in the younger peak and is the one subtype more common in women
Myeloproliferative neoplasmsLate adulthood, average 50–60; primary myelofibrosis uncommon before 60 
Splenic sequestration crisisInfants under 2 in homozygous sickle cell diseaseCan occur later in HbSC or sickle-β-thalassemia, because those spleens survive longer
Overwhelming post-splenectomy sepsisRisk greatest if splenectomy is done in the first 2–4 years of lifeWhy elective splenectomy for hereditary spherocytosis is deferred past age 4
🩺 The newborn and infant — two normal findings you must not treat
  • The physiologic nadir of infancy. Haemoglobin falls after birth as fetal red cells (shorter-lived) are cleared and erythropoietin production is switched down in a newly oxygen-rich environment, reaching its low point around 2–3 months in a term infant. A well, growing, term baby with a mild normocytic anemia at this age needs no further evaluation or treatment.
  • Haemoglobin F is protective early. A baby with β-thalassemia major or sickle cell disease is well for the first few months because HbF (α₂γ₂) does not depend on the β chain and does not participate in HbS polymerisation. Disease appears as HbF is replaced — which is also the entire rationale for hydroxyurea, which pushes HbF back up.

The specific age-related syndrome the course teaches: HIV and “inflammaging”

🔑 Virologic suppression is necessary but not sufficient ★ HY

People living with HIV now live close to normal lifespans, so the management plan has to extend past viral suppression into decades of cardiometabolic, bone, cognitive and cancer risk. The unifying mechanism is age-associated immune activation and chronic inflammation — “inflammaging”, which persists even when the virus is fully suppressed and affects both innate and adaptive immunity.

That is why a patient with an undetectable viral load and a normal CD4 count still accumulates atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, reduced bone mineral density and neurocognitive impairment earlier than an uninfected peer. “Undetectable equals untransmittable” settles transmission, not long-term comorbidity.

DomainWhat acceleratesWhat you monitor, and how often
CardiovascularAccelerated atherosclerosis; myocardial infarction and stroke at younger agesLipids and cardiovascular risk; treat raised cholesterol aggressively and control blood sugars. Conventional risk factor modification matters more here, not less
BoneOsteopenia and osteoporosis, partly inflammatory and partly drug-related (tenofovir)Bone density (DXA), vitamin D, and attention to which antiretrovirals affect bone
RenalChronic kidney diseaseCreatinine and estimated glomerular filtration rate — also drives antiretroviral dose adjustment
NeurocognitiveHIV-associated neurocognitive impairment — word-finding and short-term memory difficultyCognitive screening at routine visits
MalignancyAIDS-defining: non-Hodgkin lymphoma, cervical cancer, Kaposi sarcoma. Non-AIDS-defining: lung, liver, anal (HPV-related), head and neck, Hodgkin lymphomaAge-appropriate screening plus HIV-specific: gynecologic or rectal PAP every 6–12 months as indicated by gender and sexual history
Metabolic / drugLipid disorders, mitochondrial toxicity, body habitus change, glucose metabolism (diabetes)Adjust doses and select combinations carefully; limit highly toxic drugs
Routine baseline—Every 3–6 months: complete blood count, metabolic panel, CD4 count and viral load. Visits start at every 3 months and stretch to every 4–6 months once the patient is stable and adherent
⚠️ Three age-related traps
  • Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome is a starting phenomenon, not an aging one. It occurs within weeks to months of beginning antiretroviral therapy in someone with a low CD4 count — not twelve years into stable treatment.
  • Anemia is never “just age.” The World Health Organization thresholds are haemoglobin under 13 g/dL in men and under 12 g/dL in women regardless of age, and a fall of more than 10% from a patient's own baseline should be investigated even if the absolute number is still “normal.”
  • Iron deficiency in an older adult is a gastrointestinal lesion until proven otherwise. In an adult man or a postmenopausal woman, iron deficiency should be considered a gastrointestinal bleed until proven otherwise — the age makes this more urgent, not less.

Q: A 58-year-old man has taken antiretroviral therapy for 12 years with excellent adherence. His CD4 count is 720/µL and his viral load has been undetectable for a decade. He has newly diagnosed hypertension, an LDL of 158 mg/dL, osteopenia on DXA, and mild word-finding difficulty. He asks why this is happening now when his HIV is “controlled.” What do you tell him, and what do you monitor?

Answer

The mechanism is persistent age-associated immune activation and chronic inflammation — “inflammaging”. His immune system has stayed switched on at a low simmer for years despite full virologic suppression, and that chronic inflammatory state accelerates cardiovascular, skeletal and cognitive aging. It is the single mechanism that ties his three apparently unrelated new problems together.

What it is not: his CD4 of 720 is normal, so this is not immune failure; his viral load is undetectable, so it is not ongoing replication; immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome happens within months of starting therapy, not twelve years in; and hypertension, dyslipidemia and osteopenia are not an infectious syndrome. Cumulative antiretroviral toxicity contributes — particularly to bone and renal function — but it is not the sole driver.

Monitoring: lipids and cardiovascular risk with aggressive conventional risk-factor modification; bone density and vitamin D; renal function; cognitive screening; and age-appropriate plus HIV-specific cancer screening, including gynecologic or rectal PAP every 6–12 months as indicated. Routine labs — complete blood count, metabolic panel, CD4 and viral load — continue every 3–6 months.

LO 78Source: Anderson, People, Not Patients — Medicate, With Care · supplemented from standard prescribing and patient-safety practice for the full element list

Section 54 · Prescribing · the elements, and the older adult

Writing a Complete Drug Prescription

This objective does have a lecture behind it, and it is not a pharmacology lecture — it is Anderson’s house-call talk. That matters, because the lecture asks for two different things: recognise a poorly written prescription, and prescribe safely for an older adult. The element table below answers the first. The geriatric block near the end answers the second, and it is the half most likely to be tested, because it is the half that has a point of view.

🔑 The lecture’s own “bare minimum” — learn this list first ★ HY

Anderson’s slide reduces a prescription to five things. If a question asks what is missing, check these before anything else:

  • Drug and dose
  • Indication — the lecture flags this one with an exclamation mark, and says it matters especially for an as-needed (PRN) medication, where the patient otherwise has no way to know when to take it
  • Amount to dispense
  • Refills

The fuller element table that follows is standard prescribing practice, included because the objective line itself asks for “route of administration… and other related parameters.” Where the two disagree on emphasis, the lecture’s five win.

Abbreviations used in this section Sig from Latin signa, “write” — the directions to the patient that get printed on the label · Disp dispense — the quantity the pharmacy hands over · DEA Drug Enforcement Administration number, required for controlled substances in the United States · NPI National Provider Identifier · PO per os, by mouth · PRN pro re nata, as needed · QD / QOD / QID daily / every other day / four times daily — abbreviations to avoid, see below

The elements of a complete prescription

ElementWhat goes in itWhat goes wrong when it is missing
DateThe date writtenDetermines validity; controlled substances expire
Patient identifiersFull name, date of birth, addressDate of birth is the safety check against dispensing to the wrong person and against age-inappropriate dosing
Drug nameGeneric name preferredBrand names look alike and sound alike; generic naming reduces substitution error
Strengthe.g. 325 mgMost drugs come in several strengths; omitting it makes the prescription unfillable or dangerous
Dosage formtablet, capsule, solution, suspension, patchMatters wherever a drug exists in more than one form — especially in pediatrics
Quantity to dispenseDisp: #90★ HY Without it the pharmacist cannot know whether to supply one month or three, and cannot fill the prescription
Sig — the directionsDose + route + frequency, and duration where relevant. e.g. Take 1 tablet by mouth three times daily with vitamin CThe single most-read line on the label. Vague directions are the commonest cause of patient dosing error
Indicatione.g. for iron deficiency anemiaLets the pharmacist catch a drug/indication mismatch, and helps the patient understand what the medicine is for
RefillsA number, including zeroLeaving it blank creates ambiguity
PrescriberSignature, printed name, and identifying number (NPI; DEA for controlled substances)Legal validity
🔑 Worked example — a complete iron prescription
Date: 12 Sep 2026
Patient: Jane Doe      DOB: 14 Mar 1992
Address: 14 Elm Street, Portland, ME

Rx:   Ferrous sulfate 325 mg tablets
      Disp: #90  (ninety)
      Sig: Take 1 tablet by mouth three times daily with vitamin C,
           on an empty stomach if tolerated.
      Indication: iron deficiency anemia
      Refills: 2

[Prescriber signature / printed name / NPI]
⚠️ The patient-safety conventions — these are what actually get tested ★ HY
RuleWrite thisNever thisWhy
No trailing zero1 mg1.0 mgA missed decimal point reads as 10 mg — a tenfold overdose
Always a leading zero0.5 mg.5 mgA missed decimal point reads as 5 mg — a tenfold overdose
Write “units” out10 units10 U“U” is misread as a zero — 10 U becomes 100. The classic insulin and heparin error
Write frequency outdaily, every other day, four times dailyQD, QOD, QIDQD, QOD and QID are readily confused with each other
Spell the drug fullymorphine sulfate, magnesium sulfateMS, MSO₄, MgSO₄“MS” has meant both — two completely different drugs
Quantity in words too#90 (ninety)#90 alone, for controlled substancesPrevents alteration of the numeral
🩺 Haematology-specific prescribing points from this course

These are the details from the pharmacology sections (§16–§19) that actually change what you write on the page:

  • Oral iron — specify the salt, because the percentage of elemental iron differs: ferrous fumarate 33%, ferrous sulfate 20%, ferrous gluconate ~12%. Absorbed better in an acidic environment and without food — which is also what causes the gastrointestinal upset. Warn about black or green tarry stools, which are expected and can otherwise be mistaken for a bleed.
  • Folic acid — 400 µg daily for non-pregnant adults; 600 µg daily in pregnancy to prevent neural tube defects, with a higher dose where there is a prior affected birth or antiepileptic therapy.
  • Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents — the prescribing threshold is explicit: start only when haemoglobin is below 10 g/dL, and only for anemia of chronic kidney disease or of non-curative chemotherapy.
  • Warfarin — the prescription is inseparable from the monitoring plan and the dietary counselling: target INR 2–3 (2.5–3.5 for a mechanical valve), consistent vitamin K intake rather than avoidance, and caution with grapefruit juice and alcohol.
  • Vitamin K for warfarin reversal — route matters and belongs on the order: not subcutaneous (variable absorption), not intramuscular (haematoma risk), and when given intravenously it must be infused, never pushed, because of anaphylaxis risk.

Prescribing for an older adult — the half of this objective with a point of view

🪝 The lecture’s thesis, in one line

“The most dangerous thing I do as a doctor is…” — the talk ends on that unfinished sentence, and the answer it has spent sixteen slides building toward is write a prescription. Medications are listed alongside three other house-call lessons: people are not patients, “problem” lists are a problem, function is everything, and medications are dangerous.

⚠️ What medications are linked to in older adults ★ HY

The lecture states these as settled, not arguable: falls, delirium, dementia, disability and death — the last measured as hospital admissions and readmissions.

The four high-risk drug classes: opioids, anticholinergics, sedatives, antidepressants.

ToolWhat it isWhat it does for you
Beers CriteriaA published list of medications that are potentially inappropriate in adults 65 and olderThe standard reference for “should this person be on this drug at all?”
Anticholinergic burden scaleScores the cumulative anticholinergic load across every drug on the listCatches the patient on five individually mild drugs whose combined burden is causing the confusion
STOPP
Screening Tool of Older People’s Prescriptions		Flags drugs that should be stoppedThe deprescribing half
START
Screening Tool to Alert to Right Treatment		Flags drugs that should be started but have not beenThe under-prescribing half — the one people forget exists
The pharmacistNamed explicitly in the lecture as a resource—
🔑 “Start low, go slow — BUT get somewhere” ★ HY

The lecture quotes the familiar half of this maxim and then corrects it. Starting low and going slow is right; stopping at a sub-therapeutic dose because the patient is old is not. Under-treatment is presented as its own harm, which is exactly what the START half of START/STOPP exists to catch. Expect the exam to test the correction, not the cliché.

🧠 “There are no safe medications for…” — three slides, one structure

Three consecutive slides open with the same sentence. Each names a symptom, denies that a safe drug exists for it, offers a non-drug first line, and then concedes a reluctant second line. The structure is the teaching point.

  • Insomnia. No safe medication. First: cognitive behavioural therapy; sleep restriction / sleep compression therapy. Only “maybe, possibly, if you have to”: doxepin or trazodone.
  • Anxiety. No safe medication. First: cognitive behavioural therapy. Only if you have to: a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) or a serotonin–norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI). Note what is conspicuously not offered — benzodiazepines.
  • Neurocognitive symptoms of dementia (the “behaviours”). No safe medication, and here there is no drug concession at all. The stated treatment is “love and compassion and creativity” — meet the person where they are, not where you want them to be.

The discriminator: of the three, only dementia-related behaviours get no pharmacologic fallback. That is the one to remember.

Q: An 84-year-old woman with mild dementia is brought in by her son because she has become agitated in the evenings and is sleeping poorly. He asks for “something to calm her down.” Based on the prescribing lecture, what is the most appropriate response?

Answer

No medication — non-pharmacologic management of the behaviour. The lecture is unambiguous that there are no safe medications for “behaviours” in dementia, and unlike its insomnia and anxiety slides it offers no “if you have to” drug at all. The stated treatment is compassion and creativity — meeting the person where they are.

Every tempting distractor is in a named high-risk class: an antipsychotic or a benzodiazepine is a sedative, diphenhydramine is an anticholinergic, and both routes run straight into the falls–delirium–dementia triad the lecture opens with. If the insomnia were being treated on its own, the reluctant options would be doxepin or trazodone after cognitive behavioural therapy and sleep restriction — not a sedative-hypnotic.

Q: A resident writes: “Ferrous sulfate 325 mg tablets. Sig: 1 tablet by mouth three times daily with vitamin C. Indication: iron deficiency anemia. Refills: 2.” The pharmacist calls because it cannot be filled. What is missing?

Answer

The quantity to dispense. Running down the list: drug name, strength (325 mg), dosage form (tablets), route (by mouth), frequency (three times daily), indication and refills are all present. What is absent is “Disp: #90” — so the pharmacist has no way to know whether to hand over one month's supply or three, and cannot fill it.

Nothing else here is wrong: there is no trailing zero, no missing leading zero, and no error-prone abbreviation. Those are the other things to scan for on any prescription question.

LO 47LO 73LO 51Source: Ciraulo, Lymphatics & Spleen (Surgical Approach) — supplemented from standard trauma-surgery practice for the grading scale and the embolization pathway

Section 55 · Spleen · the injured organ

Splenic Injury — Mechanism, Grade, and the Three-Rung Management Ladder

The spleen is the most commonly injured solid organ in blunt abdominal trauma, and it is the organ whose management changed most in the last thirty years. The old answer was “take it out.” The current answer is decided by one variable — haemodynamic stability — and only then by the grade. Learn that order and every vignette in this objective resolves.

🩺 What is lectured here, and what is not — read this before you memorise the table

From the Ciraulo surgery lecture (examinable, he said it): blunt trauma is the leading cause of splenectomy; traumatic splenic injury can often be managed non-operatively; the operating room accounts for 20% of all splenectomies; splenic rupture is traumatic or spontaneous from splenomegaly; splenosis and the tear-resistant bag; accessory spleens in 20%, >80% at the hilum; splenic artery aneurysm rupturing in pregnancy; splenic abscess with gas; and the whole post-splenectomy complication and OPSI block including vaccine timing.

Supplied here because the objective asks for it and no lecture in the note set supplies it: the AAST grade I–V table, the FAST-versus-CT algorithm, the contrast blush, and proximal versus distal embolization. The new guide asks for “management strategies including medical, surgical and interventional” and for pseudoaneurysm by name — neither is answerable from the lecture alone, which is why they are here.

How to triage it: learn the three rungs and what moves you between them (stability, then blush) — that is the objective. Treat the exact centimetre cut-offs in the AAST table as reference, not as memorisation, unless your examiner taught the scale directly.

Abbreviations used in this section AAST American Association for the Surgery of Trauma — the body that publishes the organ injury grading scale · FAST Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma — a bedside ultrasound looking for free fluid · CT computed tomography · IR interventional radiology · NOM non-operative management — observation rather than surgery · OPSI overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (also written OPSS, overwhelming post-splenectomy sepsis) · LUQ left upper quadrant · MVC motor vehicle collision · Pseudoaneurysm a contained arterial rupture — blood outside the vessel wall held in only by surrounding tissue · Splenorrhaphy surgical repair of the spleen rather than removal · Splenosis autotransplanted splenic tissue seeded through the abdomen after rupture
🔑 The primary mechanism — and the four ways a spleen gets injured ★ HY

The spleen is a highly vascular organ (roughly 5% of cardiac output) wrapped in a thin capsule and suspended behind ribs 9–11. Every mechanism below works the same way in the end: the capsule tears or the parenchyma splits, and a low-pressure, high-flow organ bleeds into the peritoneum.

  • Blunt trauma — the leading cause overall. Motor vehicle collision, fall, handlebar or contact-sport blow to the left flank. Fractures of the left lower ribs are the warning sign: the ribs that protect the spleen are the ribs that lacerate it.
  • Penetrating trauma. Stab or gunshot. Less common, but far more likely to involve the hilum and the adjacent tail of pancreas.
  • Iatrogenic trauma. Usually retractor injury during upper abdominal surgery. ★ HY The operating room accounts for about 20% of all splenectomies.
  • Spontaneous / pathologic rupture. A spleen enlarged by disease ruptures under trivial or no force. Classic setting: infectious mononucleosis (hence the contact-sport restriction), also malaria, typhoid, leukemia and infiltrative disease. This is the chronic/pathologic half of the objective — see §52 for the full etiologic list.
🧠 The anatomy that dictates the operation

Four facts change what the surgeon does:

  • The splenic artery runs along the SUPERIOR border of the pancreas; the splenic vein runs along the INFERIOR border and joins the superior mesenteric vein to form the portal vein. The vein's course behind the pancreas is why pancreatitis is the commonest cause of splenic vein thrombosis, and why hilar dissection risks the tail of the pancreas.
  • The gastrosplenic ligament carries the short gastric vessels. Divide them carelessly and you devascularise the greater curve of the stomach — gastric wall necrosis is a recognised post-splenectomy complication.
  • The spleen is a segmental organ. Its arterial supply divides into segments with relatively avascular planes between them, which is what makes partial splenectomy and splenorrhaphy anatomically possible rather than wishful.
  • Accessory spleens are present in about 10–20% of people, most often at the hilum. They matter twice: they are the reason an ITP splenectomy relapses, and they are the reason a “completed” splenectomy can leave residual function.

Presentation — the signs that name the organ

FindingMechanismWhy it matters
Left upper quadrant pain and tendernessCapsular stretch and peritoneal bloodThe presenting complaint, but non-specific on its own
Kehr sign — referred LEFT SHOULDER pain ★ HYBlood irritating the left hemidiaphragm, which shares the C3–C5 phrenic nerve root with the shoulder dermatomeThe single most examinable sign. Classically worse when the patient lies flat or head-down, which pools blood against the diaphragm
Left lower rib fractures / seatbelt signDirect transmitted forceShould trigger imaging of the spleen even if the abdomen is initially soft
Tachycardia, then hypotensionClass II–III haemorrhagic shockThis is the variable that decides management, not the CT grade
Balance sign — fixed dullness in the LUQ, shifting dullness on the rightClotted blood around the spleen; free blood elsewhereHistorical but still quoted
⚠️ The diagnostic fork — stability decides the test ★ HY
  • Haemodynamically UNSTABLE → bedside FAST. Free fluid on FAST in an unstable patient means the operating room. Do not send an unstable trauma patient to CT. That single rule is worth more marks than the whole grading table.
  • Haemodynamically STABLE → CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast. This is the study that grades the injury and, critically, detects the contrast “blush” — active extravasation, meaning the spleen is bleeding right now.

The AAST grading scale — what the CT report is telling you

GradeHaematomaLacerationVascular
ISubcapsular, <10% of surface areaCapsular tear, <1 cm deep—
IISubcapsular 10–50%; intraparenchymal <5 cm1–3 cm deep, not involving a trabecular vessel—
IIISubcapsular >50% or expanding; intraparenchymal ≥5 cm; any ruptured haematoma>3 cm deep, or involving a trabecular vessel—
IV—Involving segmental or hilar vessels with >25% devascularisationAny injury with active bleeding contained within the capsule
V—Shattered spleenHilar vascular injury devascularising the spleen, or active bleeding beyond the capsule into the peritoneum

A useful compression: grade tracks depth and then vessels. Grades I–III are parenchymal; grade IV–V is where the blood supply itself is involved, and that is where non-operative management starts failing.

🩺 The three-rung management ladder — medical, interventional, surgical 🎯 SURGERY REVIEW ★ HY

This is the objective, stated exactly the way it will be asked.

  • Rung 1 — MEDICAL / non-operative management (NOM). For the haemodynamically stable patient with no blush and no peritonitis, regardless of grade in most modern protocols. It means: admission to a monitored bed, bed rest, serial haemoglobin/haematocrit, serial abdominal examination, and type-and-cross held active. NOM is the default and it succeeds in the large majority — and it succeeds more often in children, whose splenic capsules are thicker and who are managed non-operatively almost always.
  • Rung 2 — INTERVENTIONAL: angiography with splenic artery embolization. Indicated for the stable patient with a contrast blush, a pseudoaneurysm, an arteriovenous fistula, or a high grade (IV–V) injury. It is the rung that converts a patient who would once have lost the spleen into a patient who keeps it. Proximal embolization drops perfusion pressure while letting collaterals preserve the organ; distal (selective) embolization targets the bleeding vessel itself.
  • Rung 3 — SURGICAL. Haemodynamic instability despite resuscitation, peritonitis, or failure of the rungs above. Spleen-preserving options exist — splenorrhaphy (suture repair, topical haemostatics, mesh wrap) and partial splenectomy — but the unstable patient gets a total splenectomy, because the correct operation in a crashing patient is the fast one.

Two practical thresholds the lecturer quoted: if they are going to need more than 2 units of blood, take it out; and after successful NOM, watch for 2–4 days before discharge.

🎯 Surgery review #7 — the trauma standard of care, his way

What he said: if the patient is stable, splenectomy is not actually indicated (boards differ on this). You don't need the grades.

  • Stable → keep the spleen (non-operative management ± embolization).
  • In real life, grades IV and up need splenectomy. (He said grades run I–VI; the AAST splenic scale in the table above stops at V.)
  • OR — unstable at a lower grade needs splenectomy. His definition of unstable: SBP < 90 mm Hg and HR > 100/min (systolic blood pressure, heart rate).

Note the tension with the ladder above, which sends a stable grade IV–V to embolization. On his exam, answer his way: high grade or unstable → splenectomy.

⚠️ The complications — the list this objective names explicitly ★ HY
  • Rupture and DELAYED rupture. An initially contained subcapsular haematoma expands and bursts. ★ HY Classically on day 5–6 of non-operative management — the reason NOM is inpatient observation and not reassurance.
  • Splenic pseudoaneurysm. A contained arterial disruption within the injured parenchyma. It may be absent on the initial scan and appear later, and it can rupture after the patient looks well — which is why follow-up imaging is obtained in higher-grade injuries and why finding one is an indication for embolization rather than observation.
  • Splenic infarct and splenic abscess. Infarction follows devascularisation or embolization; superinfection of infarcted tissue produces an abscess, usually Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus, with fever, LUQ pain and a high mortality. Percutaneous drainage first where feasible; splenectomy for refractory cases.
  • Adjacent organ injury — the hilum's neighbours. Tail of the pancreas (pancreatic leak or fistula — suspect it when drain output stays high and drain amylase is raised); stomach (gastric wall necrosis from short gastric division); left hemidiaphragm; splenic flexure of the colon.
  • Thrombosis. Splenic and portal vein thrombosis after splenectomy, favoured by the post-splenectomy platelet surge and by low flow in the stump. Reactive thrombocytosis is expected; if the platelet count exceeds 1 million, start aspirin.
  • Subphrenic abscess, characteristically accompanied by a left pleural effusion; and postoperative haemorrhage from the splenic pedicle or short gastrics.
  • Splenosis — spilled splenic tissue seeding the omentum and mesentery. It has no reliable immune function and is usually left alone; the surgical concern is that spillage can let the underlying disease recur, which is why tear-resistant retrieval bags are used laparoscopically.
  • 🎯 SURGERY REVIEW Overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI / OPSS). The one that kills late — and once it starts it kills in 8 hours or less. Encapsulated organisms — Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, Haemophilus influenzae — because the spleen can no longer opsonise them. Worked in full at §11.

Vaccination timing, because trauma changes it: for an elective splenectomy, vaccinate 2 weeks before operating. For the unplanned, post-traumatic splenectomy that is impossible — so vaccinate before discharge (commonly about 14 days post-operatively, when the immune response is better).

Q: A 27-year-old man is brought in after a motor vehicle collision. He is alert, with a pulse of 104/min and blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg that remains stable after 1 L of crystalloid. He has left-sided lower rib tenderness and complains of left shoulder pain that worsens when the bed is laid flat. CT of the abdomen with contrast shows a 4 cm intraparenchymal splenic laceration with a focus of active contrast extravasation contained within the capsule. What is the next step, and what is the single finding that drove your choice?

Answer

Angiography with splenic artery embolization — rung 2 of the ladder.

The finding that drives it is the contrast blush: active extravasation means the spleen is bleeding at the moment of the scan, and that is what separates a patient who can simply be observed from one who needs the bleeding stopped. The grade (this is grade IV by the presence of contained active bleeding) is not the deciding variable on its own.

Note the two things that kept him off the operating table: he is haemodynamically stable after fluid, and the extravasation is contained within the capsule. Had he been hypotensive and unresponsive to resuscitation, the answer would be laparotomy and splenectomy without CT — an unstable trauma patient does not go to the scanner. The left shoulder pain worse when supine is Kehr sign, blood irritating the left hemidiaphragm and referring along the phrenic nerve; it names the organ but does not decide the management.

LO 34Source: NO single lecture in the note set works this objective — assembled from Starling physiology, the Hypercoagulable States lecture (DVT), and the Surgery/Lymphatics lecture (lymphatic obstruction)

Section 56 · Trauma · why the limb swells

Edema After a Traumatic Injury — Six Mechanisms, and the Two You Must Not Miss

Every cause of edema is a failure of one of four Starling variables: capillary hydrostatic pressure, plasma oncotic pressure, capillary permeability, and lymphatic drainage. Trauma is unusual in that it can break all four, at different times, in the same limb. The clinical skill is reading when the swelling started and what it feels like, because that is what separates expected post-injury swelling from a deep vein thrombosis or a compartment syndrome.

🩺 This objective has no lecture behind it — how to treat that

No lecture in the note set works post-traumatic edema. The Surgery lecture covers lymphedema; the Hypercoagulable States lecture mentions compartment syndrome only in passing, as a site of anticoagulant-related bleeding. Everything here is assembled from Starling physiology plus standard trauma practice.

How to triage it: the four-variable Starling frame and the timing table are what an objective phrased “mechanism and pathophysiology of various causes” is actually asking for — learn those. Compartment syndrome and DVT are the two highest-yield items because both are emergencies and both are heavily tested elsewhere. The numeric details (ΔP < 30 mm Hg) are worth knowing but are the first thing to drop if time is short.

Abbreviations used in this section Starling forces the pressures governing fluid movement across a capillary wall · Transudate low-protein fluid from a pressure problem · Exudate protein-rich fluid from a permeability problem · DVT deep vein thrombosis · ACS acute compartment syndrome · ΔP delta pressure — diastolic blood pressure minus measured compartment pressure · CK creatine kinase · AKI acute kidney injury · IL-1 / TNF interleukin-1 / tumour necrosis factor, the early inflammatory cytokines
🔑 The four-variable frame — learn this and the six mechanisms are just instances ★ HY
  • ↑ Capillary hydrostatic pressure → fluid pushed out. Venous obstruction, DVT, dependency. Produces a transudate.
  • ↓ Plasma oncotic pressure → fluid not pulled back. Hypoalbuminaemia, dilution by resuscitation. Transudate, and usually generalised.
  • ↑ Capillary permeability → protein leaks out and takes water with it. Inflammation, burns, crush. Produces an exudate.
  • ↓ Lymphatic drainage → the protein that normally leaves via lymph stays behind. Transection, nodal dissection, scarring. Produces protein-rich lymphedema, which is why it eventually becomes non-pitting.

The six post-traumatic mechanisms, in the order they appear

MechanismPathophysiologyTimingCharacter of the swelling
1. Inflammatory / increased permeability ★ HYTissue injury releases histamine, bradykinin, complement fragments, IL-1 and TNF, which open interendothelial gaps. Protein-rich exudate enters the interstitiumMinutes to hours; peaks 24–72 hLocal, warm, tender, pitting; accompanied by the other cardinal signs of inflammation. This is the expected swelling
2. Haematoma / direct haemorrhageBlood dissects into soft tissue — a mass effect first, then an osmotic load as red cells and protein break down and draw water inImmediate, may expand over hoursFocal, firm, discoloured, often fluctuant. Expanding size is the alarm
3. Venous obstruction — DVT ★ HYInjury plus immobilisation supplies all three arms of Virchow's triad — stasis, endothelial injury and a post-traumatic hypercoagulable state. Thrombus raises capillary hydrostatic pressure upstreamDays later — characteristically when swelling that was improving starts worsening againUnilateral, whole-limb, pitting, warm, with calf tenderness and a >2 cm circumference difference. See §49
4. Lymphatic disruptionLymphatics transected by the injury or by surgery, or nodes removed. The protein that normally leaves by lymph accumulates, holding water osmoticallyWeeks to months; often permanentStarts pitting, becomes NON-pitting and fibrotic; does not resolve with elevation; square toes and a positive Stemmer sign. See §48
5. Hypoalbuminaemia / resuscitation dilutionAlbumin falls three ways at once: capillary leak of albumin into the interstitium, the acute-phase fall in hepatic albumin synthesis, and dilution by large-volume crystalloid. Plasma oncotic pressure dropsDays, in the resuscitated polytrauma patientGeneralised and dependent — sacrum, flanks, both legs, periorbital. Deeply pitting. Not limited to the injured part
6. Compartment syndrome ★ HYEdema accumulates inside a non-compliant fascial compartment. Pressure rises above capillary perfusion pressure → ischaemia → more capillary leak → a self-amplifying cycle. Reperfusion and crush injury accelerate itHours — the true emergency on this listTense, wood-hard compartment; the limb is swollen but the diagnosis is made by pressure, not by size
⚠️ The two that are emergencies, and how each announces itself ★ HY
  • Acute compartment syndrome. Pain out of proportion to the injury, and pain on PASSIVE STRETCH of the compartment, are the earliest reliable signs. The classic “six Ps” are a trap: pulselessness, pallor and paralysis are LATE, and waiting for them means waiting for dead muscle. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by compartment pressure — ΔP (diastolic minus compartment pressure) below 30 mm Hg is the usual operative threshold. Treatment is emergency fasciotomy; splitting the cast or dressing is only a holding measure. Downstream: rhabdomyolysis → raised CK, myoglobinuria, hyperkalaemia and AKI.
  • Deep vein thrombosis. Suspect it whenever swelling that had plateaued or improved begins to worsen again several days after injury, particularly if the limb was immobilised. Unilateral, pitting, whole-limb. Confirm with compression ultrasonography; do not talk yourself out of imaging because “the leg is swollen because it was injured.”
🪝 Memory hook — read the clock, then read the feel

Hours → inflammation, haematoma, compartment syndrome. Days → DVT, hypoalbuminaemia. Weeks → lymphedema.

Then the texture decides the rest: hard and exquisitely painful = compartment; soft, pitting, one leg = DVT; soft, pitting, both legs and the sacrum = oncotic; firm, non-pitting, square toes = lymphatic.

Q: A 24-year-old woman sustains a closed tibial shaft fracture and is placed in a long-leg cast. Six hours later she reports severe, deep calf pain that she rates 9/10 despite opioids. Passive dorsiflexion of the toes reproduces the pain intensely. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are palpable and the foot is warm and pink. Her leg is swollen. What is the diagnosis, why are the normal pulses irrelevant, and what is the treatment?

Answer

Acute compartment syndrome of the leg — and it needs emergency fasciotomy.

The diagnosis is made by the two early signs, both present: pain out of proportion to the injury and pain on passive stretch of the muscles in the affected compartment. Splitting or removing the cast is a reasonable first manoeuvre while the operating room is prepared, but it is not the treatment.

The palpable pulses are irrelevant because compartment syndrome is a capillary-perfusion problem, not a major-artery problem. Compartment pressure only needs to exceed capillary perfusion pressure to make muscle ischaemic, and that threshold is far below the pressure required to obliterate flow in a named artery. Pulselessness, pallor and paralysis are late findings; by the time they appear the muscle is infarcting. If pressures are measured, a ΔP below 30 mm Hg confirms it.

The mechanism to be able to state: edema inside a non-compliant fascial envelope raises interstitial pressure, which collapses capillaries and thin-walled veins; the resulting ischaemia increases capillary permeability, which adds more edema — a self-amplifying cycle that does not break on its own. Watch afterwards for rhabdomyolysis — raised creatine kinase, myoglobinuria, hyperkalaemia and acute kidney injury.

LO 60Source: Lymph Node — Normal Architecture & Reactive Lymphadenopathy (Sirotnikov) · Surgery — The Lymphatic System — supplemented from standard oncologic pathology for the drainage map

Section 57 · The lymphatic system · how carcinoma travels

Lymphatic Dissemination of Carcinoma — The Route, the Sentinel, and the Drainage Map

One rule opens this objective: carcinomas spread preferentially by lymphatics; sarcomas spread preferentially by blood. Everything else is a consequence of anatomy — a tumour metastasises to whichever node happens to drain the tissue it started in, which is why a supraclavicular node can announce a stomach cancer and a testicular tumour never goes to the groin.

🩺 What is lectured here, and what is not

From the Sirotnikov lymph node lecture (examinable): lymph enters via afferent lymphatics into the subcapsular sinus, and the subcapsular sinus is the first place tumour cells land — where the pathologist hunts for metastasis. That single point is the lectured core of this objective, and the Week 11 quiz tests it directly.

Supplied here because the objective asks for “anatomic pathways” and no lecture supplies them: the drainage map (breast, stomach, testis, anal canal, lung, prostate), Virchow’s node and Troisier sign, and the sentinel node concept. The lecture never names Virchow or the sentinel node.

How to triage it: the subcapsular sinus and the carcinoma-by-lymph / sarcoma-by-blood rule are the highest-confidence facts. Of the map, the three with the strongest board and vignette history are Virchow’s node → gastric, testis → para-aortic (not inguinal), and the dentate line watershed.

Abbreviations used in this section Carcinoma a malignancy of epithelial origin · Sarcoma a malignancy of mesenchymal (connective tissue) origin · LVI lymphovascular invasion — tumour seen inside a lymphatic or vascular channel on histology · Sentinel node the first node draining a tumour bed · Subcapsular sinus the space just beneath the node capsule, where afferent lymph first arrives · Echelon a tier of nodes along a drainage chain · N stage the nodal component of TNM staging · Chyle lymph from the intestine, rich in fat and appearing milky
🔑 The pathway, step by step — and the compartment the pathologist examines first ★ HY
  1. Local invasion. Carcinoma cells lose E-cadherin-mediated adhesion, degrade the basement membrane with matrix metalloproteinases, and enter the surrounding stroma.
  2. Lymphovascular invasion. Cells enter a lymphatic capillary — easier to penetrate than a blood capillary because lymphatics have no basement membrane and loose, overlapping endothelial junctions. That single structural fact is why carcinoma prefers this route. Tumours also drive lymphangiogenesis via VEGF-C/VEGF-D.
  3. Transport to the first node along afferent lymphatics, which pierce the capsule on the convex surface of the node.
  4. ★ HY Arrival in the SUBCAPSULAR (marginal) SINUS. This is where metastatic deposits are first seen, and therefore the first compartment the pathologist examines in a sentinel node. Contrast it with the node's reactive compartments — follicles for B cells, paracortex for T cells — worked at §35.
  5. Progressive effacement of the node, then exit by the efferent lymphatic at the hilum to the next echelon.
  6. 🎯 SURGERY REVIEW Entry into the systemic circulation. Lymph ultimately reaches the thoracic duct, which empties at the junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins — so lymphatic spread becomes haematogenous spread at that point. The two routes are sequential, not alternative.
🎯 Surgery review #1 — how carcinoma travels, and how it reaches the lung

What he said: cancer spreads through the lymph nodes, typically going for the portal system. If it is metastatic to the lungs, it got there through the thoracic duct.

  • The lung route, step by step: tumour → regional nodes → cisterna chyli → thoracic duct → left subclavian–internal jugular junction → superior vena cava → right heart → the pulmonary capillaries are the first capillary bed it meets. That is why the lung is where lymph-borne tumour cells get caught.
  • The “portal system” half: the abdominal gut's venous blood drains through the portal vein, so gastrointestinal carcinoma that gets into veins lands in the liver first. Liver metastasis = came up the portal vein; lung metastasis = came up the thoracic duct (or the systemic veins).
🧠 The sentinel node — and why the concept was worth inventing

The sentinel node is the first node receiving drainage from the tumour bed. It is located by injecting blue dye and/or radiolabelled colloid around the tumour and following it.

The logic is a conditional: if the sentinel node is free of tumour, the nodes downstream of it are almost certainly free too, and a full nodal dissection can be avoided. That matters because the dissection itself is what causes secondary lymphedema — the single commonest cause of lymphedema in the developed world (see §48). Sentinel biopsy buys accurate N staging at a fraction of the morbidity.

The caveat worth knowing: spread is usually orderly, echelon by echelon, but skip metastases occur when lymphatics are obstructed by tumour and flow is diverted around the expected node.

The drainage map — the anatomic pathways worth memorising

Primary siteFirst-echelon nodesThe examinable point
BreastAxillary (levels I–III, defined by their relation to pectoralis minor) for lateral/upper quadrants; internal mammary for medial quadrantsAbout 75% of breast lymph drains to the axilla. A medial tumour with negative axillary nodes may still have internal mammary disease
Stomach, pancreas, other abdominal visceraCoeliac and para-aortic → thoracic duct → LEFT supraclavicular node★ HY Virchow's node — an enlarged left supraclavicular node from abdominal malignancy, classically gastric. The palpable finding is Troisier sign. It is left-sided because the thoracic duct drains there
TestisPara-aortic / retroperitoneal nodes★ HY NOT inguinal — the testis descended from the posterior abdominal wall and took its lymphatic drainage with it. The scrotal SKIN, however, drains to superficial inguinal nodes, which is the distinction being tested
OvaryPara-aorticSame embryologic logic as the testis
Anal canalAbove the dentate line → internal iliac / inferior mesenteric. Below the dentate line → superficial inguinalThe dentate line is a watershed for lymphatic drainage as well as for blood supply and innervation
LungHilar (bronchopulmonary) → mediastinal → supraclavicularMediastinal nodal status is the pivot of lung cancer staging and resectability
ProstateObturator and internal iliacPrecedes the classic osteoblastic bone metastases
Head and neck mucosaCervical chains (levels I–VI)An adult with a persistent, hard, painless cervical node is a malignancy until proven otherwise — and the primary is sought in the mucosa that drains there
Lower limb / vulva / penis (skin)Superficial inguinalThe common destination that makes testicular drainage feel counter-intuitive
🩺 Reading the node at the bedside — and the consequences of nodal disease
  • Metastatic node: hard, painless, fixed to underlying tissue, often matted, progressively enlarging, in an older patient. Fixation is the ominous feature — it means tumour has breached the capsule (extranodal extension), which independently worsens prognosis.
  • Reactive node: soft or rubbery, mobile, tender, with a history of local infection, and it regresses. Worked in full at §35.
  • Consequences of lymphatic dissemination: it sets the N stage and so the prognosis and the adjuvant therapy decision; nodal obstruction or dissection produces secondary lymphedema; and involvement or injury of the thoracic duct produces a chylous effusion or chylothorax — milky, triglyceride-rich fluid.

Q: A 61-year-old man has three months of epigastric discomfort, early satiety and 8 kg of weight loss. On examination there is a firm, non-tender, fixed node above the left clavicle. Name the node, explain the anatomy that puts it there, and say why a right supraclavicular node would have pointed somewhere different.

Answer

Virchow's node — a left supraclavicular node enlarged by metastatic abdominal carcinoma, here almost certainly gastric. The palpable sign carries its own eponym, Troisier sign.

The anatomy: lymph from the stomach passes through coeliac and para-aortic nodes into the cisterna chyli and then up the thoracic duct, which drains essentially the whole body below the diaphragm plus the left side above it. The thoracic duct terminates at the junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins — so the last nodal station before tumour cells enter the systemic venous circulation sits in the left supraclavicular fossa.

Why the right would mean something else: the right lymphatic duct drains only the right side of the head and neck, the right arm, and the right hemithorax. A right supraclavicular node therefore points to a lung, oesophageal, mediastinal or head-and-neck primary — not to an abdominal one.

The node's hardness, fixation and painlessness are the features that call it metastatic rather than reactive, and fixation specifically implies extranodal extension through the capsule.

LO 77Source: Armstrong, The Geriatrics Functional Assessment (September 2026, adapted from Quarella and Thieme) · Anderson, People, Not Patients

Section 58 · Geriatrics · what changes with age, and what you measure because of it

The Geriatric Functional Assessment — The 4Ms, and the Tools That Go With Them

Objective 77 asks about “age-related changes… and what should be monitored.” Section 53 answers the haematologic half — marrow cellularity, age-banded disease prevalence, accelerated aging in treated HIV. This section answers the other half, and it is the half with a lecture behind it. Here, “what should be monitored” means a named screening tool, not a blood count. The organising idea is that in an older adult function, not diagnosis, is the thing that predicts what happens next.

Abbreviations used in this section 4Ms What Matters, Medication, Mentation, Mobility — the Age-Friendly Health Systems framework · ADL activity of daily living — the basic self-care tasks · IADL instrumental activity of daily living — the tasks of running a household · MMSE Mini-Mental State Examination · MoCA Montreal Cognitive Assessment · SLUMS Saint Louis University Mental Status examination · PHQ-2 / PHQ-9 Patient Health Questionnaire, two- and nine-item versions · GDS Geriatric Depression Scale · TUG Timed Up and Go · STEADI Stopping Elderly Accidents, Deaths and Injuries — the CDC falls-prevention toolkit · RAPA Rapid Assessment of Physical Activity · CAGE-AID Cut down, Annoyed, Guilty, Eye-opener — Adapted to Include Drugs · MCI mild cognitive impairment · MOLST Medical Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment · DPOA durable power of attorney · SNF skilled nursing facility · PT / OT physical therapy / occupational therapy · AGS American Geriatrics Society · USPSTF United States Preventive Services Task Force · NIAAA National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism · CBT cognitive behavioural therapy · OSA obstructive sleep apnea · CPAP continuous positive airway pressure
🔑 Why function, and not the problem list ★ HY

Function correlates with longevity, and the lecture gives the number that makes the point impossible to argue with:

  • 75-year-olds without limitations live about 5 years longer than those with an ADL limitation, and more than 1 year longer than those limited in mobility.
  • The line to remember: the life expectancy of an ADL-disabled 75-year-old is the same as that of an independent 85-year-old. An ADL disability is worth roughly ten years of age — and much more of the remaining time is spent disabled.

That is why the geriatric assessment is defined as multidimensional and multidisciplinary — functional ability, physical health, cognition and mental health, and socio-environmental circumstances — and why the lecture says plainly that the traditional medical assessment is not comprehensive enough for an older adult with multiple comorbidities.

🧠 The 4Ms — the framework the whole interview hangs on

Four words, each with its own screening question set. The American Geriatrics Society adds a fifth, Multicomplexity.

MWhat you are actually asking
What Matters“What is the most important thing to you — in life, and right now?” Advance directive, MOLST, durable power of attorney. Goals of care.
MedicationDo you manage your own medications? Do you know their names? Do you need help organising them? Do you ever forget a dose, or take one twice?
MentationMood and socialisation; memory — losing keys, getting lost, leaving the stove on, forgetting names. Any existing diagnosis of cognitive impairment. Delirium versus dementia.
MobilityHow do you get around? Cane or walker? Can you get to the bathroom? Have you fallen — in the last 6 months, the last year, ever?

The screening tools, by domain

The lecture is explicit that you do not administer all of these. They are deployed when clinical suspicion arises during the history — “administering every tool is not logical, not practical, and will upset the average patient.” The skill being examined is choosing the right tool for the complaint you just heard.

🔑 The escalation logic — the single most testable slide ★ HY

Every domain runs brief screen → positive → longer instrument → positive → intervention. Note where the intervention is not a drug:

  • Mini-Cog → positive → MMSE / MoCA / SLUMS → positive → neuropsychiatric testing
  • PHQ-2 → positive → PHQ-9 or Geriatric Depression Scale → positive → social work, therapy and community engagement first, then medications
  • Sleep quality scale → positive → sleep hygiene first, then medications
  • RAPA, 4-Stage Balance, Timed Up and Go → positive → physical therapy referral
  • Katz / Lawton–Brody → positive → occupational therapy referral
  • Medication review for drug–drug interactions → harm potential by Beers Criteria → consider deprescribing slowly

The pattern to carry into the exam: the non-pharmacologic step always comes before the prescription — which is the same thesis as the prescribing lecture in Section 54.

🩺 ADLs versus IADLs — and why the distinction predicts disposition

ADLs (Katz) are basic self-care: bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, continence, feeding. IADLs (Lawton–Brody) are the tasks of running a life: finances, medication management, shopping, cooking, housekeeping, laundry, transport, telephone use.

IADLs fail first. A patient who can still bathe and dress but has stopped managing her own finances and medications has an IADL deficit with ADLs intact — which is the classic functional signature of mild cognitive impairment or early dementia, and is exactly the profile of the case below.

🧠 Before any tool — can this interview even happen?

The lecture puts a communication checklist ahead of every instrument, because a “failed” cognitive screen in a patient who simply cannot hear you is a false positive:

  • Can the patient talk? Hear you? See you? Do they want to?
  • Are they aware of what is going on, and do they remember? — delirium versus dementia
  • Is there family or another collateral source? Call them.

And the summary rule: talk with the patient, not at the patient.

The case — Wendy, 82

🩺 One vignette that runs all four Ms — and lands in haematology

Presentation. An 82-year-old woman with hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, type 2 diabetes, prior transient ischaemic attack, atrial fibrillation on rivaroxaban, stage 3b chronic kidney disease and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease presents with one day of left hip pain. She lives alone. Her daughter found her limping and in pain, and reports she has been “more confused lately.” The patient does not remember falling. Heart rate 105, blood pressure 102/54, temperature 99.6°F. Examination: irregularly irregular rhythm, bruising over the left lateral hip with edema and painful restricted range of motion, oriented to person, place and daughter but not time.

Through the 4Ms. Mentation — no documented impairment, but intermittent confusion, stopped driving last year after getting lost, often frustrated. Mobility — no assistive device, no reported falls, prior knee surgery, “slower than last year.” Medication — atorvastatin, rivaroxaban, metoprolol, lisinopril, sertraline, omeprazole, self-administered and sometimes mixed up; she does not know why she is on sertraline. What Matters — gardening, walking, family; advance directive completed, daughter is durable power of attorney, no MOLST on file.

What actually happened. Undiagnosed mild cognitive impairment dating from her previous “transient ischaemic attack” had been worsening. She began mixing up her medications and over-took both the rivaroxaban and the beta blocker. She fell in the kitchen, got up, and promptly forgot it. Imaging showed a non-displaced left trochanteric neck fracture with a large haematoma.

⚠️ Why this case belongs in a haematology file ★ HY

Read the chain backwards and it is an anticoagulation case: cognitive impairment → medication mismanagement → direct oral anticoagulant overdose → a large haematoma from a low-energy fall. Two crossovers worth holding onto:

  • Cognitive impairment is an anticoagulation safety problem. The capacity to self-administer is part of choosing and continuing an anticoagulant — not a separate social issue. Pair this with the anticoagulant cautions in Section 15.
  • Stage 3b chronic kidney disease changes rivaroxaban dosing, and her bradycardia-tending vital signs sit alongside a doubled beta blocker. The fall has at least three drug explanations before you reach anything neurologic.

Board-style questions from this lecture

Q: A 74-year-old woman is brought in by her son because of concern about her memory. History includes mild cognitive impairment. She lives alone, performs all basic and most instrumental activities of daily living (except personal finances and home maintenance), and drives short distances. Which one of the following can improve or maintain this patient’s cognitive ability?
(A) Exercise training   (B) Computer-based cognitive training   (C) Memory-enhancing games and puzzles   (D) Omega-3 fatty acid supplements

Answer

(A) Exercise training. In people at risk of, or diagnosed with, Alzheimer disease, exercise training may delay decline in cognitive function — with aerobic exercise possibly having the most favourable effect. Brain-training software, puzzles and omega-3 supplements do not carry the same evidence.

Note the functional detail embedded in the stem: finances and home maintenance are instrumental activities. She has an IADL deficit with ADLs intact — the signature of mild cognitive impairment.

Q: A 74-year-old woman takes 1–2 hours to fall asleep and wakes 2–4 times on at least four nights per week, sleeping 4 hours or less. She has a long history of intermittent insomnia, worse over 3 months. History includes mild-to-moderate obstructive sleep apnea (apnea–hypopnea index 15) treated with continuous positive airway pressure, which she finds reasonably comfortable and does not blame — but her insomnia interferes with using it. Which is most likely to improve her insomnia?
(A) Clonazepam   (B) Mirtazapine   (C) Cognitive behavioural therapy   (D) Trazodone

Answer

(C) Cognitive behavioural therapy. It is effective for insomnia comorbid with obstructive sleep apnea and improves adherence to continuous positive airway pressure — which is the detail the stem plants. It targets the maladaptive habits and beliefs that sustain both worry and insomnia, and adds behavioural techniques for sleep scheduling and daytime activity.

This is the sleep slide from Section 54 in question form: no safe medication for insomnia; cognitive behavioural therapy first. Clonazepam is a benzodiazepine in a patient with sleep apnea — the worst available option.

Q: A patient with Parkinson disease has a slow shuffling gait, difficulty initiating walking, and occasional falls. He walks on a treadmill to music and does standing balance exercises. What is the most efficient way to assess changes in his physical function?
(A) Timed Up and Go   (B) Standardized balance scale   (C) Gait Efficacy Scale   (D) Timed chair stands

Answer

(A) Timed Up and Go. The word doing the work is efficient. The Timed Up and Go assesses several skills at once — speed, strength and balance — by having the patient stand, initiate walking, walk 3 metres, turn as quickly as possible, and sit back down. Each of the other options measures a single component; the Gait Efficacy Scale measures confidence in walking, not physical function at all.

Q: An 86-year-old man is admitted to a skilled nursing facility after hospitalisation for urinary tract infection complicated by delirium. Before admission he lived alone. The staff physical and occupational therapists state he is ready for discharge. Which improves his chance of a successful transition back to the community?
(A) His baseline living situation   (B) His mental status   (C) The opinion of his physical and occupational therapists   (D) Having fee-for-service rather than Medicare Advantage

Answer

(C) The therapists’ opinion. A longitudinal cohort study found that occupational and physical therapists could predict which patients would have successful discharges home — while medical providers and social workers could not.

This is the section’s thesis as a test item: the people who assess function predict the outcome better than the people who manage the diagnosis.

Q: An 80-year-old patient has had frequent slips resulting in falls, without dizziness or syncope. History includes osteoarthritis, osteoporosis and mild hearing impairment. They agree to an exercise programme to reduce fall risk. Which has been demonstrated to reduce falls in older adults?
(A) Tai Chi three times each week   (B) Balance training twice each month   (C) Walking 15 minutes daily   (D) Flexibility activities three times weekly for 10 minutes

Answer

(A) Tai Chi three times each week. The effective programmes combine strength, balance and flexibility training at adequate frequency. Tai Chi delivers all three. The distractors each fail on dose or content: balance training twice a month is too infrequent, walking alone does not train balance or strength, and short flexibility sessions train neither.

Q: An 87-year-old woman has a ground-level fall, her second this year. She did not feel dizzy, lose consciousness or become confused; she “just tripped over a quilt on the floor.” Blood pressure 132/75 sitting and 130/70 standing, heart rate 72. Short runs of bigeminy, no murmur. She walks unassisted with short steps and a normal base; Timed Up and Go is normal. Vibratory and temperature sensation are decreased in both feet. Which consultation is most appropriate?
(A) Neurology   (B) Psychiatry   (C) Physical therapy   (D) Cardiology

Answer

(C) Physical therapy. The stem systematically excludes the alternatives: no orthostatic drop (not cardiology’s postural hypotension), no syncope or confusion, and the bigeminy is incidental. What remains is a mechanical fall in a patient with peripheral sensory loss — and the United States Preventive Services Task Force recommends exercise interventions to prevent falls in community-dwelling adults 65 and older at increased risk, delivered as supervised classes or physical therapy.

Do not be talked out of it by the normal Timed Up and Go. A normal score does not remove a two-fall history. A falls-prevention programme also includes home evaluation for modifications, withdrawal of psychoactive medications, minimisation of other medications, management of postural hypotension, and foot care. Falls occur in about 30% of community-dwelling older adults annually and are the leading cause of injury in this group.

Q: A 67-year-old woman on lisinopril, levothyroxine and aspirin drinks 10 oz of wine daily with dinner, as she has for most of her adult life, and wishes to continue. Which is most consistent with United States recommendations?
(A) Stop consuming alcohol   (B) Decrease to 5 oz daily   (C) Decrease to 10 oz on four days per week   (D) No change necessary

Answer

(B) Decrease to 5 oz daily. Her current intake exceeds the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism weekly recommendation for people over 65, so “no change” is wrong; four days per week at the same daily volume still exceeds the weekly threshold. Abstinence may be healthiest, but the patient has stated she wishes to continue — and 5 oz daily is within the more conservative recommendation for moderate consumption in older adults.

This is a What Matters question wearing a numbers costume. The correct answer is the one that meets the stated goal while moving toward the guideline.

🪝 The closing frame — and why it is examinable

The lecture ends on language. Ageing gets described in the vocabulary of failure — patients are “failing,” they “failed” the driving test, they “lost” their licence, it is “a shame she doesn’t remember,” and everyone jokes about a “senior moment.” The counter-thesis is one line: to have grown old is to have succeeded at every previous stage. Practically, that becomes: work with the person to set goals, revisit diagnoses, medications and values at least annually, develop the advance directive with them, and laugh, explain, and admit uncertainty.

🔑 Six-line summary ★ HY
  • Functional level correlates with longevity — an ADL disability costs roughly ten years.
  • Effective communication precedes every tool — talk with, not at; call the collateral source.
  • 4Ms: What Matters, Medication, Mentation, Mobility (+ Multicomplexity, per the American Geriatrics Society).
  • Choose tools by focus — screening everyone with everything is explicitly wrong.
  • ADLs and IADLs measure independence, and IADLs fail first.
  • The non-drug intervention precedes the prescription in every escalation pathway.

Section 59 · Atlas · what it actually looks like

The Morphology Atlas — Smear, Marrow, Node and Clinical Sign

Every objective that begins “given a clinical vignette… peripheral smear findings” is asking you to recognise something. This atlas collects the images from across the summary sheets into one place, grouped the way you would actually work through a case: the normal baseline first, then red cell shape, then the marrow, then the node, then the organisms, then the clinical sign at the bedside. Each caption carries the discriminator — the reason that picture is that diagnosis and not the one next to it.

Abbreviations used in this section PBS peripheral blood smear · MCV mean corpuscular volume · MCHC mean corpuscular haemoglobin concentration · RDW red cell distribution width · MPO myeloperoxidase · TdT terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase · RS cell Reed-Sternberg cell · SPEP serum protein electrophoresis · G6PD glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase · ITP immune thrombocytopenia · DIC disseminated intravascular coagulation · Poikilocytosis variation in red cell shape · Anisocytosis variation in red cell size · Polychromasia blue-tinged young red cells (reticulocytes) on a routine stain

1 — The normal baseline

You cannot call something abnormal until you can call the normal. Neutrophils and lymphocytes dominate; monocytes are a distant third; eosinophils and basophils together are only about 1–3%, so seeing no basophil at all on a normal smear is expected.

Each is rebuilt as real text, so it searches, reflows on a phone, and follows the theme. Use the column-hiding quiz control on any of them to test yourself.

🔑 Three discriminators hidden in that grid
  • Factor VII has the shortest half-life, so a prolonged PT/INR is the most sensitive early marker of liver disease — and why vitamin K deficiency raises PT before PTT.
  • Liver failure versus DIC: the liver makes every factor except von Willebrand factor and factor VIII (endothelium makes those). So factor VIII is preserved or high in liver failure and consumed in DIC. That single assay separates them.
  • DIC causes: “SSSTOP Making New Thrombi” — Sepsis / Snake bites / Stroke, Obstetric complications, Malignancy, Transfusion (ABO mismatch), Trauma, Pancreatitis, Nephrotic syndrome.

Ineffective haematopoiesis is the shared mechanism of MDS, megaloblastic anemia and thalassemia: cells are made but die in the marrow, giving a hypercellular marrow with a pancytopenic blood count, plus ↑ LDH, ↑ unconjugated bilirubin and ↓ haptoglobin without true peripheral haemolysis.

Ann Arbor staging — low stages are one side of the diaphragm (I = one node or nodal chain; II = two or more regions, same side), high stages cross it (III = both sides; IV = diffuse extralymphatic involvement). Every stage takes an A or B suffix: B = unexplained fever, drenching night sweats, or unexplained weight loss over 10%. Hodgkin spreads contiguously, node to node; non-Hodgkin spreads non-contiguously with common extranodal involvement.

🔑 The two that are not on that grid
  • TACO versus TRALI: TACO = hypervolemia → normotensive to hypertensive, raised BNP, distended neck veins, improves with a diuretic. TRALI = hypovolemia → normotensive to hypotensive, BNP not elevated, unresponsive to fluids.
  • Delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction: extravascular, so no haemoglobinuria. Presents over 24 h to 14 days with unexpected anemia, jaundice and a positive direct Coombs — an anamnestic response to a previously encountered non-ABO antigen. Roughly 5–10× more common than acute haemolytic reactions.
  • Allergic / anaphylactic: IgA-deficient patients make anti-IgA and need IgA-deficient (washed) products.

Chart 6 — ABO and Rh compatibility

You make antibodies against the antigen you do not have.

 Type AType BType ABType ORh(D)+Rh(D)−
Antigens on red cellsABA and BNoneDNone
Antibodies in plasmaAnti-BAnti-ANoneAnti-A and Anti-BNoneAnti-D after sensitisation
Can RECEIVE red cells fromA, OB, OAB, A, B, O — universal recipient of red cellsO onlyRh+ or Rh−Rh− only
Can DONATE red cells toA, ABB, ABABA, B, AB, O — universal red cell donorRh+Rh+ or Rh−
🧠 Plasma runs the other way — and that trips people up

For red cells: O is the universal donor, AB the universal recipient. For plasma it inverts: AB is the universal plasma donor (no anti-A or anti-B to give), and O is the universal plasma recipient. ABO antibodies are IgM and preformed without prior exposure, which is why ABO has the highest haemolytic potential and causes intravascular haemolysis. Anti-D is the only non-ABO antigen patients are routinely typed for: about 15% are D-negative, sensitisation needs as little as 1–5 mL of D-positive cells, and it causes haemolytic disease of the newborn — so save Rh-negative units for women of childbearing potential.

⚠️ Two rules that matter more than the numbers ★ HY
  • Factor V Leiden does NOT increase the risk of recurrence after a first unprovoked event — so finding it should not change how long you anticoagulate. Antiphospholipid syndrome is the one that does, it is the only one causing arterial thrombosis, and it is treated with long-term warfarin rather than a DOAC.
  • NEVER test for homocysteine or MTHFR. The work-up is: mutation analysis for factor V Leiden and the prothrombin gene; functional assays for antithrombin III, protein C and protein S; and an antiphospholipid antibody panel including the lupus anticoagulant.

And do not order the functional assays in the wrong setting, because these proteins are consumed or suppressed by the very situations that prompt the test:

Chart 8 — How long to anticoagulate

IndicationDuration
Proximal DVT or PE secondary to a transient risk factor3 months
Idiopathic (unprovoked) proximal DVT or PE“At least 3 months,” then stop or continue long-term — a shared decision
Second unprovoked DVT or PELong-term
VTE in the setting of active cancerLMWH for at least 3 months (or a DOAC; edoxaban and rivaroxaban are non-inferior but cause more upper gastrointestinal bleeding, especially with upper GI cancers)

Provoked is never 6 months; unprovoked is sometimes. Prognosis after 3 months of anticoagulation is equivalent to 6 months, so “3 months = 6 months” for provoked disease. Recurrence risk is highest in the first 1–2 years, and extended anticoagulation reduces it by over 90% — at the cost of more bleeding.

When NOT to use a DOAC: pregnancy or breastfeeding; massive PE or phlegmasia where thrombolysis is being considered; extremes of weight (>300 lb or <110 lb); altered gastrointestinal anatomy such as gastric bypass; heparin-induced thrombocytopenia with thrombosis; splanchnic vein thrombosis; recurrent VTE on therapeutic anticoagulation; antiphospholipid antibody syndrome; and major drug interactions (HIV drugs, phenytoin, carbamazepine).
