Chart 10 — Heparins: size determines everything

DrugMolecular weightTargetsSafe in renal impairment?Protamine reversalHIT risk
Unfractionated heparin~15,000 DaFactor Xa AND IIaYesCompleteHighest
LMWH (enoxaparin, dalteparin)~5,000 DaMostly Xa; hits IIa only above ~5,400 DaNo — renally clearedPartialLower
Fondaparinux~1,500 DaXa onlyNoNoneLowest — safe in HIT, no PF4 interaction

Larger molecular weight = quicker anticoagulant effect, because only a long enough chain can bridge antithrombin to thrombin (IIa). That single physical fact explains the whole column set: why unfractionated heparin prolongs the aPTT and LMWH barely does, why protamine works fully on one and partly on the other, and why anti-factor Xa activity is the right assay for enoxaparin.

Heparin adverse effects worth carrying: bleeding; hyperkalemia (unfractionated heparin inhibits aldosterone synthesis); osteoporosis with use beyond 6 months (UFH > LMWH > fondaparinux); and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia — IgG against platelet factor 4, typically at days 5–14, with a platelet fall over 50%, and thrombosis, not bleeding, as the danger. Treat by stopping all heparin and starting a direct thrombin inhibitor; never warfarin alone (limb gangrene) and never LMWH (antibody cross-reacts).

Chart 11 — Transfusion thresholds

ProductTransfuse whenStorageNotes
Packed red cellsHaemodynamically stable → Hb <7 g/dL; unstable → <8; chronically transfused → <9Refrigerated, 42 daysAcute blood loss is judged on volume lost, not on the haemoglobin
Platelets<10,000–20,000/µL if stable; <50,000 if bleeding or before a procedure; <100,000 for trauma or CNS/eye surgeryRoom temperature, 5 daysRoom-temperature storage is why bacterial contamination is a platelet problem
Plasma (FFP)INR >1.6 and/or PTT >45 s with bleeding or a planned procedureFrozen up to 1 year; 5 days thawedNeeds only ABO compatibility, no crossmatch. Consider co-administering vitamin K
CryoprecipitateDiffuse bleeding with fibrinogen <100 mg/dL; massive transfusionFrozen 1 year; 8 h thawedContains fibrinogen, factor VIII, factor XIII and von Willebrand factor

Only red cells are crossmatched. Plasma, platelets and cryoprecipitate need a compatible ABO type but no crossmatch. Immediate spin crossmatch tests ABO compatibility and is used when the antibody screen is negative; a Coombs crossmatch tests ABO and non-ABO and is used when the screen is positive; in an emergency give uncrossmatched O-negative (or O-positive) blood.

Lecture sources found after the first build — read these fresh

  • Objective 78 — writing a complete drug prescription. This was previously the one objective with no lecture behind it. It does have one: Anderson, People, Not Patients — Medicate, With Care, whose stated aims are to recognise poorly written prescriptions and to prescribe safely for older adults. §54 has been rewritten around it — the lecture’s own five-item “bare minimum,” the Beers / START / STOPP tools, the four high-risk drug classes, “start low, go slow, but get somewhere,” and the three “there are no safe medications for…” slides. Its actual lecture is Armstrong, The Geriatrics Functional Assessment, and “what should be monitored” there means a named screening tool, not a blood count. §58 now works it: the 4Ms, the tool table by domain, the escalation logic, ADLs versus IADLs, the Wendy case, and seven board-style questions from the deck. 🩺 How to add a lecture to this file

The structure is deliberately uniform, so a new set of notes drops in without redesign:

  1. Add a section with an id matching the pattern (s45-...), and add its entry both to the sidebar navigation and to the SECTION_IDS array in the script at the bottom of the file.
  2. Tag it with the objective numbers it covers, using the same lo-badge chips, plus a lo-badge src chip naming the source notes. The badges become hover tooltips automatically — the script derives them from the badge text at load.
  3. Update the coverage map — change those rows' data-st to full, update the matching cov-status chip, and add the → §N anchor link. For a partial, set data-st="part" and give the row a data-cov attribute listing the pipe-separated phrases that are covered — the tooltip highlights those and dims the rest.
  4. Move the objective out of this section, and add any new cross-cutting facts to the Master High-Yield Checklist and the one-pager.

Reference

Glossary and Abbreviations

If a short form appears anywhere in this file, its long form is here — twelve groups now, with the infection, porphyria and lymph node pathology terms added from the Week 11 lectures. Each section also carries its own abbreviation strip at the top.

Cells, counts and morphology

CBC — complete blood count
The standard automated panel: hemoglobin, hematocrit, red cell indices, white cell count with differential, and platelet count.
Hgb — hemoglobin
The oxygen-carrying protein, measured by spectrophotometry in grams per decilitre (g/dL). Four subunits, two alpha and two beta, each carrying one oxygen molecule.
Hct — hematocrit
The percentage of whole blood volume that is red cells, measured by centrifugation. Also called packed cell volume. Roughly three times the hemoglobin.
MCV — mean corpuscular volume
Average red cell size in femtolitres (fL). Under 80 microcytic, 80–100 normocytic, over 100 macrocytic.
MCH — mean corpuscular hemoglobin
Average hemoglobin mass per red cell, in picograms. Underlies normochromic and hypochromic.
MCHC
Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration — hemoglobin per unit red cell volume. Characteristically high in hereditary spherocytosis.
RDW
Red cell distribution width — variability in cell size. Raised when two red cell populations coexist.
LDH — lactate dehydrogenase
An intracellular enzyme released when cells are destroyed. Elevated in hemolysis and in ineffective erythropoiesis.
Reticulocyte
A newly released, immature red cell still containing residual RNA. The count tells you whether the marrow is responding.
Spherocyte
A round, dense red cell with no central pallor. Hereditary spherocytosis and autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
Bite cell / blister cell
A red cell with a semicircular defect where a splenic macrophage removed a Heinz body plus membrane. G6PD deficiency.
Heinz body
An intracellular inclusion of precipitated, oxidized hemoglobin. Requires a supravital stain (crystal violet).
Target cell (codocyte)
A bull's-eye red cell, from too much membrane relative to hemoglobin content. Thalassemia, sickle cell disease, liver disease, iron deficiency.
Schistocyte
An angular red cell fragment, from mechanical shearing.
Howell-Jolly body
A retained nuclear DNA fragment in a mature red cell. Its presence means the spleen is absent or non-functional.
Macro-ovalocyte
A large, oval red cell — characteristic of megaloblastic anemia.
Hypersegmented neutrophil
A neutrophil with six or more nuclear lobes. Near-diagnostic of B12 or folate deficiency.
Anisocytosis / poikilocytosis
Variation in red cell size / variation in red cell shape. Both together is anisopoikilocytosis.
Cellularity
The proportion of marrow occupied by hematopoietic cells rather than fat: normocellular, hypercellular, hypocellular. A core-biopsy word.

Iron, vitamins and the erythron

Fe²⁺ / Fe³⁺
Ferrous / ferric iron. Only the ferrous form is absorbed from the gut.
Transferrin
The plasma protein that transports iron. Picture it carrying cups that may be full or empty.
TIBC — total iron binding capacity
A measure of transferrin binding sites not saturated with iron. Rises in iron deficiency, falls in inflammation.
TSAT — transferrin saturation
The percentage of transferrin binding sites occupied by iron. Under 15% suggests iron deficiency.
Ferritin
The intracellular iron storage protein; the serum level reflects total body stores. Also an acute phase reactant, so it rises in inflammation regardless of stores.
Hepcidin
The liver hormone, driven up by interleukin-6, that degrades ferroportin and blocks iron export from cells.
Ferroportin
The only cellular iron export channel — the door hepcidin locks.
Prussian blue stain
A histochemical stain for marrow iron. Blue granules present means stores exist; absence is diagnostic of iron deficiency.
Pica / pagophagia
Craving non-nutritive substances / craving ice specifically. Strongly associated with iron deficiency.
FOBT — fecal occult blood test
Detects blood in stool not visible to the eye.
B12 — cobalamin
Vitamin B12. Obtained from animal products. Two jobs: DNA synthesis and myelin maintenance.
IF — intrinsic factor
Secreted by gastric parietal cells; B12 must bind it to be absorbed in the terminal ileum.
MMA — methylmalonic acid
Accumulates in B12 deficiency and stays normal in folate deficiency. The key discriminator.
Homocysteine
Elevated in both B12 and folate deficiency, so it cannot separate them.
THF — tetrahydrofolate
The active form of folate, required for thymidine and therefore DNA synthesis.
DHFR — dihydrofolate reductase
The enzyme that activates folic acid — and the enzyme methotrexate blocks.
Pernicious anemia
Autoimmune destruction of gastric mucosa causing loss of parietal cells and intrinsic factor.
Subacute combined degeneration
Degeneration of the dorsal and lateral spinal columns from B12 deficiency. Eventually irreversible.
EPO — erythropoietin
The kidney hormone that stimulates red cell production. Available as a drug (epoetin, darbepoetin).
ESA — erythropoiesis-stimulating agent
The drug class supplying that signal.
HIF-PHI
Hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl hydroxylase inhibitor — vadadustat. Oral; convinces the cell it is at altitude.
Ineffective erythropoiesis
Precursors produced but destroyed within the marrow before release — hypercellular marrow with a low reticulocyte count.
NTD — neural tube defect
Spina bifida and anencephaly; prevented by pre-conception folic acid.

Hemolysis and hemoglobinopathies

Haptoglobin
The plasma protein that binds free hemoglobin after intravascular hemolysis. Consumed in the process, so serum levels fall.
Hemopexin
A second scavenger, which binds free heme rather than intact hemoglobin.
Hemoglobinemia / hemoglobinuria
Free hemoglobin in plasma (pink plasma) / in urine (dark, tea-coloured).
RES — reticuloendothelial system
The macrophage network of spleen, liver and marrow that clears damaged cells and hemoglobin complexes.
DAT — direct antiglobulin test
The direct Coombs test. Detects antibody already coating the patient's own red cells.
Osmotic fragility test
Red cells in hypotonic saline. Spherocytes have no spare membrane and lyse where normal cells do not.
G6PD
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase — the red cell's only meaningful source of NADPH.
NADPH
Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate, reduced form. Powers glutathione reductase.
HbA / HbF / HbA₂
Adult hemoglobin α₂β₂ / fetal hemoglobin α₂γ₂ / α₂δ₂, raised in beta thalassemia.
HbS
Sickle hemoglobin — valine for glutamic acid at the 6th codon of beta globin.
HbH / Hb Barts
β₄ (one alpha gene remaining) / γ₄ (no alpha genes; hydrops fetalis). Both are unpartnered-chain tetramers.
HPLC
High performance liquid chromatography — separates hemoglobins for identification; now more common than gel electrophoresis.
BCL11A
The gene that switches fetal hemoglobin off after birth; the target of Casgevy.
Autosplenectomy
Destruction of the spleen by repeated infarction, as in sickle cell disease. Produces functional asplenia.
PNH
Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria — deficiency of the complement regulators CD55 and CD59, causing intravascular hemolysis and a prothrombotic state.

Transfusion medicine

FFP — fresh frozen plasma
The plasma fraction, frozen. Contains all coagulation, fibrinolytic and complement proteins.
Cryoprecipitate
The cold-insoluble precipitate formed when frozen plasma is thawed at refrigerated temperature. Rich in fibrinogen, factor VIII, von Willebrand factor and factor XIII.
Apheresis
Drawing blood from a donor, separating one component in line, and returning the rest.
Citrate
The anticoagulant in every blood bag. Chelates calcium. A large load during massive transfusion causes hypocalcemia.
Leukocyte reduction
Filtering white cells out of a product. Reduces febrile reactions and HLA alloimmunization.
Irradiation
Damaging the DNA of residual donor lymphocytes so they cannot proliferate. The only prevention for transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease.
PCC — prothrombin complex concentrate
A concentrated plasma-derived product containing vitamin K-dependent factors. 3-factor and 4-factor forms. Preferred over plasma for urgent warfarin reversal.
IVIG
Intravenous immunoglobulin — pooled, purified human antibody, dispensed from pharmacy.
MTP — massive transfusion protocol
A single activation sending a standard box of all products to the bedside.
ABO / RhD
The major blood group systems. RhD positive means the D antigen is present; about 15% of people are D negative.
HLA — human leukocyte antigen
The tissue type system. Anti-HLA antibodies from parous donors cause TRALI.
Alloimmunization
Forming an antibody against a foreign red cell antigen. Only two routes of exposure: transfusion and pregnancy.
Type and screen / type and cross
Screen = ready (type + antibody screen, no units held). Cross = reserved (units crossmatched and held for that patient).
TRALI
Transfusion-related acute lung injury. Hypotensive, normal JVP, donor anti-HLA antibodies, within 6 hours.
TACO
Transfusion-associated circulatory overload. Hypertensive, raised JVP, responds to diuresis.
GVHD
Graft-versus-host disease. Transfusion-associated form presents 1–6 weeks later with pancytopenia; prevented only by irradiation.
WBIT — wrong blood in tube
The labelling error that causes fatal ABO-incompatible transfusion.
DIC
Disseminated intravascular coagulation — simultaneous widespread clotting and clot breakdown; consumes fibrinogen.

Hemostasis pharmacology

UFH / LMWH
Unfractionated / low-molecular-weight heparin. Both act through antithrombin; chain length determines which factors are reached.
aPTT / PT / INR
Activated partial thromboplastin time (monitors heparin) / prothrombin time / international normalized ratio (monitors warfarin).
HIT
Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Antibodies to the heparin–platelet factor 4 complex activate platelets; the danger is thrombosis.
PF4
Platelet factor 4 — the protein heparin binds to form the antigenic complex in HIT.
DOAC
Direct oral anticoagulant — dabigatran and the “-xabans”.
VKORC1
Vitamin K epoxide reductase complex 1 — warfarin's target; genetic variants alter dose requirement.
CYP2C9 / CYP3A4 / CYP2C19
Cytochrome P450 enzymes. 2C9 metabolizes warfarin; 3A4 governs the -xabans and the HIV boosters; 2C19 activates clopidogrel.
P-gp
P-glycoprotein — a drug-transport pump; all three -xabans are substrates.
CrCl
Creatinine clearance — a measure of kidney function used to dose-adjust anticoagulants.
COX / TXA₂
Cyclooxygenase / thromboxane A2 — aspirin irreversibly acetylates COX-1, abolishing thromboxane for the platelet's lifespan.
P2Y12
The platelet ADP receptor blocked by clopidogrel, prasugrel, ticagrelor and cangrelor.
GP IIb/IIIa
Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa — the fibrinogen receptor and the final common step of platelet aggregation.
PAR-1
Protease-activated receptor 1 — the thrombin receptor on the platelet, blocked by vorapaxar.
PDE / cAMP
Phosphodiesterase / cyclic adenosine monophosphate — dipyridamole and cilostazol raise cAMP to keep platelets calm.
tPA
Tissue plasminogen activator — alteplase. Converts plasminogen to plasmin, which degrades fibrin.
TXA
Tranexamic acid — an antifibrinolytic, the mirror image of the “-plase” drugs.
TFPI
Tissue factor pathway inhibitor — a natural anticoagulant blocked by marstacimab and concizumab in hemophilia.
G-CSF / GM-CSF
Granulocyte, and granulocyte-macrophage, colony-stimulating factor. Given as filgrastim and sargramostim.

Sepsis and HIV

SIRS
Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome. No longer defining for sepsis but still used by the US Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.
SOFA / qSOFA
Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (score ≥ 2 ≈ 10% mortality) / quick SOFA (respiratory rate ≥ 22, systolic pressure ≤ 100, altered mentation).
NEWS2 / MEWS
National Early Warning Score, 6 parameters including oxygen saturation / Modified Early Warning Score, 5 parameters, more sensitive.
MODS
Multi-Organ Dysfunction Syndrome — the older term for the end state of septic shock.
PAMPs / DAMPs
Pathogen-Associated / Damage-Associated Molecular Patterns. Viral sepsis works through DAMPs, not PAMPs.
LPS
Lipopolysaccharide — the most prominent gram-negative trigger.
Procalcitonin
The one sepsis marker that points to a cause — elevation indicates a bacterial etiology.
PSS
Post-sepsis syndrome, affecting 50% of survivors.
ART
Antiretroviral therapy. Called HAART in the 1990s.
NRTI / NNRTI / INSTI / PI
Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (competitive, chain-terminating) / non-nucleoside (allosteric) / integrase strand transfer inhibitor / protease inhibitor.
gp120 / gp41
The env products — the binding protein and the fusion protein.
p24
The gag capsid antigen; easiest HIV protein to detect in serum, and the basis of 4th-generation testing.
PIC / RTC
Pre-integration complex / reverse transcription complex — chaperoned into the nucleus by capsid material.
NAT
Nucleic acid test (HIV-1 RNA PCR) — the third tier of the CDC algorithm; a positive result there means acute infection.
ARS
Acute retroviral syndrome — primary HIV infection. Non-exudative pharyngitis is the discriminator from strep.
IRIS
Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome — paradoxical or unmasking; median 48 days after starting ART.
PJP
Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. Cholesterol not ergosterol in the cell wall, which is why TMP/SMX and not an azole.
TMP/SMX
Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole — treatment and prophylaxis for PJP, and prophylaxis for toxoplasmosis.
TDF / TAF
Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (more nephrotoxic, more bone loss) / tenofovir alafenamide (less).
PrEP / PEP
Pre-exposure prophylaxis (~99% effective for sexual transmission) / post-exposure prophylaxis (start within 72 hours, take for a month).
U = U
Undetectable equals untransmittable — CDC threshold < 200 copies/mL. Evidence: the PARTNER trial.

The laboratory — methods and artefacts

Coulter principle (impedance)
A cell crossing a narrow aperture changes electrical impedance. Each pulse is one cell; pulse height is proportional to size. Gives RBC + MCV, platelets + MPV, and the total white count.
Flow cytometry
Separates cells by forward scatter (size) against side scatter (complexity and granularity). The basis of the automated white cell differential, and of the scattergram flags.
SLS — sodium lauryl sulfate
The cyanide-free hemoglobin reagent. Lyses cells, oxidises heme, and forms a stable coloured complex read photometrically at 555 nm.
PLT-F
The fluorescent platelet channel. Stains platelet rough endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria with oxazine, counting by content rather than size. Correlates with CD41/CD61; used below 50 × 10³/µL.
RDW — red cell distribution width
The width of the impedance size distribution, calculated as SD of volume / MCV. Normal 11.4–14.5. Raised with a normal MCV means two populations.
Immature platelet fraction
Newly released platelets — the platelet equivalent of the reticulocyte count. Used to detect marrow recovery after transplant days before the count rises.
Accuracy vs precision
Systematic bias reduces accuracy (suspect the instrument, recalibrate); random bias reduces precision (may be intrinsic to the assay). Platelets vary 15–20% intrinsically; the MCV is very tight.
Autoverification
Automatic release of results when there are no flags and values are near normal, without human review.
Ghost cells
Cells that lysed during collection or processing. Low forward and side scatter, gated out as debris; a lot of them means a degraded sample.
Monolayer / feather edge
The monolayer is where cells sit evenly spaced without overlapping — the only region morphology should be read in. The feather edge distorts cells and manufactures spherocytes.
Wright–Giemsa stain
Eosin plus methylene blue, devised in 1902. Hematoxylin is a basic dye staining acidic DNA blue; eosin is an acidic dye staining basic cytoplasmic protein pink.
Cold agglutinin
An antibody clumping red cells at low temperature. Clumps count as one large cell → low RBC, high MCV, and an impossibly high MCHC. Resolved by warming the sample to 37 °C.
Pseudothrombocytopenia
A falsely low platelet count from EDTA-dependent clumping. Confirmed on the smear; resolved by redrawing into citrate.
Codocyte / dacryocyte / acanthocyte / echinocyte
Target cell (excess membrane for the contents) / tear-drop cell (myelofibrosis) / spur cell, few irregular spicules (liver) / burr cell, many even spicules (uremia, or a drying artefact).
Polychromasia
Larger blue-grey red cells on the smear — reticulocytes. The morphological equivalent of a raised reticulocyte count.
Parasitaemia
The percentage of red cells infected in malaria. Reported with every smear; drives treatment intensity and monitors response.

White cells and immunodeficiency

ANC — absolute neutrophil count
White cell count × % neutrophils — an absolute number, never a percentage. Under 1,000 infection risk climbs; under 500 endogenous flora escape control; under 200 no inflammatory response is possible.
Left shift
Circulating immature granulocyte precursors — bands, metamyelocytes, myelocytes — because the marrow is releasing cells early under demand.
Auer rod
A needle-shaped cytoplasmic inclusion in a myeloblast. A marker of malignancy, specifically a myeloid leukemia.
Döhle body / toxic granulation / vacuolisation
The three reactive neutrophil changes — retained rough endoplasmic reticulum, coarse dark granules, and phagocytic vacuoles. Signs of a cell working hard, not a malignant clone.
Leukemoid reaction
Severe leukocytosis with immature cells in the blood that may mimic a neoplastic proliferation. Differential: myelofibrosis and a space-occupying marrow lesion.
Leukoerythroblastic picture
Immature white cells plus nucleated red cells plus tear-drop cells together — disturbed marrow architecture.
N:C ratio / clonality
Nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio: decreased favours reactive, increased favours malignant. A monoclonal, uniform population favours malignancy; a variety of appearances favours a reactive process.
B symptoms
Fever, night sweats, weight loss — systemic features raising concern for lymphoma or leukemia.
Duffy null
A common variant, particularly in people of African ancestry, giving a constitutionally lower neutrophil count with no increased infection risk. The same antigen is Plasmodium vivax's red cell receptor.
CGD — chronic granulomatous disease
NADPH oxidase / cytochrome b558 mutations; phagocytes cannot generate reactive oxygen species, so catalase-positive organisms survive inside them. Diagnosed by nitroblue tetrazolium or the neutrophil oxidative index.
Catalase-positive
An organism that destroys its own hydrogen peroxide, leaving a CGD phagocyte nothing to borrow: S. aureus, Aspergillus, Serratia, Nocardia, Burkholderia.
BTK — Bruton tyrosine kinase
Mutated in X-linked agammaglobulinemia; the block sits at the pre-B cell, so there are no CD19/CD20 B cells, no plasma cells and no tonsils.
CATCH-22
DiGeorge syndrome: Cardiac abnormality, Abnormal facies, Thymic aplasia, Cleft palate, Hypocalcemia, chromosome 22q11 — one third/fourth branchial pouch migration defect.
SCID / TREC
Severe combined immunodeficiency; screened for at birth by T-cell receptor excision circles, a by-product of normal T-cell receptor rearrangement. An absolute lymphocyte count below 2,000/µL warrants evaluation.
ADA — adenosine deaminase
The autosomal recessive SCID enzyme. Accumulated purines inhibit ribonucleotide reductase; because the defect is systemic, neurological problems can persist after a successful transplant.

Bleeding and clotting

PT / INR / aPTT
Prothrombin time (extrinsic + common, most sensitive to factor 7) / its standardised form, the number warfarin is dosed against / activated partial thromboplastin time (intrinsic + common, most sensitive to factors 8, 9, 11, 12).
Mixing study
Patient plasma mixed 1:1 with normal pooled plasma. Corrects → factor deficiency. Fails to correct → inhibitor. Incubate 30–60 min at 37 °C to catch a slow factor 8 antibody.
The 50% rule
Roughly 50% of a factor is enough for hemostasis — which is why clotting times only prolong well below normal, and why adding an equal volume of normal plasma corrects a deficiency.
D-dimer
A fragment carrying two D regions, released only when factor 13-cross-linked fibrin is degraded by plasmin. A marker of clot turnover, not merely of clotting.
Sodium citrate tube
The light-blue-top coagulation tube. Citrate binds calcium reversibly so the laboratory can restart clotting; the 9:1 blood-to-citrate ratio must be exact or times are falsely prolonged.
VWF:Ag / VWF:RCo
Von Willebrand factor antigen (how much protein) versus ristocetin cofactor activity (how well it works). A ratio under about 0.5–0.7 means a qualitative, type 2 defect.
Ristocetin
A withdrawn antibiotic that forces von Willebrand factor onto platelet GPIb. Its side effect became the assay's mechanism.
HMWM / ADAMTS13
High molecular weight multimers carry most of von Willebrand factor's activity; ADAMTS13 is the protease that trims them. Losing the large ones causes bleeding; failing to trim them causes TTP.
GPIb/IX/V vs GPIIb/IIIa
The von Willebrand factor receptor (absent in Bernard–Soulier — low ristocetin, large platelets) versus the fibrinogen receptor, CD41/CD61 (absent in Glanzmann — everything but ristocetin low).
Emicizumab (Hemlibra)
A bispecific antibody bridging factor 9a and factor 10, reproducing factor 8a's cofactor geometry. Works despite an anti-factor-8 inhibitor, and falsely shortens the aPTT.
DDAVP — desmopressin
Releases stored von Willebrand factor and factor 8 from endothelial Weibel–Palade bodies. First-line in type 1 von Willebrand disease; potentially harmful in type 2B.
TMA — thrombotic microangiopathy
Small-vessel thrombosis with mechanical red cell destruction. TTP, HUS and aHUS all have normal PT, aPTT and fibrinogen — which is what separates them from DIC.
Eculizumab
An anti-C5 monoclonal antibody; the targeted therapy for atypical HUS, where the alternative complement pathway runs unregulated.
Virchow's triad
Endothelial cell damage, blood stasis, and a hypercoagulable state — the three categories of thrombosis risk.
Factor V Leiden / activated protein C resistance
The R506Q mutation that prevents protein C from cleaving factor 5a. The commonest thrombophilia (~5% of Caucasians, 20–30% of VTE) and one of the least dangerous (RR 3–5×).
Prothrombin G20210A
A 3′ untranslated region mutation raising pre-messenger-RNA stability, so more prothrombin is made. The protein is normal — hence molecular, not functional, testing.
Purpura fulminans
Neonatal dermal microvascular thrombosis with skin necrosis in homozygous protein C or S deficiency. The purpura is a consequence of the clotting, not of bleeding.
Lupus anticoagulant
A double misnomer: patients need not have lupus, and it prolongs clotting in vitro while promoting thrombosis in vivo. Fails to correct on mixing but corrects with added phospholipid.
dRVVT
Dilute Russell viper venom test — a phospholipid-dependent clotting assay, more specific than the aPTT for a lupus anticoagulant.
HIT / PF4 / 4T score / SRA
Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia — antibody against the heparin–platelet factor 4 complex, days 5–14, prothrombotic despite the low count. The 4T score (Thrombocytopenia, Timing, Thrombosis, oTher cause) decides whether to test; the serotonin release assay resolves a conflicting immunoassay.
Anti-Xa
Anti-factor 10a activity. The only valid assay for low-molecular-weight heparin and fondaparinux, because only a long heparin chain bridges antithrombin to thrombin for the aPTT to sense.
Argatroban / lepirudin
Direct thrombin inhibitors used in HIT, where no heparin compound and no warfarin alone may be given.

Blood and lymphoreticular infection

Reservoir
The population that maintains a pathogen in nature between human cases. Humans for dengue and malaria; rodents for hantavirus, Lassa and plague; livestock and birds for Crimean–Congo; the Egyptian fruit bat for Ebola and Marburg; cats for Bartonella; the white-footed mouse for Babesia.
Vector
An arthropod in which the organism replicates before transmission. Mere carriage on the mouthparts delivers too small a dose — “you can't be a vector unless the organism grows in you.” No vector exists for the filoviruses, hantavirus or Lassa.
Dead-end host
A host in which infection is accidental and does nothing for the organism — humans in plague. Contrast the reservoir host, which humans are for dengue and malaria.
Epizootic
An outbreak in an animal population. US plague epizootics occur in squirrels, prairie dogs and chipmunks.
Peri-domestic
Living close to humans but not with them — the rat populations that drove the plague pandemics.
Extrinsic / intrinsic incubation
Time from blood meal to infectivity in the vector (dengue 8–10 days) / time from bite to symptoms in the human (dengue 4–7 days).
Pleomorphic
Having no fixed shape or size. Characteristic of Arenaviridae (50–300 nm) and of Bartonella.
“Sandy” / arenavirus appearance
The granular look of arenavirus particles on electron micrograph, caused by host ribosomes (~30 nm) internalized during assembly. Latin arena = sand.
Coccobacillus
A bacterium neither quite a coccus nor quite a bacillus — fat rods that look almost round. The three to know: Bartonella, Haemophilus, Bordetella.
Argyrophilic
“Silver-loving” — demonstrable by a silver stain such as Warthin–Starry. The short list: Bartonella, spirochetes, Legionella, Helicobacter pylori.
Bubo
An acutely swollen, exquisitely tender regional lymph node from intense hemorrhage and swelling — the lesion that names bubonic plague.
Bipolar (“safety pin”) staining
Uptake of stain at both ends of the bacillus with a pale middle — the appearance of Yersinia pestis on Gram or Giemsa stain.
Proventriculus
The valve between a flea's esophagus and midgut. Y. pestis multiplies there until it blocks the valve, so the flea starves, bites frantically and regurgitates bacteria into every wound.
Acral gangrene
Necrosis of the coldest, most distal tissue — fingers, toes, ears, nose — from microvascular thrombosis. Literally where “Black Death” comes from.
Transovarial transmission
Passage of an organism from an infected female arthropod to her eggs. It does not occur for Babesia or Borrelia, which is why every Ixodes nymph must first feed on an infected mouse.
Thick versus thin smear
Thick = red cells pre-lysed, parasites concentrated → a sensitive screen (“is it there?”). Thin = parasites seen inside intact red cells → speciation and parasite density (“which one?”). Both use Giemsa.
Hemozoin
The inert polymer into which Plasmodium converts the toxic free heme released by digesting hemoglobin. Chloroquine blocks that conversion, so heme accumulates and kills the parasite.
ACT
Artemisinin-based combination therapy, e.g. artemether–lumefantrine — the treatment for chloroquine-resistant malaria.
RTS,S/AS01 (Mosquirix)
The malaria vaccine. Recombinant P. falciparum surface protein made in yeast, fused to hepatitis B surface protein purely as a carrier, with the AS01 adjuvant. It targets the sporozoite, stopping the parasite before the liver.

Heme synthesis, porphyria and lead

ALA — δ-aminolevulinic acid
The first committed intermediate of heme synthesis. Elevated in both acute porphyria and lead poisoning.
PBG — porphobilinogen
The intermediate made from ALA by ALA dehydratase. The discriminator: elevated in acute porphyria (block below it), normal in lead poisoning (block above it).
ALAS1 / ALAS2
ALA synthase, the first and rate-limiting enzyme. Heme inhibits ALAS1, so a downstream block removes that feedback and floods the pathway with precursors. ALAS2 is the erythroid isoform — a gain-of-function mutation in it causes X-linked dominant protoporphyria, the one porphyria that is not loss-of-function.
PGC-1α
A transcriptional co-activator induced by fasting that drives ALAS1. Why fasting and low carbohydrate intake provoke attacks — and why glucose and insulin, which suppress it, are treatment.
Hemin
The acute-attack drug. It restores the end-product negative feedback that shuts ALAS1 off.
AIP — acute intermittent porphyria
The most common acute porphyria (80% of acute cases). Autosomal dominant, PBG deaminase, only a partial deficiency — hence onset at 15–50. Triad: visceral abdominal pain with normal imaging, neurologic dysfunction, psychiatric disturbance.
PCT — porphyria cutanea tarda
The most common porphyria overall. Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD). Blistering photosensitivity, milia, hypertrichosis, tea-coloured urine; associated with hepatitis C, alcohol, iron overload and end-stage renal disease, with hemochromatosis mutations in two-thirds.
Hypertrichosis
Excessive hair growth — in PCT over the cheeks, temples and eyebrows. The feature that does not photograph.
Milia
Small white keratin cysts in the skin, part of the PCT picture.
ZPP — zinc protoporphyrin
Accumulates when lead inhibits ferrochelatase. The lead screening test, reflecting the prior three months.
Burton's lines
The gingival lead line; dense lines also appear at the epiphyses of long bones.
Saturnine gout
Gout caused by lead nephropathy — from Saturn, the alchemical name for lead.

Lymph node pathology and the lymphomas

Germinal center
The reactive centre of a secondary follicle. Dark zone = centroblasts undergoing somatic hypermutation; light zone = centrocytes being selected on affinity. A reactive one is polarized; follicular lymphoma is not.
Tingible body macrophage
A macrophage full of the apoptotic debris of B cells that failed selection — the “starry sky.” Present in reactive germinal centers and in Burkitt lymphoma; absent in follicular lymphoma.
Mantle zone / marginal zone
The cuff of small naive B cells around a germinal center / the paler outer rim of memory B cells beyond it. The normal counterparts of mantle cell and marginal zone lymphoma.
Paracortex
The interfollicular T-cell zone. Expanded in infectious mononucleosis, dermatopathic lymphadenopathy, peripheral T-cell lymphomas — and, the trap, in mixed cellularity Hodgkin lymphoma.
Reed–Sternberg cell
Binucleate cell with well-rounded cherry-red macronucleoli and a perinuclear halo. B-cell lineage with the B-cell program switched off: CD30 strong, CD15 ~75%, PAX5 weak, CD20/OCT2/CD45 negative. Under 10% of the cells in the node.
Popcorn (LP) cell
The diagnostic cell of nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma — multilobated, vesicular chromatin, irregular nucleolus, and a fully retained B-cell program (CD20, OCT2, BOB1, CD45 all positive).
Lacunar cell
A Hodgkin/Reed–Sternberg cell with retraction artifact producing a clear space around it. Characteristic of nodular sclerosis.
Emperipolesis
Intact, viable lymphocytes and plasma cells passing through a histiocyte without being digested — the buzzword of Rosai–Dorfman disease. Contrast hemophagocytosis, where the engulfed material is debris being destroyed.
Atretic follicle · onion-skinning · lollipop sign
The three morphologic buzzwords of hyaline vascular Castleman disease: a small regressed follicle of pale dendritic cells, concentric rings of mantle lymphocytes, and a hyalinized vessel penetrating the follicle.
Proliferation center (pseudofollicle)
The pale nodules of CLL/SLL, containing prolymphocytes and paraimmunoblasts. Not a reactive germinal center — the surrounding architecture is effaced and there are no tingible body macrophages or mantle zones.
Smudge cell
A disrupted tumour cell crushed during smear preparation. Read “smudge cells” → think CLL.
Richter transformation
Progression of CLL/SLL to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma — a rapidly enlarging nodal or splenic mass, driven by newly acquired TP53 or MYC mutations.
Paratrabecular pattern
Marrow lymphoid aggregates hugging the bony trabeculae — classically follicular lymphoma (marrow involved in 40–70%); CLL/SLL can mimic it.
Lymphoepithelial lesion · monocytoid cells
Atypical lymphoid cells invading and destroying glandular epithelium / lymphoid cells with abundant pale cytoplasm giving clearing around each nucleus. Together, the morphology of MALT lymphoma.
Cerebriform nucleus
A nuclear outline folded like a brain surface — the Sézary cell. Distinguish from the flower cell of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma, which has distinct petal-like lobes.
Epidermotropism · Pautrier microabscess
Migration of atypical lymphocytes into the epidermis / clusters of them forming collections within the upper epidermis. Both are features of mycosis fungoides.
Dermatopathic lymphadenopathy
A reactive node draining chronically inflamed skin — preserved architecture, reactive germinal centers, paracortex full of histiocytes, dendritic cells and pigment-laden macrophages. Calling it involved would wrongly upstage a mycosis fungoides patient.
Hallmark cell
The diagnostic cell of anaplastic large cell lymphoma — an eccentric horseshoe-shaped nucleus with a pale paranuclear area. ALCL and classic Hodgkin lymphoma are the two CD30-positive lymphomas.
Ki-67
A proliferation marker labelling every cell not in G0. High and polarized in a reactive germinal center; low in indolent B-cell lymphomas; over 95% in Burkitt lymphoma.
